SANTIAGO, Chile--First quarter economic activity and domestic demand in Chile have decelerated at a faster pace than expected, and gross domestic product for the period could grow around 4.4% year-on-year according to preliminary data, central bank governor Rodrigo Vergara said Wednesday.

In 2010-2012, GDP grew at over 5.5% annually, above the economy's trend rate of 5%, sparking concerns of overheating.

For 2013, growth is expected at around 5%, according to central bank and government estimates.

Regarding the strength of the peso against the dollar, Mr. Vergara, speaking to the local Asimet trade group, reiterated the bank can't rule out intervening in the market to weaken the currency, but that such a move can be very costly.

title: DJ UPDATE: Chile Finance Min: Capital Controls Used Only As Last Resort
text:
--Government's $5 billion, peso-denominated bond issue schedule aims to ease pressure on peso

--Quantitative easing to blame for strong currencies in several Latin American nations

--Finance Minister reiterates central bank autonomously decides whether to intervene

SANTIAGO, Chile--Capital controls are measures of last resort and the Chilean government won't easily implement them to stem the strength of the peso in relation to the dollar, Finance Minister Felipe Larrain said Friday.

Earlier this week, the peso traded at 20-month highs versus the dollar, prompting concerns that exporters continue to lose their competitiveness and calls for intervention.

Mr. Larrain said the government is contributing to reducing pressure on the local currency and, to that effect, on Thursday disclosed a $5 billion local bond issue schedule for this year.

By issuing bonds denominated in pesos, he said, the government aims to reduce its dollar sales on the local market, which is already flooded with dollars as investors seek more-attractive returns on their investments than in industrialized nations where interest rates are near zero.

Mr. Larrain reiterated that the aggressive stimulus Japan, the U.S. and the E.U. had injected into their economies were mostly to blame for the strength of the peso.

"The rest of the world is suffering the effects of quantitative easing," Mr. Larrain told assistants at Banco BCI seminar, adding that the currencies of Chile and several other Latin American countries were taking a beating.

"Europe, Japan, and the U.S. don't have any more room to use fiscal or monetary policies so they turn to injections of liquidity. The problem is that successful emerging-market nations are paying the consequences," he said.

As a result of the peso's sharp gains this week, many market participants were betting that the central bank would disclose intervention measures following its monthly monetary-policy meeting late Thursday.

While the bank didn't announce an intervention, it mentioned, in its post-meeting communique, that the peso had continued firming in multilateral terms. It also said copper prices, a key indicator for the peso as Chile produces one-third of the world's copper, had fallen on international markets, hinting that the peso wasn't in line with its fundamentals.

The finance minister sits in on the bank's monthly policy meetings and voices his opinion, but he doesn't have a vote on the five-person governing council.

Asked if he had discussed intervention with central-bank authorities, Mr. Larrain told reporters on the sidelines of the seminar that "no issue was taboo."

He reiterated, however, that to intervene in the local currency market is the prerogative of the autonomous central bank.

title: UPDATE 1-Chile central holds key rate steady, eyes strong peso
text:
* Central bank says peso has further appreciated in multilateral terms

* Central bank, gov't met earlier Thursday to discuss peso strength

* Currency at same level that triggered intervention in 2011

(Recasts throughout; adds central bank's comments, analyst quote)

By Anthony Esposito

SANTIAGO, April 11 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank kept its key rate steady at 5.0 percent on Thursday, as expected, and underscored that the peso currency has continued appreciating across the board and that domestic demand remains dynamic.

It is the second meeting in a row the bank has referred to the peso's appreciation in "multilateral" terms in its post-meeting communique.

The central bank also mentioned that commodities prices, especially for copper - Chile's top export - have receded in recent weeks.

"The fact that the central bank mentioned copper prices are falling yet the peso keeps appreciating reflects that the monetary authority notices an uncoupling of the peso with its fundamentals," said Alejandro Puente, economist at BBVA Chile.

The peso typically moves in line with copper prices, as higher prices mean more dollars entering the local market due to sales of the red metal. The inverse is true of lower prices.

In a public display of unease with the matter, Finance Minister Felipe Larrain met with Central Bank President Rodrigo Vergara prior to the monetary policy meeting to discuss the peso's strength.

The local currency climbed to 465.50 per U.S. dollar on Tuesday - the same level that had triggered a central bank currency intervention in early 2011.

"We have a prior meeting with the president of the central bank, where we will discuss in depth the issue of the peso and other matters," Larrain told reporters earlier on Thursday.

The central bank has kept its benchmark lending rate

steady at 5.0 percent since a surprise cut in January 2012, as buoyant growth, low inflation and a strong peso - as well as persistent economic threats from abroad - keep its hands tied.

"The labor market is still tight and domestic demand remains dynamic. Credit conditions are somewhat more restrictive," the central bank said in its post-meeting statement.

Analysts surveyed in the central bank's latest poll said they saw the benchmark rate holding steady at least through December before being hiked to 5.25 percent within 11 months.

The bank kept its monetary policy bias broadly neutral, which in standard monetary policy parlance means it neither spurs nor curbs economic growth.

The peso has been buoyed by Chile's robust economy, an attractive rate differential and healthy prices for copper. So-called quantitative easing measures adopted in major economies have also helped fuel the peso's appreciation.

The peso was one of the strongest performers against the U.S. dollar among 152 currencies tracked by Reuters after appreciating 8.48 percent last year and has accumulated an additional gain of around 2 percent in 2013.

Though the peso "is likely to remain under strengthening pressure from capital inflows charged by global liquidity and attracted by solid fundamentals and high interest rates," there is limited room for additional appreciation, as an exchange rate closer to 460 per dollar increases the likelihood of intervention, said RBS economist Felipe Hernandez.

Chile's central bank deployed a dollar-purchasing program in 2011, increasing its foreign reserves by $12 billion, to curb peso strength after it appreciated to 465.50 per dollar, then its highest level in over 2-1/2 years.

In recent weeks, the bank has said a currency market intervention is one of the tools at its disposal, but it has also highlighted the costs associated with such a move.

SURGING DEMAND

The bank is also concerned with reining in robust domestic demand, which has been growing faster than gross domestic product, helping to fuel a widening current account deficit.

Analysts have said the bank could raise its key rate to rein in buoyant demand sooner than forecast, but it may have to incur a currency intervention before a rate hike to avoid further stoking the strong peso.

Over the weekend, bank board member Enrique Marshall said the bank will act if the local economy maintains dynamism "above what is reasonable," and interest rates are the best instrument at the entity's disposal.

Sturdy domestic demand, an economy near full employment and solid levels of investment have protected the world's No. 1 copper producer from a sharp slowdown on the back of global economic woes, but many analysts are now worried about overheating.

Those fears have not yet materialized in the form of inflationary pressures. Chile's consumer price index posted a 0.4 percent rise in March, its fastest pace since October, but the 12-month figure of 1.5 percent remained well below the central bank's tolerance range of 2 percent to 4 percent.

"Headline and core inflation measures are around 1 percent and 2 percent year-on-year, while inflationary expectations in the policy horizon remain around the target," the post-meeting statement said.

Elsewhere in the region, inflation in Brazil pierced the government's target ceiling in March for the first time in over a year. However, the rise was slightly less than expected, fueling bets the country's central bank could wait until May to start hiking interest rates.

In Mexico, the annual inflation rate also climbed above the central bank's target ceiling in March, crimping policymakers' ability to lower borrowing costs as the peso currency soared to 20-month highs.

Mexico's central bank cut its key rate to an all-time low of 4 percent in early March in what was seen as a bid to tamp down its currency, but the peso has kept appreciating, and is up about 6.8 percent so far this year.

(Writing by Anthony Esposito, additional reporting by Santiago Newsoom and Moises Avila; editing by Bernadette Baum, G Crosse)

title: Chile's Peso Marginally Weaker Prior to  Central Bank  Policy Meeting
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile--The Chilean peso was marginally weaker in recent trading Thursday, after retreating the previous session from a 20-month high on a "verbal intervention" from Chile's finance minister.

The peso was recently at CLP468.60 to the dollar, from Wednesday's close of CLP468.50.

On Wednesday, the Chilean currency pulled back from levels near where the central bank last intervened in the exchange market in 2011, when it launched a $12 billion program to weaken the peso, after Finance Minister Felipe Larrain said he would meet with central bank President Rodrigo Vergara this week to discuss the "worrisome" exchange rate, in what was characterized as an attempt to talk down the local currency.

"The peso retreated yesterday solely because of Larrain's verbal intervention, ignoring external factors, and today we were seeing a lot of institutional selling of pesos because the dollar is at an attractive rate," said Ronald Volpi, head of currency spot market at EuroAmerica.

Local traders said the central bank's monetary policy meeting scheduled Thursday afternoon was pressuring investors to close out short positions on the dollar. The monetary authority is expected to refer to the exchange rate in the policy statement to be issued immediately afterward.

"The central bank always says in its statement that 'the peso has appreciated.' The question is, are they going to do something about it?," Mr. Volpi said.

title: Chile Stocks Close Marginally Higher
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile--Chile's IPSA select stock index ended marginally higher Wednesday, ignoring strong gains among U.S. and European shares, as analysts believe there was some profit-taking in the local market after Tuesday's 1.2% surge.

The IPSA closed 0.1% higher at 4353.6, while market volume increased to 114 billion Chilean pesos ($243 million) from CLP84 billion Tuesday.

The local index made a strong move over the 4300-point level this week, rebounding from a five-session losing streak last week.

But Wednesday, the IPSA did not take its cues from the Dow Jones Industrial Average or the Stoxx Europe 600, which rose broadly with strong economic data from China and Europe, and minutes from the U.S. Federal Reserve that did not shake the confidence in the central bank's support for the U.S. economy.

As the U.S. and Europe are among the country's main trading partners, the local index usually takes direction from economic and political developments in those markets.

"The local market moved considerably higher yesterday, and today there might have been some profit taking, especially around shares that rebounded from last week's heavy losses," said German Guerrero, partner at MBI Inversiones.

Heavyweight retailer Cencosud (CNCO, CENCOSUD.SN) closed 0.2% lower to CLP2,780.8, after posting a 1.1% gain Tuesday, while Latam Airlines Group (LFL, LAN.SN) declined 0.5% to CLP9,886.6 after surging 2.5% the previous session.

However, another big winner from Tuesday, steel producer CAP (CAP.SN), rose 0.8% to CLP15,557.0

In other local markets, the peso closed at CLP468.50 to the dollar, down from Tuesday's 20-month high of CLP466.80, after what has been characterized as a "verbal intervention" from Chile's finance minister, who announced he would meet this week with central bank officials to talk about the "worrisome" exchange rate.

The currency hit 20-month highs this week and seemed headed to the CLP465 level where the central bank last intervened in 2011, when it launched a $12 billion, year-long intervention program.

The central bank will hold its monetary policy meeting Thursday and may refer to the exchange rate in its policy statement issued immediately afterward.

In the fixed-income market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central-bank bonds, or BCUs, ended higher.

The yield on five-year BCUs closed at 2.59%, up from 2.57% Tuesday, while the yield on 10-year BCUs also closed higher, at 2.47%, from 2.46% the previous session. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

title: Chile  Peso Ends Weaker After Finance Minister's 'Verbal  Intervention '
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile--The Chilean peso pulled back Wednesday from a 20-month high after what has been characterized as a "verbal intervention" from Chile's Finance Minister, who announced he would meet this week with central bank officials to talk about the "worrisome" exchange rate.

The peso ended at CLP468.50 to the dollar, down from Tuesday's close of CLP466.80, after trading in a range of CLP467.00 to CLP469.30.

The currency hit 20-month highs this week and seemed headed to the CLP465 level where the central bank last intervened in 2011, when it launched a $12 billion, year-long intervention program.

Early Wednesday, though, the peso began to retreat as investors started closing out short positions and locking in profits, according to local traders. Then Finance Minister Felipe Larrain stepped in with what was widely seen as a "verbal intervention."

"We are in full coordination mode with the central bank. We will meet either tomorrow or the following day [Thursday or Friday] with the central bank president [Rodrigo Vergara]...without a doubt this is a situation that worries us," said the official, who sits on the central bank's monthly monetary policy meetings but doesn't vote on decisions, to reporters.

The central bank will hold its monetary policy meeting Thursday and may refer to the exchange rate in its policy statement issued immediately afterward.

"The peso was already retreating from its high against the dollar, add to it that Larrain will meet with the central bank, and all of that motivates people to close out short positions or bet on a possible intervention, sending the peso lower," said Eugenio Cortes, a trader at EuroAmerica, who doesn't foresee an intervention unless the peso breaks through the CLP465 resistance level.

In the fixed-income market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central-bank bonds, or BCUs, ended higher.

The yield on five-year BCUs closed at 2.59%, up from 2.57% Tuesday, while the yield on 10-year BCUs also closed higher, at 2.47%, from 2.46% the previous session. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

title: Chile  Peso Closes at 20-Month High, Near  Intervention  Levels
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile--The Chilean peso closed at a new 20-month high against the dollar Monday, extending the previous session's move toward levels at which the central bank intervened in 2011.

The peso ended at CLP466.80 to the dollar, versus Friday's close of CLP468.80, after trading in a range of CLP466.80 to CLP469.50.

On Friday, the Chilean currency broke through the CLP470 resistance level of the past 18 months.

"The peso had a hard time breaking through the resistance level, but now we are clearly reaching probable intervention levels, or at least that's how the market is viewing it," said Eugenio Cortes, a trader at EuroAmerica.

When the peso firmed to CLP465 in early 2011, the central bank launched a $12 billion, year-long intervention program to weaken the currency.

Mario Del Campo, a trader at Banco Consorcio, believes the central bank would step in if the peso strengthens to a level around CLP460, "but only if there's a lot of pressure on the government to intervene, and right now I don't see the government too concerned about it."

The bank's latest monetary-policy report, released last week, showed the monetary authority sees the peso trading in line with its fundamentals.

In the fixed-income market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central-bank bonds, or BCUs, ended unchanged and weaker.

The yield on five-year BCUs closed unchanged at 2.53%, flat with Friday, and the yield on 10-year BCUs closed at 2.45%, down from 2.49% the previous session. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  rally on Fed stimulus hopes
text:
* Poor U.S. jobs data fuels bets on continued Fed stimulus

* Brazilian real jumps nearly 1.5 pct, crosses 2/dlr mark

* Mexico peso jumps 1 pct to 19-month high

* Chile peso hits 1-1/2-year high; intervention eyed

By Walter Brandimarte

SAO PAULO, April 5 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real jumped nearly 1.5 percent while the Mexican peso hit a 19-month high on Friday after weaker-than-expected U.S. jobs data upheld expectations of continued monetary stimulus by the Federal Reserve.

Other Latin American currencies also rallied as hopes for a prolonged bond-buying program by the U.S. central bank added to the support from Thursday's announcement of unprecedented monetary stimulus by the Bank of Japan.

The Chilean peso closed at a more than 1-1/2-year high, nearing levels that, according to analysts, could trigger a central bank intervention.

The Mexican peso initially weakened after data showed that hiring by employers in the United States, Mexico's main trading partner, hit a nine-month low in March.

Although the data raised doubts about the recovery of the world's largest economy, bets that the worrisome jobs outlook would keep the Fed's monetary stimulus in place eventually bolstered higher-yielding emerging market currencies.

The Mexican peso reversed losses to jump 1 percent to 12.1849 per dollar.

"U.S. payrolls were bad, fueling expectations that a loose monetary policy will remain in place in the United States," said a trader with a large Brazilian bank in Sao Paulo.

The Brazilian real strengthened past the psychologically relevant level of 2 per dollar for the first time in over two weeks.

The gains were also fueled by rumors that the government could ease a financial tax known as IOF over fixed-income investments by foreigners, traders said. A spokesman at Brazil's Finance Ministry declined to comment.

The real is unlikely to gain much further, however, as Brazilian policymakers seem likely to keep the exchange rate near the 2-per-dollar mark, considered by analysts as an appropriate level to avoid inflation pressures without hurting exporters.

Upholding that view, a senior official on President Dilma Rousseff's economic team told Reuters that "the exchange rate is fine where it is."

In Chile, however, policymakers looked increasingly likely to intervene to stem currency gains as the peso closed at 468.80 per dollar, increasing year-to-date gains to more than 2 percent.

"The trend for the peso is still positive. We see the market is shorting the dollar. The next level investors will test is 465 (per dollar), and then we can expect an intervention," said Matias Madrid, chief economist with Penta bank in Santiago.

title: Chile  Peso Ends At 20-Month High, Nearing  Intervention  Levels
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile--The Chilean peso closed at a 20-month high against the dollar, breaking through a significant resistance level and nearing levels at which the central bank intervened in 2011.

The peso ended at CLP468.80 to the dollar, versus Thursday's close of CLP470.00, after trading in a range of CLP468.60 to CLP471.30.

"According to fundamentals, the peso should have weakened today, but there's likely a big dollar sale in the market underpinning the peso," said Gloria Soto, chief currency trader at FXCM Chile.

When the peso firmed to CLP465 in early 2011, the central bank launched a $12 billion, year-long intervention program to weaken the currency.

"At these levels, we expect the central bank will start buying dollars soon," Ms. Soto said.

But not all market participants agree, as some see the intervention risk closer to CLP460.

In the last two sessions, large dollar sales from institutional investors have given the peso strength.

"On Thursday, it was mining companies. Today, it was the private pension-fund managers," said currency trader Flavio Magnasco.

"Only the dollar sales flows have taken the peso below CLP470, because all the other signs point to a weakening exchange rate for the peso."

In the fixed-income market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central-bank bonds, or BCUs, ended lower in reaction to a lower-than-expected gain in a gross domestic proxy index for February.

The central bank reported the Imacec GDP proxy index grew 3.8% year-on-year in February, well below the 5.1% analysts expected.

A deceleration in economic activity pushes a possible rate increase further away.

The yield on five-year BCUs closed at 2.53%, down from 2.56% Thursday, and the yield on 10-year BCUs closed at 2.49%, down from 2.56% the previous session. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

2 Apr 2013 10:17 EDT DJ  Chile Central Bank Raises 2013 GDP Outlook to 4.5%-5.5% Range

By Carolina Pica

SANTIAGO, Chile--The resilient Chilean economy will likely grow at a brisk pace this year amid tame inflation and low unemployment, but it still faces risks from the euro zone, possible copper price decreases and dynamic domestic demand, the central bank said Tuesday.

In its first Monetary Policy Report for the year, the central bank upwardly revised its gross domestic product growth outlook to a range between 4.5% and 5.5% and slightly reduced its year-end inflation view to 2.8%, still very close to its 3% target.

It warned, however, the economy faces both external and internal risks and that these risks could have repercussions on the current account, which this year is expected to post a deficit of 4.4% of GDP.

"An abrupt change in external conditions, such as reduced terms of trade or less favorable financial conditions, could mean costly adjustments for the nation," bank Governor Rodrigo Vergara said in a speech to the Senate Finance Committee where he presented the report.

On the international front, the bank said that while the outlook for the U.S and China has improved, the euro zone faces several threats that could have local repercussions. The Chilean economy relies heavily on its exports, especially its copper exports, and China, the U.S. and Europe are the main destinations for Chilean goods.

For 2013, the monetary authority increased its copper price estimate to an average $3.50 a pound, from $3.40 in its previous report, and cautioned that a brusque decrease in international copper prices due to real or financial factors would have a significant effect on the current account, domestic demand and on inflation.

Still relatively high copper prices, robust domestic growth in the past three years, a wide spread between local and international interest rates and a weak dollar globally have all contributed to a firmer peso in relation to the dollar. In 2012, the peso appreciated around 8% versus the greenback and has gained another 1% so far this year.

The central bank said that while the currency has firmed both against the dollar and against a basket of currencies in recent months, its gains are no different than those seen in other commodity-producing or emerging-market nations. It added that when measured in real terms the peso's exchange rate is on the stronger end of those values consistent with long-term fundamentals, but still within the bank's comfort zone. A stronger peso makes Chile's exports less competitive abroad.

In his prepared remarks, Mr. Vergara reiterated intervening in the currency market to weaken the peso, like the bank did in 2011, can be costly.

As to the internal risks the local economy faces, the pace at which domestic demand continues to grow is also a concern for the bank, Mr. Vergara said.

Domestic demand this year is seen gaining 6.1% year-on-year on the back of sizable investments, especially in mining and energy projects, and also on robust private consumption.

Mr. Vergara noted that data for the first quarter of this year indicate that strong retail, automobile, appliance and home furnishing sales point to still dynamic private consumption.

"The biggest risks are in relation to persistently elevated dynamism in domestic demand," Mr. Vergara said.

Strong domestic spending could, in the medium-term, put additional pressure on the labor market, the use of installed capacity and inflation, he said.

Regarding monetary policy, the bank noted the baseline interest rate scenario it used for this report fixed the benchmark overnight lending rate, or TPM, at its current level of 5% for the near term, in line with the most recent bank's polls of expectations.

In January 2012, the central bank reduced the TPM 25 basis points to 5% and has held it there ever since, citing opposing factors such as the global economic slowdown, financial tensions from the euro zone's debt crisis and domestic demand that hasn't decelerated as quickly as anticipated.

"The TPM is at levels considered neutral, although its current level is high when compared with the rest of the world," Mr. Vergara said.

In the report, the bank noted that the spread with industrialized nations poses monetary policy challenges for many emerging-market nations, including Chile.

title: Chile Peso Closes Weaker on Chinese, U.S. Manufacturing Data
text:
The Chilean peso closed weaker against the dollar Monday on disappointing Chinese and U.S. manufacturing data.

The peso closed at CLP472.30 to the dollar, versus Thursday's close of CLP471.50, after trading in a range between CLP472.10 and CLP473.20.

As China and the U.S. are among Chile's main trading partners, the peso often takes its cues from U.S. and Chinese economic developments.

The peso has been trading between CLP470 and CLP475 to the dollar since the beginning of the year and traders are looking for volatility.

"It's boring," said Martin Ferrer, head of the currency desk at Capital FX.

Chile's economic growth and speculation about a central bank intervention should the peso cross the CLP470 resistance level have kept the Andean currency trading rangebound, Mr. Ferrer added.

The central bank intervened in the currency market when the peso firmed to the CLP465 level to the dollar in early January 2011. It bought a total $12 billion at a rate of $50 million a day during that year.

In the fixed-income market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central-bank bonds, or BCUs, ended unchanged from Thursday in a quiet session.

The yields on five-year BCUs closed at 2.60% and the yield on 10-year BCUs closed at 2.54%. Bond yields and prices move inversely.

title: Chile gov't says looking at ways to tame peso's gains -report
text:
SANTIAGO, Feb 24 (Reuters) - Chile's government is studying measures to stem the peso's gains against the U.S. dollar such as selling more local currency debt, the finance minister was quoted as telling a local newspaper on Sunday.

The peso, which has been boosted by Chile's solid economic growth and healthy prices for top export copper, ranked among the strongest foreign currency performers against the U.S. dollar among 152 currencies tracked by Reuters in 2012.

Finance Minister Felipe Larrain said last month that the government would support any intervention by Chile's independent central bank to weaken the strong peso.

In Sunday's interview with daily La Tercera, Larrain said the government was "studying some measures of macro-prudence due to the risks to the dollar."

Among possible steps, he mentioned establishing debt ceilings for certain state institutions, curbing public spending or issuing more peso-denominated debt.

The Chilean peso has firmed 1.12 percent against the dollar since the start of the year and gained 8.48 percent in 2012, making Chilean exports less competitive in global markets.

Larrain reiterated his opposition to capital controls to stem inflows from abroad.

"Under extreme circumstances, they might be considered but I'm skeptical about their effect. We will try not to take that path," he was quoted as saying.

He said the peso, like other emerging market currencies, was feeling the effect of U.S. quantitative easing and expressed concern about the possible impact of Japan's decision to pursue economic stimulus measures.

"There's an enormous increase in the amount of money with an extremely low interest rate," he said.

title: Finance Minister Says Chile Studying Measures to Weaken Peso - Newspaper
text:
The Chilean government is studying measures to weaken the peso, such as limiting state companies' dollar-denominated debt, La Tercera newspaper reported Sunday, citing Finance Minister Felipe Larrain.

The peso's appreciation versus the U.S. dollar has prompted agricultural, wine and manufactured-goods exporters' calls to the central bank and the government to weaken the peso as a strong local currency hurts exports' competitiveness.

Like other currencies in the region, the peso has strengthened around 10% to the dollar since early 2012, but unlike the authorities of Colombia, Peru or Brazil, the Chilean central bank has chosen not to act over the past year.

In Chile, a central bank intervention depends solely on the monetary authority decision.

"Should the bank intervene, we would support it," Mr. Larrain said to La Tercera.

Among the steps to limit dollar inflows to Chile, the government could reduce state companies' bond issues abroad. Copper producer Corporacion Nacional del Cobre de Chile, or Codelco, and oil and gas company Empresa Nacional del Petroleo SA, or Enap, are some of the state-owned firms that issued debt in dollars in recent years.

The Finance Minister also ruled out establishing controls on foreign capital, arguing they don't limit the total amount of dollars arriving in Chile and make credit more expensive.

The government recently announced a local debt program of as much as $5 billion for 2013. In 2012, it had a program for as much as $6 billion.

title: Chile  finance minister would support cbank  intervention  on peso
text:
* Peso boosted by strong Chile growth, copper

* Chile's central bank last intervened in 2011

* Larrain sees emerging markets remaining strong

DAVOS, Switzerland, Jan 26 (Reuters) - Chile's government would support any intervention by the country's independent central bank to weaken the strong peso, Finance Minister Felipe Larrain said on Saturday.

"The central bank may decide to intervene but it is their own decision ...if they do, we would certainly support them," Larrain told Reuters in a television interview at the World Economic Forum in Davos.

"We're trying to prevent further appreciation," he said.

The peso, which has been boosted by Chile's robust economic growth and healthy prices for top export copper, ranked among the strongest foreign currency performers against the U.S. dollar among 152 currencies tracked by Reuters in 2012.

Last month, central bank president Rodrigo Vergara reiterated that intervening in the local peso currency market was a tool at the bank's disposal, but that if it hadn't intervened so far it was because it hadn't been deemed necessary.

The central bank deployed a dollar-purchasing program in 2011 to curb peso strength after it appreciated to its highest level in more than 2-1/2 years at 465.50 per dollar.

Larrain said it was hard to counter the weight of U.S. quantitative easing: "Against this massive QE, we have a few tools but not many."

Chile's central bank has kept rates steady since a surprise cut in January 2012, as it weighs external risks against a buoyant domestic economy.

Due to robust domestic demand and investment, Chile's small, export-dependent economy has for the most part fared better than expected despite slowing demand from top trade partner China and fallout from the euro zone crisis.

Larrain added that the global economic picture was somewhat rosier at this year's Davos than in 2012.

"We're not yet out of the woods. The real economy still needs to undergo some tough work and the financial markets are helping but it's not to say this is over," Larrain said.

"It is the emerging markets that will continue pulling the world economy again in 2013."

(Reporting by Emma Thomasson; editing by Jason Neely)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  lower; Mexico peso hit by rate cut fears
text:
* Mexico peso falls 0.4 pct to lowest level in 2 weeks

* Chile peso drops with copper prices, intervention fears

* Brazil real closes flat due to Sao Paulo holiday

By Walter Brandimarte

RIO DE JANEIRO, Jan 25 (Reuters) - The Mexican peso led Latin American currencies lower on Friday as investors, fearing a possible interest rate cut by the country's central bank, pocketed some of the currency's recent gains.

In Brazil, the real closed flat at 2.0305 per dollar in an extremely thin market due to a holiday in Sao Paulo, the country's financial center.

Regional currency losses were exacerbated by the peso's fragile technical position on the Chicago exchange, where investors have placed large bets for a stronger Mexican currency. Analysts say such bets could quickly reverse, prompting the peso to sell off.

The peso dropped 0.4 percent to trade at 12.698 per dollar, after touching its weakest level in over two weeks.

It has lost around 1 percent since last Friday, when the Mexican central bank said it could ease its monetary policy if inflation continues to cool and the economy loses steam. Lower rates could reduce the allure of peso-denominated assets.

The central bank's warning represented an abrupt reversal from its previous threat to raise interest rates, leaving some investors wondering whether policymakers were actually more concerned about the strength of the currency.

"The central bank's about face, coming as it did after a bout of peso strength, is likely to be viewed by many as a first sign of a possible policy response if the peso gains further ground," Morgan Stanley's analyst Luis Arcentales wrote in a research note.

Elsewhere in Latin America, the Chilean peso lost 0.3 percent to 471.80 per dollar, pressured by lower prices of copper, Chile's top export.

Fears that Chilean policymakers may intervene in the market to curb the currency's strength also weighed on the peso, which has gained about 1.5 percent since the beginning of the year.

title: As Rhetoric Heats Up,  Currency  War Risks Rise
text:
Guido Mantega is finally getting some company.

In September 2010, the Brazilian finance minister caused a mini commotion when he declared that the world was gripped by a "currency war." Mr. Mantega complained that the hyper-loose monetary policies pursued by advanced countries, coupled with the exporter-backed exchange-rate manipulations of China, were deflecting unwanted "hot money" into emerging market countries and forcing them to take retaliatory currency-weakening measures of their own. Those remarks, which evoked the specter of the vicious cycle of beggar-thy-neighbor policies that exacerbated the Great Depression, triggered much debate and even provided the title for a bestselling book by investment banker James G. Rickards. But at the time economic pundits mostly dismissed it as an alarmist reading of what was really just a post-crisis policy realignment.

Two and a half years later, Mr. Mantega's bandwagon is getting some fellow riders. With the yen having lost 13% of its value against the dollar in four months as the Bank of Japan has caved into demands from new Prime Minister Shinzo Abe for looser monetary policy and with the U.S. Federal Reserve well into a new round of open-ended "quantitative easing," currency-war warnings are coming thick and fast. And they're coming from figures that might be expected to take a more sober view of the world.

In separate speeches Tuesday, outgoing Bank of England Gov. Mervyn King expressed fear that the global financial system was facing a wave of competitive currency depreciations and Deutsche Bundesbank President Jens Weidmann chastised the Bank of Japan for policies that "could lead to an increasingly politicized exchange rate." That followed similar warnings this month about the fallout from Japan's actions by St. Louis Fed President James Bullard and European Central Bank board member Benoit Coeure, and a complaint from Jean-Claude Juncker, Luxembourg's prime minister who heads the Eurogroup of finance ministers, that the euro was "dangerously high."

Emerging market governments are also piping up. Among others, Russian and South Korean central bankers have warned that other countries may follow Japan's lead and weaken their currencies.

By the reckoning of the Royal Bank of Scotland's foreign-exchange strategy team, 2013 could see this current round of "currency fracas morph into something more internationally combustible." So, in preparation for a global currency war, they came up with a matrix showing which central banks have the most "intent" and/or "capacity" to intervene. The top scorers on both counts: the banks of Chile, Thailand, Malaysia and, somewhat surprisingly, Sweden.

It might be tempting to dismiss all this as mere hyperbole. The situation is far less severe than the brutal currency wars of the 1930s, which were intrinsically linked to trade restrictions that governments used to protect their national industries and which drained world trade to a trickle. For now at least, governments are too respectful of the World Trade Organization to go down that route.

But a strongly held view exists that extreme monetary easing and proactive currency strategies, which lie outside the purview of WTO regulations, represent protectionism by another name. Either way, we are at risk of a series of tit-for-tat measures doing great harm to the global economy. The end result could be an all-out trade war or a wholesale loss of confidence in paper money, along with surging inflation.

By speaking about this threat, policymakers often justify their own bad behavior. Mr. Mantega might have taken a holier-than-thou stance when he attacked the Fed and the People's Bank of China but it gave him an excuse to launch Brazil's own intervention strategy, including a tax on capital inflows, to weaken its currency, the real.

In a similar vein, the BOE's Mr. King accompanied his cautionary remarks Tuesday with statements that the pound needed a 25% depreciation to rebalance the struggling UK economy and that his central bank would resort to more quantitative easing if needed.

Such statements do little to breed mutual trust among trading nations. Countries need to acknowledge the negative international impact of their policies and, where possible, foreswear actions that undermine global trade. (The Fed, for one, could simply acknowledge the self-evident truth that quantitative easing weakens the dollar and creates imbalances in the global economy-even if its intent is to boost domestic rather than external demand.) Only then can countries come together in the mutual interest of a free-floating currency system that enhances world commerce and promotes shared prosperity.

(Michael Casey is managing editor for the Americas at DJ FX Trader, a foreign-exchange news service from Dow Jones Newswires and The Wall Street Journal. His new book on the global financial system, "The Unfair Trade," was published in May. Write to Michael Casey at michael.j.casey@dowjones.com.)

title: *DJ Chile Government Concerned About Peso Strength -Finance Minister
text:
24 Jan 2013 16:11 EDT *DJ  Chile Central Bank  Must Judge Whether Intervention Is Merited

24 Jan 2013 16:11 EDT *DJ  Chile Finance Minister Felipe Larrain Spoke in Interview

24 Jan 2013 16:14 EDT DJ  Chile Government Concerned About Peso Strength -Finance Minister


   By Carolina Pica and Laurence Norman 

DAVOS, Switzerland--The Chilean government is concerned about the strength of the peso, which on Thursday closed at a 16-month high against the dollar, and has taken measures such as reining in the growth of fiscal spending to ease pressure on the currency, Finance Minister Felipe Larrain said Thursday.

The peso has gained more than 10% since early 2012 and is reaching levels that prompted a $12 billion intervention program in January 2011.

"We share the concern about the exchange rate," Mr. Larrain said in a interview on the sidelines of the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland.

"Exchange-rate pressures come from a very high level of international liquidity of the major currencies, in particular of the dollar."

The government has attempted to partially offset the peso's gains through eased taxation for derivatives, keeping fiscal spending growth slower than gross-domestic-product growth and improving exporters' competitiveness.

Exporters, especially those in the agricultural sector, have been calling on the government to take more measures and on the central bank to intervene.

Mr. Larrain, who can voice an opinion at the central bank's monthly policy meetings but has no say in policy decisions, said the bank has made it clear it would step in if there were a compelling case for doing so.

In an interview earlier this week, central bank governor Rodrigo Vergara didn't provide any clues on whether there is an intervention looming, but he did warn that both the benefits and costs of such a move must be weighed.

"[The central bank] has to judge if there are enough reasons to intervene," Mr. Larrain said.

Regarding any new sovereign issues, Mr. Larrain said the government was open to new issue, but that there is currently no need to tap international markets.

"If we do it, it's because the market conditions are right...We believe it will be very tough to beat what we did in 2012 in terms of the yield and the spread."

In October, Chile issued $1.5 billion in 10-year and for the first time, 30-year bonds. The issue obtained the lowest yields ever for an emerging-market nation.

23 Jan 2013 11:28 EDT DJ  Chile Central Bank  Vergara: Closely Monitoring Peso Strength Vs Dollar

--Chile central bank always monitoring peso market, but currency still within comfort range

--Increase in productivity can offset loss of competitiveness on stronger peso

--Central bank satisfied that local market understands housing bubble warning

By Carolina Pica and Matthew Cowley

SANTIAGO, Chile--The Chilean central bank is keeping a close eye on the strength of the peso, although it remains in line with long-term fundamentals, its president said Tuesday.

Rodrigo Vergara said the currency is at the stronger end of the bank's comfort range and, if it remains appreciated for long periods, it can damage the country's industrial base.

The peso strengthened 8% against the dollar in 2012, in part because of the monetary easing of developed economies such as the U.S and Europe to jump start growth. That hurts Chile's exporters, making their products more expensive, leading to fresh calls for the central bank to intervene.

The institution intervened to rein in the currency in 2008 and 2011, and Mr. Vergara said it still has that tool. But he stressed intervention isn't the be-all and end-all for currency woes, adding there are always costs as well as benefits.

"The central bank doesn't have a magic formula to control the exchange rate," the central bank governor said in an interview. "Capital controls, for example, can distort a market and sometimes, they just don't work at all."

For Mr. Vergara, who travels later Wednesday to Davos, Switzerland, to participate in the World Economic Forum , increasing productivity would be a better way to deal with the loss of competitiveness that comes from a stronger currency.

"Structural reforms are really the way to deal with the strength of the peso, and we have seen some improvement in Chile's productivity in recent years," he said at his wood-paneled corner office at the central bank's headquarters in downtown Santiago.

Chile's benchmark rate has stood at 5% for the last year, compared with the near-zero levels in industrialized economies. That spread, together with a positive economic growth outlook, has led to heavy capital flows into emerging markets. But Chile hasn't seen a significant increase in short-term speculative inflows.

"We've seen inflows but mostly aimed at [long-term] investments and this has been offset somewhat by outflows as Chilean companies and private pension fund managers invest abroad," Mr. Vergara said.

As in other emerging markets, the Central Bank of Chile is having to walk a fine line on monetary policy, balancing a risky global outlook with a buoyant domestic economy. Economists say that any downturn in the global economy might prompt interest rate cuts, while signs that domestic demand is overheating could trigger interest rate increases.

The export-intensive Chilean economy grew faster than expected in 2012, at an estimated 5.5%--a figure that's especially eye-catching given that inflation ended the year at 1.5%, well below the bank's 3% target.

Robust domestic demand, amid low unemployment and rising salaries, was an important reason behind the growth surge last year, but, according to Mr. Vergara, investment also kept pace, keeping inflation pressures in check.

For 2013, the central bank is expecting growth to slow to around 4.75%, as demand for exports is decelerating. Chile is particularly dependent on copper, which accounts for 60% of exports and has seen prices come off from highs seen in 2011, although they remain close to record highs.

Mr. Vergara said consumer demand nonetheless has been decelerating and should continue to slow in 2013. He said he doesn't see any major risks to prices in the short term and, gradually, inflation should return to the 3% target. On the other hand, the external outlook remains fragile. All that adds up to the central bank's decision to keep rates on hold and to maintain a neutral bias, he said.

"This is a balance that can change at any moment," Mr. Vergara said.

That equilibrium is also reflected in market expectations. According to the bank's most recent monthly poll of more than 60 analysts, most expect a quarter-percentage-point increase in the benchmark rate by the end of the year to tame domestic demand. But one-fifth of the analysts see a rate cut by year-end, and another 20% see a half-point hike.

Mr. Vergara mused that the split probably reflects whether people emphasize the internal or external factors. There aren't many periods in history when there's been such a contrast between two opposing economic forces, he added.

Meanwhile, Mr. Vergara said he is "satisfied" that his warnings about the possibility of a housing bubble developing in some parts of the country had been heeded. "I'm satisfied that our message was heard," he said.

title: Chilean Peso Weakens On  Intervention  Speculation
text:
The Chilean peso weakened against the dollar in early trading Wednesday as the current peso levels prompted traders to speculate the central bank could intervene in the currency market.

The central bank launched a year-long intervention program when the peso firmed to the CLP465 level to the greenback in early January 2011.

"The peso is moving on possible new intervention programs," said Hernan Jimenez, an analyst at Forex Chile.

title: Currency  Rally Hems In Latin America
text:
The recent rally in Latin American currencies has exporters in the region renewing calls for central-bank and government action to slow the appreciation they fear will blunt their competitive edge at a time of slowing demand for their exports.

In Chile, Colombia and Peru, the dollars are pouring back in as global economic jitters have subsided and U.S. investors again seek the higher returns on investments that emerging markets offer.

A strong local currency and high labor and energy costs are creating "a perfect storm" for exporters, said Wilfred Leigh, chief executive at Chilean vintner Bethwines.

"One solution would be to increase our wine prices but, as Europe is our largest market, if we raise prices nobody there would buy our wines," Mr. Leigh said. "Europeans are undergoing their own crisis."

Brazilian exporters blamed their strong currency, the real, for last year's drop in the country's trade surplus as exports declined 5% and imports fell only 1%.

"We're facing price competition not only in export markets but also in the domestic market," said Flavio Castelo Branco, chief economist of the Brazilian Confederation of Industries.

Calls by exporters for intervention in Chile picked up in recent weeks when the peso reached a three-month high against the U.S. dollar, twice closing around 470 Chilean pesos to the dollar, a psychological level at which investors estimate the central bank could intervene. That is where the peso was when the bank launched a yearlong intervention program in January 2011.

Others see renewed intervention as unlikely. They say the cause of the current appreciation is dollar weakness partly tied to the Federal Reserve's largess.

"At 470, investors buy dollars and the peso depreciates," said Sergio Tricio, head of research at Forex Chile.

Chilean central-bank governor Rodrigo Vergara gave no clues in an interview as to whether the bank would take action to curb peso strength. "Some sectors have benefited from significant price increases abroad," he said. "Others have a more complicated outlook. So naturally, some manufacturing or agricultural sectors have been much more affected than others and they speak out against this."

Currency intervention across Latin America has varied, with Brazil the most active in managing swings and Mexico among the most hands-off.

Nomura Latin America strategist Benito Berber said currency appreciation is bound to be an issue in the region in 2013, noting recent statements by Colombian officials about weakening the Colombian peso.

Moves to weaken local currencies could lead investors to shop around when choosing where in the region to park funds, since depreciation of the currencies reduces the gains on local-currency bonds. "It's something they take into account," Mr. Berber said.

Mexico's peso is one of the most-traded emerging-market currencies, and as a result it is among the most vulnerable to swings in investor mood.

The Mexican peso last week reached its strongest level since September 2011, moving below 12.60 pesos to the dollar. Finance Minister Luis Videgaray said the government and central bank will maintain the policy of accumulating foreign reserves as a "prudential measure" against bouts of international market volatility.

Colombia's Finance Minister Mauricio Cardenas shrugged off cries for greater action to curtail Colombian peso strength, saying the recent appreciation is "transitory" and that the exchange rate would soon return to 1,800 Colombian pesos to the dollar.

The Colombian central bank currently buys at least $20 million a day, and the Finance Ministry makes discretionary dollar purchases.

"The problem goes beyond simply buying dollars...it requires more aggressive and more audacious measures," including possibly capital controls, said Augusto Solano, who heads a Colombian flower exporters association.

Costa Rica is planning just that. The government this week proposed to Congress temporary measures including stiff taxes on financial gains by foreign investors that are transferred out of the country. President Laura Chinchilla last week described short-term capital inflows as "genuine weapons of mass destruction" for receiving economies.

--Tom Murphy in Sao Paulo, Darcy Crowe in Bogota and Carolina Pica in Santiago contributed to this article [ 01-22-13 1941ET ]

title: UPDATE: Chile  Central Bank  Holds at 5%, Bias Still Neutral
text:
--Central bank weighs robust local economy against a still risky international outlook

--Base rate seen at 5% at least through the first half

--Central bank not likely to intervene in peso market just yet, analysts say

(Updates with comments from analysts starting in paragraph fourteen)


 
   By Carolina Pica 
 

SANTIAGO, Chile--For the 12th consecutive month, the Central Bank of Chile kept its benchmark interest rate steady, while maintaining its neutral rate bias.

At its monthly monetary-policy meeting Thursday, the central bank held the overnight interbank lending rate, known locally as the TPM, at 5%, in line with analysts' expectations. The 13 economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires had expected the bank to stand at 5%.

Like it did in its previous 11 meetings, the central bank weighed contrasting factors such as the risks stemming from the euro zone and the U.S. and the performance of the local economy, which has grown at a robust pace with mild inflation and low unemployment.

In January-November 2012, the country's gross domestic proxy index grew 5.7%, surpassing expectations that GDP grew 5.5% in the whole of 2012.

Inflation, according to recently reported data, ended 2012 at 1.5%, below the central bank's target of 3%, with a tolerance range of one percentage point around that target.

In its post-meeting communique, the bank said activity and demand are in line with its outlook and, while inflation is below 2%, long-term inflation expectations are in line with its target.

The central bank also briefly mentioned the peso's strength versus the dollar. A wide spread with U.S. rates, relatively high copper prices, the dollar's global weakness and the resilience of the local economy have all contributed to firming the Andean currency.

"In this recent month, the peso has appreciated slightly with respect to the dollar," it said.

In recent sessions, the peso has been trading near a psychologically important level at CLP470 and flirting with the CLP465 trading level that triggered the bank's $12 billion intervention program in early 2011.

On the international front, the bank said that while there are still risks in the euro zone and the U.S., international financial conditions have improved.

In addition, the monetary authority said the economies of developed nations remain weak while China, Chile's main trade partner, is showing positive signs of growth.

The prices of fuels abroad have increased, while copper, the country's biggest export, has held at prices similar to those seen in December, the bank said. International crude oil prices can pressure local inflation as the country imports 98% of the fuels it consumes. A strong peso, however, relieves some of these pressures as imports get cheaper when the peso firms.

The bank maintained its neutral rate bias, reiterating, as in previous months, that any future changes to the TPM will depend on the impact of domestic and international macroeconomic conditions on inflation expectations.

Analysts, meanwhile, don't foresee any changes in monetary policy for most of 2013.

"For the bank to make any move, the outlook abroad would have to improve dramatically while the economy here decelerates and inflation moves closer to the central bank's target," said Cristobal Doberti, chief economist at local investment bank BICE Inversiones.

Analysts expect the TPM to hold steady at 5% at least through the first half of the year. The bank's most recent monthly poll of analysts' expectations shows a rate increase isn't expected until sometime in the second half of this year.

"When the international outlook takes a turn for the better, we could see a rate increase," said Felip Jaque, senior economist at Banco Bilbao Vizcaya Argentaria's (BBVACL.SN) Chile unit .

Regarding currency market intervention, analysts said the bank's mention of the slight firming the peso has seen in recent sessions is a signal that it won't intervene unless the peso strengthens further.

Most analysts think the peso will have to cross the CLP460-threshold before the bank begins buying dollars to weaken the local currency.

"Despite the small change in language from last month's statement, the bank is saying that at these levels, it won't intervene," Mr. Doberti said.

In recent public appearances, central bank chief Rodrigo Vergara has said that while intervention can't be ruled out, it's a costly measure.

--Graciela Ibanez contributed to this article

title: UPDATE:  Chile Intervention  Depends Solely on  Central Bank  -President
text:
--Chile government closely monitoring peso's value against the dollar, president says

--Prudent fiscal spending has reduced strengthening pressure on peso

--Currency strength likely topic at upcoming summit of Latin American, Caribbean states

(updates with additional comments from President Pinera)


 
   By Carolina Pica 
 

SANTIAGO, Chile--While the Chilean government closely monitors the strength of the country's peso in relation to the dollar, as this appreciation curbs the export sector's competitiveness abroad, market intervention is the prerogative of the autonomous central bank, President Sebastian Pinera said Thursday.

The peso has been trading firmer against the dollar so far this year, nearing levels that triggered a $12 billion intervention program in early 2011.

"The peso's appreciation is in large part due to the depreciation the dollar has seen globally," Mr. Pinera said in a press conference with foreign correspondents.

He added the government has contributed to reducing mounting pressures on the currency by keeping fiscal spending at prudent levels, maintaining fiscal spending growth slower than gross domestic product growth.

Mr. Pinera pointed out that while Chile's GDP has grown at an average of about 6% since he took office in early 2010, fiscal spending has been gaining at around 5%.

In 2012, the peso firmed around 8% against the dollar, and so far this year, it's hit three-month highs during several sessions as it trades near an important psychological barrier at CLP470 to the dollar.

But Chile isn't the only country in the region grappling with a strong currency as the U.S., the European Union and other large economies continue to inject additional stimulus into their economies.

Many Latin American nations have been weathering the global financial crisis with healthy growth, but their success has also fueled capital inflows as investors seek better returns. Several nations, such as Brazil and Peru, have seen currency-market interventions to counter the strength of their currencies versus the dollar.

Later this month, Chile will be hosting the first summit of the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States, or CELAC by its Spanish acronym, and the topic of currency strength will likely come up during the gathering.

"The topic is one we're concerned with and we're obviously going to discuss this at the CELAC summit as it affects many countries in the region," Mr. Pinera said.

The CELAC summit, which follows a similar summit in Santiago of CELAC and the E.U., will take place on Jan. 27 and 28.

title: Chile  Peso Ends At Three-Month High Amid New  Intervention  Calls
text:
The Chilean peso strengthened to close at a three-month high against the dollar Wednesday amid new intervention calls to the central bank from exporters who seek a weaker peso.

The peso ended at CLP470.70 to the dollar, versus Tuesday's close of CLP472.00, after trading in a wide range of CLP470.70 to CLP473.15.

Gains in copper prices after Alcoa Inc. (AA), the world's largest aluminum producer, reported strong fourth-quarter results contributed to the peso's gains.

As Chile produces one-third of the world's copper, the peso often moves in line with the industrial metal's price.

Manufacturer exporters in Chile asked the central bank to launch an intervention program as the peso's current level is hurting their competitiveness and threatening their survival.

During most of 2011, the central bank intervened in the currency market when the peso firmed to CLP465.40 to the dollar, buying a total of $12 billion.

If the central bank doesn't intervene soon, "many small exporters will die," said Roberto Fantuzzi, who leads the Asexma manufacturing exporter trade group.

The 2011 intervention "came late," he added in a statement.

Fears of intervention have prompted investors to buy dollars when the peso reaches or crosses the level of CLP470 to the dollar.

Agricultural exporters have also called for intervention, but the bank has repeatedly said the peso has traded in line with its long-term fundamentals.

In the fixed-income market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central-bank bonds, or BCUs, ended flat.

The yield on five-year BCUs ended at 2.80%, while the yield on 10-year BCUs closed at 2.72%, both unchanged from Tuesday. Bond yields and bond prices move inversely.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real,  Chile  peso drop on verbal  intervention
text:
* Chile finance ministry, central bank to discuss peso strength

* Brazil won't roll over dollar auctions with repo agreement -Estado

* Brazil real drops 0.5 percent; Mexican peso drops 0.3 percent

By Danielle Fonseca and Moises Avila

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Jan 8 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real dropped on Tuesday on signs that the country's central bank does not want the currency to gain much further, while the Chilean peso weakened after that country's finance minister expressed concern about the impact of a strong exchange rate on exports.

Most Latin American currencies also fell as investors took a weak Wall Street session as a cue to pocket part of a recent rally, driving the Mexican peso 0.25 percent lower.

Brazil's real led losses in the region, falling 0.4 percent to 2.0373 per dollar, after local news agency Estado quoted an anonymous central bank source as saying that, at current exchange rates, the bank would not roll over the dollars it had sold with repurchase agreements late last year.

"That could be an indication that the central bank doesn't want the real too close to two per dollar," said a trader at a large Brazilian bank.

A central bank spokesman said the bank would not comment on a story based on an anonymous source.

Those dollar auctions were part of Brazil's strategy to provide liquidity to the foreign exchange market at the end of the year, when greenbacks are usually more scarce as Brazilians vacation abroad and foreign companies remit profits to their headquarters.

Although the central bank's most recent intervention was designed to strengthen the real and avoid additional inflation pressures, analysts believe policymakers also do not want the real to gain past two per dollar, which could hurt exporters.

In Chile, the peso erased early gains to close 0.21 percent weaker at 472.20 per dollar after Finance Minister Felipe Larrain said the government and the central bank may come up with "coordinated action" to prevent the currency from gaining further.

The Chilean peso has rallied more than 1 percent in the first few days of 2013, on top of gains of nearly 8.5 percent in 2012.

"The peso started the day stronger as foreign banks sold dollars," said Eugenio Cortes, head of forward contracts at EuroAmerica. The currency pierced the level of 470 per dollar when investors started buying dollars again and the finance minister came with his "verbal intervention," he added.

Local analysts say the central bank would be compelled to intervene if the peso strengthens past 467 to the dollar.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  weaken; Mexico peso slumps
text:
* Brazil's real down 0.52 pct despite central bank intervention

* Mexico's peso slips 1.43 pct, Chile's peso off 0.67 pct

(Adds comment, updates prices, changes dateline, previous SAO PAULO)

By Jean Arce

MEXICO CITY, Dec 21 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso tumbled by the most in five months on Friday after U.S. budget negotiations stalled and Brazil's real weakened despite efforts by the country's central bank to lift the currency.

Brazil's real shed 0.52 percent to 2.0732 per dollar, while Mexico's peso tumbled 1.43 percent to 12.9444 per dollar. The peso hit its weakest level since early December and headed for its worst one-day loss since late July.

Markets fell on Thursday after a budget plan proposed by a Republican leader failed to win support from his own party, raising the chances that austerity measures kick in next year.

U.S. lawmakers are struggling to come up with a deal to avert $600 billion worth of tax increases and spending cuts, a combination that could push the world's largest economy back into recession next year.

"The risk is rising that (talks) are going to drag into next year," said Delia Paredes, an analyst at Mexico's Banorte-IXE.

A U.S. economic downturn could hit Mexico the hardest among Latin American countries, since it sends nearly 80 percent of its exports to its northern neighbor.

Bets on a deal by U.S. lawmakers before the end of the year had spurred gains in riskier assets, such as Latin American currencies. Mexico's peso hit a two-month high last week.

Brazil's central bankintervened twice earlier in the day, selling up to $4 billion in two auctions with repurchase agreements. The auctions were designed to increase the supply of foreign exchange before year-end, but traders and analysts said they aim at curbing excessive losses in the Brazilian real.

The central bank said after the market close that it will sell up to $2 billion on the spot market on Dec. 26 with a repurchase agreement.

"After all the central bank has done, I think it wants the foreign exchange rate below 2.1 per U.S. dollar. It can even strengthen past 2.05 per dollar," said Reginaldo Siaca, manager at Advanced brokerage in Sao Paulo.

Chile's peso shed 0.67 percent to 478 per dollar to close at its weakest in two weeks.

title: UPDATE:  Chile  Peso  Intervention  Hasn't Been Needed - Central Bank  Head
text:
--Intervention hasn't been warranted as peso still in line with fundamentals

--Growth seen robust in 2013, but economy faces domestic and external risks

--Central bank concerned about possible housing bubble; Government rules out bubble forming

(Updates with more comments from Rodrigo Vergara and Finance Minister Felipe Larrain)

SANTIAGO, Chile--The Central Bank of Chile hasn't intervened in the peso market to weaken the currency against the dollar as this "hasn't been necessary," Central Bank Governor Rodrigo Vergara said Wednesday.

As the peso has firmed some 8% versus the dollar this year, exporters have clamored for central bank or government moves to depreciate the peso. Exports, the backbone of the Chilean economy, lose competitiveness when the peso firms.

Mr. Vergara, speaking at the Icare local business forum and later to reporters, reiterated that intervention can be costly.

"Intervention has its benefits and it has its costs and while it's a policy that's always available, we will use it if the benefits outweigh the costs," he said, adding that the peso remains in line with its long-term fundamentals although on the stronger end of the bank's tolerance levels.

In early 2011, when the peso was trading at near three-year highs, the bank launched a year-long, $12 billion intervention program.

"If we intervened in previous occasions, it was because we saw the benefits of such a move," the central banker said.

Earlier this week, the central bank released its quarterly Monetary Policy Report and its most recent Financial Stability Report.

In the former, it raised its outlook for both 2012 and 2013, while pointing out that the economy, which has been growing at a brisk pace, isn't immune to both internal and external risks.

The bank raised its 2012 gross domestic product outlook to a year-on-year gain of 5.5%, in line with analysts and markets.

"Growth this year has been surprisingly high," Mr. Vergara said, adding that the bank's initial growth view was a percentage point lower than its recently revised estimate.

GDP is expected to grow between 4.25% and 5.25% in 2013, on the bank of healthy domestic demand and investments, while facing risks from the slowdown in the euro zone and a widening current account deficit.

The central bank also mentioned a possible housing bubble as a risk to the local economy. In its Financial Stability Report, the bank said strong real estate demand had boosted housing prices in certain areas to record highs, which could lead to a potential surge in medium-term mortgage lending.

"We didn't use the phrase 'housing bubble' as it can lead to misunderstandings, but there's been a steep price increase along with significant debt which can produce a vulnerability. So our first move is to issue a warning about what could happen in the future," Mr. Vergara said.

Finance Miniter Felipe Larrain, meanwhile, applauded the central bank's revised outlook as it is in line with the government's view but ruled out a nascent housing bubble.

Mr. Larrain told reporters the government is monitoring the real estate sector to avert any such bubble.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  gain modestly after Fed
text:
* Fed pledges to pump more money into the U.S. economy

* Chilean peso gains for 7th session to 2-month high

* Brazil real gains 0.1 pct, Mexico peso flat

By Walter Brandimarte

RIO DE JANEIRO, Dec 12 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies rose modestly on Wednesday after the Federal Reserve pledged to inject more money into the U.S. economy, potentially driving up dollar inflows to emerging markets.

The Fed's decision to replace an expiring stimulus program with a fresh round of Treasury debt purchases, combined with its pledge to keep interest rates near zero until the jobless rate falls to 6.5 percent, is likely to keep alive investor appetite for emerging-market currencies and stocks.

A number of domestic factors curbed gains in Latin American foreign exchange markets, however.

In Mexico, a holiday kept local markets closed, leaving the peso to trade nearly unchanged at 12.740 per dollar in overseas trading.

In Chile, investors grew increasingly cautious of a possible central bank intervention as the peso gained for a seventh consecutive session.

The Chilean currency ended 0.17 percent higher at 474.20 per dollar, its strongest level in two months, also helped by a rise in prices of copper, the country's main export product.

Brazil's real ended 0.1 percent stronger at 2.0742 per dollar, also supported by two central bank auctions of dollars with repurchase agreements.

The auctions are aimed at providing dollar liquidity at year-end, but also suggest the central bank does not want the real to weaken too much for fear of inflation.

"The recent actions and comments from central bank officials show the bank wants a stronger real as they fear inflation pressures," said Sidnei Nehme, a director at NGO brokerage in Sao Paulo.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  firm; Venezuela bonds rally
text:
* Venezuelan 2027 bond hits highest price since January 2008

* Chile peso up again, some see cenbank intervening

* Mexico peso up 0.5 pct, Brazil real flat

By Walter Brandimarte

RIO DE JANEIRO, Dec 11 (Reuters) - Venezuelan bonds rallied for a second session on Tuesday on expectations of a regime change in the oil-exporting nation, while Latin American currencies rose as German data on investor confidence and hopes of a U.S. budget deal supported appetite for risk.

Venezuela's global 2027 bonds, the most actively traded, reached their highest price since early 2008 as President Hugo Chavez underwent surgery in Cuba for a cancer recurrence, raising the prospect of new presidential elections, even as Chavez named a successor.

The 2027 bonds last traded 1.4 points higher at a bid price of 102.367.

Yield spreads between Venezuelan bonds and safe-haven U.S. Treasuries tightened 3 basis points to 749 basis points according to JPMorgan's EMBI+ index, showing investors' appetite for the country's assets was the strongest since September 2008.

Before leaving Venezuela, Chavez named his vice president and foreign minister, Nicolas Maduro, to take over, should he become incapacitated. Chavez, who is due to begin a new six-year term on Jan. 10, urged supporters to vote for Maduro in the event of an election.

"We are encouraged that President Chavez asked for voter support for his candidate since this suggests an electoral transition as opposed to the alternative strategy to allow the VP to finish the entire six-year term," Siobhan Morden, head of Latin America strategy at Jefferies & Co. Inc., wrote in a research note.

CURRENCIES GAIN, EXCEPT REAL

Elsewhere in Latin America, most currencies rose after a key index of German investor sentiment rose sharply in December, supporting optimism about the world economy.

The appetite for risk further grew as the S&P 500 index

ended at its best level since Election Day, buoyed by hopes of a resolution to the U.S. budget impasse.

The Mexican peso rose 0.5 percent to 12.7435 per dollar, while the Chilean peso edged 0.1 percent higher to 475.00 per greenback, its strongest level in nearly two months.

It was the sixth straight winning session for the Chilean peso, which led some traders to believe the country's central bank could soon act to curb currency gains.

On the other hand, the Brazilian real closed practically unchanged at 2.0770 per dollar after the central bank announced two auctions on Wednesday to sell as much as $1.5 billion on the spot market with repurchase agreement.

The announcement added to the market perception that Brazilian policymakers do not want the real to weaken. Confirming that perception, a member of Brazil's economic team said the real was at a satisfactory level when it traded around 2.03 and 2.04 reais per dollar.

title: Chile CorpGroup Still Interested in Local Fuel Assets - Chairman
text:
--CorpGroup would be interested in fuel company Terpel's local assets

--Terpel has 97 convenience stores in Chile, an attractive target for CorpGroup's retail division

--"We're interested in the real-estate and the convenience store businesses," CorpGroup Chairman says

By Graciela Ibanez

SANTIAGO, Chile--After more than 70 acquisitions in the retail sector over the past five years, Chilean conglomerate CorpGroup SA still has an appetite for another deal and would again bid for fuel company Terpel's local assets should the opportunity arise, said CorpGroup Chairman Alvaro Saieh.

That opportunity may come soon enough, given a deadline for Terpel's controlling shareholder to sell the unit. If a renewed bid by CorpGroup is ultimately successful, it will consolidate CorpGroup as one of Chile's top convenience store operators, and would add significantly to its real-estate holdings.

"We're interested in the real-estate and the convenience-store businesses, but we would need a partner [to run Terpel's 200 gas stations]," Mr. Saieh said in an interview last month.

Terpel has 97 convenience stores in Chile.

In 2011, Mr. Saieh's CorpGroup, along with state-owned oil company Empresa Nacional del Petroleo SA, or Enap, and Peruvian conglomerate Grupo Romero, bid for Terpel's Chilean assets, but lost to holding company Quinenco SA (QUINENCO.SN), which had offered $320 million to Terpel's controller, Chilean fuel and forestry conglomerate Empresas Copec SA (COPEC.SN).

Terpel Chile could be up for sale again if the Supreme Court upholds an April Antitrust Court ruling that rejected Quinenco's bid, as the holding company already has a 13% market share in the fuel distribution sector. The Supreme Court doesn't have a date for its ruling.

Copec is under a separate antitrust deadline to divest its Terpel Chilean assets by the end of November.

Terpel's convenience stores are an attractive target for CorpGroup's SMU retail division and real-estate operations.

SMU, which plans to consolidate its operations over the next two years after a flurry of acquisitions in Chile and Peru, has developed the convenience store format in Chile's largest cities.

The Chilean retailer, which reported a 29% increase in sales to 1.029 trillion pesos ($2.16 billion) in the first-half of the year, plans to finance its organic growth by raising cash from listing shares on the Santiago Stock Exchange and in the U.S. next year.

Mr. Saieh said he won't venture SMU into a new country, such as Colombia, where CorpGroup has been aggressively expanding this year through its banking unit CorpBanca (BCA, CORPBANCA.SN).

CorpBanca, Chile's fifth largest bank in terms of loans, will consolidate its operations in Colombia over the next two years after it purchased the Colombian unit of Spanish Banco Santander SA (SAN, SAN.MC) and closes the acquisition of Colombian Helm Bank SA (PFHELMBAN.BO) in the first quarter of 2013.

"The Colombian market offers big expansion opportunities as it's less developed than the Chilean market and Colombia has a population that is three times Chile's," Mr. Saieh said.

In Latin America, Chilean banks are the most active lenders, with domestic credit to the private sector at some 70% of the country's gross domestic product. In Colombia it's about 45% of GDP, according to the World Bank.

In Colombia, CorpBanca, which will have a 7% market share after the Helm Bank acquisition, plans to target middle and lower income individuals as it already has a presence in the higher income segment, Mr. Saieh said on the 45-million people country.

As a long-time banker, Mr. Saieh jumped into Chile's intervention discussion after the peso has firmed nearly 8% versus the dollar so far this year.

"If intervention was easy, the central bank would have already done it."

With the peso at CLP482 to the dollar, agricultural exporters are asking the bank to intervene in the currency market to weaken the Andean currency as a strong peso hurts their revenue.

In 2011, the central bank launched a yearlong intervention program when the peso firmed to CLP465.40 in early January of last year.

A similar move isn't likely at the moment as the peso is still in line with its fundamentals, Central Bank Governor Rodrigo Vergara has said several times.

title: MARKET TALK:  Chile Central Bank Intervention  Seen Farther Away
