title: UPDATE: Chile on Track to Grow 5% In 2012 - Central Bank  Governor
text:
--Effects of slower global growth on Chile have been softer than expected

--Peso intervention not warranted, central bank governor says

--Peso still in line with fundamentals, although on stronger end of comfort range

(Adds quotes, details beginning in the sixth paragraph)

SANTIAGO, Chile--The Chilean economy remains on track to grow around 5% this year, as the worsening global outlook hasn't hit the Andean nation as hard as expected, central bank governor Rodrigo Vergara said Thursday.

Chile's gross domestic product, which relies heavily on exports, is expected to grow between 4.75% and 5.25% year-on-year in 2012, following gains of 6.1% and 6.0%, respectively, in 2010 and 2011.

Inflation, meanwhile, remains mild and is expected to end the year at 2.5%, below the central bank's target of 3%.

Mr. Vergara warned that despite tame inflation, pressures are looming on the horizon, especially in light of a tight labor market, robust domestic demand and a closed output gap.

Demand this year is seen growing 5.6% year-on-year, while the unemployment rate is currently at 6.4%, a level which economist say puts the local economy at nearly full employment.

The good health of the Chilean economy, as well as a weak dollar globally and still high copper prices, have contributed to keeping the peso strong against the greenback.

So far this year, the peso has gained nearly 10% against the dollar, prompting calls from agricultural exporters for central bank intervention and government measures to weaken the local currency.

Mr. Vergara, who has previously said the bank could never rule out intervention although it could be costly, said the monetary authority hasn't intervened because it hasn't been warranted.

"We reserve the right to intervene if the situation merits it. If we haven't done so it's because we believe that this isn't the case for now," he said at a conference hosted by local charity Hogar Mision de Maria.

The peso's appreciation "is a source of concern for the central bank," Mr. Vergara said, but he noted the peso's gains weren't isolated. "If we compared ourselves to Brazil, Colombia, Peru and Mexico, the peso's appreciation is in line with these other countries."

He reiterated that an intervention would only have temporary effects and unlike in 2011, when the bank bought $50 million a day for a total $12 billion to weaken the peso, the Andean currency is still in line with its fundamentals, although on the stronger end of the bank's comfort range.

title: UPDATE 1- Chile  cbank says not the moment for  forex intervention
text:
* Chilean peso has strengthened nearly 8 pct this year

* Cbank says reserves itself right to intervene

* Chile cbank president says peso strength a worry

(Recasts with central bank president quote, context)

SANTIAGO, Oct 25 (Reuters) - The Chilean peso's strength remains a worry but it isn't the moment to intervene in the foreign exchange market to stem its appreciation, central bank president Rodrigo Vergara said on Thursday.

The peso has strengthened nearly 8 percent this year, sparking market speculation over a potential intervention.

"Yes, it's a worry. We reserve ourselves the right to intervene if the situation deserves it, but if we haven't done it yet it's because we don't think it's the moment at least for now," Vergara told a business forum.

The central bank deployed a dollar-purchasing program last year, which lasted through December, to curb peso strength after it appreciated to its highest level in more than 2-1/2 years at 465.50 per dollar.

The peso was trading around 0.52 percent stronger at 478.50 per dollar on Thursday morning, buoyed by encouraging data from Britain and China and the U.S. Federal Reserve's latest commitment to support growth. Vergara's comments didn't appear to affect its movement.

Chile's peso has firmed as an attractive interest rate differential compared with the developed world and high levels of foreign investment have kept dollars flowing into Chile, which is seen growing around 5 percent this year.

The central bank's benchmark interest rate is 5 percent, compared with a U.S. overnight rate that is less than 0.25 percent, a gap that attracts capital to the South American nation.

title: EMERGING MARKETS- Chile  up on China data, Brazil may  intervene
text:
* Chinese manufacturing survey points to economic recovery

* Data shows Germany being sucked into euro zone crisis

* Brazil's Mantega admits "dirty float" of the currency

* Mexico peso drops 0.12 pct, Chile peso up 0.35 pct

(Adds detail)

By Walter Brandimarte and Lorena Segura

SAO PAULO, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Chile's peso bounced back from a two-month low o n Wednesday after data pointed to a stronger economic performance in China, the region's top trading partner, and a top buyer of Chilean copper.

After slipping for four straight sessions to trade at its weakest since August, C hile's peso strengthene d 0 .3 5 p ercent a fter data showed Chinese manufacturers' output reached a three-month high in October, while order books were at their highest level since April.

"The peso is supported by China's strong manufacturing data, which boosted copper prices and European stocks," said Jose Manuel Briceno, an analyst with GKFX in Santiago.

Copper, Chile's main export product, traded slightly higher on the London Metal Exchange.

The Mexican peso dipped 0. 1 2 percent, however, as investors remained worried about the global economy after business surveys suggested Germany is being sucked into the euro zone crisis.

The peso slumped to a nearly six-week intraday low on Wednesday, breaking past 13 per dollar before bouncing back to trade at 12.99.

Data on Wednesday showed Mexican annual inflation eased in the first half of October from a 2-1/2 year high, bolstering expectations that the central bank will keep borrowing costs steady into 2014. [nL 3E8LO5LY].

The U.S. Federal Reserve said it would stick to its stimulus plan until the job market improves, in line with expectations.

The Fed's asset buying scheme is expected to help support demand for higher-yielding, riskier assets in coming months. A nalysts said that demand for Mexican assets could keep the peso from breaking past 13 per dollar. [ID :nL1E8LNFFD]

"We still have the idea that the exchange rate can return to levels around 12.80 plus or minus 10 centavos, " said Rafael Camarena, a n economist at Santander.

DIRTY FLOAT

In Brazil, the real edged up 0.1 percent to 2.0250 per greenback.

T raders were unwilling to push it much stronger amid e xpecta tions that the central bank could intervene in the foreign exchange market again to stop the currency from strengthening.

The bank intervened on Monday after a two-week hiatus with an auction of reverse currency swaps - derivative contracts that emulate the purchase of dollars in the futures market.

With the sale, the central bank rolled over about half of the contracts that expire on Nov. 1, leaving traders speculating that it could offer more swaps in the next few days to complete the rollover, or even increase the stock of reverse swaps if dollar inflows pick up.

In the latest sign of the government commitment to a weaker currency, Finance Minister Guido Mantega acknowledged in an interview that the real is now subject to a "dirty-floating" regime in which policymakers intervene to keep an exchange rate favorable to the local industry.

The constant threat of intervention has sapped volumes and liquidity of the Brazilian foreign exchange market, keeping the real in an increasingly tight trading range.

"We still work with a trading band of 2.0-2.1 reais per dollar, but the truth is that this range has been tightening. The central bank now intervenes whenever the real nears the level of 2.02 per dollar," said Mauricio Nakahodo, an economic research consultant with Tokyo-Mitsubishi bank in Sao Paulo.

title: Chileans Debate a  Currency Intervention  as Peso Strengthens
text:
The debate over whether Chile's central bank should try to weaken the peso heated up this week as the peso remains strong against the dollar, but a consensus about such a measure is still far off.

With the peso closing Tuesday at CLP472.80 to the dollar, the Andean currency has firmed 10% against the greenback this year, making it one of the world's top gainers versus the dollar in 2012.

The peso's current trading level is close to the CLP465 level seen in January 2011, when the central bank launched a yearlong intervention program and bought a total of $12 billion at a rate of $50 million a day.

While market participants say the current level is enough to justify an intervention, they agree there's little the central bank can do when the dollar weakens against most of the world's currencies.

"The peso isn't as out of line with its fundamentals as it was in the past and the central bank has more dollar reserves than in 2011," said Sergio Tricio, head of research at Forex Chile.

One of the reasons for intervening is to accumulate reserves, former central bank Governor Vittorio Corbo recently said. The central bank raised its foreign currency reserves to 15% of gross domestic product with its 2011 intervention.

On Monday, President Sebastian Pinera jumped into the intervention debate and attributed the strong peso to the previous administration's increase in public spending.

"If we raise public spending, we will further strengthen the peso," Mr. Pinera said in a radio interview, after having recently sent to Congress the country's 2013 budget. That fiscal budget will grow 4.8% year-on-year to some $62 billion, while the central bank estimates gross domestic product will grow between 4.75% and 5.25% this year.

"To control the peso/dollar parity, we're implementing responsible fiscal policy," Mr. Pinera said.

To calm agricultural producers' calls for intervention, Mr. Pinera said, the central bank is monitoring the currency market and will take measures when it deems these are appropriate. Chile is an export-based economy and the country's revenue decreases when the peso strengthens.

For a central bankintervention to be effective in weakening the peso, the bank will have to buy a total of about $10 billion, analysts said. With the 2011 intervention and its $12 billion purchase, the peso weakened some 8% against the dollar.

"If we want to reach a similar effect this year, the bank should buy $12 billion or more," said Nathan Pincheira, senior analyst at Banchile Inversiones.

Another factor to consider in an intervention scenario is the need to offset the economic effects of the increase in central bank reserves. In 2011, the central bank issued $2 billion in short-term fixed-income instruments and $10 billion in both peso-denominated and inflation-indexed bonds to neutralize the intervention.

"The 2011 sterilization plan triggered an increase of around 90 basis points in the yield of 10-year peso-denominated bonds and 30 basis points in the yield of 10-year inflation-indexed bonds," said Mr. Pincheira.

Central bank Governor Rodrigo Vergara, meanwhile, has reiterated that the costs of an intervention would outweigh the benefits of such a move.

Despite the high costs, if the peso continues to strengthen against the dollar, the central bank would intervene anyway as the government isn't likely to adjust fiscal policy to cool down the appreciating pressures on the peso, Credit Suisse said in a research note.

title: EMERGING MARKETS- Chile  peso slumps on  intervention  concerns
text:
* Chile cenbank president doesn't rule out intervention

* Colombia says will keep up dollar purchases

* Mexican peso falls 0.31 pct; Brazil real up 0.28 pct

(Recasts, adds comments)

By Moises Avila and Jean Arce

SANTIAGO/MEXICO CITY, Sept 28 (Reuters) - Chile's peso slumped by the most in seven weeks on Friday after the central bank warned it could act to curb currency gains, while Colombia pledged to keep buying dollars in its market to fight peso strength.

The Chilean peso lost nearly 0.8 percent to change hands at 474.60 per U.S. dollar after central bank chief Rodrigo Vergara said policymakers may intervene during "exceptional periods" in which the exchange rate is significantly out of line with fundamentals.

The move by Chile pushed it closer to the stance of policymakers in Brazil, Colombia and Peru who have been intervening in markets to fight dollar inflows that have lifted their currencies and hurt exporters.

"The central bank's comments weakened the peso because they leave the door open for a possible intervention. The market isn't just speculating about the possibility of dollar purchases, but also bank deposit requirements," said Rodrigo Sarria, a trader at Celfin Capital in Santiago.

The peso has gained more than 9 percent so far this year, making it the second strongest performer among the 152 currencies tracked by Reuters.

Stimulus measures announced by the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank boosted Latin American currencies this quarter. The measures are expected to drive down yields on U.S. and European fixed-income instruments, making emerging market assets more attractive.

The Chilean peso gained 5.5 percent against the dollar in the third quarter, while Mexico's peso firmed 4.5 percent. Brazil's real shed 0.8 percent against the greenback in the quarter after Brazil's central bankintervened.

Colombia's central bank held its benchmark interest rate steady on Friday, and it pledged to extend daily dollar purchases to keep a lid on the peso.

The central bank said it would buy at least $3 billion in the foreign exchange market via auctions from Oct. 1 through March 29, 2013, to take pressure off the peso currency.

The Colombia peso slipped 0.1 percent on Friday, bringing its decline for the quarter to 0.9 percent, hurt by central bank dollar purchases.

The Mexican peso lost a modest 0.31 percent to trade at 12.8660 per dollar as concerns about Spain made investors cautious about taking risks in emerging markets.

A stress test on Spanish banks showed the institutions need a total of 59.3 billion euros in extra capital, but uncertainty persisted about whether Spain will ask for a bailout that would let the European Central Bank begin buying its bonds.

"We could see a whole to wave of pressure related to Spain," said Jorge Gordillo, an analyst at CI Banco in Mexico City, saying that concerns about Spain could weigh on the peso in the coming week. "We think that it will be in October when Spain will ask (for a bailout), and if this happens the peso and stock markets are going to take it well."

Barclays analysts said the Mexican peso could outperform its emerging market peers in Latin America and Asia because its central bank is unlikely to intervene.

Banco de Mexico research published on Friday said emerging market attempts to stem capital inflows during the last round of Fed easing had a limited effect in the longer term.

Steps pursued by countries such as Brazil, Chile and Colombia, including new taxes on investment, higher bank reserve requirements and tariff reforms, may even make investors see them as a riskier bet, the research paper said.

The Brazilian real decoupled from the rest of the market, rising 0.28 percent to 2.0255 per dollar, as investors tried to influence the currency's closing rate at the end of the month.

Brazilian policymakers have pledged to move aggressively to offset expected capital inflows from the easy monetary conditions in the developed world.

A senior government official recently told Reuters that Brazil will defend the level of 2 reais per dollar "like a wall."

title: UPDATE 2- Chile central bank  may  intervene  in  forex  market, if needed
text:
* Peso weakens 0.51 pct vs U.S. dollar after comments

 * Nominal currency appreciation common in emerging markets 

(Adds comments, details, context)

 By Felipe Iturrieta

 SANTIAGO, Sept 28 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank may intervene in the foreign exchange market to stem the peso's

strength if such a move is justified, bank president Rodrigo Vergara said on Friday.

 "In exceptional periods, the central bank reserves the right to intervene," Vergara told business leaders during an event in Santiago. " What is an exceptional period? An exchange rate that is significantly out of line with regard to its fundamentals for a relatively long period, because transitory things have less importance." 

 The peso dropped 0.51 percent to trade at 473.40 per U.S. dollar following Vergara's comments, and closed 0.76 percent weaker at 474.60 per dollar on Friday. The local currency has firmed nearly 10 percent this year on the back of prices for top export copper and firm local economic data.

 The nominal appreciation of the Chile's currency is a phenomenon common to all emerging markets, Vergara said. 

 South American officials, concerned that stronger domestic currencies will price their exports uncompetitively in the global market and drag on growth, have in the past intervened in the forex market to limit currency gains. 

 The central bank used a dollar-purchasing program last year to damp down the peso after it appreciated to its highest in more than 2-1/2 years at 465.50 per dollar. 

 "The central bank's comments weakened the peso because they leave the door open for a possible intervention. The market isn't just speculating about the possibility of dollar purchases, but also bank deposit requirements," said Rodrigo Sarria, a trader at Celfin Capital in Santiago.

 Tightening bank deposit requirements could slow the pace of credit expansion and curb domestic demand without having to hike interest rates, thus avoiding a further influx of capital that could boost the peso. 

 The peso's real exchange rate, which is an index the bank uses to show how competitive the peso is against a basket of currencies, is at the low end of values coherent with its long-term fundamentals, Vergara said.

Chile's central bank has maintained its key rate at 5 percent since a surprise cut in January, as it weighs solid domestic growth against external woes. 

 The world No.1 copper producer's small, export-dependent economy has so far resisted euro zone debt woes and slowing Chinese demand better than previously expected. 

 Vergara said one of the risks for the local economy was brisk domestic consumption, which adds inflationary pressure in the medium term.

"The reduction of internal risks for the economy happens via a necessary moderation of domestic demand," Vergara said.

 The central bank earlier this month raised its forecast for domestic demand, which has been a pillar of Chile's economy, to 5.6 percent growth this year, from a previous forecast of 5.2 percent.

title: Chile Central Bank  Governor Reiterates  Intervention  Has Costs
text:
While the Chilean peso trades at a one-year high against the dollar and exporters clamor for intervention to weaken the local currency, Rodrigo Vergara, the governor of the Central Bank of Chile, reiterated Thursday that such a move has its costs.

In 2011, the central bankintervened in the market through daily purchases of $50 million for a total of $12 billion--which increased the bank's foreign currency reserves to 15% of the country's gross domestic product.

In a speech posted on the bank's website, Mr. Vergara said no measures such as intervention and capital controls are "cost free."

"A sterilized intervention worsens the balance sheet of the central bank as the interest rate on foreign reserves is lower than the interest rate on domestic debt," he said.

Interventions can increase international reserves during periods where access to international financing is tighter and they can also reduce misalignments, according to the central banker.

"Nonetheless, as it is not simple to define when there is a clear misalignment, there is always the risk of acting too soon, in which case the intervention will be ineffective," Mr. Vergara said in prepared remarks delivered at the International Journal of Central Banking's fourth annual conference.

Regarding the quantitative easing measures central banks in developed economies adopted, Mr. Vergara said while these in principle should be good news for emerging markets as they aim to boost growth, they could have negative effects such as the "significant appreciation of the domestic currencies."

title: Chile Central Bank  Must Be 'Careful' if It  Intervenes  -Ex Chief

Although the Chilean peso has appreciated 10% versus the dollar so far this year, the central bank has remained hands-off while some of its peers in the region are taking steps to weaken their currencies against the dollar.

The agricultural-export community, one of the victims of a strong peso, recently asked the central bank to intervene.

"The central bank has to be very careful with market intervention," said Mr. Corbo on the sidelines of a seminar organized by financial-advisory firm Picton Advisors.

A distortion in the peso's parity against the dollar or the need to accumulate reserves are the two reasons for intervention; otherwise, an intervention would be useless, Mr. Corbo added.

While Chile has a free-float currency policy, the central bank already increased its foreign currency reserves to 15% of gross domestic product with its 2011 intervention.

The central bank can't rule out a peso intervention, but the cost of such a move would be too high, the current governor, Rodrigo Vergara, recently said.

On top of a strong peso, rising energy costs are also hurting agricultural exporters. Chile has some of the highest power-generation costs in the region as the Andean country imports thermal sources such as natural gas, coal and diesel, which represent a combined 62% of the country's installed capacity.

Chile's energy costs are a hurdle for the country's competitiveness and threaten its economic growth, Mr. Corbo said.

Energy costs could continue to rise after the Supreme Court recently halted the $5 billion, 2,100-megawatt Hacienda Castilla power project. The country needs to double its current 15,000-megawatt installed capacity over the next decade to keep up with projected demand and the cancellation puts this increase at risk.

"Energy costs are a problem" and Chile needs to reduce them to maintain growth, said Mr. Corbo.

The central bank recently revised its GDP growth estimation upwards to between 4.75% and 5.25% this year.

title: WRAPUP 1-Fed's QE3 stirs LatAm differences over  currency
text:
* Brazil restarts currency intervention after Fed

 * Speculation that Chile, Colombia could follow

 * Mexico's QE3 enthusiasm stands out from crowd 

 By Krista Hughes and Michael O'Boyle

 MEXICO CITY, Sept 14 (Reuters) - The U.S. Federal Reserve's latest round of stimulus spotlights  a gulf between Mexico and its Latin American neighbors as the region girds itself for a likely revival of the "currency war."

 While Mexico embraced the Fed's decision to start a third round of bond-buying, Brazil vowed to unleash an arsenal of new measures to combat what it fears could be a sharp appreciation in its currency. 

 A stronger real could not come at a worse time for Brazil, which is battling slowing growth with a raft of measures to boost the domestic economy. This contrasts with Mexico, which is growing roughly twice as quickly as its rival and has been fretting about a weak peso pushing up prices. Close links to the United States give it a big stake in stronger U.S. growth.

 "Mexico is clearly one of the few countries in Latin America where you don't have any resistance to peso strength, and you are unlikely to do so, because the central bank prefers a hands-off attitude," said Clyde Wardle, a strategist at HSBC in New York. "That does set Mexico apart."

 Latin American currencies surged to new highs after the Fed's news, with Chile's peso hitting a one-year high against the U.S. dollar and Mexico's rising to a five-month peak on bets that yield-seeking investors will flood to the region, driving asset prices higher.

 During the Fed's second round of bond buying in late 2010 and the first half of 2011, a rush of capital pushed the Brazilian real up 12 percent against the dollar while the Mexican and Chilean pesos both gained 8 percent.

 Economists said a fresh round of currency intervention was in the cards, with Brazil kicking off o n F riday with two central bank interventions in two hours. Speculation is mounting about increased efforts in Chile and Colombia as well.

 South American officials, worried that a rise in their currencies will price their exports out of the market and drag on growth, have a history of intervening to limit currency gains.

 But in Mexico, policymakers face a different dynamic as the peso - one of the most liquid emerging market currencies and often used as a hedge for emerging market risk - has weakened about 30 percent since before the financial crisis.

 Mexican central bank Governor Agustin Carstens told Reuters the Fed's new bond buying program, dubbed QE3, would help the economy, giving no sign policymakers would try to stem the peso's rise. 

 In fact, Carstens said the stronger peso would help limit inflation by making imported goods cheaper - a much-needed break for the Banco de Mexico, which is confronting a spike in inflation to its highest level in more than two years due to fresh food prices. 

 MEXICO AT ODDS

 Mexico's laissez-faire stance will put it in a different class from Latin American counterparts that intervene to cap currency gains, like Brazil, which also fears competition from Asian powerhouse China and its yuan.

 Countries that keep their currencies cheap will face higher prices for imported goods at the same time a flush of cheap money probably drives commodity prices higher, economists said.

 Although price pressures are subdued in Chile, Colombia and Peru - meaning their central banks may not worry too much about the downside of intervention - inflation accelerated to 5.24 percent in Brazil last month.

 "QE3 will end up having two different kinds of effects on inflation," said BNP Paribas economist Nader Nazmi. 

 "In countries that fight against appreciation... the price of commodities will increase. This could lead to higher inflation in countries that do not allow their exchange rate to appreciate."

 Reacting to higher inflation by raising interest rates would make currencies even more expensive, a policy Catch-22 that the region faced during the Fed's previous stimulus, when Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega coined the term "currency war."

 The phrase has been adopted by officials in Colombia, whose peso has been the fourth-biggest gainer worldwide this year, firming 7 percent since January despite back-to-back interest rate cuts. The peso rose 0.4 percent on Friday.  

 "This shows that we should not remain silent in Colombia and that we will have to respond to these kinds of decisions from the United States," Finance Minister Mauricio Cardenas said.

 Chile's Finance Minister Felipe Larrain had said even before the Fed's Thursday announcement that the country was worried about another round of stimulus, and the peso is approaching levels that have sparked intervention in the past. 

 "These levels for the peso are a concern for authorities. Although we don't expect imminent action, such as an outright intervention, we do expect to see in the short-term, over the next 30 days, verbal interventions or announcements that try to contain the currency's appreciation," said Ruben Catalan, senior analyst at Bci in Santiago.

title: DJ Chile Fruit Exporters Anxious Over Peso's Gains; Worry About Industry
text:
--Fruit-export trade group Fedefruta reiterates need for central-bank intervention

--Producers and exporters still not familiar with hedging instruments

--Fedefruta asks for government help while the Chilean peso remains strong 


 
   By Graciela Ibanez 
 

SANTIAGO, Chile--The Chilean peso's 9.2% surge against the U.S. dollar this year is making Chile's fruit producers and exporters anxious as some 70% of their $4 billion annual sales are denominated in dollars.

A stronger local currency--on the back of the country's solid economic growth--is lifting the fruit-production sector's costs, which are largely denominated in pesos, to some 70% to 100% of revenue.

Fresh fruit accounted for 5% of Chile's 2011 exports.

While government officials have cheered Chile's economic performance in times of global uncertainty, the fruit-export trade group Fedefruta isn't happy and has called on the central bank to intervene in the currency market to weaken the peso.

"With a strong peso, no one will want to invest in [agricultural] production," said Fedefruta President Cristian Allendes in an interview Monday.

Last year, the Central Bank of Chileintervened in the currency market after the peso had firmed to a 32-month high at CLP465.40 to the dollar in the first days of January. The bank bought a total of $12 billion at a rate of $50 million a day.

This year, the peso hasn't crossed the CLP470 psychological level--it is currently trading at around CLP474 to the dollar--and central bank Gov. Rodrigo Vergara said last week it would be expensive for the bank to intervene.

Among fruit producers, kiwi and plum producers are the most concerned with the current peso level as their costs are nearly matching their revenue, Mr. Allendes said.

Since the mid-2000s, exporters have had to live with a stronger peso. Currency hedges became more common in the industry, but only large exporters and producers are familiar with them despite efforts from Fedefruta to promote these instruments across the industry.

"It's a fragmented industry where around 80% of fruit producers are small- and medium-size, and they don't know how the hedging system works," said Mr. Allendes.

When the peso weakened to nearly CLP520 to the dollar in late May and early June, producers and exporters took forward contracts for only $200 million, or 5% of the industry's sales, Mr. Allendes said.

Most of the sector's sales are denominated in dollars, but 30% of revenue is in euros, which exporters also convert to dollars. Fedefruta is trying to promote both dollar and euro forward contracts.

Mr. Allendes recently met with other non-mining export trade groups to coordinate a public-opinion campaign. Non-mining exporters want Chileans to become aware of how the strong peso is eating into their competitiveness abroad.

"If investments in production fall, the Chilean regions that depend on agriculture and fish farms would see jobs tumble," he said.

The mining industry, which represents 60% of exports and 15% of gross domestic product, meanwhile, have a natural hedge against the strong peso as the currency usually moves in line with prices of their products, especially copper.

Mr. Allendes also wants to see help from the government while the peso remains strong versus the dollar.

"The government could give us more money to promote our exports abroad, so an increase in sales could partially offset a stronger peso," he said.

The government contributes around $10 million a year to the agriculture-exporting sector for advertising campaigns abroad, and Mr. Allendes would like to see that figure grow to at least $50 million for each of the next three years.

The government could also invest more in infrastructure projects such as roads in the agricultural-intensive regions, he said.

President Sebastian Pinera, meanwhile, earlier this week said exporters will have to learn to cope with the strong peso.

"We will have to live with the exchange rate very similar to what we have now. For some sectors, it is a problem, and they will have to adjust," Mr. Pinera said during a visit to Australia.

title: UPDATE:  Chile Central Bank  Can't Rule Out Peso  Intervention  -Governor
text:
--Conditions not right for peso market intervention

--New intervention could hurt central bank balance sheet

--Legal delays in energy projects could slow growth in coming years

(Adds comments and quotes from central bank governor, starting in fifth paragraph)


 
   By Carolina Pica 
 

SANTIAGO, Chile--The Central Bank of Chile can't rule out intervening in the peso market, although the costs of such a move would outweigh the benefits, bank governor Rodrigo Vergara said Friday.

Following the European Central Bank's bond purchasing announcement earlier this week, the peso on Friday firmed to a 12-month high against the dollar.

Mr. Vergara said the bank could intervene if the peso were out of line with its fundametals, which isn't the case for the Andean currency.

"If the peso were significantly and persistently out of line with its fundamentals, intervention would be used as an exceptional measure," Mr. Vergara said.

"The central bank doesn't give up the possibility of an intervention. We've done it before and we could do it in the future," he said.

As Chile's economy depends heavily on its exports, a strong peso cuts into the competitiveness of its products abroad.

In recent years, the central bankintervened in 2008 and then in 2011. In last year's intervention program, it bought a total $12 billion at a rate of $50 million a day.

Following that intervention, the bank increased its foreign currency reserves to 15% of gross domestic product.

According to Mr. Vergara, further increasing these reserves could bring financial costs and put a crimp in the bank's balance sheet.

"It's important to understand that interventions have financial costs that all Chileans end up paying because the central bank buys dollars and finances these purchases through domestic debt that is more expensive than the returns obtained from the foreign reserves, so we have to be extremely responsible and prudent because these costs are relevant," the central banker said.

He reiterated, as he's done in previous speeches, that a free-floating exchange rate is the best defense mechanism against international volatility.

Regarding the measures the European Central Bank announced this week concerning bond purchases, Mr. Vergara warned markets should remain cautious.

"The [ECB] announcement is a step in the right direction, but one should remain cautious as this isn't the first time we've heard 'this time is for real.' There are many other measures and reforms to be carried out," the central bank governor said.

The central bank doesn't usually comment on local policies so it was unexpected for Mr. Vergara to also comment on recent local court rulings that have held up electricity generation projects.

The delay of several large generation projects will likely increase power costs, which are already among the highest in the region and possibly curb economic growth, Mr. Vergara said.

"These [electricity] problems will manifest themselves a few years from now and they'll have repercussions on productivity and eventually on growth," he said.

SANTIAGO, Sept 7 (Reuters) - Chilean Central Bank President Rodrigo Vergara said on Friday that existing "worry" over the strong Chilean peso did not yet warrant intervention in the foreign exchange market.

title: Fed Easing Could Boost Some  Currencies , but Not All
text:
Last time the Federal Reserve bought bonds, the dollar dropped between 5% and 10% against most of the world's currencies.

If the Fed goes ahead with more easing later this year, the greenback's decline is likely to be more selective, investors and analysts say.

On Friday, Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke said the central bank would provide additional support for the economy "as needed," in a speech that appeared to lay out the case for a third round of bond buying known as quantitative easing.

As those measures would involve printing more dollars and pushing down yields on U.S. debt, investors are looking at other currencies to hold.

Their options are more limited than they were two years ago, the last time the Fed pursued easing. Central banks from Brazil to Switzerland have clamped down on trading in their currencies by intervening in the market or cutting interest rates, all in a bid to curb volatility and shield exporters.

As a result, investors have increasingly turned to currencies like the Chilean peso, Mexican peso and South Korean won, where central banks have lately adopted a lighter touch.

"It's been a global race to the bottom between [actions by] a lot of central banks, and it doesn't look like it's going to ease off," said Bob Gelfond, chief executive officer of New York-based hedge fund MQS Asset Management, which holds G10 currency positions.

Analysts say the Chilean and Mexican pesos should appreciate on another round of Fed easing, given expectations that those central banks will hold rates steady in the coming months. The Chilean and Mexican pesos have outperformed other Latin American currencies over the last three months, appreciating over 7% against the dollar since June 1.

By contrast, the Brazilian real has weakened 0.5% in the same period and the Colombian peso is nearly unchanged. Brazil's central bank has cut interest rates nine times over the past year, including another cut Wednesday, and has intervened directly in the foreign-exchange market to devalue the real and help local exporters.

"If it weren't for bank intervention, the Brazilian real could rally another 5% or 6%, but with the central bank sitting there," investors are more reluctant to buy the real, said Michael Mata, portfolio manager of the $700 million ING Global Bond Fund. Mr. Mata said he plans to buy the Mexican peso if the Fed launches another round of easing.

Another winner is the South Korean won, which was the top Asian currency gainer in the past three months amid looming intervention risk in Indonesia, Japan and India. After a surprise rate cut in July, South Korea's central bank held rates steady in early August.

However, even the more hands-off central banks have a breaking point. A Norwegian central bank official warned on Thursday that policy makers won't tolerate continued strength in the krone, which rose to a 16-week high against the dollar this week.

Chile's central bankintervened last year, launching daily dollar purchases to stem its currency's strength. It could do so again if the peso strengthens to 470 to the dollar, analysts say. Friday, the peso was at 480.10 versus the dollar.

But the market still sees a greater risk of the Fed easing than of some other central banks becoming more aggressive. For example, some of the Australian dollar's gains were eroded recently by signals from policy makers that the strong currency is weighing on the economy. But the Aussie is still up 6.3% against the U.S. dollar since June 1, and the Reserve Bank of Australia looks unlikely to cut interest rates soon.

--Erin McCarthy contributed to this article.

title: Chile peso on rise, could break 470/dlr with US stimulus
text:
SANTIAGO, Aug 29 (Reuters) - Chile's peso will probably continue to appreciate in line with the Andean nation's strong economic fundamentals during the rest of the year and may even break technical resistance at the 470-per-dollar level if the United States unleashes a new round of monetary stimulus, analysts said.

The peso has gained around 8 percent versus the dollar since the start of the year to trade near 480 per dollar, a level Finance Minister Felipe Larrain said has the government's attention.

Analysts see the peso trading in a range of 475 to 485 per dollar over the coming weeks, short of levels which have triggered central bankintervention in the past, as the market awaits clear signs of extra stimulus in the United States and Europe.

Markets are awaiting a speech by U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Ben Bernanke in Jackson Hole, Wyoming on Friday for hints on a third round of stimulus, which likely would translate into dollar inflows to emerging economies, and push up local currencies.

"There's a strong psychological level at 473-470 (pesos per dollar) because there's more of a chance the Chilean central bank will intervene," said Sergio Tricio, head of research at Forex Chile. "But if quantitative measures in the United States are used, the peso could break that level," he said on Tuesday.

The central bank used a dollar-purchasing program last year, which lasted through December, to beat back the peso after it appreciated to its highest level in more than 2-1/2 years at 465.50 per dollar.

Earlier this month, Chile's central bank held its key interest rate steady at 5.0 percent for a seventh straight month, saying energy and food prices could pick up in coming months, and mentioned the appreciation in the peso in what was viewed as a signal to the market.

"It's not just the key interest rate's level, but it's the neutral stance regarding rates that the central bank has maintained up until now that's helped support the peso," Jorge Selaive, chief economist at bank BCI in Santiago said on Wednesday.

The economy of Chile, the world's largest copper producer grew 5.5 percent in the second quarter, year-on-year, bolstered by mining, retail, forestry, agriculture and brisk domestic demand.

The peso has firmed as an attractive interest rate differential compared with the developed world and high levels of foreign investment have kept dollars flowing into Chile.

Analysts say the currency has some room to appreciate before any concrete intervention measures. Conversely, if expectations for stimulus are dashed and risk aversion returns, the peso could abruptly weaken to 500 per dollar.

"It's likely we'd see some action on the part of the central bank or government if the peso breached 470 (per dollar). It's a complicated level when we have falling prices for our exports and sliding export volumes ... the sector's competitiveness is already facing a very complicated scenario," BCI's Selaive said.

Chilean exporters have been asking the central bank to take action to stem the peso's strength to help make prices for their products more competitive.

The peso's current strength is attuned to Chile's economic reality, the former president of the central bank, Jose De Gregorio, told Reuters last week.

"The peso is within a range that is consistent with Chile's economic fundamentals ... we said it when we intervened in 2011. The tension of the currency will last for a very simple reason: Chile is a strong economy and has extremely favorable conditions," De Gregorio said.

In 2008, the monetary authority intervened after the peso firmed to 431 per dollar.

By Rachel Uranga

MEXICO CITY, Aug 21 (Reuters) - Brazil's real slipped on Tuesday after the central bank moved to curb its rise against the dollar, while Chile's peso firmed on hopes the European Central Bank will soon begin buying Spanish and Italian bonds.

Brazil's central bank, which had not waded into the market for several weeks, sold $350.2 million of reverse currency swap contracts, which mimic the purchase of dollars in futures markets.

The central bank was seen again signaling to markets that it wanted to keep the real from reaching a point where it would hurt local industries competing against cheaper imports.

"The market is being told 'don't move,'" said Pedro Tuesta, a Latin American currency strategist with Washington-based 4Cast. "The central bank has a lot of money. You don't defy a $350 billion central bank and one that is very willing to use its power," he said referring to the bank's reserves.

The real weakened 0.05 percent to 2.0166 per dollar. The real has been mostly trading between 2 per dollar and 2.05 per dollar since the end of June on the threat of central bank intervention.

In addition to acting to protect local exporters, Brazil's policymakers have acted to strengthen the currency if it weakens so much that it could raise import prices and stoke inflation.

The move to weaken the real comes after a spate of upbeat data showing that Brazil's economic doldrums may be hitting bottom. Last week the country reported the economy in June grew at its fastest pace in 15 months and retail sales clocked a surprising leap.

STIMULUS EXPECTATIONS WEIGH

Chile's peso gained 0.44 percent to 482.6000 as the price of copper, its top export, rose sharply on hopes for stimulus to the global economy from major central banks.

Copper for delivery in three months gained 1.72 percent in London, buoyed by both the outlook for Europe and expectations the United States and China may also provide more stimulus.

European central bankers on Monday sought to quash speculation that it will buy bonds of Spain and Italy to push down borrowing costs, but investors and traders contined to see hopes that the debt crisis is closer to resolution.

In Mexico, the optimism had a different affect on the peso with some traders selling off Latin America's most liquid currency to buy up European assets, Tuesta added.

title: Chile  peso surges on economy, but space before  intervention
text:
SANTIAGO, Aug 10 (Reuters) - Chile's peso, currently trading near 11-month highs, is likely to keep appreciating on the back of strong economic growth, but has room to gain another 3 percent against the dollar before any eventual central bankintervention, traders and analysts say.

The small, export-dependent economy of world No.1 copper producer Chile is bracing for fallout from the euro zone crisis and a slowdown in global demand, especially from top trade partner and metals consumer China.

But it expanded 5.5 percent during the first half of the year, one of the world's fastest rates, and this growth combined with interest rates held steady at 5 percent in recent months has lured foreign capital, in turn boosting the local peso.

"There are no external factors which justify such a strong increase in the peso. So the only explanation can be the local economy, which makes the country attractive to foreign capital," said Sergio Tricio, head of research at the Forex Chile brokerage.

The currency has appreciated 9.37 percent against the dollar year-to-date. It grazed a September 2011 peak at 474.80/dlr on Thursday before easing slightly, though traders and analysts are betting the central bank would likely only step in around the 460 level.

The central bankintervened last year when the peso rose to 465.50 per dollar, and made its move in 2008 when the currency rose to 430 per dollar.

But the bank says it has no intervention level trigger and focuses on whether the real exchange rate, which shows how competitive the peso is against a basket of currencies, is in line with fundamentals.

"With the calculations that we have now done, a real exchange rate that is out of balance would be equivalent to 460 pesos. I don't think anything would happen before that level," said Matias Madrid, chief economist at Banco Penta in Santiago.

"Chile is not a safe-haven, but the good performance of the economy, a copper price which hasn't fallen as much (as during the 2008 global crisis), as well as the interest rate differential, given the rate is no longer seen falling, make it attractive," he added.

Central Bank President Rodrigo Vergara on Tuesday said he expected trade in the peso to remain volatile in coming months, citing prices for main export copper and international financial turmoil.

But he added that exchange rate flexibility remained the best tool to face volatile external conditions, and many in the market think the bank would opt for verbal intervention before taking any measures such as dollar purchases.

"It doesn't mean we flatly rule out the possibility of intervening when we consider the exchange rate to be out of alignment with fundamentals," he told a business forum on Tuesday. "We intervened significantly in both 2008 and in 2011."

Forex Chile's Tricio thinks the central bank could mention the peso in next week's interest rates decision statement, if the currency appreciates to the 470 level, as a signal to markets that the bank can always intervene to weaken the currency if necessary.

Foreign capital inflows boost the supply of dollars available in the country, which are then cashed into pesos, boosting the local currency. But a stronger currency makes exports less competitive.

Foreign investors who bought dollar forwards from local banks, are allowing the contracts to expire, betting the peso will continue to appreciate, meaning short-term capital is remaining in the country.

Once those contracts expire, the local banks who covered the operations by buying dollars locally sell them, which injects U.S. currency into the local market, boosting the peso.

Foreign bets against the peso in the futures market have fallen to $7.645 billion, down from a record near $10 billion three months ago, according to central bank data through Aug. 8.

title: UPDATE:  Chile Central Bank  Head: No Peso  Intervention  Planned
text:
--Central Bank likely won't intervene in currency market despite peso strength

--Letting the peso float freely allows the currency to absorb shocks and react quickly

(Adds comments from Vergara, background, in the fifth through ninth paragraphs.)

SANTIAGO, Chile (Dow Jones)--Despite the Chilean peso trading 7% stronger against the dollar since the year began, the central bank doesn't have any plans to intervene in the peso market, bank Governor Rodrigo Vergara said Thursday.

In early 2011, when the peso was trading at three-year highs against the dollar, the bank launched a $12 billion intervention program.

"[Market] intervention is only for extraordinary situations and it's not in our plans for now," he told reporters at a press conference.

However, he noted that a central bank can never rule out such a move if needed, but that the costs of intervening for a free-floating currency are very high.

Vergara said the peso's exchange rate, when expressed in real terms, is in line with its long-term fundamentals.

When the bank intervened in 2011, it said the peso's real exchange rate had deviated from its fundamentals.

During a presentation to the Icare local business forum, Vergara said a free-floating currency, such as Chile's peso, is preferable to a pegged currency as it absorbs both internal and external shocks.

"It also allows for quicker [economic] adjustments when conditions rapidly change," Vergara said.

In the 1980s and 1990s, the Chilean peso was first fixed to the dollar and then moved in a narrow trading band, set by the central bank. In 1999, the central bank began to let the currency float freely.

* Chile peso gains 1.06 percent, copper up 1 percent

By Caroline Stauffer

SAO PAULO, April 2 (Reuters) - The Mexican and Chilean pesos strengthened on Monday after manufacturing data from the world's two largest economies beat forecasts, though Brazil's real weakened on "the specter of intervention."

Data showed new factory orders in China rose to an 11-month high in March while growth in U.S. manufacturing surpassed economists' expectations in February.

China and the United States are Latin America's top trade partners. The price of metals such as copper, exported by many Latin American countries, rose after the manufacturing data pointed to sustained demand from the world's economic giants.

"The data showed growth is generally holding up reasonably well, commodities prices are making significant gains," said Nick Chamie, head of emerging markets research at RBC Securities in Toronto.

Chile's peso gained the most out of the region's currencies, ending 1.06 percent stronger to bid 483.1 per U.S. dollar. That was its strongest close in two weeks.

Copper for delivery in three months rose 1 percent.

Chile gets more than half of its export earnings from the red metal, a key component in electrical and electronic equipment.

"This was a completely favorable scenario for the peso," said one trader in Santiago.

Mexico's currency, which had weakened for the five previous sessions, gained 0.7 percent to 12.7281 per dollar.

The Mexican peso is particularly sensitive to U.S. manufacturing data as many Mexicans work in U.S. factories and the United States buys nearly 80 percent of Mexico's exports by value.

REAL BUCKS TREND

Brazil's real, however, weakened 0.31 percent to close bidding 1.8277 per dollar. Government measures to weaken the currency and data showing the pace of manufacturing in Brazil had slowed for a third straight month weighed.

"The ongoing specter of intervention on the part of the government is the key reason," said RBC's Chamie.

"We also had a weaker-than-expected PMI," he said, referring to Markit's Brazil Manufacturing Purchasing Manager's Index.

The index edged down to 51.1 last month from 51.4 in February.

Brazil's central bank often purchases dollars in the spot market on days the currency is strengthening as policymakers aim to weaken the real in an effort to make Brazil's manufacturing exports more competitive.

The government has also raised its financial transactions or "IOF" tax and on March 12 extended its scope to foreign debt maturing in up to five years. Some traders have sold the real fearing the government could take additional measures like extending the tax to all financial transactions.

Investors are also down on the real because Brazil's central bank is expected to lower interest rates in coming months. That would curb potential returns in Brazil as economic growth slows.

"Even if they aren't introducing new currency measures, these are all factors that will restrain the real," said Nicholas Bennenbroek, head of currency strategy at Wells Fargo in New York.

"Chile has had one of the stronger currencies because inflation is favorable and the central bank is not likely to cut rates," he added.

The real strengthened 2.17 percent in the first quarter of 2012, reaching just a third of the Chilean peso's gains.

(Additional reporting by Froilan Romero in Santiago)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-LatAm  currencies  fall as China manufacturing slows
text:
* Brazil real falls to lowest since Jan. 9; intervention seen

* Chile peso sheds 0.74 pct; top export copper at two-week low

* Mexico peso off 0.69 pct, real ends down 0.18 pct

By Caroline Stauffer

RIO DE JANEIRO, March 22 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies weakened on Thursday as faltering factory activity in China cast doubt on the Asian giant's appetite for the region's commodities and surprisingly weak European data added to global growth fears.

China's industrial activity fell for the fifth straight month in March, a purchasing managers index showed.

In Europe, German and French manufacturing suffered sharp declines in March that even the most pessimistic economists had failed to predict, according to PMI data..

"When there's negative news out of China, Europe or the United States you have this risk-off trade," said Kathryn Rooney Vera, an emerging markets analyst at Bulltick Capital Markets.

"Bad news out of China pushes Latin American currencies weaker because China is a huge commodity consumer - that's the main driver here," she said.

Chile's peso shed 0.74 percent to bid 487.2 per dollar. It was the peso's weakest close in two weeks and its biggest single-day drop since March 6.

Copper prices fell to a two-week low on expectations of lower demand from China, the world's biggest metals consumer, and Europe. Chile is the world's top copper exporter, and its mines produce 30 percent of the world's copper supply.

Brazil's real weakened for a fourth day, losing 0.18 percent to bid 1.8207 per dollar. Declining industry performance in China, Brazil's top trading partner, led to the real's weakest close since Jan. 9.

Still, Finance Minister Guido Mantega said on Thursday the central bank would continue intervening to keep the real from gaining ground as it tries to maintain the competitiveness of Brazil's already expensive exports and spur economic growth. .

The central bank bought dollars on Feb. 6 for the first time since September of last year. The real has weakened 5.5 percent since it waded back into the market.

"They are intervening at 1.8 to stop the real's momentum, but I have a hard time, barring a significant global situation that would impact all of Latin America, seeing it going above 1.9," said Eduardo Suarez, currency strategist at Scotia Capital.

Though analysts doubt the interventions will drastically weaken the real, the efforts have led some to recommend the region's other currencies.

"Mantega and (President Dilma) Rousseff have made no bones about their intention to intervene, and for that reason we aren't extremely bullish on the real. ... The Finance Ministry should not be dictating monetary policy, but that's what you see going on here," said Bulltick's Rooney Vera, who favors the Mexican peso.

PESO RESPECTS MOVING AVERAGE

Latin American currencies mostly weakened despite signs of recovery in the United States, the world's largest economy. New U.S. claims for unemployment benefits dropped to a four-year low last week, a government report said.

Mexico, which sends nearly 80 percent of its exports to the United States, saw its currency weaken 0.69 percent, to 12.7948 on risk aversion from the Chinese and European data.

But traders said the peso isn't likely to change its appreciation tendency because the Latin America's only fully convertible currency stayed below an important technical signal.

"I think the key resistance is the 200-day moving average, which is 12.935," said Alfredo Puig, a trader at Vector brokerage in Monterrey. "There's been resistance at 12.85, and I think there will be at 12.90 as well."

Colombia's peso strengthened 0.08 percent to 1,759.7 after the country posted 6.1 percent growth in the last quarter of 2011 versus the year-earlier period. Foreign investment and expanding consumer credit helped shield Colombia from global economic troubles.

title: Chile  cenbank has no trigger for  FX intervention
text:
PUNTA DEL ESTE, Uruguay, March 1 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank does not have a set level that triggers intervention in the foreign exchange market, central bank board member Enrique Marshall said on Thursday.

The Chilean peso has firmed by 7.85 percent since the start of the year, putting increasing pressure on the central bank to resume its dollar purchases on the market to stem the local currency's appreciation, which hurts exporters.

Many Latin American currencies have strengthened as regional economic growth attracts investors seeking higher returns than they can get in more developed markets. That has prompted currency interventions by central banks in Brazil, Colombia and Peru.

"We don't have any reference level for intervening or not. We have to evaluate and have to see if the circumstances justify it and that's what we've done in the past," Marshall told reporters on the sidelines of a seminar on macroprudential policies organized by the International Monetary Fund and Uruguay's central bank.

He said the bank's policy was to intervene in "special or extraordinary" circumstances.

The peso is currently bidding at 481.50 per dollar. When the central bank intervened last year, it was trading at 465.50 and the bank made its move in 2008 when it reached around 430 pesos per dollar.

Commenting on the wider economy, Marshall said credit growth of about 12 percent was a "reasonable" level and had a healthy correlation to the rate of economic growth.

"In Chile what we are observing is an expansion of credit but it is still within a limited range, therefore there is no particular concern about that growth," he said.

Chile's central bank board said holding its key interest rate steady at 5.0 percent in February was coherent and pointed to a gradual and paused process of rate moves, minutes of the bank's rate-setting meeting showed.

(Reporting by Hilary Burke and Malena Castaldi; Editing by Andrew Hay)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  FX  mixed; Brazil real wilts on cenbank threat
text:
* Traders bet on further Brazil intervention measures

 * Chile's peso ends at 5-month high on Greece deal

 * Brazil's real slips 0.2 pct, Mexico's peso up 0.32 pct 

(Recasts throughout; adds closing prices)

 By Michael O'Boyle

 MEXICO CITY, Feb 9 (Reuters) - Brazil's real slipped on Thursday as traders poised for another round of central bankintervention, while Chile's peso firmed to a five-month high, driven by optimism that Greece will get its next bailout deal.

 Brazil's central bank threw its weight into the spot market on Monday for the first time since September in a bid to limit gains in the real, which has surged so far this year and is again threatening the competitiveness of local exporters.

 The real  dipped 0.2 percent to 1.7207 per U.S. dollar, pulling away from the key 1.70-level that many think the central bank and government may try to defend with more interevention or capital controls.

 While the central bank has not bought dollars since Monday, Joao Medeiros, head of trading at Brazilian brokerage Pioneer, said traders moved to the sidelines on expectations that policy makers could enter the market around the 1.7120 level.

 "That's it for free trading," Medeiros said.

 Still, analysts think Brazil will be unable to do much more than slow the real's advance due to a tide of dollar flows washing into Latin America's top economy. Intervention efforts have been repeatedly deployed in recent years around the region.

 Flows are being driven by a spate of corporate dollar bond sales, including Brazil's biggest ever by Petrobras, strong foreign investment in infrastructure projects, and a renewal of global interest in Brazil's stock market.

 "There is a lot of flow from corporates, which will come anyway. In a way there's too many dollars in the market right now," said Pedro Tuesta, Latin America analyst with 4Cast Inc in Washington.

 The real could get a bigger shock if the government revives a tax on foreign investment in the stock market, which was removed last year after global markets swooned.

 But improving economic data from the United States and China, Latin America's top trading partners, as well as expectations that central banks in Europe and the United States will keep interest rates low for years to come, has renewed appetite for riskier assets across the board.

 Latin American currencies were among the top emerging market assets during the first five weeks of 2012, when they posted their biggest gains since a rebound from the credit crisis in early 2009. 

 Worries about Greece and intervention efforts cooled the advance this week, but demand for riskier assets was lifted on Thursday after Greek leaders clinched an austerity deal on reforms needed to secure a second international bailout and avoid a disorderly default. 

 Chile's peso bid 0.55 percent stronger to end at 475.00 per dollar, a five-month high.

 Following the peso's recent sharp gains, traders say if the currency strengthens beyond 470 per dollar, Chile's central bank could start voicing concern about the exchange rate. But dollar purchases are seen as unlikely unless the peso breaches at least the 460 barrier and possibly even lower.

 Mexico's peso firmed 0.32 percent to 12.6750 per dollar. Central bank authorities are likely welcoming recent currency gains that could help cool inflation pressures.

 Mexico's annual inflation rate pierced the central bank's 4 percent ceiling for the first time in over a year in January.

 Investors sought protection in case consumer prices keep rising by piling into Mexican inflation-linked bonds, or Udibonos, pushing prices upward and yields lower.

 The yield on the December 2014 Udibono bid down almost 9 basis points to 1.28 percent. Strategists at Banorte project its yield could fall to a key support level at 1.20 percent and may break even lower to 1.07 percent. 

(Additional reporting by Helio Barboza in Sao Paulo and Rachel Uranga in Mexico City; Editing by Gary Crosse)

title: Fitch Affirms Chile at 'A-'; Outlook Stable
text:
Release date - 19072023

Fitch Ratings has affirmed Chile's Long-Term (LT) Foreign-Currency (FC) and Local-Currency Issuer Default Ratings (IDRs) at 'A-' with a Stable Outlook.

A full list of rating actions is at the end of this rating action commentary.

Key Rating Drivers

Credit Strengths and Weaknesses: Chile's ratings are supported by a relatively strong sovereign balance sheet, with government debt/GDP well below peers, solid governance indicators and a track record of credible macroeconomic policies centered on an inflation-targeting regime and flexible exchange rate. These strengths are balanced by per capita income that Fitch projects will remain low relative to peers, high commodity dependence and weak external leverage and liquidity metrics.

Constitutional Reform Uncertain: Chile is preparing a second draft of a new constitution to be put to a vote this December following an unsuccessful first attempt in 2022. An expert commission finished a pre-draft in May that is more moderate and in line with the current charter than the first proposal. It includes principles that must be respected in the final text (e.g. property rights, Congress current structure, and BCCh independence) and some social rights subject to availability of resources. In Fitch's view, the new draft would not impair Chile's economic model or sustainability of public finances.

The final text will be prepared by the Constituent Council elected on May 7. The council is dominated by the political right, who won the two-thirds majority needed to control the council and make amendments to the pre-draft unopposed. Amid this backdrop, there could be risk that the final draft veers farther to the right, raising the chances of a rejection in the referendum. Early polls show that over half of Chileans would vote 'no' to the current draft.

Limited Reform Agenda Progress: President Gabriel Boric has had limited success on his tax reform agenda amid low popularity and political gridlock. While his government has pushed through some legislation in Congress (e.g. mining royalty bill), the rejection of his flagship tax reform (2.7% of GDP) in March was a major setback. The government will propose a new tax bill. Given the opposition's stance against new taxation, it is likely to focus on administrative measures and incentives for private investment. If passed, it is unclear how much revenue it could ultimately generate and whether it could fully fund President Boric's campaign promises for higher social spending. The government estimates that the mining royalty bill approved in May will yield 0.5% of GDP annually.

The government presented a pension reform bill in late 2022, which has not made much progress in Congress. The Boric administration's challenges in advancing his agenda and in raising taxes to address spending pressures could result in renewed social discontent and/or fiscal slippage.

Weaker Fiscal Balances: In line with the Ministry of Finance (MOF), we forecast the general government (GG) balance to return to a deficit this year. However, we expect a larger deterioration, with the deficit at 2.7% of GDP compared with the MOF's 1.9%. While we forecast deficits to narrow over the forecast period through 2025, we expect them to remain above 2.0% of GDP. In 2023, tax receipts should continue adjusting to softer economic activity and falling copper revenues, though these will be partially offset by higher tax intake tied to lithium. Meanwhile expenses are rising due to higher pension benefits and a larger interest burden. The outlook faces downside risks as a stronger-than-expected El Nino could lead to additional spending.

Debt Prospect Deterioration: Over the medium term, we expect GG debt to GDP to continue rising given the level of budget deficits and sizable below the line items, i.e. capitalization of state-owned enterprises, student loan purchases, recognition bonds and replenishing sovereign funds. Fitch projects GG debt/GDP to rise to 39.7% of GDP at end-2023 from 38.0% in 2022 and to follow an upward path through the forecast period to 42.5% in 2025. This still compares favorably with the 'A' median of 50.6%, but the percentage of interest/revenues has surpassed the current 'A' median (3.6% versus 2.7%).

Softer Post-Pandemic Growth: We expect GDP growth to decelerate to 0% in 2023 before recovering to 2.4% in 2024, as activity rebalances due to declining private consumption and investment (likely also impacted by political uncertainty) amid a restrictive monetary policy stance. Activity should be supported by government consumption as counter-cyclical fiscal policy is implemented to contain a bigger economic correction. Net exports should also support GDP as Chile benefits from higher global demand for essential metals needed for the energy transition, offsetting a weaker than expected impact from reopening in China.

In the medium term, we see growth returning to the pre-pandemic trend of 2.0% (2015-2019), supported by copper production as new projects coming online offset near-term operational challenges and old project delays.

Monetary Policy to Ease: Chile's central bank, the BCCh, has held the monetary policy rate at 11.25% since October 2022, which, coupled with lower fuel and food prices, a softer labor market, and a strengthening peso, has helped to lower inflation. With headline inflation falling to 7.6% in June from 12.8% in October and inflation expectations at the 12- and 24- month horizons closer to the 3% target midpoint, the BCCh indicated that the start of an easing cycle is near in its previous monetary policy meeting in June. We expect the BCCh to cut slowly as core inflation has fallen at a slower rate than headline and remained well above the target midpoint at 9.1% in June.

Moderating External Vulnerabilities: We expect the current account deficit to narrow substantially to 3.5% of GDP in 2023 from 9.0% in 2022 driven by an improvement in the trade balance as exports rise, buoyed by China's reopening despite fall in copper prices, and imports fall amid lower oil prices and household spending.

The BCCh plans to boost FX reserves by USD10 billion over June 2023 to June 2024 amid a weaker external liquidity position due to last year's USD25 billion FX intervention program. Chile's access to the IMF's Flexible Credit Line amounting to USD18.5 billion offers additional liquidity support.

ESG - Governance: Chile has an ESG Relevance Score (RS) of '5' for both Political Stability and Rights and '5' [+] for the Rule of Law, Institutional and Regulatory Quality and Control of Corruption. Theses scores reflect the high weight that the World Bank Governance Indicators (WBGI) have in our proprietary Sovereign Rating Model (SRM). Chile has a high WBGI ranking at 73.5, reflecting its long track record of stable and peaceful political transitions, well established rights for participation in the political process, strong institutional capacity, effective rule of law and a low level of corruption.

RATING SENSITIVITIES

Factors that Could, Individually or Collectively, Lead to Negative Rating Action/Downgrade

Public Finances: Markedly higher government debt/GDP and/or depletion of sovereign assets, for example reflecting persistent large fiscal deficits driven by strong social spending pressures;

External Finances: Renewed sharp deterioration in external finances and liquidity, for example due to a copper price shock.

Factors that Could, Individually or Collectively, Lead to Positive Rating Action/Upgrade

Public Finances: A declining trajectory of government debt/GDP and/or a rebuilding of fiscal buffers, for example reflecting fiscal consolidation;

Macroeconomic: Improvement in medium-term economic growth prospects that helps raise GDP per capita, ease social tensions and improve fiscal dynamics.

Sovereign Rating Model (SRM) and Qualitative Overlay (QO)

Fitch's proprietary SRM assigns Chile a score equivalent to a rating of 'BBB+' on the LT FC IDR scale.

Fitch's sovereign rating committee adjusted the output from the SRM to arrive at the final LT FC IDR by applying its qualitative overlay (QO) relative to the SRM output, as follows:

Macro: +1 notch added to offset the deterioration of inflation and GDP growth volatility variables in the SRM due to the current position in the economic cycle, which Fitch expects will be temporary, and would otherwise add excess volatility to the rating.

Fitch's SRM is the agency's proprietary multiple regression rating model that employs 18 variables based on three-year centered averages, including one year of forecasts, to produce a score equivalent to a LT FC IDR. Fitch's QO is a forward-looking qualitative framework designed to allow for adjustment to the SRM output to assign the final rating, reflecting factors within our criteria that are not fully quantifiable and/or not fully reflected in the SRM.

Best/Worst Case Rating Scenario

International scale credit ratings of Sovereigns, Public Finance and Infrastructure issuers have a best-case rating upgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a positive direction) of three notches over a three-year rating horizon; and a worst-case rating downgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a negative direction) of three notches over three years. The complete span of best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings for all rating categories ranges from 'AAA' to 'D'. Best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings are based on historical performance. For more information about the methodology used to determine sector-specific best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings, visit https://www.fitchratings.com/site/re/10111579.

REFERENCES FOR SUBSTANTIALLY MATERIAL SOURCE CITED AS KEY DRIVER OF RATING

The principal sources of information used in the analysis are described in the Applicable Criteria.

ESG Considerations

Chile has an ESG Relevance Score of '5' for Political Stability and Rights as WBGIs have the highest weight in Fitch's SRM and are therefore highly relevant to the rating and a key rating driver with a high weight. As Chile has a percentile rank below 50 for the respective Governance Indicator, this has a negative impact on the credit profile.

Chile has an ESG Relevance Score of '5' [+] for Rule of Law, Institutional & Regulatory Quality and Control of Corruption as WBGIs have the highest weight in Fitch's SRM and are therefore highly relevant to the rating and are a key rating driver with a high weight. As Chile has a percentile rank above 50 for the respective Governance Indicators, this has a positive impact on the credit profile.

Chile has an ESG Relevance Score of '4' [+] for Human Rights and Political Freedoms as the Voice and Accountability pillar of the WBGIs is relevant to the rating and a rating driver. As Chile has a percentile rank above 50 for the respective Governance Indicator, this has a positive impact on the credit profile.

Chile has an ESG Relevance Score of '4' [+] for Creditor Rights as willingness to service and repay debt is relevant to the rating and is a rating driver for Chile, as for all sovereigns. As Chile has track record of 20+ years without a restructuring of public debt and captured in our SRM variable, this has a positive impact on the credit profile.
