title: B. Central: Current account recorded a deficit equivalent to 9% of GDP in 2022
text:
During the year 2022, the current account registered a deficit of US$27,102 million, equivalent to 9% of the gross domestic product (GDP), informed the Central Bank this Monday through the document Balance of Payments, International Investment Position and External Debt corresponding to the mentioned fiscal year.

The result was explained by the income from foreign investment in Chile and the deficit of the services trade balance; meanwhile, the goods trade balance was positive.

The financial account recorded net capital inflows of US$25,387 million, determined by the decrease in reserves of the Central Bank of Chile (BCCh), as part of the foreign exchange intervention program, and by direct and portfolio foreign investment in Chile.

At the end of the year, the net international investment position (IIP) increased its debit balance with respect to 2021, to US$55,435 million (18.1% of GDP, in annual terms). The result was due to the indebtedness of the financial account and the decline in the valuation of assets.

The external debt, as compared to the end of 2021, decreased to US$233,325 million (76.4% of GDP), due to the fall in the value of government and corporate bonds. Meanwhile, the residual short-term external debt stood at US$68,234 million, mainly due to payments by non-financial companies.

Goods trade balance

The balance of trade in goods recorded a surplus of US$3,807 million in the period, following the increase in exports and imports.

Shipments of goods amounted to US$98,548 million, representing an increase of 4.0% over the previous year, explained by a 5.5% increase in prices and a 1.5% drop in volume terms. The result was driven by shipments of industrial products, while mining and forestry and livestock exports declined.

Mining exports fell by 2.9% to US$56,489 million. The result was explained by lower copper prices and, to a lesser extent, lower volumes. This effect was partly offset by lithium carbonate exports, which rose sharply, in line with international prices.

Shipments of agricultural, forestry and extractive fishing products fell by 1.6%, totaling US$6,643 million. The result reflected lower exports of fruit, mainly blueberries and apples; this effect was partially offset by higher shipments of cherries.

Industrial shipments grew by 18.6% to US$35,417 million. The boost came mainly from the chemical industry, where lithium-derived products stood out, and from the food industry, led by salmon shipments.

Imports of goods totaled US$94,741 (FOB) and US$104,530 million (CIF).

Compared to the same period of the previous year, and considering the results in CIF terms, imports registered an increase of 13.1%, reflecting a 14.9% increase in prices, while in terms of volume, they fell by 1.5%. The increase in intermediate goods predominated in the result; to a lesser extent, imports of consumer and capital goods also contributed.

Imports of intermediate goods grew 22.1%, totaling US$56,268 million. The result was led by imports of energy goods, where diesel was the most important. The rest of the intermediate goods also grew, driven mainly by chemical products.

Imports of consumer goods increased by 3.2% to US$28,505 million. The impulse came from imports of non-durable consumer goods, especially clothing and gasoline. Meanwhile, there was a generalized fall in imports of durable goods, with the exception of automobiles, which increased.

Imports of capital goods registered a level of US$19,757 million, which represented an increase of 5.6%, led by increased purchases of buses, trucks and cargo vehicles.

Services trade balance

The services balance recorded a deficit of US$14,824 million. Exports totaled US$8,529 million and imports US$23,353 million, after growing 42.8% and 27.7%, respectively.

Both exports and imports were driven by an increase in all categories: Transportation, Travel and Other services.

In the case of exports, the result was led by air transport services, mainly for passengers. There was also an increase in air operating leasing services and business, professional and technical services.

Imports were led by maritime freight services, in line with the high level of international prices in this market. Imports of financial services and tourism services also increased.

Income

Net income presented a negative balance of US$16,520 million, determined by the income accrued from foreign direct investment in Chile.

On the other hand, income from Chilean investments abroad presented an increase, in line with the performance of investments associated with the maritime transport, energy and mining sectors.

Transfers

Net transfers recorded a surplus of US$434 million. The recovery of the balance with respect to the previous year is explained by the normalization of personal remittances abroad, after they increased in line with the partial withdrawals of pension funds and fiscal aid.

title: Bloomberg warns that "the last traces of Chile's reputation as the most stable country in Latin America are being erased".
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile - The instability experienced during the last few months in Chilean assets "are erasing the last traces of the country's reputation as the most stable in Latin America," warned Bloomberg.

In its analysis, the agency indicated that the volatility of the Chilean peso is the highest in the world after the Russian currency, while local swap rates have oscillated at an almost unprecedented pace. That unpredictability has pushed many investors to the sidelines, with the nation's sovereign dollar debt now trading at levels similar to the Philippines, rated two notches below Chile.

Chile's fall from grace has been a long time coming. It began even before the social outbreak three years ago that paralyzed much of the country and shocked investors dazzled by a sense of security from three decades of steady growth and low inflation. Now, there seems to be no remedy for the decline. Even a new constitution that many had warned would undermine investment and growth only announced further declines last month.

"Chile used to be synonymous with stability and security, but now that's a distant memory," said Mario Castro, a fixed-income strategist at Banco Bilbao Vizcaya Argentaria SA in New York. "There has been a structural change in Chile, involving institutional deterioration and a shift toward a welfare state that will increase fiscal pressure."

Volatility has hit new highs recently as emerging-market currencies were hit by a stronger dollar at a time when Chile struggles to finance one of the world's highest current-account deficits. That pushed the peso to record lows in July and triggered the largest intervention program in the central bank's history.

In 2017, Chile was rated AA- by S&P Global, on par with market favorites such as Taiwan and the Czech Republic. Then, a growing fiscal deficit led to a downgrade to A+ that year, followed by another cut to A in 2020.

Now, even that rating seems to flatter Chile, with its dollar debt trading at yields similar to BBB-rated countries like the Philippines, and well above Saudi Arabia, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

"There are downward pressures on Chile's rating," said Valerie Ho, portfolio manager at Doubleline Group LP in Los Angeles. "Chile's vulnerabilities are a weaker growth outlook, uncertainty about future policy in the mining sector and spending plans."

Chile's Finance Ministry did not respond to a request for comment.

What really shook Chile and the markets out of their 30-year slumber were the October 2019 riots that brought the military back onto the streets and saw the then-president nearly besieged in La Moneda palace. "Nothing has been the same since," Bloomberg highlights.

The market-friendly policies that have characterized the country since the 1980s were questioned, as were the parties that have dominated politics since the end of Augusto Pinochet's dictatorship in 1990.

Now, President Gabriel Boric heads Chile's most leftist government in half a century, pushing for constitutional change, while seeking to increase taxes on the mining industry, improve labor rights and redesign a pension system based on personal savings. All this against the backdrop of stagnant growth, the fastest inflation in three decades and a soaring current account deficit.

Chile's current account gap will narrow sharply next year as the economy contracts while inflation slows. At the same time, many expect the price of copper, which accounts for about half of exports, to improve, while production of the metal should increase.

In addition, Chile is already one of the few countries in the world expected to present a nearly balanced budget this year.

"Chile will improve over time and will look closer to what it was before," said Andres Abadia, economist at Pantheon Economics. "However, returning to being a safe haven in Latin America will depend on how the rules of the game are maintained in the new constitution."

For now, investors are struggling to understand all the changes. The peso's 30-day volatility has outpaced that of the Brazilian real and Colombian peso.

"For many years, inflation was basically nowhere and rates were not moving," said Carlos Fernandez-Aller, global head of FX and emerging markets macro operations at Bank of America. "A five basis point move in Chile was a big deal. Now it's a completely, completely different story."

title: Fall of the Chilean peso reflects the difficulty of the battle against the strength of the dollar
text:
The Chilean currency received a boost in mid-July with a US$25 billion intervention by the Central Bank, but has recently had one of the worst performances in the region in an example of how difficult the battle to counter a rampant dollar is, according to a Reuters analysis.

It is now threatening to break the 1,000 pesos per dollar barrier again after reaching a historic low of close to 1,050 pesos in July, when the Central Bank launched its plan of spot sales of dollars for up to 10 billion dollars and exchange hedging instruments for the same amount.

In addition, it offered a currency swap plan for up to US$5 billion. The move successfully helped to eliminate peso volatility.

However, as the dollar soars and interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve impact global currencies from the British pound to the Japanese yen and Chinese yuan, the effect of the intervention in Chile fades.

In the past two months, the currency has weakened 6.5% against the dollar, trailing the region's major currencies in Brazil, Mexico, Peru and Colombia. And it could weaken further after Friday's end of the intervention program, as set.

"Probably in the short term, maybe in October, we will see 1,000 pesos (per dollar) and maybe it will extend historical maximum that we have," said Angel Rubilar, senior analyst at Santiago-based Libertex. The currency is now worth 968 units to the dollar.

Chile is not alone in having to defend its currency. Currency interventions have increased in India, the Philippines and Korea in recent weeks, while Japan's central bank has just spent a record 2.8 billion yen (US$19.7 billion) in the foreign exchange market.

That intervention, after the yen fell to a 24-year low of nearly 146 per dollar, triggered a sharp rebound of more than 5 yen per dollar, although the currency fell back to around 144.7.

Diego Mora, market strategist at XTB Latam, said the Chilean central bank's intervention helped reduce the chances of aggressive moves, but the measure has its limits.

"The intervention was successful for the objective sought by the Central Bank, which was to control exchange rate volatility but not the price," he said, adding that markets had already incorporated the end of the intervention.

"We have seen a reduction in volatility. The possibility of seeing aggressive rises is less," he added.

Chile, the world's largest copper and second-largest lithium producer, is also grappling with annual inflation of around 14% through August, weak red metal prices and a recession expected by 2023, compounding the impact of the strong dollar.

Currency strategist Juan Prada of Barclays said tightening global financial conditions were increasing pressure on some regional markets particularly susceptible to external global economic shocks.

"We have identified Chile and Colombia as vulnerable, and the COP (Colombian peso) and CLP (Chilean peso) have underperformed their Latin American peers" since the September meeting of the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee.

However, the Chilean Central Bank has given no indication of further intervention. Analysts and traders say that, despite the pressures, another intervention would be "hasty" and could jeopardize long-term stability by affecting reserve levels.

"Reserves are not infinite," Mora referred. "To the extent that a Central Bank has less direct foreign currency reserves, the country becomes riskier with its long-term rates," he said.

With information from Reuters

title: ANALYSIS-Chile's sliding peso reflects tough battle vs rampaging dollar
text:
SANTIAGO, Oct 3 (Reuters) - Chile's sliding peso got a shot in the arm in July from a huge $25 billion central bank intervention, but in recent months has been one of the region's worst performers, showing how hard the battle is for policy makers countering a rampaging dollar.

The Chilean currency is threatening to breach the 1,000 peso per dollar line once again after it hit a record low near 1,050 pesos in July. That milestone led the central bank to launch a plan to sell $20 billion in dollars and FX hedging instruments, backed up by a $5 billion currency swap and peso liquidity program.

That move successfully helped cull wild volatility.

However, as the U.S. dollar soars and interest rate hikes by the U.S. Federal Reserve hammer global currencies from the British sterling to the Japanese yen and Chinese yuan, the impact of Chile's intervention has faded.

In the last two months the currency has weakened some 6.5% versus the dollar, trailing major regional currencies in Brazil, Mexico, Peru and Colombia. It is likely to weaken more after the central bank ended its intervention program on Sept. 30.

"Probably in the short term, maybe in October we'll see 1,000 pesos (to the dollar) and maybe we'll beat our historic low," said Angel Rubilar, a Santiago-based senior analyst at Libertex. The currency is now worth 968 per dollar.

Chile is not alone in having to defend its currency. FX interventions have increased in India, the Philippines and Korea in recent weeks, while Japan's central bank spent a record 2.8 trillion yen ($19.7 billion) in the FX market last week.

That intervention, following the yen's slump to a 24-year low of nearly 146 to the dollar, triggered a sharp bounce of more than 5 yen per dollar, although the currency has drifted down again to around 144.7.

'RESERVES AREN'T INFINITE'

Diego Mora, a market strategist for XTB Latam, said that Chile's central bankintervention had helped reduce the chances of aggressive currency moves, but had its limits.

"The intervention was successful for what the central bank needed, which was controlling volatility in the exchange rate, but not the price," said Mora, noting that markets were already pricing in the end of the intervention next week.

"The possibility of a sharp crash is lower."

Chile, the world's top producer of copper and the No. 2 for electric vehicle battery metal lithium, is also grappling with annual inflation at some 14%, weakening copper prices and a predicted recession, compounding the hit from the strong dollar.

Currency strategist Juan Prada at Barclays said the tightening of global financial conditions was ramping up pressure on some regional markets particularly susceptible to external global economic impacts.

"We have identified Chile and Colombia as vulnerable, and COP (Colombian peso) and CLP (Chilean peso) have underperformed LatAm peers" since the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee meeting in September, he said.

Chile's central bank, however, has given no indication that it would intervene again. Analysts and traders say that despite pressures, another intervention would be "hasty" and could risk longer-term stability by denting levels of reserves.

"Reserves aren't infinite," Mora added. "If the central bank has less direct reserves of foreign currency, the country becomes riskier with its long-term interest rates."

title: Dollar approaches $1,000 again due to global uncertainty and analysts believe that the CB should not think about a new  intervention  yet.
text:
At a time when the end of the current foreign exchange intervention by the Central Bank is approaching, the dollar once again appears on the horizon as a threat. Already rising steadily in the last week and a half, this Monday it lashed out strongly and closed with a rise of more than $20, reaching $992. This is its highest level since July 15 ($975), just the day after the exchange intervention, when the U.S. currency climbed to its historical maximum of $1,051.

In addition, the dollar recorded its eighth consecutive day of increase, if the two holidays on working days that took place during the Fiestas Patrias are discounted, accumulating a gain of $93.61 since September 12.

But this situation is not just Chile's. The Chilean peso is losing strength amid fears of a global recession that is pushing commodity prices into a slump. World markets are internalizing a new scenario where the US Federal Reserve would raise its interest rate harder and longer in order to control inflation. This leads investors to avoid risky assets, highlighted Bloomberg. Along with the Chilean peso, most currencies fell sharply against the dollar on the day, with the euro and the pound sterling, for example, at historic levels.

Also on Monday morning, the Central Bank's advisor, Stephany Griffith-Jones, said that the issuing institution "is closely monitoring" the dollar's movements, while participating in an activity organized by the Universidad de O'Higgins.

This scenario comes only four days before the Central Bank ends its intervention program. And although during the morning there was speculation as to what the Central Bank would do given this new situation, this question ended in the afternoon, as it issued a communiqué reaffirming the end of this process.

"The Central Bank of Chile informs that, as foreseen in the announcement dated July 14, 2022, the program of foreign exchange intervention and preventive provision of liquidity in dollars will end on Friday, September 30, 2022. Therefore, as of October 2, 2022, spot dollar sales, FX swap and Repo operations will cease", said the Central Bank.

As of the aforementioned date, the CB informed that "only the renewal of the stock of forward dollar sales operations will be offered, at market conditions, of the stock in force as of today, for the equivalent of US$ 9,110 million. If any auction is declared void, this amount will be rescheduled for the following week".

This renewal scheme will be in effect until Friday, January 13, 2023. Eventual changes to this renewal mechanism, as a result of changes in market conditions, will be announced in due course, he said.

The Central Bank's evaluation of the intervention is positive: "The Council of the Central Bank of Chile considers that the program of foreign exchange intervention and preventive provision of liquidity in dollars has achieved the objective of helping the proper functioning of the foreign exchange market, facilitating the adjustment of the economy and the financial markets to external and internal conditions".

For this reason, the Board maintains its commitment to the floating exchange rate regime, and reserves "the option to intervene in the exchange market in exceptional circumstances if it considers that the proper functioning of the financial market is at risk", it added.

According to the Central Bank's information, of the total amount destined to the sale of spot dollars, as of today a total of US$ 5,950 million has been allotted and that by the end of Friday this amount will reach US$ 6,100 million out of a total of US$ 10,000 million.

With this process, the Central Bank's international reserves went from US$45 billion to US$39 billion.

Experts agree that this is not the time for the CB to go out again with an intervention program, since the causes are global and the appreciation of the currency is in line with the fundamentals, so there are no signs of a misalignment. "Behind the most recent rise we recognize mainly external factors. The price of copper has retreated and the global dollar has gained value, reaching record highs, given the prospect of more aggressive Fed rate hikes," comments Bci's chief economist, Sergio Lehmann. However, he states that "we see that risk premiums on Chilean assets remain very high. Uncertainty, although it reveals better defined edges today, is still high". This, for Lehmann, is mainly due to political factors. "Important discrepancies are recognized within the government coalition on key issues, such as pension reform, trade agreements, figures related to Chile's development in recent years and others, which introduce volatility".

Tomás Flores, economist at Libertad y Desarrollo (LyD), adds that "this new rise of the dollar in Chile is being repeated in several countries as a consequence of the present and future rise of interest rates in the US. At the same time, the cut in growth projections for the world is affecting the prices of commodities, including copper, which additionally affects our currency".

Another view is provided by economist Patricio Rojas, of Rojas y Asociados, who argues that "as the expectation is that the United States will raise interest rates more strongly and the possibility of a deeper deceleration and even recession in some parts of the world, the dollar will of course gain ground. This is the origin of the peso's depreciation".

What the authorities should doFor now, economists point out in that the CB has to wait. "A dollar at $990 we all agree is not a sustainable value over time. Clearly the timing of the end of the Central Bank's intervention is not the best given the global context. And therefore, thinking about some kind of intervention will be within its powers," says Rojas.

Martina Ogaz, an economist at Euroamerica, adds that "for the moment, I believe that the conditions have not been met to extend intervention, as the current depreciation of the parity has been in line with the fundamentals and has not registered anomalous volatility or spread to other local markets.

Juan Ortiz, senior economist at OCEC-UDP, shares the same view: "I believe that the conditions are not yet in place. The peso has depreciated sharply as a result mainly of the strengthening of the multilateral dollar. The CB intervenes when it considers that, due to exchange rate fundamentals, the exchange rate is misaligned, which is not the case today, as can be seen from the behavior of the peso with respect to other currencies".

Lehmann points out that "the Central Bank will monitor the evolution of the exchange market with special care. Today the exchange rate misalignment is high, around 10% according to our models, and volatility is extraordinarily high. If this worsens and affects the functioning of the financial market, the Central Bank will intervene, but we do not see that for now".

title: Chile  confirms end of  foreign exchange intervention  even as peso drops
text:
Chile's central bank confirmed plans to end its foreign exchange intervention program at the end of the month, even as the peso reached its lowest level since the bank began selling dollars in mid-July.

The program will end as scheduled on Sept. 30, after which the bank will only renew forward contracts as they expire, according to a statement released Monday. It will no longer sell dollars in the spot market.

The bank chose to make the announcement on a day when the peso was among the worst performing currencies in the world amid broad risk aversion sentiment and as the intervention program begins to wind down.

The currency depreciated 2.2% against the dollar, bringing its fall in the last three weeks to more than 12%. It currently stands at 992 pesos to the dollar.

"The Council remains committed to the floating exchange rate regime, reserving the option to intervene in the foreign exchange market in exceptional circumstances if it considers that the smooth functioning of the financial market is at risk," the statement said. The program achieved its objective of assisting the "proper functioning of the foreign exchange market".

The bank will renew US$9.11 billion in forward sales operations and any auctions that are declared void will be rescheduled for the following week. The renewal program will be valid until January 13, the monetary policy institute said.

On Friday, the bank announced plans to sell US$50 million a day in the spot market this week and renew a total of US$2.21 billion in forward sales. The forward renewal and rescheduling schedule will continue to be reported every Friday.

title: Dollar starts sixth day on the rise and surpasses $950 two weeks before the plebiscite
text:
The intense bullish pressures of last week are once again imposing themselves on the dollar, pushing it above the $ 950 mark in a local and international investment environment that favors the appreciation of the US currency.

According to Bloomberg, the dollar is up $ 9.60 to trade at $ 954.20 at 9 am.

Last week was the week of the greatest advance for the exchange rate in all its history of free floating, with an increase of $ 67.60 in the set of five upward days (transactions on holiday Monday were minimal, which did not prevent a rise in the price).

"The dollar continues on its upward path on the eve of the exit plebiscite next Sunday, September 4 in Chile. Despite the Central Bank's recent intervention, we could see the exchange rate above $1,000 again in the days leading up to the referendum," said FX Globe market analyst Sergio Cisternas.

In addition, copper fell 0.12% to US$ 3.64 per pound on the London Metal Exchange, contributing to the weakening of the Chilean peso.

Global dollar The rise of the dollar is also due to international factors linked to a decrease in investors' confidence regarding future financial conditions, as it is expected that the US Federal Reserve will not hesitate to raise interest rates sharply.

The dollar index - which measures the global strength of the dollar - traded higher for the fourth consecutive day, rising 0.20% to 108.38 points.

"The next key event to gauge U.S. dollar risk will be this Friday's speech by Fed Chairman Jerome Powell at the Jackson Hole symposium," wrote analysts at Saxo Bank.

The anticipation of such an event, in the absence of an August policy meeting, has led all types of riskier assets to experience pullbacks.

According to Oanda senior analyst Craig Erlam, "traders will be looking for more clarity when Powell speaks, and seem to think his appearance will take the form of a dovish warning".

title: War and pandemic return Mexico and Latin America to era of high rates
text:
In the fight against pandemic inflation, Latin America led the world into a new era of money scarcity. Eighteen months later, there is no sign that being the first in will help the region become the first out.

Last August 11, the Bank of Mexico and Peru's central bank announced what were their tenth and thirteenth consecutive interest rate hikes, respectively. Forecasters do not believe that any of them are over yet. In Brazil, one of the world's first hikers in March 2021, there is a chance it could stop. Still, specialists said this week they expect to keep rates in "significantly contractionary territory for a sufficiently prolonged period."

Latin America's central bankers, of course, are not the only ones who missed their targets by a mile during the worst price crisis in decades. But, amid signs that the inflationary wave may be peaking, they have a particular reason to remain vigilant.

A local history of hyperinflation means that even simple contracts such as rents are tied to past price increases, helping inflation to take hold. in the opposite direction to central bank policies that attempt to control demand.

'It has to wait'And on top of that, the region's currencies, mostly strong performers this year thanks to higher rates and commodity prices, have been wobbling again in recent weeks.

What Bloomberg says..."Inflation resilience reflects the lag between rate hikes and their effect on the economy. Those effects are held back by two other factors: the adverse external scenario, which weakens emerging currencies and pushes up tradable prices; in addition, fiscal measures adopted by some Latin economies fuel the very inflation whose effects they seek to alleviate."

--Adriana Dupita, Latin American economist.

Currency falls, especially when the US and other developed economies are raising their own interest rates, are a classic path to runaway prices in Latin America. That gives central bankers another incentive to keep policy tight, and perhaps use other tools as well. Chile intervened in currency markets last month and others may follow suit.

"There is a possibility that many may have to wait until 2024 to cut rates," says Gabriel Casillas, chief economist for Latin America at Barclays Plc. Economists surveyed by Bloomberg suggest easing could begin a bit sooner, but not before the second half of next year.

Inflation continues to accelerate in many Latin American nations, with Mexico and Chile recently posting multi-decade highs. In Argentina, which has endured two decades of wild economic swings, it topped 70 percent, prompting the central bank to raise interest rates by nearly 10 percentage points on Thursday. Overall, the region has the world's fastest price growth outside war-torn Eastern Europe, data compiled by Bloomberg show.

Brazil experienced a sharp drop in prices last month, though it was largely due to energy tax cuts pushed by President Jair Bolsonaro, who is running for re-election in October.

'Part of the toolkit'Latin American currencies are also at risk from the end of the pandemic commodity boom, as well as from US interest rate hikes that will continue well into 2023.

For most of the year, they have held up better than most against the rising dollar. Brazil's real and Mexico's peso are among a handful of currencies that posted gains, although they have lost ground from mid-year highs.

Others have seen steeper declines. Chile's central bank reversed the peso's slide in mid-July by announcing it would spend $25 billion over several weeks to buy it.

With interest rates already high enough to threaten economic growth, and many Latin American countries holding large amounts of foreign currency, other central banks may resort to such measures as part of the fight against inflation, says Daniel Titelman of the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean.

"We've seen large enough depreciations, in a region that, generally speaking, has accumulated reserves," he says. "That's part of the toolkit you have, in the same way that Chile did."

title: Rosanna Costa, president BCCh: 'I am the person of the crises'.
text:
(Bloomberg) -- Just hours after speaking to Bloomberg Markets, Rosanna Costa extinguished a looming currency crisis by announcing the biggest intervention in the history of Chile's central bank in the foreign-exchange market.

The only hint of the drama unfolding in the background were occasional interruptions from her assistant asking her to verify the details of a document. Smiling, polite, the president of the Central Bank of Chile apologized as she moved into an adjoining room. The central bank looked calm in the midst of an increasingly frantic market.

Costa, 64, has experience in crisis management. Days before he took over as director of budgets at the Finance Ministry in 2010, Chile was rocked by one of the biggest earthquakes in history. The cost of the damage amounted to billions of dollars. Since becoming a central bank policymaker in January 2017, she has had to deal with the impact of a wave of social protests over inequality and poor public services that paralyzed the country and often turned violent. More recently, he helped the economy navigate through the covid-19 pandemic.

Since taking over as central bank president in February, Costa has raised interest rates to the highest level in more than two decades in an attempt to curb the fastest inflation in a generation, as well as the threat to the currency in mid-July. Moreover, as a former member of a right-wing government, he is directing monetary policy after Chileans voted in the most left-wing government in 50 years, electing Gabriel Boric as the country's president.

"I seem to be the crisis person," Costa told Bloomberg Markets. The interview, which took place on July 14, has been edited for length and content.

BLOOMBERG MARKETS: How do you feel at the central bank after having a very different job as deputy director of the Institute for Liberty and Development, a free-market think tank?

ROSANNA COSTA: I knew the central bank. It was my first job after leaving university. I was here for about 10 years and I would say that the bank was my second school, especially when you come straight out of university, the work makes its mark.

BM: Did you ever plan to be president of the central bank?

RC: It was never in my thoughts. I think that in each of the jobs I have had, I have looked for the space to grow and contribute. And, above all, to enjoy the job, beyond the tensions or the complexity of it. When I refer to enjoyment, I'm talking about being passionate about what you are doing.

BM: Are you passionate about what you are doing today as president of the central bank?

RC: The central bank offers a platform to be able to contribute to your country. There are many areas of work within the bank. Today, inflation has been presented as a phenomenon, but it was absent for many years. You can see the cost to families, to households, and I have a great platform to contribute to the fight against that. That motivates me.

BM: Do you still enjoy it when you have days when it seems like a crisis is looming like today?

RC: Stress management is something you learn over time, and I'm old enough to know that. That's not to say it doesn't exist, but you know and recognize yourself, and you find your own way to manage it. I have a very supportive family; I have important emotional support. You learn to manage stress and balance life.

BM: When you get home from work, do you still read academic papers or do you find a way to relax and do other things?

RC: This is getting into the more intimate territory of my home. I don't easily disconnect from work, not at all. But I really enjoy family time, family gatherings. Having my own family close by is the most valuable thing to me.

BM: It is currently such a tumultuous time for the markets that there is a lot of contradictory information. How do you handle all the data?

RC: We work within a structure. We apply or make decisions today so that their effects are seen over time. We work based on what is the medium-term perspective, so we have to understand very well what is happening, what are the forces behind it and how to project it forward. It is a challenge.

Working in the unknown is always a challenge. Controlling inflation two years in advance helps us avoid overreacting in the present. We have very well-prepared technical teams. There are top-level management teams overseeing that work. There is a bureau that, as a whole, is a group made up of people who know a lot about the issues and are very committed. Together we make decisions that are as informed as possible.

BM: Do you read all the bank analysts' reports that so often tell you what to do, and do you consider all the opinions of the market and investors?

RC: We don't have our windows closed, but we don't read everything that is published either. We look at what is said, see if the arguments make sense. We contrast with what we have and with what the evidence tells us, knowing that the evidence tells us about the past and that we are building the future. And, if there is relevant information, we take it into account, obviously without getting dizzy.

BM: What qualities do you consider you have that help you deal with crises or difficult times?

RC: I am a person who listens a lot and who seeks to generate agreement among the board members. But I am also a person who makes decisions when it is time to make them. This is an institution that makes its decisions collegially, so it is important to build trust and work together. That is something that excites me, something I am born to do.

BM: How does it feel to be the first woman president of the central bank and to work in an environment historically dominated by men?

RC: I was once told that I could easily work in teams of men and that the difference was not very noticeable. I don't know what they meant by that [laughs]. In my family we were only two sisters, but I was always very close to my father. At that time he studied to be a commercial engineer at the university, since pure economics did not exist in Chile. I also went to a coeducational school.

BM: During the social unrest of October 2019, you were a member of the bank's board of directors. Were the riots a shock for you?

RC: The way the riots manifested themselves was a shock.

BM: Did it change in any way the opinion you have about Chile's economic model?

RC: I can't really answer that as president of the central bank.

BM: I guess that is one of the main differences between your work here and your time in the think tank. You cannot freely express your political views.

RC: They are different institutions. But the exposure, the public part of that work, was never what attracted me most. I was interested in the research work.

title: Dollar falls below 900 Chilean pesos and copper rises in value
text:
The US dollar closed this Monday for the first time below 900 Chilean pesos since it surpassed this psychological barrier in July and began an escalation that led it to break the ceiling of 1,000 pesos, forcing a double intervention of the Central Bank of Chile.

According to local operators, the North American currency oscillated between 884 and 898 pesos and closed at 891.15 pesos, which implies a negative variation of 0.71% with respect to the previous day.

The fall of the dollar coincides with the rise on Monday of the price of copper - the main engine of the Chilean economy - which appreciated by 1.67% on the London Metal Exchange (LME), for the third consecutive time.

The "Grade A" spot pound was quoted at 3.59722 US dollars compared to 3.53825 on Friday and 3.49811 on Thursday, reaching its highest level since last July 4, when it reached 3.64507 per pound.

In this context, experts believe that the price of the dollar will continue its downward trend also due to the policy of the Federal Reserve (Fed), which last week already announced that it will not opt for such aggressive rate and interest rate hikes.

title: The Big Mac Index
text:
The Big Mac Index was invented by The Economist in 1986, according to its website, as a light-hearted guide to determine whether countries' currency quotes worldwide are at their "correct" level or are "undervalued" or "overvalued." It is based on the theory of purchasing power parity (PPP), which says that price levels between two countries should tend to be equal in the long run, i.e., an identical basket of goods in each country will cost the same once the currencies have been exchanged.

The Economist does not use a basket but a world standard hamburger, the Big Mac which, for example, as of June 2022 cost 3,400 pesos in Chile, while in the US its price was US$5.15. The relation between both prices gives us a Big Mac exchange rate of 660.19 pesos, which would be its "correct" level. Now, if we compare this level with the official quotation of the Chilean peso as of June, which was 928.43 pesos for one dollar, we find that the official Chilean peso would be weaker, more Chilean pesos for one dollar with respect to its "correct value", by 28.9%.

This situation occurs, according to The Economist website, with the majority of currencies worldwide that would be in a race to devalue, with the exception of a few currencies such as the Swiss franc, which would be rather "above its value" by 30.3%, the Norwegian krone (21.6%) and the Uruguayan peso (18.1%).

The underlying problem is the revaluation of the U.S. dollar, the highest in 20 years, and the fact that the rival currency, the euro, from a ratio of US$ 1.15 in December 2021 fell in a few months to a rate of US$ 0.98, less than one dollar for one euro. There are many explanations for the revaluation of the dollar; one of them, that it is "a post-pandemic evil" due to the excess of spending, and another, which associates it to the problem of inflation and the increase in interest rates by the US Federal Reserve.

However, it is convenient to analyze the behavior of the dollar not in nominal terms with other currencies, but in real terms; which means taking into account the relation of prices with other economies, for which the US Federal Reserve (Fed) calculates a Real Broad Dollar Index, where levels above 100 mean a "real revaluation". If we start in January 2006 with an index equal to 100, we find that the index as of June 2022 is 115, which reflects a real appreciation of 15%.

First of all it should be noted that a strong dollar is neither recent nor is it post-pandemic, since its trend is already observed as of March 2015, which continued with COVID-19 in 2020 and continues until now. Therefore, it seems unreasonable to associate the real appreciation of the dollar only to increased fiscal spending in times of pandemic.

Second, while there is a relationship between dollar appreciation and the Fed's interest rate, it is worth keeping in mind that prior to its rate hike in mid-March, already the real appreciation as of February 2022 was 10%. Then, the increase of its interest rate from 0.25% in March to 1.15% in June shows an additional appreciation of the dollar of 5%, so it would not be the only explanation for its appreciation.

The context is undoubtedly high inflation and the problem is that central banks believe that in order to curb inflation, interest rates must be raised, on the understanding that it is a demand-only inflation due to the expansion of the quantity of money, so by raising their interest rates they make money expensive and lower prices.

Additionally, several central banks in South America let their currencies depreciate due to the recent fall in commodity prices and although the devaluation nominally encourages exports, on the other hand, it makes imports more expensive, so they had to intervene in their exchange markets, as the Central Bank of Chile did.

Bolivia is not yet in the middle of the vortex of high inflation and strong depreciation, so we must preserve the economic stability achieved as a heritage of all Bolivians.

Gabriel Loza Tellería is an economist, self-employed and Bolivarian.

title: *Fitch Rtgs: Chile, Colombia Large Current Account Deficits Are a Vulnerability
text:
26 Jul 2022 10:28 ET  Press Release: Fitch  Rtgs: Chile, Colombia Large Current Account Deficits Are a Vulnerability

The following is a press release from Fitch Ratings :

Fitch Ratings -London-26 July 2022: Chile's (A-/Stable) and Colombia's (BB+/Stable) current account deficits (CADs) will remain large in 2022 due to continued strong import growth and high profit remittances by companies in the commodities sector, Fitch Ratings says. Large CADs are a vulnerability as external financing conditions tighten, and if domestic political uncertainty begins to weigh on FDI prospects, external pressures could build. Fitch has revised its forecasts for both countries' 2022 CADs. We now see Chile's at 6.2% of GDP, compared with 6.4% in 2021. For Colombia, our updated 2022 forecast sees the CAD little changed, at 5.6% of GDP from 5.7%. We had forecast the CADs to moderate this year to 4.1% and 4.6%, respectively, on higher prices for commodity exports and lower imports. Our new forecasts reflect continued high domestic demand driving strong import growth while commodity export prices are volatile. Copper prices have fallen to pre-Ukraine war levels and oil prices have retreated from their peak. Profit remittances from private oil and mining companies remain another significant factor.

Wide CADs increase vulnerability to tighter global financing conditions and a global economic slowdown and possible recession. Political uncertainties are a further consideration, with a new leftist government about to take office in Colombia, while in Chile there is a coming referendum on a new constitution. Combined with the tougher global backdrop these uncertainties could affect the financial accounts through both FDI and portfolio flows. Chile's proposed new constitution will be put to a popular referendum in early September and irrespective of its outcome, uncertainties will persist. In Chile, the administration of Gabriel Boric that took office in March has thus far demonstrated fiscal pragmatism, committing to tax increases to meet social spending pressures. But its ability to deliver these remains unclear in the face of a split Congress. Similarly in Colombia, the appointment of finance minister Jose Antonio Ocampo suggests a pragmatic approach. But while incoming president Gustavo Petro has toned down his initial rhetoric, his proposal to halt new oil exploration has weighed on investor sentiment, and details on tax and pension reforms are yet to be worked out. The Chilean peso and Colombian peso have come under greater pressure in the past month than many other emerging-market currencies in the face of a stronger U.S. dollar. Depreciation should help to facilitate external adjustment over time, but can amplify existing macroeconomic challenges by pushing inflation higher.

It also directly affects debt/GDP ratios. Colombia and Chile's currency composition deteriorated during the Covid-19 pandemic as they relied increasingly on external debt to fund their large fiscal deficits. Chile's foreign-currency share of debt rose to nearly 35% at end-2021 from 21% at end-2019, while Colombia's rose to about 40% from close to 34%. Central banks have been proactive, raising rates aggressively and helping to support policy credibility. But reserves have still fallen, notably in Chile, from a peak of USD55 billion in October 2021 to USD45 billion in June 2022. Chile's central bank opted to intervene in the FX market this month, announcing USD10 billion of sales in the spot market and USD10 billion in hedging instruments until end-September and a currency swap plan for up to USD5 billion to boost liquidity in dollars complemented by a liquidity program in pesos. This has boosted the peso, but will weaken external liquidity metrics. And Chile replaced its USD23.9 billion IMF flexible credit line (FCL), with a much smaller USD3.5 billion short-term facility. Colombia has not intervened to date. Its external liquidity metrics are stronger with reserve coverage of current account payments at more than seven months (versus just over three for Chile). title: Strong dollar rattles much of Latin America's economy
text:
An important factor in the depreciation of currencies against the dollar is the constant interest rate hikes by the U.S. Federal Reserve.

The U.S. dollar has experienced an unusual appreciation in recent weeks, which has caused several Latin American currencies to devalue, with the inevitable consequences for the public coffers and domestic economies of the countries in the region.

A large part of the products that make up the family basket in Latin America are imported and paid for in dollars, as well as important resources such as hydrocarbons and raw materials.

A POST-PANDEMIC EVIL

"After a pandemic in which the economy was stimulated comes a great phenomenon called inflation. When central banks start to raise interest rates and begin to see a possible recession, growth has to be curbed," financial analyst Andres Moreno told EFE.

"There was runaway growth in the world, everything recovered faster than expected. With better interest rates and a possible recession, international capital is more risk-averse and prefers to go to more solid economies. This translates into a devaluation of the currencies of emerging countries," he adds.

Another important factor in the depreciation of currencies against the dollar is the constant interest rate hikes by the US Federal Reserve (Fed), the last one on June 16 to 1.50%.

DOLLAR: ANOTHER PAIN FOR ARGENTINA

In Argentina, the strengthening of the dollar adds to the country's macroeconomic imbalances and reinforces the weakness of the peso itself, as a result of 64% year-on-year inflation, the shortage of international currency, devaluation expectations, the fiscal deficit and political uncertainty.

"The dollar is going to build on a problem that Argentina had before," said Gabriel Caamaño, an economist at the Ledesma consulting firm, to EFE, who warns that there are already discussions that inflation could reach three digits.

Argentina applies strong exchange controls to authorize the entry and exit of dollars at the official exchange rate, which has led to a proliferation of parallel exchange rates on the stock market and the black market.

The expectations of devaluation and the weakness of the Argentine peso are reflected in a gap of more than 147 % between the official exchange rate and the "blue" or parallel exchange rate, which this week reached 338 pesos.

STRONG INTERVENTION IN CHILE

Alarm bells went off in Chile on July 14, when the dollar reached an all-time high of 1,051 pesos. This dizzying escalation precipitated that same day a historic intervention in the foreign exchange market by the Central Bank for an amount of 25 billion dollars until September.

The intervention is proving to be "successful", as it has managed in just four days to push the dollar back below 1,000 pesos, according to experts.

"Before the exchange intervention, the peso was among the most devalued currencies in the world, despite the fact that Chile has relatively stable and healthy economic fundamentals. The appreciation of the dollar had reached 20%, but thanks to the intervention it has been reduced to 12%," Francisco Castañeda, of the Universidad Mayor, explained to EFE.

COLOMBIA: A DOLLAR WITH POLITICAL INFLUENCE?

The dollar in Colombia reached a record high of 4,625 pesos on July 12, driven by world volatility due to fears that the United States could enter a recession that could turn global.

The country will be governed as from August 7 by the leftist Gustavo Petro, but market analysts consider that the political situation has little influence on the behavior of the exchange rate, since the Colombian peso has accumulated so far this year a depreciation of 10.5% in the official quotation.

"Part of what is happening in Colombia and Chile is that they are countries highly exposed to raw materials: oil in the case of Colombia and copper in the case of Chile, and both have had price reversals. This means that we have two currencies with high sensitivity in this environment", says the chief economist of BBVA Research, Alejandro Reyes.

So far, Banco de la República's policy of not intervening in the value of the dollar has been successful and, after last week's record high, the dollar has entered an adjustment trend, with four days of declines, and last Thursday it closed at 4,410 pesos.

THE RESILIENT MEXICAN PESO

The Mexican peso closed at 20.51 per dollar on July 19, the same figure as on December 31, 2021, according to official data from the Bank of Mexico (Banxico).

Janneth Quiroz, chief economist at Monex Group, emphasizes to EFE that in the first half of the year the Mexican peso maintained the levels of the end of 2021 with an appreciation of 0.1%, closing at 20.13 pesos per U.S. dollar on June 30.

PERUVIAN SOL SOMEWHAT OPAQUE AGAINST THE DOLLAR

In Peru, in the first days of July, the exchange rate of the dollar experienced an increase of 3.8 % on average, in the interbank quotation, towards the end of the period from July 1 to July 12.

In those days, 3.97 soles had to be given per dollar, as opposed to 3.82 soles on average last June, according to figures from the Central Reserve Bank of Peru (BCRP).

THE DOLLAR DECLINES IN BRAZIL

In Brazil, the US currency has suffered a merry-go-round and, contrary to the rest of the region, accumulated a decline of only 2.43% from January to July 20.

However, since last May, the dollar has gradually strengthened in the Brazilian market, after having lost up to 15.35 %, although the impact of the rise of the greenback has not been as great as in some of the neighboring countries.

According to Joelson Sampaio, professor at the Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV), the strengthening of the dollar should continue in Brazil and other emerging countries in the face of "the expectation" of a further increase in interest rates and inflation in the US.

THE "DOLLARIZED" COUNTRIES

In Ecuador, the appreciation of the dollar has generated concern due to the rising cost of exports, and, although the measure benefits, on the other hand, imports, domestic sales depend on the purchasing power in a country in recurrent economic crisis.

"We are very concerned because we are living through times that have not been seen in the last two decades," with a dollar appreciation "as strong as the one that is happening," Felipe Ribadeneira, president of the Ecuadorian Federation of Exports (Fedexpor), told EFE.

The strengthening of the dollar means that Ecuadorian exports are losing competitiveness in destination countries, whose currencies are depreciating.

Meanwhile, the revaluation of the dollar hardly affects Panama, and rather benefits it, since it is a country of services and more of an importer than an exporter.

Unlike Ecuador and El Salvador, Panama has had the dollar since its foundation as an independent state after its separation from Colombia in 1903.

The high value of the dollar has not affected El Salvador's exports, which in fact have remained on the rise despite inflation.

According to the Central Reserve Bank, total exports between January and June 2022 totaled US$3,256 million, with a 16.8% growth.

In addition, imports reached $8,934.4 million, registering a 27.2 % increase. And although bitcoin is a legal tender since 2021, the economy is not "bitcoinized".

Ricardo Castaneda, coordinator of the Central American Institute for Fiscal Studies (Icefi) for El Salvador and Honduras, tells EFE that the incidence or effect on the economy in general is minimal, due to the dollarization in force since 2001.

However, this could affect groups such as exporters who do not send their products to the U.S. but to other countries, as their products will be less competitive.

THE EURO IS THE PROBLEM IN CUBA

In Cuba the dollar has not had a significant rise, but the euro has registered a steady rise for the past month, above the U.S. currency.

Until last Tuesday, the European bill was exchanged in the informal market at 124 Cuban pesos (cup). The official rate is 24.54 pesos.

The increase of the euro began in mid-June, coinciding with the entry into force of a directive of the Central Bank of Cuba (BCC) that prevents consulates from changing to other currencies the income from procedures invoiced in cup.

A few days later, several consulates confirmed that they would charge in euros. Many Cubans travel to Central American countries to undertake their journey to the United States.

At the beginning of 2021, the country launched a package of economic reforms known as Tarea de Ordenamiento, which established an official exchange rate of 24 cupS for each dollar. However, on the street the greenback was trading on Tuesday at 118.

A DOLLAR THAT HURTS THE U.S. ITSELF.

The United States closed 2021 with a trade deficit of 27 % and this trend could continue this year if the dollar remains strong against the euro.

Broadly speaking, with a weaker euro, European goods and services become more attractive to the United States, while domestic producers become much less competitive internationally.

This could affect domestic production in sectors such as machinery, vehicles or the chemical industry, major sectors within U.S. exports to Europe.

"Europe today has a little bit more inflation, but it's in a stronger position in terms of international competition. So it's going to be a little easier to export and a little less attractive for them to import products from the U.S.," Carol Osler, professor of Financial Markets and Institutions at Brandeis International Business University, told EFE.

title: Central Bank intervention  in the U.S. dollar market does not impress swap rates
text:
The Central Bank of Chile (BCCh) began its largest foreign exchange intervention in history last week. The dollar market reacted strongly, but the effect on swap rates was more diluted.

Two-year peso-Camero swap rates fell only 11 basis points to 9.71%, down from the previous week's high of 10.05%, but up from 8.39% at the beginning of the month. More notably, five-year rates rose 18 basis points from the previous week to 7.49%, even as U.S. Treasury rates fell.

The BCCh unveiled a US$25 billion intervention program on July 14, triggering a sharp rebound in the peso from historic lows. But the dollar sales and an increase in the monetary policy rate failed to ensure that inflation will decelerate soon, or that an end to tighter monetary policy is in sight.

"The shorter part of the swap curve fell because a stronger peso should reduce pressure on inflation, but that good run was not enough to benefit longer swaps," said Sebastian Ide, manager of Banco de Chile's money desk. The long end of the curve was more impacted by local risk factors, he said.

Investors remain concerned that the peso will fall again against the dollar when intervention ends in September, considering that Chile is running its largest current account deficit since at least 1997. There are also concerns about the size of the intervention, which is equivalent to almost half of the central bank's reserves.

"The risks to the central bank's future credibility could be very high," said Felipe Alarcón, chief economist at Euroamerica in Santiago. "It is critical that the intervention is successful."

Daily salesOn top of this, intervention this week will be lower: US$150 million a day in the spot market and US$350 million in forwards, compared to US$200 million and US$500 million, respectively, last week.

Two-year inflation breakevens, a gauge of price expectations over that period, fell to 7.1% last week from 7.6% the previous week.

"Despite central bank intervention and a lower dollar, there are still strong upside risks to consumer prices," said Jaime Achondo, general manager of brokerage Fynsa. Among these are possible increases in transport and energy prices, and further economic stimulus from the government.

President Gabriel Boric this month announced an additional US$1.2 billion aid package, which the government insists will not impact inflation. This comes on top of a US$3.7 billion package announced in April. In addition, the government may unfreeze public transport prices from 2023, said Finance Minister Mario Marcel.

However, some think the breakevens should compress in the coming weeks as inflation nears a turning point.

"Inflation could be close to peaking, with the economy likely to enter recession by the end of the year," said Mariano Alvarez, fixed income manager at LarrainVial. "Betting on nominal bonds over CPI-indexed bonds is starting to make sense."

title: Chilean dollar continues its decline below $ 930 on new copper price hike
text:
On the fifth day since the Central Bank's banking intervention began, the dollar in Chile marks this Friday new declines, dropping below the $ 930 barrier.

At the opening, the exchange rate fell $ 5.05 to $ 923, which places the Chilean peso as the fourth emerging currency with the best daily performance, according to Bloomberg.

This, while copper rises 1.94% on the London Metal Exchange to US$ 3.344 a pound, and the dollar index - which compares the U.S. currency with a basket of six other currencies - falls 0.17% to 106.625 points.

"The U.S. currency has been trading flat for the past week, after the dollar's sharp fall due to the Central Bank's intervention to alleviate the currency's pressure on the national economy. However, fears of a global recession as a result of the strong rate hikes being carried out by the world's main central banks to contain the escalation of prices is having a strong impact on the greenback", explains XTB Latam's senior market analyst, Juan Ortiz Godoy.

So far, the sale of dollars by the central bank has totaled US$ 2,735 million at the close of trading on Thursday. While spot sales represent 70.75% of the total, forward sales account for the remaining 29.25%.

This is in line with the program of foreign exchange intervention and preventive provision of liquidity in dollars, which includes an amount of up to US$ 25 billion until September 30, 2022, with the sale of spot dollars for up to US$ 10 billion and the sale of foreign exchange hedging instruments for an amount of up to US$ 10 billion.

At the international level, attention is focused on how the greenback may be influenced by the monetary policy meeting of the US Federal Reserve, where it is expected to raise the interest rate by 75 basis points next week to control inflation.

"We believe that the exchange rate will continue its upward trend despite the drops it has been experiencing in some days. The exchange rate could go for $ 915 - $ 920, to possibly rebound to $ 900 and continue its upward trend if we see further falls in copper and an appreciation of the dollar at a global level", states Godoy.

title: Will Chile's rising dollar and inflation be brought under control?
text:
The main economic concern in Chile today is the strong inflation we are experiencing, 12.5% annualized, as of June of this year. The pressure of internal prices is so high that the Central Bank raised the Monetary Policy Rate, TPM, on May 9 to 9% and has just raised it (July 13, 2022) by 75 points, to 9.75%, which reduces once again the money supply and will raise again the interest rates of the Chilean economy which, in June 2022, were at 26.3% the consumer rate and 12.99% the commercial rate. Actions aimed at reducing domestic demand (consumption and investment) and productive activity to reduce inflation.

However, the results have been slow, we are observing a slow adjustment of the IMACEC in 2022, from 6.8% in February to 6.40% in May, while the unemployment rate is also adjusting slowly, while prices have not stopped growing, moreover, recent data indicate that, in June, inflation, annualized, reached 12.5%. This indicates that inflationary pressures in Chile were not only due to internal factors (pension withdrawals -savings- and more fiscal spending, in universal FPI, for example), which translated at the time (2021) into a strong increase in the demand for consumer and capital goods and services, impacting prices. If this were the case, the results in inflationary control would have already been noticed.

We know that our prices are also rising due to external factors such as the increase in the price of our imports: oil, wheat and others; due to the increase in costs, due to problems in transportation logistics, which still persist; due to the reappearance of outbreaks of the pandemic, due to Russia's invasion war in Ukraine, which still continues, among others.

Higher values mean higher input values and higher domestic production costs (such as the higher price of wheat, which pushes up the price of bread) or raise the prices of imported goods and services for direct sale (automobiles, electronic devices and others). For all these imported goods and services, we must then pay more dollars, which we have to buy in the domestic exchange market, increasing the demand for dollars and pushing up the exchange rate and depreciating our peso against the dollar.

The value of the exchange rate appears today as our great conjunctural concern. But it is of vital importance to control inflation, since a high percentage of it is explained by external factors.

In this regard, it can be stated that both the international economic situation mentioned above, as well as the inflationary and recessive expectations of the world economy, which surround it, are factors of uncertainty due to which economic and financial agents abandon the stock markets and take refuge in dollars, affecting the exchange rate of our currency with respect to the dollar.

This situation is expected to normalize in the short term, although in the meantime the stock market mood is not firm and some stock markets continue to fall and others recover slightly, basically because it is expected that the US Federal Reserve, FED, will raise the reference rate again to control its high inflation (9.1%), which would bring new impacts of depreciation of our currency against the dollar. It will be necessary to remember that also the political uncertainty, at a national level, drives up the exchange rate in Chile.

The current intervention of the Central Bank in the exchange market is trying to control the strong expansion observed in the exchange rate in Chile, which in one month rose from 863.95 pesos per dollar (June 14) to $1,042.97 on July 14. It could be affirmed that the impact was materialized by the single announcement, which made the dollar fall to $972.40 the day after the announcement, Friday July 15, and achieved at the beginning of the Central Bank's sales in the exchange market, on Monday July 18, a reduction to $947.89, a value that includes for this day, an increase in the price of copper, which operated in the same direction as the official intervention, increasing the supply of dollars and making the dollar fall.

Then, apparently, the effects of the intervention will not be very high and, perhaps, we will have rather high and undesired fluctuations of the exchange rate. These results show how difficult it will be to contain inflation in our country and the high costs that will surely be paid in terms of containing productive activity and increasing unemployment.

Víctor Salas Opazo

Department of Economics

University of Santiago de Chile

title: Chile 's volatile peso extends rally after  central bank intervention
text:
SANTIAGO, July 20 (Reuters) - Chile's peso has enjoyed an extended rally since the central bank last week announced a $25 billion intervention to buoy the currency after a series of historic lows, but it may face a bumpier path in the coming weeks.

At Tuesday's close, the peso finished up 1.81% at 923.80 per dollar, taking its gains to 13.21% from a historic low of 1,045.80 on Thursday, before the intervention.

On Monday, the peso was aided by a hike in the price of copper, of which Chile is the world's largest producer, but the currency continued its strong run on Tuesday even as the price of the metal fell.

"For a lot of people the question is why the (exchange rate) keeps (improving) after the intervention and fall of copper today," said Jorge Selaive, chief economist of Scotiabank Chile, adding that other internal factors are aiding the peso's ascent.

Selaive said a "brutal" drop in risk fund shares in the country's AFP pension system is leading to investment in more conservative funds, resulting in AFPs selling dollars, aiding the exchange rate.

As well, he said the central bank hasn't announced how it will "sterilize" the intervention, or remove the excess dollars it is injecting into the system through daily currency auctions, but signs point to the bank letting bonds with less than a 360-day maturity expire.

Many of those bonds were issued at lower rates before a recent string of rate hikes.

"So the effect of the lowered interest rate will concentrate in that time frame," he said.

Another contributing factor is that foreign investors are holding off on buying dollar futures contracts, he said.

"They're waiting for the exchange rate to stabilize at new levels to reevaluate their strategy in Chile," Selaive said.

A global surge in the U.S. dollar has pushed down currencies worldwide, but Chile's peso has been particularly volatile, partly due to its floating exchange rate.

That has made it more susceptible to speculation related to copper's fluctuating price and political uncertainty over a proposed new constitution, as well as the recent intervention, according to Victor Salas and other economists at the University of Santiago.

"This is going to be an unclear, unclean drop in the exchange rate," in terms of the number of pesos that a U.S. dollar can buy, Salas said, adding that the real effect will take weeks to see.

(Reporting by Fabian Cambero and Alexander Villegas; editing by Richard Pullin)

title: Dollar continues to plummet following  Central Bank intervention
text:
The dollar in Chile continues to show signs that the Central Bank's intervention in the local greenback market is having an effect. The U.S. currency started the day down, and the Chilean peso is also favored by the rise in the price of copper.

"At the moment it has been seen that the objective (of the intervention) has been achieved, but we will pay close attention to the economic data that we will know in the United States in the next few days, as well as the news regarding world economic growth", says the head of trading studies at Capitaria, Ricardo Bustamante.

However, the initial rise is the lowest since the autonomous agency announced the injection of US$25 billion into the dollar market through various exchange instruments.

At the beginning of operations, the dollar lost $7.07 with respect to yesterday's close and was trading at $919.95. Thus, the greenback is heading for its third consecutive day down, where it accumulates a loss of $131.1.

According to Bloomberg data, the dollar in Chile is at its lowest level in three weeks.

The Chilean peso is also favored by the rise in the price of copper. The three-month reddish metal quotation gains 1.93% to a value of US$3.35 per pound.

"For today we expect a bearish day for the dollar against the peso, which could break $920 and go in search of $900 due to the appreciation that copper has brought, and due to the uncertainty before the US rate decision$, projects BeFX analyst Camilo Celedón.

However, the greenback at international level recovers again after three down days. The dollar index gained 0.24%.

Markets have cut expectations of a US interest rate hike of 100 basis points next week and now see a 23% probability of such a hike after authorities poured cold water on that option, notes Reuters.

"For the exchange rate we see a stable but downward price, thanks to the notorious advance in the copper price, the stable price of the dollar index and the still notorious effect of the Central Bank's intervention in our country, which practically sold half of its dollar reserve in order to control the value of the exchange rate", states XTB Latam's senior market analyst, Francisco Roman.

So far today, the Chilean peso is the sixth most appreciated currency in the world against the dollar and the second among the group of currencies of emerging countries, according to Bloomberg.

title: Chile's Finance Minister seeks to calm investors after turbulent week
text:
Chile's Finance Minister Mario Marcel assured investors that the nation's giant copper industry would remain competitive despite plans to raise taxes, and that the new government would protect the country's reputation for fiscal discipline.

His comments come after a week in which the peso depreciated to record lows, in part due to falling copper prices and political concerns over a new constitution and tax law, before recovering after central bank intervention.

"Chile is approaching tax reform with an open mind," Marcel said in an interview with Bloomberg TV. The government needs to secure funding for its social program and at the same time investment in the copper industry. "We have a competitive mining environment and we don't want to damage it," he said.

Marcel is in New York this week as part of the Chile Day event, where government officials and private company executives promote investments in the country. This is the first Chile Day since the start of the pandemic and the issue of tax reform has come up in Marcel's meetings in the United States.

Chile's Congress will begin discussion of the tax bill on Wednesday. President Gabriel Boric's administration seeks to raise revenues equivalent to 4.1% of gross domestic product, mainly by increasing personal income taxes, creating a wealth tax and increasing mining royalties.

The tax reform has been criticized by local mining companies. Fitch Ratings said earlier this month that, as initially proposed, it would weaken the sector's competitive position relative to global peers.

Peso advances

Marcel's visit comes just days after Chile's central bank announced a US$25 billion intervention program to prop up the peso, prompting a 13% rally in the currency in just three trading sessions.

The move capped a turbulent week in the currency market in which the peso extended its losses even after monetary policymakers raised the key interest rate by 75 basis points, more than many anticipated.

The central bank's intervention was "very timely," Marcel said, as in the days leading up to the announcement volatility had risen to unjustifiable levels and interest rate differentials had widened.

Marcel also commented that the days of early pension withdrawals, in which Chileans took more than US$50 billion out of their savings during the pandemic, were a thing of the past.

"There was a big turnaround in the discussion on the latest pension withdrawal with a large majority against the measure," Marcel said. "The authorities and MPs realized that withdrawals create far more harm than good."

title: Chile  tells U.S. investors about  foreign exchange intervention  and tax plans
text:
New York, 18 Jul. The Chilean government explained to US investors on Monday its latest intervention measures in the foreign exchange market and the tax reform plans of President Gabriel Boric, with the message that it continues to be "an open economy".

The "Chile Day" event organized by InBest and which had been planned as an occasion to "position Chile as a leading exporter of financial services in Latin America" was rather an exposition of the need for these economic policies of a government that a priori can be seen as less friendly to capital due to its leftist ideology.

The governor of the Chilean Central Bank, Rosanna Costa, and the Minister of Finance, Mario Marcel, spoke, explaining the expansive policies that Chile had to apply to get out of the pandemic crisis and how it has now had to apply adjustments in the face of a very high accumulated inflation (12.5% in the last 12 months) and a dollar at historic highs that exceeded the 1,000 peso barrier.

Costa emphasized that the country, although it has suffered an unprecedented shock in recent years, enjoys "a solid institutional framework" that will allow it to face the high public debt and, even more of a priority because it is now "the main concern", to aim at lowering inflation to 3% within two years, he stressed.

For his part, Marcel -an economist well regarded in the business world- acknowledged that his country is facing an unprecedented accumulation of problems: high raw material prices, rising private consumption, a historically expensive dollar and supply bottlenecks, which have forced his government to adopt restrictive monetary policies.

He took for granted that the recession will arrive this year, but he expressed hope that in early 2023 there will be a recovery, thanks to last Thursday's "successful intervention" in the exchange market, which in a few days allowed the exchange rate to drop below the psychological barrier of 1,000 pesos per dollar.

On the other hand, Marcel dedicated the last part of his speech to defend the fiscal reform planned by the Government to revert a fiscal distribution "currently seen as unfair" and also to correct the fact that the tax burden is now much lower than in other countries of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).

title: Dollar opens below 1,000 pesos after  Central Bank intervention
text:
Santiago de Chile, July 18. The U.S. currency continued to fall in Chile this Monday after the intervention announced by the Central Bank last Thursday, with an injection of 25 billion dollars to the market to contain a historic escalation above 1,000 pesos.

Although it is still at high levels, at the beginning of trading the US currency averaged 945 pesos, a fall of almost 3% and more than 100 pesos in two days, according to the Chilean Electronic Stock Exchange.

In addition, the rise in the price of copper played in favor of the Chilean currency, with futures fixed at 2.78 % at 3.32 dollars per pound of the red metal, the main export of the South American country.

The intervention announced by the Central Bank will be through the sale of spot dollars for an amount of up to 10 billion dollars, the sale of currency hedging instruments for an amount of up to 10 billion dollars and a currency swap program for an amount of up to 5 billion dollars from July 18 to September 30, 2022.

This move, expected by the markets, came on the same day that the dollar reached its all-time high of 1,051 pesos per unit and one day after the issuer raised benchmark interest rates by 75 points to 9.75% to try to curb inflation.

The Chilean economy grew by a historic 11.7% in 2021, after a sharp 5.8% drop in 2020 due to the pandemic, and recorded cumulative inflation of 7.2%, the highest in 14 years.

In May, the government lowered its growth forecast for 2022 from 3.5% to 1.5% and raised its 12-month cumulative inflation estimate for the end of the year to 8.9%.

The issuer did not make an intervention of such magnitude since March 2020 November 2019 (20 billion dollars), when the peso reached 828.36 units per dollar and the country was plunged into the biggest social crisis in its recent history, with protests that left at least thirty dead. EFE
