title: Dollar maintains its free fall after  Central Bank intervention  and copper price hike
text:
The dollar in Chile continues its downward trend, which started after the announcement of the Central Bank's intervention in the dollar market. In addition, the rise in the price of copper and the weakening of the greenback at international level give another hand to the Chilean peso.

At the beginning of trading, the dollar fell $33.72 after Friday's close and traded at a value of $944.78 . Thus, in two days, the US currency has lost more than $100 and continues to move away from the $1,000 barrier.

On the other hand, copper helps the Chilean peso after registering a rise in its three-month price. Copper futures are up 2.78% to a value of US$3.32 per pound.

Prices of copper and other industrial metals rebounded on Monday as investors bought back positions on news of government support for the economy in China, the main metals consumer, and a weaker dollar, Reuters noted.

"This is still a bear market rebound, and it is too early to predict whether this will turn into a consolidation and a recovery," Saxo Bank's head of commodity strategy in Copenhagen, Ole Hansen, told the news agency.

Meanwhile, the international dollar weakened again after falling on Friday on expectations that the next rate hike by the U.S. Federal Reserve (Fed) will not be 100 basis points and will be moderated to 75 basis points. The new forecasts are based on recent statements from Fed members.

Along these lines, the dollar index is down 0.47% from the previous close and is moving away from its 20-year high.

"It is possible that we may see some additional correction of the dollar in our country, to return in the coming days with possible rises considering the more fundamental fundamentals of the exchange rate", commented the head of trading studies at Capitaria, Ricardo Bustamante.

However, the senior market analyst of XTB Latam, Juan Ortiz Godoy, states that "the factors that are appreciating the US currency are still latent, so we could see higher levels in the exchange rate as the days go by while the fears of an economic recession continue to persist and copper continues to fall".

So far today, the Chilean peso is the currency that has appreciated the most against the dollar in the world, according to Bloomberg.

title: Central Bank intervention  in the dollar market should help bonds in  Chile
text:
The Central Bank of Chile's intervention in the dollar spot market announced Thursday night triggered the largest daily rally in the peso in four decades and lowered swap rates and bond yields. Its impact will reverberate through the market for weeks.

The bank plans to sell US$10 billion in the spot market by September 30, plus a similar amount of foreign exchange hedges and US$5 billion in swaps. The peso appreciated as much as 9.9% on Friday following the announcement.

How the dollar market works: Banks, brokers and more than US$1.2 billion traded per dayThe peso's new strength should help restore the local bond market.

"We expect greater liquidity in fixed income markets and a consequent fall in long-term yields," analysts at Larrain Vial, including head of research, Leonardo Suarez, wrote in a report.

The rebound in the peso eased the outlook for import costs and inflation, prompting a 22 basis point drop in two-year swap rates on Friday from an all-time high of 10.05%. The yield on Chilean Treasury bonds maturing in 2026 fell 35 basis points on the same day, while one-year break-even inflation plunged to 9.5% from an all-time high of 10.2%.

"The fall in the exchange rate should imply a moderation of inflation expectations, this should benefit nominal rates over UF rates," said Marco Gallardo, deputy fixed income manager at BICE Inversiones. However, in the short term he still prefers to bet on short UF bonds, considering that inflation will be higher in the coming months as the peso recovers, he said.

Falling from highsThere are still structural factors that will slow the adjustment in fixed income, said Sergio Lehmann, chief economist at BCI. Bond recovery "will be happening anyway, but without reaching the values of a few years ago," he commented. "In that sense there is already damage in our markets."

Crisis, what crisis?It was a bold move on the part of the central bank, given that they only have US$45.8 billion in foreign currency reserves, which represents about 5.2 months of imports. They had little choice, however, after the Finance Ministry's announcement that it planned to sell US$5 billion had almost no impact on the market a few weeks ago.

"This is probably one of the most successful interventions by the central bank in its history of interventions," Jorge Selaive, chief economist at Scotiabank Chile, said in a tweet on Friday. The program just goes into effect today.

The plan is big enough to have an impact, but it will probably take several sessions for the market to fully absorb its impact, said Nathan Pincheira, chief economist at Fynsa, who forecast the peso could reach 920 pesos to the U.S. dollar in the coming weeks. The currency closed at 974 pesos to the dollar on Friday.

Before the central bank's intervention, the peso had depreciated 21% since the beginning of June. Alvaro Vivanco, director of emerging markets strategy at NatWest Markets, described the situation as a "full-blown currency crisis". It remains the worst performing currency in the world during that period, even after Friday's rally.

Confidence in the peso had fallen so low that it even gave up 4% on Thursday, the day after monetary policymakers raised the key interest rate by 75 basis points to 9.75%.

In an interview on Friday, central bank president Rosanna Costa said the foreign exchange market retained adequate liquidity, but that the board was concerned about the "cumulative effect" of peso volatility on other markets. She also emphasized that the measures were aimed at "making the peso more stable" and not directly at the level of the currency.

title: Central Bank  of  Chile intervenes  in  foreign exchange  market
text:
The Central Bank's intervention was highly expected by the market, given the significant increase in volatility in the foreign exchange market. The intervention is appropriate because the market had been depreciating in addition to what the fundamentals indicated.

Martina Ogaz, analyst at Euroamerica

The Board of the Central Bank of Chile announced that, in order to facilitate the Chilean economy's adjustment to uncertain and changing domestic and external conditions, it decided to implement a program of foreign exchange intervention and preventive liquidity provision in dollars, for up to US$25 billion, starting next Monday, July 18, through September 30, 2022.

Through a statement published on Thursday night on the entity's official website, it pointed out that the external determinants of the exchange rate in Chile have continued to deteriorate "significantly. In particular, since the beginning of June the global dollar has appreciated about 7% and the price of copper has fallen approximately 30 percent. In a context of local uncertainty that remains high, this has continued to put downward pressure on the Chilean peso".

In recent days, however, they acknowledged that "the peso depreciation has occurred with unusually high intensity and volatility, which has strained the price formation of the exchange market. The persistence of this scenario increases the likelihood of significant distortions in the functioning of the financial market in general".

In particular, the intervention in the foreign exchange market considers: the sale of spot dollars for an amount of up to 10 billion dollars and the sale of foreign exchange hedging instruments for an amount of up to 10 billion dollars.

The monetary effects in local currency of the operations of this intervention will be duly sterilized, explained the bank, "so that the provision of liquidity in pesos is consistent with the monetary policy rate".

Regarding the provision of dollar liquidity, although the dollar money market is functioning adequately, the Board considered it appropriate to offer a "preemptive" foreign exchange swap program for up to 5 billion dollars. This will be complemented by a peso liquidity program through over-the-counter REPO operations at the same maturities.

The Central Bank will inform at the end of each week the amount and other terms and conditions of the following week's auctions. It will also publish timely information about the operations carried out, indicating in aggregate form the amounts of these operations. The Board reiterated that it will continue to use all the tools at its disposal to maintain the normal functioning of domestic and external payments, and that inflation will remain within the 3% target over the two-year policy horizon.

For her part, the Central Bank's highest authority, Rosanna Costa, admitted that "it was a complicated decision. Our objective is for the exchange rate to be at a level more consistent with its fundamentals".

Following the announcement of the intervention, the dollar recorded a sharp decline on Friday, after a successive wave of record highs that took the currency above $1,050 in Thursday's session. At Friday's opening, the dollar traded at $997.00, down $54 from Thursday's close, then moved to $1,000 levels before dropping again and deepening its retreat to close at $978.50, down $72.5.

Samuel Carrasco, senior economist at Credicorp Capital, commented on the announcement: "We value positively the magnitude of the intervention program, which in turn, should be complemented with a somewhat hawkish monetary policy path and reinforcing the message that rates will remain high for most of 2023".

For his part, Sergio Lehmann, chief economist at BCI, considered that "there were sufficient arguments for intervention".

title: Who are the favorites to replace Boris Johnson in the United Kingdom?
text:
The former Minister of Finance Rishi Sunak and the Deputy Minister of International Trade Penny Mordaunt, obtained enough support to pass to the second round of votes to elect the successor of the British Prime Minister, Boris Johnson, reported the television channel 'Sky News'.

According to this media, Sunak has the support of no less than 50 party colleagues and Mordaunt, at least 30. To advance to the second round a candidate must have the support of at least 30 members of the Conservative Party. Among the candidates who made it through to the second round on July 13 were: former Finance Minister Rishi Sunak; Foreign Secretary Liz Truss; Finance Minister Nadhim Zahawi; former Foreign Secretary Jeremy Hunt; Deputy International Trade Minister Penny Mordaunt; House of Commons committee chairman Tom Tugendhat; Attorney General for England and Wales Suella Braverman; former Equalities Minister Kemi Badenoch.

Later in the day, Graham Brady, chairman of the 1922 Committee, or the Conservative Private Members' Committee, announced that six candidates for the position of U.K. prime minister advanced to the second round of voting. The second round of voting will be held on July 14.

A total of 11 MPs declared their desire to run for Conservative leader and British prime minister, but three of them - Transport Minister Grant Shapps, former Health Minister Sajid Javid and former Conservative Party deputy prime minister Rehman Chishti - withdrew from the race. A candidate must have the support of at least 30 party members to advance to the second round, and more may be held until only two contenders remain. The winner will then be elected by the entire Conservative Party membership, which currently numbers about 200,000, with voting to be conducted by postal ballot. Boris Johnson, in office as Prime Minister since July 2019, announced his resignation following a flurry of resignations from his ministers and senior officials.

An unprecedented crisis in the British government broke out after a sex scandal with MP Christopher Pincher, a Johnson supporter, accused of harassing two visitors to a London club. Johnson, who will remain in office until a new Chief of Staff is appointed, leaves the United Kingdom mired in a deep economic crisis and with the highest inflation recorded since 1982.

"The Council of the Central Bank of Chile, in order to facilitate the adjustment of the Chilean economy to the uncertain and changing internal and external conditions, has decided to implement a program of foreign exchange intervention and preventive provision of liquidity in dollars, for an amount of up to 25 billion dollars starting next Monday [July 18] and until September 30, 2022," the agency stated in a press release.

The Central Bank detailed that the intervention in the exchange market contemplates the sale of spot dollars for an amount of up to 10 billion dollars, in addition to the sale of exchange hedging instruments for a similar amount.

"Since the beginning of June, the dollar at a global level has appreciated close to 7% and the price of copper [Chile's main export product] has fallen approximately 30%, this, in a context of local uncertainty that remains high, pressures the Chilean peso downwards", explained the issuing agency.

This month in Chile the dollar surpassed for the first time in history the barrier of 1,000 Chilean pesos, and this July 14 closed at 1,051 pesos.

title: Intervention  announcements lower the dollar in  Chile  and increase the purchasing power of travelers
text:
The dollar reacted downward on Friday in Chile after the announcement by the Central Bank of an exchange and liquidity intervention of up to 25 billion dollars to facilitate the adjustment of the economy in view of the uncertain internal and external conditions that have taken the currency to historic prices in the South American country.

The U.S. currency fell as much as 50 pesos at the beginning of the day's trading, almost the same 51 pesos it rose on Thursday, when it reached 1,062 pesos, making it the largest increase since 1999. After midday it averaged 992 pesos.

The market reacted to the announcement of intervention by the Central Bank, which on Thursday night stated that "in order to facilitate the adjustment of the Chilean economy to the uncertain and changing internal and external conditions'', it will begin on Monday, July 18, a program of exchange intervention and preventive provision of liquidity for up to 25,000 million dollars. The measure will be extended until September 30.

Simultaneously, the Chilean peso strengthened after a depreciation that "has occurred with an unusually high intensity and volatility", which since the beginning of the year has been around 20%, according to the Central Bank. The appreciation of the local currency occurred despite a new fall in the value of copper, Chile's main export, which has contracted by around 30% since the beginning of June.

Chile imports all the oil it consumes, as well as natural gas and diesel, and almost 2/3 of the products that make up the basket used to calculate inflation are imported.

The advance in the price of the dollar occurs in a context of global strengthening of the currency and the strong fall of copper, which is also hit by the drop in the growth of China, the main buyer of the Chilean red metal.

The autonomous Central Bank described the measures adopted by its Board as exceptional and said that they are in line with its monetary policy, which responds to an inflationary target and exchange rate flexibility.

Finance Minister Mario Marcel said that "we believe that it has been appropriate that it has used its powers for this purpose''.

Chile's 12-month inflation is 12.5%, and so far this year stands at 7.1%, more than double the Central Bank's target of 3%, which it expects to recover in about two years, after further adjustments to its interest rate, which it raised from 9% to 9.75% on Wednesday.

title: CORRECTED-UPDATE 2- Chile central bank  announces $25 billion  intervention  amid U.S. dollar advance
text:
(Corrects sales program calendar to reflect end date of September 30, not July 30)

SANTIAGO, July 15 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank agreed to a $25 billion intervention in the foreign exchange market due to the galloping advance of the U.S. dollar in recent weeks.

In a statement released Thursday night, the bank said the peso has depreciated with unusually high intensity and volatility over the last few days, putting pressure on the prices of the foreign exchange market.

"The persistence of this scenario raises the probability that significant distortions will be generated in the functioning of the financial market in general," the statement said.

The announcement boosted the local currency, which gained 4.73% on Friday morning, dropping below 1,000 units per dollar. The previous day it closed with a drop of 3.7% to the minimum historical 1,045.80/1,046.10 units per dollar.

The bank said it decided to intervene due to the U.S. dollar's strong global advance since June, the drop in the price of copper, Chile's main export, and "local uncertainty."

"This is a welcome development, particularly if combined with a decisive conventional monetary policy strategy," Alberto Ramos, an economist at Goldman Sachs, said in a report.

"However, there are limits to what the central bank can achieve given the very challenging domestic and external context and when taking into account the limited amount of foreign exchange reserves."

The bank announced a $10 billion sales program on the spot market from July 18 to September 30 and the sale of foreign exchange hedging instruments for the same amount.

"The monetary effects in local currency of the operations of this intervention will be duly sterilized, so that the provision of liquidity in pesos is consistent with the monetary policy rate," the bank said.

Additionally, to increase the provision of liquidity in dollars, it will offer a currency swap plan for up to $5 billion, complemented by a liquidity program in pesos.

"These exceptional measures are consistent with the monetary policy scheme, based on an inflation target and exchange rate flexibility," the statement said.

Earlier in the week, the bank had said that the current deterioration of the local currency has not significantly affected the financial system, although it said it would continue to assess the situation in order to act if necessary.

title: Chile intervenes  in the exchange rate with US$ 25 billion to defend the peso
text:
Chile's central bank announced plans to support the peso after the country's currency plummeted to a record low, fueling inflation that is already at nearly four times the target.

Thursday night, the country's monetary authority said it will carry out a $25 billion foreign exchange intervention between July 18 and September 30. The plan includes up to $10 billion in spot market dollar sales and currency hedging that could amount to the same amount.

"With the global recession narrative beginning to dominate the investment landscape, the Chilean central bank is trying to stop the downward momentum in its currency," said Todd Schubert, head of fixed income research at Bank of Singapore. The fall in copper prices has led to a sharp depreciation of the peso, as Chile is the world's largest copper producer, he said.

The Chilean peso fell to a record low of 1,060.40 per dollar on Thursday as the U.S. currency strengthened globally and copper prices plunged. The peso has already depreciated nearly 19 percent this year.

The announcement of the intervention came after Finance Minister Mario Marcel said the government was studying ways to alleviate the effects of the weaker currency and urged the central bank to comment on the matter.

Monetary policy makers have already extended aggressive interest rate hikes in an effort to tame annual inflation that probably rose to 12.7 percent in June, according to estimates in a Bloomberg survey. A weaker currency makes imported goods more expensive, adding to price pressures.

Political uncertainty is also hurting the peso. Chile is approaching a referendum on Sept. 4 on a proposed new constitution. Polls show that more voters are inclined to reject the draft document, while a bill to reduce the majority needed to reform the current charter is making its way through congress.

The central bank implemented exchange rate measures in 2019, when the peso collapsed amid mass street protests, and again in 2020, at the start of the pandemic. The policies included dollar sales and currency swaps.

title: The  Central Bank  of  Chile  decided to  intervene  with the sale of USD 25 billion to contain the historic rise of the dollar.
text:
The Central Bank of Chile announced its intervention with a USD 25 billion program in view of the historic rise of the dollar that has been affecting the country in recent weeks.

The Central Bank's intervention consists of the sale of spot dollars for up to USD 10 billion and the sale of foreign exchange hedging instruments for the same amount. "The Council of the Central Bank of Chile, in order to facilitate the adjustment of the Chilean economy to the uncertain and changing internal and external conditions, has decided to implement a program of foreign exchange intervention and preventive provision of liquidity in dollars, for an amount of up to USD$ 25 billion starting next Monday, July 18 and until September 30, 2022″, communicated the entity.

Likewise, the Central Bank stated that "the Board considers appropriate to offer, on a precautionary basis, a foreign exchange swap program for an amount of up to USD 5,000 million. This will be complemented by a liquidity program in pesos through over-the-counter REPO operations at the same terms".

In Chile, the dollar has climbed to historic prices. During this Thursday, the US currency closed at $1,051 (USD 1.05) and this intervention of the Central Bank is added to the "verbal intervention" of the beginning of the week when the entity stated that it would implement measures "if necessary".

In addition, the Central Bank of Chile raised its interest rate by 75 basis points to 9.75%. The agency explained that this decision was applied due to the implications of global inflation and the decision of the U.S. Federal Reserve to increase its interest rate by 75 basis points.

Details of the intervention

In a conversation with Infobae, the general manager of Empresas Golden, Wilfredo Araya, commented that the Central Bank's intervention "will be carried out in different stages so that the outflow of dollars from the country is gradual", pushing down the value of the exchange rate.

Wilfredo Araya explained that one of these stages is the spot sale or instantaneous sale of dollars. "To cope with a rapid fall in the exchange rate is the direct sale of current dollar reserves by the Central Bank, equivalent to USD 10 billion, which is what is known as spot selling."

Another stage of the Central Bank's decision is the foreign exchange intervention for another USD 10 billion. The expert explained that "in the general market, different entities such as importers or exporters hedge against risk volatility through contracts such as forward contracts, where I fix the price for a certain period of time with the option of renewing the contract if I wish to continue protecting the exchange rate". In this case, the Central Bank, as counterparty, "would decide to close the contracts and sell the dollar forward contracts. The liquidation of these contracts through the sale of dollars would mean that we would be talking about USD 10 billion". The effect of this would have a short-term impact, but not instantaneous.

Finally, for USD 5 billion, a swap program will be carried out, which "in simple terms, is a program regarding the valuation of the dollar as a result of interest rates between connections, or transactions, with different countries". As long as interest rates continue to increase, "the transaction cost gap in different countries, which is known as swap, has a greater increase, and this has an impact on the price". In view of this, what the Central Bank would do is "to make a swap program so that this transactional cost of dollars with international entities, international economies, also has a much lower impact".

title: Dollar sets new high in  Chile ,  Central Bank  does not rule out  intervention
text:
The dollar remained this Tuesday in Chile above 1,000 pesos and reached the historical maximum of 1,026 pesos, after the Central Bank announced on Monday in a statement that it does not rule out taking containment measures.

According to local operators, the US currency is quoted between a maximum value of 1,026.43 pesos and a minimum of 996.80 pesos, awaiting the closing of the day.

The day before, the Board of the Central Bank assured in a statement that the exchange rate "could obstruct the price formation of the exchange market and stress the evolution of other sectors of the financial market".

This "would require the Bank's intervention in order to ensure the proper functioning of the economy," the report added.

Experts blame the escalation of the dollar, which has been at a high for days, on the context of the global strengthening of the currency and the fall in the value of copper, the country's main export, due in part to the restrictions that China maintains in several cities due to covid-19.

"The price of copper has fallen nearly 20% since the beginning of June, which has generated a deterioration in the terms of trade of our economy" and at the local level "the significant current account deficit, high inflation and uncertainty levels have increased the sensitivity of the economy," the statement said.

According to the London Metal Exchange, the red metal, of which Chile is the world's main producer, fell to 3.3 dollars per pound on Wednesday, a 3.31% decrease with respect to the previous day and its lowest value in more than a year and a half.

Key meeting of the Central Bank

A key meeting starts this afternoon: the Monetary Policy Meeting that the central bank holds every month to decide on possible changes in the benchmark interest rate.

This rate is already at its highest value since 2001 (9%) after a 75-point increase last June, and on Wednesday it will be known whether or not a new increase will take place in order to contain the inflation that the country is going through.

Chile accumulates a 12.5% price increase in 12 months, the highest level since 1994, and according to experts consulted by the Central Bank could close the year at 11%.

After a historic GDP rebound of 11.7% in 2021, the largest expansion in four decades, the Chilean economy is showing signs of cooling and estimates of the issuing entity point to GDP growth this year between 1% and 2%. (I)

title: BofA estimates that the rate will reach 10% in  Chile  this year and does not rule out  Central Bank intervention
text:
When the dollar touched $ 1,000 again, and after it was known that in June inflation advanced 12.5% in twelve months, all eyes are once again on the Central Bank. This Wednesday, Bank of America (BofA) will announce the adjustment that the Central Bank will apply to the monetary policy rate (TPM), which is expected to be 50 basis points, leaving it at 9.5% .

The U.S. investment bank expects that Wednesday's adjustment will be followed by another of the same magnitude in September - higher than the 25 bps previously contemplated - which would raise the interest rate to 10% by the end of this cycle, above the 9.75% previously anticipated.

The financial entity expects "aggressive language" from the Board of the issuing institute in this week's meeting, as a result of the pressures and the Chilean peso's pass-through, and the higher inflation expectations in the latest surveys. "We expect the Central Bank to convey a higher rate peak and forward guidance, which will entail a delay in the expected rate cuts," reads a report released on Monday.

The analysis also recalls that the bank's corridor contemplated rate cuts since December. But BofA expects the downward adjustments to begin in March, "amid the looming recession," which would lead to the end of next year's MPR reaching 7.5%. In addition, the investment bank estimates that this year inflation will close at 11%, falling to 5.5% by the end of 2023.

And the dollar? BofA's view is that the peso's weakness this year is due "mainly to weakening global fundamentals", as a result of the copper price falling 20% so far this year, the increase in oil prices and the increase in interest rates in the US.

"Chile has suffered one of the worst terms of trade shocks in the region - copper exports, oil imports - and we see the current account deficit rising to 7% of GDP this year," the bank warns.

The entity recalls that last year the pressure on the peso was "clearly explained by internal factors, including greater political uncertainty due to the political transition and the risks of the Constitution". Now, the agency considers that if the Magna Carta proposal is rejected -now its base scenario given recent polls- "this could provide some support to the peso, although we believe that the noise about changes to the Constitution will persist".

The analysis also states that while they do not rule out a dollar selling program by the Central Bank, this is not their base scenario either. "We see more likely a targeted foreign exchange intervention on days of excessive market fluctuations not driven by fundamentals and low liquidity," the report states, which specifies that some recent days saw "excessive fluctuation."

"We believe that the external weaknesses of the Chilean economy - very high current account deficit, private capital outflows - make it more difficult for the Central Bank to sell a large amount of dollars," they detail, adding that "more aggressive language and slower cut guidance should also help the currency."

title: Concern in Chile over the effects of record dollar prices
text:
The dollar in Chile suffered a strong rise never seen before, which has awakened concern among experts about the consequences this may have on domestic and foreign trade.

The dollar in Chile reached $1,000 for the first time in history and minutes later the currency "moderated", dropping to $970. The rise of the North American currency was registered around midday on Wednesday.

The day began with the dollar at a value of $959, eight pesos more than last Tuesday's close, and after that it began to rise precipitously, according to the Chilean Electronic Stock Exchange website. At 10:05 a.m., the North American currency was at $963.75 and exactly one hour later it reached $975. However, at 11:22 a.m. it reached $980.65, and a few minutes before 11:40 a.m. it was quoted at $1,000.

At the same time that this was happening, the value of copper closed in the red again. Copper is Chile's main export product, and according to the Chilean Copper Commission (Cochilco), the metal was at the price of USD 3.414 per pound, which represents a 3.61% drop. This is the lowest value recorded for this commodity since November 2020.

Reactions to the historic rise

For Wilfredo Araya, executive director of Empresas Golden, the price of the currency is "historic" and is consecrated "as a strong resistance in the face of possible new rises". The expert added that these increases would be "justified by the strong fears of a world recession that would start in the United States", which would spread "to the main economies of the world and to the emerging markets".

Araya pointed out that in Chile this rise could mean a new increase in the interest rate fixed by the Central Bank in its Monetary Policy Meetings. In case the latter happens, "it would bring strong inflationary pressures in our country. With this, it is estimated that the Unidad de Fomento (UF), in the short term, could reach $35,000 (USD 36.05)".

The UF is a unit of measurement exclusive to Chile that is used to express the prices of leases, purchase and sale of apartments in Chile. It is also used by Isapres to define their prices to citizens and even by insurance companies to charge their premiums. It is not identified as a currency, but rather "as an indicator of the value of the Chilean currency, which is increasing in line with inflation".

Finally, Araya emphasized that it is necessary to be attentive "to what will be the decision of the Central Bank" of Chile and if "there is an intervention, particularly in the sale of dollars" to "contain the rise in the exchange rate" in the country.

Political uncertainty in Chile

The rise of the dollar has provoked a debate in Chile. For José Raúl Godoy, head of Analysis of the investment company XTB Latam, the political uncertainty in Chile would also influence the North American currency. "In domestic matters, political uncertainty has influenced, given by the exit plebiscite, together with the economic uncertainty from the tax reform. This is generating a depreciation effect of the Chilean peso, which in fact, is one of the most depreciated globally and therefore we see an increase in the exchange rate", said Godoy to Emol.com.

Another point that has been debated is the possibility that the dollar will officially go above $1,000 in Chile, something that is not so impossible. "The greenback at $1,000 pesos is already a reality and we should not be surprised if we continue to see an uptrend that, both technically and fundamentally, are fully justified," said Renato Campos, chief analyst at Admiral Markets.

Finally, Chile's Minister of Finance, Mario Marcel, called for calm on all sides in the face of this rise. "We must be calm about the fact that factors that in the past made Chile especially vulnerable to the exchange rate are no longer there today, we do not have exchange mismatches in companies or in the financial system that could generate an impact", said the Secretary of State.

title: Dollar rises sharply at the open and sets new record high above $940 amid global strengthening of the  currency
text:
The exchange rate began Tuesday's session under pressure, as has been the trend in recent days, with a jump of $ 12.6 with respect to yesterday's close, standing at $ 940.1 at the opening .

The depreciation of the Chilean peso is in line with the global advance of the US currency. The dollar index - which measures the greenback against the main world currencies - expanded by more than 1%. Likewise, the euro, which is one of the currencies with the greatest weight within this index, succumbs and falls to its lowest level in the last 20 years.

The euro falls to a 20-year low against the dollar and parity is only a matter of time.

Fears of a global economic recession are once again the main concern among investors, which has increased their appetite for the dollar and turned it into a safe-haven asset.

Another factor hitting the Chilean peso is copper. The commodity fell 2.85% on the London Metal Exchange, reaching US$ 3.541 per pound.

According to Cochilco, the downward cycle in the price of the red mineral has been influenced in part by "the risk of recession increased as the rhetoric of aggressive monetary policy rate hikes to reduce inflation in the United States and Europe takes hold in the short term".

The Commission recalled on Friday that "during June price dynamics were dominated by global macroeconomic risks and their impact on demand for the metal."

XTB Latam's senior analyst, Juan Ortiz, mentioned that "as long as market fears of a recession continue, where analysts and large investment banks are increasingly raising the probability of a recession, we will continue to see falls in the price of the metal and thus directly impact the exchange rate".

Under this scenario, the head of research at Capitaria, Ricardo Bustamante, indicated that it is not ruled out that the dollar "could go for new historical highs, in the midst of a further fall in the price of copper". In fact, he did not rule out that the U.S. currency could reach $ 950 under this scenario.

He added that "the local uncertainty before the exit plebiscite and due to the proposed tax reform is an additional ingredient that supports the weakening of the peso, generating an additional advance of the dollar in our country".

In the same line, the chief analyst of Admiral Markets, Renato Campos, remarked that two months before the exit plebiscite on the proposed new Constitution drafted by the Constitutional Convention, "it generates uncertainty among investors due to its result and the impact it may have on local politics and economy".

Bci Estudios recalled in a report sent today to its clients that "the Chilean peso has lost value significantly in the last two months, due to the expectations of important rate increases by central banks of developed countries, especially the Fed, which has led to an outflow of foreign flows".

The entity pointed out that "the exchange rate is at its historical maximums and its deviation of variables is close to levels of possible intervention by the Central Bank of Chile, adding to what has been done by the Treasury".

title: New dollar records do not move the  Central Bank  and remains firm in its position of not  intervening
text:
The records set every day by the dollar for the Central Bank have an explanation and that is why the autonomous organization remains firm in its position of not intervening in the U.S. currency market in Chile. The vice-president of the entity, Pablo García, also pointed out that their efforts are in containing inflation and not in the exchange rate policy, unless it presents movements that cannot be explained.

"There are many reasons that I could use to understand the dynamics and direction of the exchange rate issue, but for the Central Bank's effect, we must remember that if the concern is inflation, the instrument is monetary policy. The exchange rate policy does not have the objective of maintaining an inflation control strategy, that is something we left behind many years ago", said García in the framework of an Icare seminar.

The dollar again surpasses $930 in the face of a sharp drop in copper prices.In the activity called "Strengthening the Capital Market towards the Future" at the meeting "Chilean Capital Market: Improvements in Financing for SMEs and Individuals", García defended the Central Bank's position, stating that the dollar is rising internationally, the price of copper is falling, we are facing "the worst quarter in equities in the world for many decades" and we have a "high deficit in our current account", among other reasons.

Economic activity confirms signs of deceleration: Imacec grew 6.4% in May"We have to take into account that it is not enough to observe exchange rate movements, but one has to see movements that are not substantially linked to more fundamental dynamics," he added.

The economist also highlighted that the measure of having a floating exchange rate allows for a better cushioning of external impacts, and reiterated that the Central Bank will only act in the dollar market in exceptional situations.

Jorge Selaive: "If the Central Bank is saying that the fall of the peso is explained by copper and the appreciation of the dollar I would suggest that they review their models"."Intervention has to be linked to movements that are producing significant financial tensions, liquidity problems, that there are problems with our fixed income and this is not being observed", concluded the economist, who invited people to give their opinion on the behavior of the Central Bank in this matter, taking into consideration "the policy framework that we have and see through it how one takes certain eventual intervention decisions".

title: Dollar opened lower on Tuesday after Treasury  intervention  and copper rally
text:
The exchange rate fell by $10.80 at the opening of trading on Tuesday. The parity was trading at $904.60 at the time of this note after a strong rise of $14.10 on Friday to its historical maximum value ($915.40).

Ricardo Bustamante, head of trading studies at Capitaria, stated that the dollar has shown a strong fall at the beginning of the week after last Friday's intervention by the Ministry of Finance, who will sell US$ 5,000 million dollars for two months, with a cap of US$ 200 million per day. "This measure seeks to generate a weakening of the dollar locally, after having approached $920, its highest value in history, amid external and internal factors that supported this rally," he said.

"While this intervention could generate some additional weakening in the short term, close attention to the other fundamentals of the exchange rate, especially copper which has been key in recent times," he warned, adding that "if we see falls in the red metal again due to fears about the global economy, added to local uncertainty as we approach the plebiscite on the new constitution, it is likely that the rises in the U.S. currency will soon return."

Nataly Venegas, FXGlobe market analyst, noted that "internationally this morning it has been flat (0.6%). This is due to the decline in inflation expectations that prompted a reassessment of the outlook for aggressive interest rate hikes, although market volatility dampened a broader decline."

At the local level, he specified, "the strong rebound of copper is coupled with the strength of the Chilean peso against the dollar. With a variation of 1.51%, the red metal touched 3.8 usd/lb. This generates bullish expectations, as the market would be assuming the deceleration. In addition, the intervention to be carried out by the Treasury in Chile for the next 60 days is considerable (...) In the local market, in terms of volume, US$800 million are traded, so the daily amount to be sold by the Treasury generates pressure for the dollar, taking a bearish path during these two months. It is likely that this morning we will find ourselves with a downward price, towards the $880/$850 areas".

Juan Ortiz Godoy, senior market analyst at XTB Latam, believes that the exchange rate will continue its upward trend "where it could seek $900 as a first correction target and at the same time act as support. However, we will have to see the real impact of the Treasury's decision to sell US$ 5 billion to counteract the escalation".

title: Lowering the dollar by secretariat?
text:
At its June meeting, the US Federal Reserve raised its monetary policy rate by 75bp, above market expectations, generating global concern about the possible recession that could affect the world's main economy. In his testimony last Wednesday, Chairman Powell pointed out that both the interest rate hike and those to come could cause a recession, and that avoiding it depends on factors beyond the Fed's capabilities, with a nod to fiscal policy and banking supervision. He also reiterated that it is not possible to fail in this task and that inflation in the United States must return to 2% annually.

This scenario generated a substantial drop in the price of commodities, where copper has been substantially affected, falling by 16.7%, from US$ 4.55 per pound at the beginning of the month to US$ 3.79 per pound today, which implies an annualized loss of exports of US$ 9.6 billion. Additionally, it is usual for the prices of a large part of our export basket to be affected in correlation with what has been observed with the red metal. In turn, the financial angle of the rise in interest rates has raised the dollar index by close to 3%, which explains part of the devaluation of currencies such as the Australian dollar and the Japanese yen.

However, both the real effect, the expected cycle for U.S. activity, and the financial effect precipitated a substantial devaluation of the Chilean peso, which rose from $857 per dollar in mid-June to $920 in the latest transactions, implying a drop of 7.3%. Given that nearly 70% of the CPI basket is made up of tradable goods, concern has arisen about the pass-through coefficient to domestic prices and the difficulty this implies for monetary policy.

"Given that close to 70% of the CPI basket is composed of tradable goods, concern has arisen about the pass-through coefficient to domestic prices and the difficulty this implies for monetary policy."

In this context, the Ministry of Finance announced the liquidation of up to US$ 5 billion, with a daily maximum of US$ 200 million, for the next 60 days. This is not the first time that the Treasury carries out this action and in fact, in 2020 it sold US$ 15 billion, which rose to US$ 33.9 billion during last year. These sales respond to the cash planning of an institution that receives part of its income in dollars, while most of its expenses are in Chilean pesos.

Notwithstanding the above, it is necessary to specify this operation in greater detail, since the available balance in dollars in other Public Treasury assets at the end of April was US$ 2.7 billion, while the FEES and the FRP were US$ 14.3 billion. I imagine that the monies held in the latter two funds will not be used for dollar/peso cash programming.

Probably the worst expected effect of this decision is that the market will perceive it as an exchange intervention to lower the value of the dollar in Chile. This would be very unfortunate, since, given the overall characteristics of the phenomenon, it will not have a significant effect on the nominal exchange rate, as previous interventions by the issuing institution have shown.

title: Marcel dismisses government actions and ability to influence the dollar, but warns that impact on inflation is minor
text:
The Minister of Finance, Mario Marcel, dismissed the Government's capacity to be able to take measures that could intervene in the dollar market in Chile after the quotation of the US currency broke milestones every day. The Secretary of State pointed in this matter to the Central Bank and added that the work of the Executive must go on the side of how to cushion the effects of this rise in inflation.

"The Government cannot do much in exchange matters, because the sovereign funds have a very limited magnitude and very different from the Central Bank, which has international reserves, liquidity lines and has other mechanisms that it can use if it so decides", said Marcel in a press conference in La Moneda after a cabinet meeting.

Dollar continues unstoppable and registers new record highs in the face of the copper plungeThe former president of the Central Bank took the opportunity to explain that the current rise of the dollar is explained by the weakening of copper and the monetary rate policy promoted by the US Federal Reserve, among other factors.

Former Minister of Finance Rodrigo Valdés adds to the position of not intervening in the dollar market despite the new historical maximum."We have no control over those phenomena that occur at a global level and that are the ones that are pressuring the dollar at the margin. Now the exchange rate policy in Chile, as we well know, is the responsibility of the Central Bank", he added.

However, Marcel contextualized that the rise in the dollar does have an impact on inflation in Chile, but that in this case it would be lower as it is a rise generated by international and not local factors.

"But of course the increase is important and we will see how we can reinforce some protection and support mechanisms that we have implemented, which have the capacity to adjust to how inflation behaves in the country", concluded the Minister of Finance.

Tax reform The Minister of Finance was also asked about the tax reform, which will be presented next week. In this regard, Marcel highlighted the process of citizen dialogues on this issue and reiterated that this tax initiative is focused on people with higher incomes and mining.

"This is a reform in which the greatest contribution is going to come from those with higher incomes and from the sources of evasion and avoidance, which in our consultations emerged as one of the things that most outrages people", commented Marcel.

On the mining side, the Secretary of State will take the mining royalty proposal to the Senate, where such an initiative is being discussed.

"The details will be made known on the same day that the tax reform is presented", added Marcel, who scheduled for July 1st the activity to deliver the project in relation to taxes.

title: Former Finance Minister Rodrigo Valdés supports position of not  intervening  in dollar market despite new record high
text:
The dollar in Chile continues its tendency to set a new record high each day, and experts support the position that the Central Bank should not intervene, for now, in the exchange market, despite the fact that the U.S. currency is already above $900.

The dollar continues unstoppable and records new historical highs in the face of the copper plunge.Now it was the turn of former Finance Minister Rodrigo Valdés. "The strength of the intervention is very limited. The effects every time the Central Bank intervenes are seen over time, but they are not a magic ball that will return the exchange rate to $800, they are just a few pesos", said the economist in an interview with Radio Infinita.

Corbo dismisses CBintervention for the rise of the dollar in Chile: "You have to be Tarzan to change its appreciation".His position is similar to that of the former president of the Central Bank, Vittorio Corbo, and the current vice-president of the autonomous organization, Pablo García.

The former Secretary of State during Michelle Bachelet's second government also warned that the dollar reserves are not enough to venture into an intervention in this market.

Central Bank reaffirms decision not to intervene in the dollar market in spite of new historical quotation."They are not to play at intervening as an Asian country, that is very dangerous, because one can run out of reserves when one really needs them", he added.

The Catholic University academic also pointed out that "there is nothing unusual in the market to suggest that an intervention would make it work better, and therefore, the effect would be very minimal".

In this line, Valdés dismissed that the Central Bank should intervene in the dollar market in case there are pressures or calls from the political sector, such as the Congress. "Politicians are always going to be arguing against the Central Bank. It is part of why it has autonomy," he concluded.

Tax reformThe economist participated in the tax dialogues and called for an evaluation of the process once it is complete. This, in view of voices such as that of the president of the Confederation of Production and Commerce (CPC), Juan Sutil, who expected more pre-legislative work, and in view of the other positions that already highlight the process for having promoted meetings on the subject.

"It is important to calibrate, because we are seeing many pieces together. To see that the result of everything together does not cause too many serious problems for the investment. I understand that the structure is well thought out, but now we have to see that things come together," commented the director of the General Electricity Company (CGE), a company owned by the Chinese giant State Grid International Development (SGID).

The former Finance Minister also recalled that the last two tax reforms, during the second terms of Bachelet and Sebastián Piñera, underwent "radical, very profound changes in the process".

On the other hand, Valdés put forward his ideas of disintegrating the tax system in order to simplify it and expand tax collection beyond the wealthiest sector of the population.

"Let's all pay more taxes, that means raising the rates of the global complementary, not only to the richest, but much lower", pointed out the economist, who added that he is concerned about the wealth tax: "It is very politicized, but we will see what rates they propose and if the set of these things makes sense or not".

On how he sees the burden of the current economic agenda, with reforms such as pensions, taxes and labor, Valdés pointed out that "it is something that is very difficult to digest for the economy and therefore it has to be done in a sequence, in a gradual way, that avoids deepening problems. This is not easy and implies less investment, at least in the transition, because it is more expensive to do business".

Regarding the new Constitution, Valdés reiterated his disappointment with the process, but did not define his position regarding the upcoming plebiscite to approve or reject the text elaborated by the Constituent Convention.

title: Central Bank  reaffirms its decision not to  intervene  in the dollar market despite new historical high
text:
The dollar registered a new historical maximum this Thursday, when it surpassed the $900 barrier, but this will not be a reason for the Central Bank to try to influence its price, since the rise has logical explanations, according to the organization's view.

"There are good precedents to say that what has happened recently is linked to the fact that the U.S. Federal Reserve (Fed) was half asleep regarding inflation", commented the vice-president of the Central Bank (CB), Pablo García, in the framework of a seminar of the Faculty of Economic and Administrative Sciences of the Universidad Austral de Chile (Uach).

The Metropolitan Region and the central and southern zones boosted the GDP in the first quarter of this year.In the activity of launching the Quarterly Regional Gross Domestic Product, García referred for the second day to the exchange rate issue and stressed the idea that the rise of the dollar in Chile "responds to global phenomena. The dollar in the world is getting stronger (...) All the currencies in the world have tended to depreciate against the dollar".

Dollar continues its escalation and surpasses the $900 barrier in the face of the copper plungeAlthough the vice-president of the Central Bank added that internal factors have pushed the dollar's price close to $150 or more, he emphasized that the increases from $815 are explained by the abrupt increase in rates by the Federal Reserve and the possible future increases that this organization and the market see in view of the advance of inflation.

"This is a much more aggressive rate hike scenario than I thought a month and a half ago, that is what is behind (the rise in the dollar)," said the economist.

The Central Bank considered the option of applying an even greater increase in the interest rate at its last meeting.In view of this scenario, García explained that the criteria for the Central Bank to intervene in the dollar market are not met. The vice-president of the Central Bank pointed out that the behavior of the dollar in Chile is normal in relation to the fact that it responds to the floating exchange rate of the Chilean peso, that these movements can be explained and that they are not yet considered "disruptive for the macroeconomy".

In addition, he quoted the expression of the former president of the Central Bank, Vittorio Corbo, who said that "you have to be Tarzan to change the appreciation of the dollar" at this time.

Corbo dismisses CBintervention due to the rise of the dollar in Chile: "You have to be Tarzan to change its appreciation".However, García stated that the Central Bank's action with its interest rate hikes has allowed counteracting part of the effect of the Fed's actions.

"If we did not have the interest rate we have today and we were just realizing, like the Fed, that there is an inflationary problem, it is a good thing we realized it a year ago (...) The impact we would be experiencing would be much greater", commented the economist when asked about a possible intervention in the exchange market.

title: Corbo dismisses CB  intervention  for dollar hike in  Chile : "You have to be Tarzan to change its appreciation".
text:
The dollar continues to rise and climb to new all-time highs. The currency reached $891 early Wednesday morning, affected mainly by the international scenario of rate hikes by the Federal Reserve and the slowdown in China due to the impact of the confinements determined by the authorities to contain the pandemic.

In spite of this historical rise of the U.S. currency in the country, the former president of the Central Bank, Vittorio Corbo, does not see room for the issuing institution to make an exchange intervention, since he affirms that the appreciation of the dollar is explained by reasons aligned with the fundamentals that move that currency.

"First, the Central Bank always studies very carefully if there are misalignments that cannot be explained by its fundamentals, and the second thing is that if it is misaligned, it can be corrected with an intervention", explained Corbo when participating in the XX Economic Perspectives Seminar "Economic Scenario under Pressure", organized by Sura Inversiones.

The economist added that "this is a dollar appreciation problem: you have to be Tarzan to change the appreciation of the dollar, and therefore I see it as unlikely. That is written in the CB's rules. First there has to be a misalignment that cannot be explained by fundamentals, but now there is a rationale that explains the rise of the dollar, which is international appreciation". For this reason, "I see it very unlikely (an intervention) at this juncture, especially with the uncertainty we are going to have in the coming months. We have to save our ammunition".

Rates: "The remedy has to produce effects".In his analysis, Corbo also addressed the problem of inflation, which today stands at 11.5% in twelve months. "Inflation expectations and inflationary compensations in the two-year term continue to be well above the inflation target and those in the 10-year term reach 4.4%. Overheating is still present and indexation mechanisms increase the risk that high inflation becomes more persistent," warned the economist.

He pointed out that "to reduce overheating, the Central Bank has been raising the interest rate, this year's Budget reduces public spending by 25% in real terms and no new withdrawals have been approved".

In this context, he noted that "the contraction of final demand has affected both private consumption and investment", and said that this factor, together with lower food and fuel price inflation as a result of the global slowdown, "will contribute to reduce inflation".

Therefore, he foresees that "new interest rate hikes should be more moderate, to end this cycle at around 9.5% and begin to decline later when inflation begins to move towards the CB's 2% target".

Therefore, for Corbo "we are close to the end of the bullish cycle, because the remedy is already in the patient and has to produce its effects. Antibiotics do not have effects when they are just taken, you have to be patient for them to have effects".

title: Wall Street's critical assessment of Chile
text:
Citi: "Political uncertainty casts doubt on whether fiscal policy will remain as prudent.Although Chile maintains solid macroeconomic fundamentals, Citi's economist following Chile, Fernando Jorge Díaz, says political uncertainty sows a knob of doubt about the country's attractiveness as an investment destination, highlighting, for example, ongoing debates about the growth model and the pension system.

What's your general view of Chile's macroeconomic moment?

The risk of overheating has increased substantially this year. Although the economy is recovering from the downturn in 2020, fiscal policy has become even more expansionary.

On the other hand, although commodity prices are very high and there are very favorable terms of trade for Chile, the peso is very depreciated. That's a combination that, in general terms, is quite inflationary. Moreover, if we look at the components of the inflationary rise, we see that the price of tradables, which are not very affected by the exchange rate, is rising. The inflation of the most stable prices, that is, excluding energy and food, is also rising.

There is a macroeconomic policy, especially fiscal policy, which is being procyclical and I don't know if it is worrying or not, but it will imply that in the future, when the economy has negative shocks again, the space to cushion them through expansionary monetary and fiscal policies will be smaller. That is the risk associated with the policies that are generating this overheating of the economy.

In this context, what would be the implications of a fourth withdrawal of the PFAs?

Regarding the impact on the cycle, if it is going to overheat the economy more or not, probably, each withdrawal has a lower impact on the product. Probably, more people won't spend that money because they already have liquidity than they didn't spend before. So the impact on the level of activity and the level of employment is probably marginal.

What we see with the different withdrawals is that each time the impact on the capital market is greater. At the beginning, the PFAs sold more liquid assets, mainly external, but with the pace of withdrawals they have to sell a little more domestic assets, which means that those withdrawals have a greater impact on the prices of financial assets.

The ability of the Central Bank to try to smooth that adjustment in portfolios is diminishing. This is also consistent with the fact that withdrawals are more disruptive to the domestic capital market.

Does the Central Bank have the capacity to contain rising inflation?

Yes. They have the necessary tools. Monetary policy acts with a lag, so it can no longer operate for the reasons that made inflation so high in September. So, in the short term inflation is going to be high. Fiscal policy was very different from what the Central Bank calibrated in its base scenario and that is why inflation is rising today. In the medium term, with the CB acting decisively, it will manage to control inflation.

Has Chile lost its attractiveness as an investment destination?

Chile still has solid macroeconomic fundamentals. For example, if we were to measure the quality of the Central Bank as a stock, it's high, while debt - although higher - is still lower compared to other developing countries. What is true is that political uncertainty casts doubt on whether fiscal policy will remain as prudent as in the past, which adds to the question of what Chile's growth model will be.

Clearly there are unmet social demands, that's why the country is in this constitutional process - what's not clear is how those demands are going to be met. We've seen in other countries in the region that, in that, they compromise the growth model, which in the medium term is usually problematic. At the end of the day, if we look at which countries have improved their quality of life the most in recent decades, they are the ones that have grown the most, Chile being an example of this.

While all of them are valid, there are discussions today that were not there before. For example, there is the one related to the size of the State and the services it should provide to the population, which should include how this greater public spending is financed. There is also the discussion on what to do with the pension funds, raising the question of whether there is going to be a large public pension fund, whose criteria for the administration of its portfolio we do not know.

The challenges Chile is facing are evident and that is why asset prices are discounting greater uncertainty going forward.

JPMorgan: "Today the market is demanding a higher risk premium than the country has been accustomed to".The Chilean economy is growing 5% above its potential level and an approval of a new withdrawal of the AFP fund "would exacerbate the imbalances," says Diego Pereira, economist for Chile at JPMorgan, based on calculations presented to PULSO. It is in this context that he also states that the market is valuing investment in Chile with greater risk.

What is your analysis of Chile's current macroeconomic situation?

Activity was 5.7% above the pre-pandemic level (6.8% if we exclude mining). Some 70% of the expansion is explained by the trade sector, 25% by services and only 12% by industry. This anatomy of expansion is typical of consumption booms and overstimulated economies, which is consistent with household income growing by about 27% of GDP since Covid came out, as of September this year, with pension withdrawals accounting for 78% of such accumulation of available liquidity. In our estimates, this has led the level of activity to be 5% above its potential level, which is consistent with the inflationary acceleration we are experiencing.

What would new withdrawals from the PFAs imply?

I defined the fourth withdrawal as flirting with a mini-financial crisis, self-created by impulses associated with politics and not the economy. And unfortunately we are seeing some of the effects associated with the increased likelihood that the Senate will end up approving such a measure. From a macroeconomic standpoint, a fourth withdrawal would exacerbate the imbalances discussed above, pushing inflation up, and currency depreciation. Consumption would gain again, but the marginal impact would be smaller than the effect of the previous withdrawals when we think of the total impact on the level of activity. This is explained by higher inflation and the central bank's reaction by raising rates to avoid an even more damaging de-anchoring of expectations.

Does the central bank have the capacity to contain rising inflation?

In my baseline scenario, I discount a restrictive stance by the Central Bank, taking rates to levels it considers neutral. But I see the path as very dependent on whether or not the fourth withdrawal is approved.

If approved, I see the policy rate at 3.75% and 6.5% by the end of 2021 and 2022, respectively. If not approved, at 3.25% and 5%.

Has Chile lost its attractiveness as an investment destination?

For financial investment, attractiveness is defined by the expected return, which is associated with risk. Today the market demands a higher risk premium than the country has been accustomed to, especially for assets denominated in local currency. And we cannot forget that the premium associated with financial investment also impacts real investment, the key to growth. There can be scenarios with sustained growth and sub-optimal redistribution, as is argued to have occurred in Chile in recent years. But we cannot have sustained redistribution processes without growth.

Goldman Sachs: "People are looking at Chile with some concern".The Chilean economy is seriously overheated, in the eyes of Goldman Sachs' chief economist for Latin America, Alberto Ramos. Part of that is explained, in his view, by an "overstretched" fiscal stimulus, precisely what calls into question Chile's short-term macroeconomic management and has begun to change the perception of the country's distinctly prudent political economy.

What is your general view of Chile's current macroeconomic situation?

It's a reality that the Chilean economy is overheated, the output ratio is already positive and it's going to stay positive throughout 2023, so it will continue to drive up inflation, although not all sectors are fully recovered. Certainly, there is heterogeneity, for example, in the labour market. However, the truth is that the economy is already operating above the natural limit of its capacity.

It is the fastest growing economy, it is the one with the highest level of vaccination and it has a huge fiscal stimulus. It would be necessary, then, to moderate the stimulus to consumption, so that the economy begins a path of more moderate, but sustainable and balanced growth.

In this context, what would be the implications of approving a fourth withdrawal from the PFAs?

The stimulus to consumption, through the fourth withdrawal of pension savings, would take place at a time when it is not necessary. What is required is to lower the pressure on inflation a little and also, in the medium and long term, it is important to have some savings so that people can withdraw them when they lose the capacity to generate income.

It seems to me that it would be prudent not to make the pension withdrawal now, given that at this cyclical moment in the economy less stimulus to consumption is needed.

How do you assess the Central Bank's reaction?

The decision seems to me to be quite correct. The Central Bank's objective is to lower inflationary pressure, because the economy is clearly overheating. If you don't control inflation you're going to have a much bigger impact on future growth, so raising the interest rate is a sign of a Central Bank that's quite determined and committed to reducing it.

You have to keep in mind that lowering inflation is social policy, because inflation is a regressive tax that makes it more difficult for low-income families. Therefore, it is very important, from a dynamic point of view, to lower inflation now so that we can return to growth at an acceptable rate and with a balanced economy in terms of monetary policy.

Has Chile lost its attractiveness as an investment destination?

The thesis that Chile was a country that was positively differentiated from the rest of Latin America seems to be changing. That's no longer so true because short-term macroeconomic management itself, with fiscal stimulus a bit overdone, with high inflation and a Central Bank having to validate an interest-rate shock to bring it down, shows that the "political economy" of fiscal management is changing quite a lot. It seems that we are going to go down the path of an economy with a greater presence of the State, more interventionist. There's a risk that it's veering away from a slightly more conventional and orthodox macro model, towards a more interventionist and potentially more populist one.

People are looking at Chile with some concern. They don't know what's going to happen, but there's a question mark there that there wasn't in the past.

title: Fitch Affirms EFE LT Foreign  Currency  and LT Local  Currency  IDR at 'A-'; Outlook Stable
text:
Release date - 05082021

Fitch Ratings has affirmed Empresa de los Ferrocarriles del Estado (EFE) of Chile Long-Term Foreign Currency (FC) Issuer Default Rating (IDR) and Long-Term Local Currency IDR at 'A-' with a Stable Outlook.

Fitch also affirmed EFE's USD500 million 3.068% senior unsecured notes due in 2050 at 'A-', the same level as EFE's FC IDR.

KEY RATING DRIVERS

Status, Ownership and Control Assessed as Very Strong

EFE is fully controlled by the state of Chile. A board of directors is appointed by the Chilean Economic Development Agency, which depends on the Ministry of Economy. Chile's Ministry of Transportation represents the formal interaction between EFE and the central government; defines the operating framework of EFE and prepares triennial investment plans jointly with EFE. The Treasury Ministry approves investment plans, annual budgets and borrowing. EFE is subject to official audits by the Comptroller General of the Republic, the superior oversight body, and to the rules of the Comision Mercado Financiero (CMF), the securities and insurance regulator in Chile.

Support Track Record Assessed as Very Strong

EFE has received consistent support from the government. EFE receives transfers from the nation for operating expenses (mainly maintenance cost) and capex. For both domestic and foreign debt, interest and capital payments are paid directly from the state of Chile to EFE's creditors. Every investment project has been done with federal transfers or through new debt. Local bonds are directly guaranteed by Chile. This support is expected to continue in the following years.

Sociopolitical Implications of Default Assessed as Strong

EFE's railroad network has the most extensive coverage and connectivity in Chile, which positions EFE as a critical link for the country's global supply chain. Given the social and economic discontent that could take place in Chile during an interruption of service, Fitch expects the state would try to continue providing service regardless of the contingency, event or debt default situation. The interruption of EFE will affect other entities due to its connectivity with ports and other means of transport, such as Metro de Santiago.

Financial Implications of Default Assessed as Very Strong

Chile is in charge of paying EFE's debt service. The state covers the debt service without EFE's intervention. A default of EFE would be comparable to Chile's own default and would lead to temporary closure of any market funding for both the state and EFE.

Standalone Credit Profile (SCP)

EFE's SCP assessed at 'b'

EFE's SCP is assessed at 'b', which reflects a Weak assessment for revenue defensibility, a Midrange assessment for operating risk, and a Weaker financial profile because leverage (Fitch's net adjusted debt to EBITDA) is over 100.0x in Fitch's rating case scenario. EFE's SCP also reflects peer comparisons.

The Weak revenue defensibility assessment reflects the highly subsidized tariff regime that does not allow for full cost recovery with revenues from core business activities alone, despite adequate passenger demand in recent years. As a result, EFE requires government transfers to close the gap between its own revenues and operational costs.

The Midrange operating risk assessment reflects the nature of the entity, characterized by high operating expenditure. EFE's operating expenditure registered a 2016-2020 CAGR of 5.7%, above the operating revenue CAGR of 3.7%. The result was mostly driven by the drop of revenues following the global pandemic and its impact on mobility and passenger flow. However, EFE was able to adjust operating expenditures by 9% in 2020, evidence of austerity amid a challenging environment. EFE presents an adequate supply of resources and labor with limited volatility. Capital planning management is assessed as neutral to EFE's operating risk.

EFE's net adjusted debt has increased in recent years and is expected to continue increasing given financing needs to implement the Chile sobre Rieles program. According to Fitch's rating case, it will exceed 100.0x EBITDA throughout the rating case scenario for 2021-2025. This is due to weak operational balance and increasing debt, leading to a Weaker financial profile.

Debt Ratings

The ratings of EFE's USD500 million 3.068% senior unsecured notes due in 2050 is affirmed at 'A-', the same level as EFE's FC IDR.

DERIVATION SUMMARY

Fitch views EFE as a government-related entity (GRE) of the Chilean state and equalizes its ratings with those of the sovereign. This reflects a score of 50 points under our GRE Rating Criteria. The 'b' SCP does not affect EFE's IDR.

Under its GRE Criteria, Fitch classifies EFE as an entity linked to the Chilean government and applies an equalized approach based on its assessment of the strength of linkage with and incentive to support by the Chilean government. EFE's GRE support score is assessed at 50, reflecting a combination of a Very Strong Status, Ownership, and Control; Very Strong Support Track Record and Expectations; Strong Sociopolitical Implications of Default; and Very Strong Financial Implications of Default.

The 'b' SCP also reflects the peer comparison. The SCP assessment combined with a GRE Score of 50 leads to the 'A-' IDRs.

KEY ASSUMPTIONS

Fitch's Key Assumptions Within Our Rating Case for the Issuer

Fitch's rating case is a through-the-cycle scenario that incorporates a combination of revenue, cost and financial risk stresses. It is based on Fitch's sovereign group macro projections and incorporates the following assumptions:

Revenue from core business to gradually recover to pre-pandemic levels until 2024;

Operating costs will grow in line with historical performance, considering projected inflation;

New debt in the amount of USD3.2 billion for 2021-2025, following EFE's expected disbursement schedule and financing need for Chile sobre Rieles.

RATING SENSITIVITIES

Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to negative rating action/downgrade:

EFE's Long-Term IDRs could be downgraded if the sovereign rating is downgraded, or on a weaker assessment of strength of linkage or incentives to support, leading to an overall score below 45 points under our GRE Criteria, which Fitch deems to have a low probability.

Negative rating action on EFE's IDRs would result in similar action on the ratings of EFE's senior unsecured USD500 million notes due in 2050.

Factors that could, individually or collectively, lead to positive rating action/upgrade:

Positive rating action on Chile's IDRs would result in similar action on the ratings of EFE and its senior unsecured USD500 million notes due 2050.

BEST/WORST CASE RATING SCENARIO

International scale credit ratings of Sovereigns, Public Finance and Infrastructure issuers have a best-case rating upgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a positive direction) of three notches over a three-year rating horizon; and a worst-case rating downgrade scenario (defined as the 99th percentile of rating transitions, measured in a negative direction) of three notches over three years. The complete span of best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings for all rating categories ranges from 'AAA' to 'D'. Best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings are based on historical performance. For more information about the methodology used to determine sector-specific best- and worst-case scenario credit ratings, visit https://www.fitchratings.com/site/re/10111579.

LIQUIDITY AND DEBT STRUCTURE

Liquidity improved in 2020, driven by the recent issuance of USD500 million of international bonds in 2020. The pandemic delayed capex and new debt translated into higher cash for EFE. Considering investments are expected to pick up once mobility restrictions are phased out, we see the current improvement as temporary.

EFE's YE 2020 debt totaled CLP1,886 million, 78.2% of which is in local bonds, 18.4% international bonds and 3.4% in bank loans. The bonds schedule is bullet amortization and all local bonds have the state guarantee; international bonds and bank loans do not have a guarantee. However, interest and capital payments are paid directly from the state of Chile to EFE's creditors. While the substantial use of bullets is a negative factor for its debt structure, EFE's SCP is supported by the extended debt maturity profile and strong access to onshore and offshore capital markets.

ISSUER PROFILE

EFE Group is the major infrastructure and transportation service provider in Chile. It is fully owned by the state of Chile, supporting the company's operations, investment plan and debt service. EFE focuses on three segments: passenger, cargo transportation and real estate management.

ESG Considerations

Unless otherwise disclosed in this section, the highest level of ESG credit relevance is a score of '3' - ESG issues are credit neutral or have only a minimal credit impact on the entity, either due to their nature or the way in which they are being managed by the entity.

REFERENCES FOR SUBSTANTIALLY MATERIAL SOURCE CITED AS KEY DRIVER OF RATING

The principal sources of information used in the analysis are described in the Applicable Criteria.

PUBLIC RATINGS WITH CREDIT LINKAGE TO OTHER RATINGS

The ratings of EFE are supported by the ratings of Chile
