Derivative instruments classified as hedges are accounted for as cash flow hedges.

In order to classify a derivative as a hedging instrument for accounting purposes, the Company documents (i) as of the transaction date or at designation time, the relationship or correlation between the hedging instrument and the hedged item, as well as the risk management purposes and strategies, (ii) the assessment, both at designation date as well as on a continuing basis, whether the derivative instrument used in the hedging is highly transaction effective to offset changes in inception cash flows of the hedged item. A hedge is considered effective when changes in the cash flows of the underlying directly attributable to the risk hedged are offset with the changes in fair value, or in the cash flows of the hedging instrument with effectiveness between 80% to 125%.

The total fair value of a hedging derivative is classified as assets or financial liabilities in Other non-current if the maturity of the hedged item is more than 12 months and as other assets or current liabilities if the remaining maturity of the hedged item is less than 12 months. The ineffective portion of these instruments can be viewed in Other gains (losses) of the Consolidated Statements of Income. The effective portion of the change in the fair value of derivative instruments that are designated and qualified as cash flow hedges are initially recognized in Cash Flow Hedge Reserve in a separate component of Equity. The income or loss related to the ineffective portion is immediately recognized in the Consolidated Statement of Income. The amounts accumulated in Equity are reclassified in Income during the same period in which the corresponding hedged item is reflected in the Consolidated Statement of Income. When a cash flow hedge ceases to comply with the hedge accounting criteria, any accumulated income or loss existing in Equity remains in Equity and is recognized when the expected transaction is finally recognized in the Consolidated Statement of Income. When it is estimated that an expected transaction will not occur, the accumulated gain or loss recorded in Equity is immediately recognized in the Consolidated Statement of Income.

Derivative instruments are classified as held for trading unless they are classified as hedge instruments.

This allowed us to supply our customers and consumers with our products and maintain safety in the workplace. Fair value hierarchies

The financial instruments recorded at fair value in the Statement of Financial Position are classified as follows, depending on the method used to obtain their fair values:

Level 1   Fair values obtained through direct reference to quoted market prices, without any adjustment.
Level 2   Fair values obtained through the use of valuation models accepted in the market and based on prices other than those of Level 1, which may be directly or indirectly observed as of the measurement date (adjusted prices).
Level 3   Fair values obtained through internally developed models or methodologies that use information which may not be observed or which is illiquid.

Note 15 Business Combinations

a) Bebidas Bolivianas BBO S.A.

On May 7, 2014, the Company acquired 34% of the stock rights of Bebidas Bolivianas BBO S.A. a Bolivian closed stock company that produces soft drinks and beers in three factories located in the cities of Santa Cruz de la Sierra and Nuestra Señora de la Paz. The amount of this transaction was US$ 24.303.000, equivalents to ThCh$ 13,776,885. On December 9, 2015, the Company paid an increased of capital for an amount of US$ 2,720,000, equivalents to ThCh$ 1,921,245. On June 8, 2016 and November 10, 2016, the Company paid an increased of capital for an amount of US$ 2,221,696, equivalents to ThCh$ 1,510,420 and US$ 1,019,970, equivalents to ThCh$ 663,951, respectively. This transaction did not change the percentage of participation because both partners concurred in proportion to their current participation.

On August 9, 2018, the Company acquired an additional 17% of the shares of BBO for an amount of US$ 8,500,000, equivalents to ThCh$ 5,457,935, remaining with a 51% stake in BBO, on this date the Company proceeded to consolidate this business.

The Company has determined the fair values of assets and liabilities for this business combination (see Note 1 - General information, letter D).

On September 20, 2018, the Company paid committed capital of US$ 1,530,029 (equivalent to ThCh$ 1,044,688) in BBO. This transaction did not change the percentage of participation because both partners concurred in proportion to their current participation.

On June 28, 2019 and on July 11, 2019 the subsidiary CCU Inversiones II Ltda. made capital contributions to Bebidas Bolivianas BBO S.A. for an amount of US$ 1,249,713 (equivalent to ThCh$ 849,630) and an amount of US$ 178,305 (equivalents to ThCh$ 122,210) respectively. This transaction did not change the percentage of participation because both partners concurred in proportion to their current participation.

b) Cervecera Guayacán SpA.

On August 31, 2018, the subsidiary Cervecería Kunstmann S.A. (CK) acquired an additional 30.0004% of the stock rights of Cervecera Guayacán SpA., for an amount of ThCh$ 361,560, equivalent to 39,232 shares and the subscription and payment of ThCh$ 470,711, equivalent to 49,038 shares. As a consequence above mentioned CK has the 50.0004% stake in Cervecera Guayacán SpA.

The Company has determined the fair values of assets and liabilities for this business combination (see Note 1 - General information, letter D).

c) Bodega San Juan S.A.U.

In December 2018, the subsidiary Viña San Pedro Tarapacá S.A. (VSPT) signed an agreement to acquire a part of the Pernod Ricard wine business in Argentina. The purchase agreement, subject to local regulatory approval, included the Argentine wine brands Graffigna, Colón and Santa Silvia, which represent approximately 1.5 million boxes of 9-liter wine bottles per year. Bodegas Graffigna has a winery warehouse in the province of San Juan, two fields in the same province, and a field in Mendoza.

On January 28, 2019, the Argentine subsidiary Finca La Celia S.A. established the company Bodega San Juan S.A.U. making a capital contribution of ARS 100,000, in order to use it as a vehicle for the acquisition of the Graffigna, Colón and Santa Silvia wine business of Pernod Ricard Argentina S.R.L., in addition to the purchase of Graffigna winery and the Pocito vineyards, Cañada Honda and La Consulta.

On May 31, 2019, the subsidiary VSPT made a capital contribution to the subsidiary Finca La Celia S.A. by US$ 14,000,000, equivalent to ThCh$ 9,910,040 and on the same date the subsidiary Finca La Celia S.A. made a capital contribution to Bodega San Juan S.A.U. for US$ 2,806,820, equivalent to ThCh$ 1,986,836.

On May 31, 2019, Bodega San Juan S.A.U. through a deed of sale became the owner of the businesses associated with the operation of the winery and the Pocito and Cañada Honda vineyards.

Main assumptions for impairment calculation

Goodwill assigned to the CGUs is subject to impairment test on an annually basis or more frequently if there are signs of potential impairment. These signs may include a significant change in the economic environment that could affect the business scenario, new legal provisions, operational performance indicators or the disposal of an important part of a CGU. The impairment loss is recognized for the amount by which the carrying amount of the CGU exceeds its recoverable amount. The recoverable value of each CGU is determined as the highest amount between its value in use and its fair value minus the cost of selling. The management considers that the value in use approach, determined by a discounted cash flow model, is the most reliable method to determine the recoverable values of the CGU.

The following describes some considerations applied when determining the corresponding values in use of the CGUs that have Goodwill and / or intangible assets with indefinite useful life assigned:

Projection period: A five-year horizon is considered for all units / brands. An exceptionally longer period of time (no longer than ten years), is considered for those units / brands that require a longer maturation period.

Cash Flow: To determine the value in use, the Company has used cash flow projections in line with the time horizon described above, based on budgets, strategic plans and projections reviewed by management for the same period of time. Given the maturity of our business, these budgets have been historicaly consistent with the results.

Management's cash flow projection included significant judgements and assumptions relating to perpetual growth rates and discount rates.

Perpetual growth: Although the Company expects a higher volume and price growth in the medium and long term, a nominal growth of 3% has been assumed for the perpetuity in Chilean units, which is a conservative assumption considering the historical capacity and nature of the business where the company operates. In the case of Paraguay and Argentina a perpetuity rate of 3.0% and 2.5% are used respectively, which are composed by the average inflation rate of the United States of America mentioned above, plus a percentage of the potential long-term GDP in each country.

Discount rate: Corresponds to the nominal WACC (Weighted Average Cost of Capital) rate of each country.

Note 22 Right of use assets and Lease liabilities

The Company has implemented IFRS 16 as of January 1, 2019. This means recognizing the right of use assets for the goods subject to operating lease contracts and a liability equivalent to the present value of the payment associated with the contract.

Considerations:

- Identification of the asset for right of use: As part of the contract review and analysis process, the Company identified assets by right of use associated with identifiable and non-substitutable lease contracts, which were classified under the item Right of use assets. - The Company mainly has warehouses, offices, vehicles and land leased contracts. - Interest rate used for the measurement of the financial liability: The Company determined the interest rate based on the currency and the term of the lease contracts. The average incremental borrowing interest rate applied to lease liabilities used is 3.2%. - Term of the contract: The Company evaluated the lease clauses, market conditions, costs related to the termination of the contract and early cancellation.

Other considerations:

1) During the initial measurement of lease agreements, the Company applied exemptions for leases with remaining terms less than 12 months and leases with a value lower than US$ 5,000 (ThCh$ 3,747) as of January 1, 2019. These leases have been considered as short term, therfore no right of use asset or lease liability has been recognized. 2) The Company excluded initial direct costs from measuring the right of use asset at the date of initial application. 3) The Company analyzed the lease terms on a case-by-case basis, in those with an option to extend or terminate the lease.

For leases previously classified as financial leases, the Company recognized the carrying amount of the lease assets and the lease liabilities immediately before the transition as the carrying amount of the assets for the right to use and the lease liabilities on the date of the initial lease recognition.

As a consequence of the aformentioned, the Company recorded the right of use asset under the item Right of use assets, and Current and Non-Current Lease liability in the Consolidated Financial Statements. Also it has modified the nature of the lease expenses, eliminating the operating expense offset by the expense of depreciation and a financial cost. The short-term and low-value leases are still going through the Consolidated Financial Statement of Income. Finally, the presentation in the Consolidated Statement of Cash Flows was modified. The main portion of lease payments are presented in cash flow from financing activities and the interest associated to leases are presented in cash flow from operating activities.

The current value of the agreement amounted to ThCh$ 10,403,632 as of December 31, 2007. The agreement also grants CCU the right or option to acquire the assets contained in the agreement (real estate, furniture and facilities) as from month 68 of the lease. The lease rentals committed are according to the conditions prevailing in the market.

At the time of sale, the Company recognized ThCh$ 3,108,950 as a gain for the building portion not leased by the Company and ThCh$ 2,276,677 as a liability that was deferred until completion of the building. At this time, the Company recorded the transaction as a financial lease.

On February 28, 2018, the Company carried out an amendment to the contract with Compañía de Seguros de Vida Consorcio Nacional de Seguros S.A., recording a balance debt of UF 608,375, with 3.95% annual interest and maturity on February 5, 2048.

The Company records a liability for the payment of an irrevocable severance indemnity, originated by collective and individual agreements entered into with certain groups of employees. The so-determined value is presented at the current value by using the severance benefits accrued method. Capital Management

The main purpose, when managing shareholder's capital, is to maintain an adequate credit risk profile and a healthy capital ratio, allowing the access of the Company to the capitals market for the development of its medium and long term purposes and, at the same time, to maximize shareholder's return.

Earnings per share

The basic earnings per share is calculated as the ratio between the net income (loss) for the period attributable to equity holders of the parent and the weighted average number of valid outstanding shares during such term.

The diluted earnings per share is calculated as the ratio between the net income (loss) for the period attributable to equity holders of the parent and the weighted average additional common shares that would have been outstanding if it had become all ordinary potential dilutive shares.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazilian real snaps three-day rally; eyes weekly gains
text:
* Brazil's real outperforms peers for the week
    * Chilean peso tracks sharpest weekly decline since August
2020
    * Latam stocks index set to fall for the week

    By Shreyashi Sanyal
    Jan 15 (Reuters) - Brazil's real bucked a three-day winning
streak on Friday after data showed the first decline in retail
sales in seven months, although the currency is set to
outperform its Latin American peers for the week on improving
risk sentiment.   
    The real fell 1% against the dollar as
official figures showed Brazilian retail sales surprisingly fell
in November mainly driven by a sizeable fall in sales of food
products.    
    "The survey breakdown suggests that those components that
were performing well during the peak of the pandemic are now
contracting (food/beverages/supermarket or furniture/home
appliances), while others components that were more negatively
affected during that period keep recovering (apparel or cars),"
Citi strategists wrote in a note.
    Global risk sentiment showed signs of improving early in the
week, which has put the real on track to cap the week with gains
of 2.6%. 
    However, a travel ban imposed by Britain over a Brazilian
variant of the coronavirus hurt the mood on Friday.
    The MSCI's index for Latin American currencies
 was set to end the week higher, adding 1.3%. 
    Most risky assets have gained this week on anticipation of a
faster pace of global economic recovery as COVID-19 vaccines
start to roll out across the world. Sentiment was also boosted
by hopes of a fiscal boost from a $1.9 trillion U.S. stimulus
plan.  
    The Mexican peso fell 0.6% on Friday, but was set for
its sharpest weekly gain in nearly one month on improving
economic data points.
    Among weekly decliners, Chile's peso led the descent
to tumble over 3% for the week. Chile's central bank announced
during the week a plan to purchase $12 billion over the next 15
months to replenish and expand foreign currency reserves.
    However, analysts expect substantial near-term weakness in
the peso, despite the intervention by Chile's central bank. The
currency dropped 1.2% in early trading. 
    Oil-exporter Colombia's peso fell 0.5% and was also
set to drop for the week tracking losses in crude prices.
    Equities across emerging markets fell on Friday, with the
MSCI's index for Latin American stocks set for
weekly declines of 1.6%.

title: Goldman Sachs highlights  Central Bank  measures and rules out inflationary pressures
text:
A positive vision has Goldman Sachs on the Central Bank international reserve replenishment and expansion program. While the announcement generated a sharp depreciation of the Chilean peso and the investment bank sees no signs of a widespread and persistent uptick in inflationary pressures.

"We believe that the measure is necessary to strengthen Chile's external mattresses, particularly in light of the post-protest experience of October 2019, which led to an unprecedented weakening of Chile's peso, which required strong intervention from the Central Bank," Goldman Sachs said.

The announcement of the dollar purchase plan raised doubts about the direction inflation could take, in the face of a possible sustained rise in the dollar.

In fact, the US currency rose $15 following the announcement of the BC, then closed today's trades with a drop of $13.34 to $728.5.

However, the investment bank believes that "negative surprises" in economic data, coupled with sustained progress in coronavirus contagions, would keep inflation levels under pressure, following the uptick at the end of last year.

"We still see no signs of a widespread and persistent uptick in inflationary pressures. Domestic activity has been negatively surprised in recent months, and the imposition of new social restraint measures to counteract the increase in new cases of COVID is likely to affect recovery in the short term. So while inflation has surprised considerably upwards, the expectation that the output gap could close by the end of 2022 has probably remained virtually unchanged," goldman Sachs says.

Second withdrawal from AFPsThe investment bank emphasized that the uptick in inflation at the end of 2020 is explained only by transitional factors: rising consumption as a result of the first and second withdrawals of 10% of pension funds.

In this regard, Goldman estimates that the Central Bank maintains current monetary policy, at least throughout 2021. However, he emphasized that a scenario of greater control of the coronavirus could lead to a shift towards normalization.

"We hope that the Committee will continue to signal the maintenance of the current monetary policy stance until the end of 2021. However, positive news of COVID vaccination efforts and a possible decrease in new infections may begin to change the central bank's assessment towards an earlier normalization of the policy stance," Goldman concludes.

title: Bolivia's President-Elect Expected to Boost Public Spending -- Market Talk
text:
1403 ET - Bolivia's incoming president, Luis Arce , will likely boost public spending, leading to bigger fiscal deficits as he aims to get Bolivia out of a deep economic contraction, says Oxford Economics. Arce, the former finance minister of ex-president Evo Morales , was elected on Sunday. Oxford says his economic policy probably won't change much from his time in the Morales administration, when poverty declined. Oxford notes his economic management was "marked by large public spending that failed to generate hard currency inflows and that didn't bolster the development of the private sector. This makes us doubtful about expecting something radically different from him." (ryan.dube@wsj.com; @duberyan)

1346 ET - Chile will hold a referendum on Sunday to write a new constitution, which could "entrench greater state intervention in the economy," Capital Economics says. That could help Chile's economy recover faster than others in Latin America; however, the constitution-writing process is also expected to fuel uncertainty, the firm says. "Political uncertainty is now the main certainty in Chile," it says. "Sunday's landmark referendum on constitutional change could be the start of a long and complex process to alter its political landscape." If the referendum is approved, Chileans will elect in April the assembly that will write the charter. (ryan.dube@wsj.com; @duberyan)

1128 ET - Russia's central bank is likely to keep interest rates on hold in the short term as the ruble's weakness feeds through to higher inflation, Capital Economics says. Further interest-rate cuts are "off the table" for as long as inflation continues to rise toward the central bank's 4% target and the ruble remains "on the back foot," Capital Economics economist Liam Peach says. However, inflation will peak in the coming months and begin to fall in the first half of 2021, prompting the bank to cut rates by 25 basis points in February, he says. The central bank left its policy rate at 4.25% Friday. USD/RUB last trades down 0.5% at 76.2478. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1047 ET - U.S. and eurozone third quarter economic growth figures due next week are viewed as backward looking so will probably have a limited impact on the euro-dollar exchange rate, Unicredit says. Other data scheduled in coming days including durable goods orders, consumer confidence, personal income and personal consumption expenditure in the U.S. and the ifo's German business climate index will have a "greater impact" on EUR/USD, Unicredit 's Roberto Mialich says. The German business climate index is likely to show a "renewed decline" in business confidence, which should "curb any further EUR/USD rally much beyond 1.18 for now," he says. EUR/USD rises 0.1% to 1.1830. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1044 ET - The world economy has recovered about 60% of the output lost in the first half of the year, but recoveries in most parts of the world have already slowed and prospects now vary according to countries' success in controlling the virus, Capital Economics says. "The outlook for Europe has darkened as second waves have prompted new restrictions and fiscal support is being scaled back," says the forecasting firm. The U.S. looks more resilient, with risks in both directions relating to the virus and to the possibility of post-election fiscal stimulus. Inflation will stay very low everywhere, implying that the era of unprecedented monetary policy support is set to continue for at least the next couple of years, Capital Economics says. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

1041 ET - The European Central Bank 's October 29 policy meeting is unlikely to materially impact the euro as further stimulus measures aren't expected until the end of the year, Unicredit says. "[ECB ] President Christine Lagarde is expected to delay the announcement of further monetary policy expansion--in the form of more asset purchases under the pandemic emergency purchase program facility--to the final Monetary Policy Committee meeting of 2020 on December 10," Unicredit 's Roberto Mialich says. EUR/USD rises 0.2% to 1.1839.(renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1006 ET - The absence of an increase in global risk aversion has stopped the euro and sterling from falling considerably against the dollar despite rising coronavirus cases and Brexit risks, Unicredit says. Given the second coronavirus wave and the threat of a no-deal Brexit, "one might have imagined" EUR/USD and GBP/USD would fall towards 1.16 and below 1.28, respectively, "if not further," Unicredit 's Roberto Mialich says. The "resilience" the two exchange rates reflects the dollar's role as a safe-haven currency, he says. The dollar has "lost momentum" recently on hopes for another U.S. fiscal stimulus package and news that Brexit negotiations will continue until mid-November. EUR/USD rises 0.1% to 1.1833 and GBP/USD falls 0.2% to 1.3059. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0933 ET - Spain has replaced Mexico as the most vulnerable economy in the world to Covid-19, according to Oxford Economics. After Spain and Mexico, the Philippines, the U.S., and Brazil rank as the most vulnerable economies. On the other hand, economies like Switzerland, Australia, New Zealand and Mongolia remain the least vulnerable. "The global economy has become more vulnerable to Covid-19 with a 30% of growth in new cases since August," says Evghenia Sleptsova, senior economist at the forecasting firm. Big parts of the Northern Hemisphere are being afflicted by the second wave of the pandemic and this has far outweighed some improvements in epidemiology in some emerging markets, such as Brazil and India, Sleptsova says. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

0902 ET - A new U.S. administration under Democrat Joe Biden may hurt the U.K. government 's chances of agreeing a trade deal with the U.S. any time soon, as President Donald Trump has backed the U.K. leaving the EU and emboldened the Brexit movement, Frederique Carrier at RBC Wealth Management says. Although Biden's position is less well known, the Obama administration opposed preferential trade terms for a U.K. "out of Europe," she says. Moreover, given the size of the European Union compared with the size of the U.K., Biden is unlikely to prioritize a U.K. trade deal. With U.S.-U.K. free trade deal talks on hold until spring because of the pandemic, Biden could pause all negotiations while re-examining U.S. trade policy, Carrier says. (anthony.orunagoriainoff@dowjones.com)

0853 ET - Bank of Canada is unlikely to cut its main interest rate further, despite similar considerations under way at the Reserve Bank of Australia -- which traders tend to think of as Canada's antipodal twin, senior economists at CIBC Capital Markets tell clients. CIBC says clients have inquired about another BOC rate cut, or even negative rates, given Australia's central bank is setting stage for another cut next month. "It's clear to us that the Bank of Canada , having passed over the opportunity to go below 0.25% when the economy was in even more dire straits in the spring, believes that lower rates ... would not be helpful," firm says. It adds BOC Gov. Tiff Macklem has been forthright that negative rates are not under active consideration. (paul.vieira@wsj.com, @paulvieira)

0835 ET - Economists at PNC Financial Services advise clients the Bank of Canada 's main interest rate will remain as is until 2024, arguing that is the time required to absorb the spare economic capacity the pandemic has created. BOC Gov. Tiff Macklem said in July he expects the benchmark rate, of 0.25%, to remain unchanged for at least two years. PNC said Canada's recovery will unfold in "fits and starts" after a rapid upswing in growth in 3Q, likely 40%-plus at an annual rate. Despite heavy dose of government stimulus, PNC said the economy will face stiff headwinds. For instance, it expects demand for energy to slow, and renewable power to eat into market share from conventional sources. It does not expect GDP to return to prepandemic levels until 2023. (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

title: New Chile Constitution Could Give State Bigger Economic Role -- Market Talk
text:

"Political uncertainty is now the main certainty in Chile," it says. "Sunday's landmark referendum on constitutional change could be the start of a long and complex process to alter its political landscape." However, inflation will peak in the coming months and begin to fall in the first half of 2021, prompting the bank to cut rates by 25 basis points in February, he says. (anthony.orunagoriainoff@dowjones.com)

After surviving an impeachment vote last month, opposition lawmakers are now planning to convene in November to consider another motion to oust him. That comes after newspaper El Comercio reported that Vizcarra was implicated by a witness in an alleged corruption scheme during his time as governor of the southern Moquegua state. He denies wrongdoing. Prosecutors say they will investigate, and political analysts say it is increasingly likely that Vizcarra will face legal troubles when he steps down in July. (ryan.dube@wsj.com; @duberyan)

1403 ET - Bolivia's incoming president, Luis Arce , will likely boost public spending, leading to bigger fiscal deficits as he aims to get Bolivia out of a deep economic contraction, says Oxford Economics. Arce, the former finance minister of ex-president Evo Morales , was elected on Sunday. Oxford says his economic policy probably won't change much from his time in the Morales administration, when poverty declined. Oxford notes his economic management was "marked by large public spending that failed to generate hard currency inflows and that didn't bolster the development of the private sector. This makes us doubtful about expecting something radically different from him." (ryan.dube@wsj.com; @duberyan)

1346 ET - Chile will hold a referendum on Sunday to write a new constitution, which could "entrench greater state intervention in the economy," Capital Economics says. That could help Chile's economy recover faster than others in Latin America; however, the constitution-writing process is also expected to fuel uncertainty, the firm says. "Political uncertainty is now the main certainty in Chile," it says. "Sunday's landmark referendum on constitutional change could be the start of a long and complex process to alter its political landscape." If the referendum is approved, Chileans will elect in April the assembly that will write the charter. (ryan.dube@wsj.com; @duberyan)

1128 ET - Russia's central bank is likely to keep interest rates on hold in the short term as the ruble's weakness feeds through to higher inflation, Capital Economics says. Further interest-rate cuts are "off the table" for as long as inflation continues to rise toward the central bank's 4% target and the ruble remains "on the back foot," Capital Economics economist Liam Peach says. However, inflation will peak in the coming months and begin to fall in the first half of 2021, prompting the bank to cut rates by 25 basis points in February, he says. The central bank left its policy rate at 4.25% Friday. USD/RUB last trades down 0.5% at 76.2478. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1047 ET - U.S. and eurozone third quarter economic growth figures due next week are viewed as backward looking so will probably have a limited impact on the euro-dollar exchange rate, Unicredit says. The German business climate index is likely to show a "renewed decline" in business confidence, which should "curb any further EUR/USD rally much beyond 1.18 for now," he says. EUR/USD rises 0.1% to 1.1830. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1044 ET - The world economy has recovered about 60% of the output lost in the first half of the year, but recoveries in most parts of the world have already slowed and prospects now vary according to countries' success in controlling the virus, Capital Economics says. "The outlook for Europe has darkened as second waves have prompted new restrictions and fiscal support is being scaled back," says the forecasting firm. The U.S. looks more resilient, with risks in both directions relating to the virus and to the possibility of post-election fiscal stimulus. Inflation will stay very low everywhere, implying that the era of unprecedented monetary policy support is set to continue for at least the next couple of years, Capital Economics says. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

1041 ET - The European Central Bank 's October 29 policy meeting is unlikely to materially impact the euro as further stimulus measures aren't expected until the end of the year, Unicredit says. "[ECB ] President Christine Lagarde is expected to delay the announcement of further monetary policy expansion--in the form of more asset purchases under the pandemic emergency purchase program facility--to the final Monetary Policy Committee meeting of 2020 on December 10," Unicredit 's Roberto Mialich says. 1016 ET - Statistics Canada estimates that travel restrictions imposed by Canadian authorities to contain the spread of Covid-19 had a direct cost on the country's tourism industry of up to C$23B and the loss of up to 406,000 jobs. The indirect impact on economic sectors that supply the tourism sector could lead to a further loss in GDP of up to C$13.8B and another 143,000 jobs. The data agency said travel restrictions will reduce GDP by up to 1.7% versus 2019, and account for over 14% of the total virus-induced decline in output. Tourism accounts for 2% of Canadian GDP. Canada has, among other things, mostly closed its border to foreign tourists, including the US. Meanwhile, provinces in Atlantic Canada have imposed their own restrictions on travel from within other parts of the country.(paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

1006 ET - The absence of an increase in global risk aversion has stopped the euro and sterling from falling considerably against the dollar despite rising coronavirus cases and Brexit risks, Unicredit says. Given the second coronavirus wave and the threat of a no-deal Brexit, "one might have imagined" EUR/USD and GBP/USD would fall towards 1.16 and below 1.28, respectively, "if not further," Unicredit 's Roberto Mialich says. The "resilience" the two exchange rates reflects the dollar's role as a safe-haven currency, he says. EUR/USD rises 0.1% to 1.1833 and GBP/USD falls 0.2% to 1.3059. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0953 ET - Brazil's inflation was higher than expected in the month through mid-October, but the backdrop for consumer prices remains comfortable enough that the country's central bank should be able to stay calm in coming months, according to Alberto Ramos, an economist at Goldman Sachs. Brazil's statistics agency says Friday consumer prices rose 0.94% in the month through mid-October, the biggest increase for the period since 1995, as food prices increased rapidly. Airfares and the price of electronics and home appliances rose more than expected, but core and services inflation is still tracking at low levels, Ramos says. Brazil has a large output gap and high unemployment, which should help keep inflation under control going forward, Ramos says. (jeffrey.lewis@wsj.com)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil's real on a tear despite bleak outlook; Latam stocks gain
text:
* Brazil's real at near two-month high
    * Stocks rise as U.S., China services data brews optimism
    * Chile's peso falls; C.bank to scale back NDF intervention

 (Adds details, updates prices)
    By Susan Mathew and Ambar Warrick
    June 3 (Reuters) - Brazil's real surged on Wednesday after
industrial output in the country fell less than expected, while
Latin American stocks surged as major global economies were seen
recovering from the coronavirus' economic rout. 
    The real rose 2.4% to a near two-month high as
industrial production in Brazil fell 18.8% in April at its
fastest pace on record due to coronavirus containment measures,
but the drop was less than the estimated 29.2% slide.
 
    "It still highlights that GDP will fall dramatically in Q2 –
perhaps by 10%-12% quarter on quarter," said William Jackson,
chief emerging markets economist at Capital Economics.
    "It will also provide (the monetary policy committee) with
plenty of reason to cut interest rates further later this
month."
    The real has been one of the worst-performing emerging
market currencies this year, but a recent bout of risk appetite
has lifted it from record lows, even as pandemic and political
woes persist.
    Hopes of a broader economic recovery gained momentum as
readings showed business activity in the United States and China
beginning to recover. 
    Sao Paulo listed stocks extended gains to a fourth
session with financials serving as the biggest boost to the
Bovespa. 
    Most other Latam stocks also rose, tracking Wall Street
higher as the U.S. job market was also seen stabilizing.
    Chile's peso rose 1.3% after the country's central
bank said it would gradually scale back its foreign exchangeintervention program in the non-deliverable forward (NDF) market
amid lower peso volatility.
    One-month NDFs on the peso were trading at
770.31 to the dollar by 1902 GMT, compared with the spot rate of
770.30.
     The central bank also said it was speaking with its U.S.
and Chinese counterparts to broaden the country's foreign
exchange lines.
    Argentina's debt restructuring saga continued. A prominent
group of the country's creditors said its restructuring proposal
was in line with an International Monetary Fund assessment of
what would be sustainable and called for a deal to help the
country avoid a costly default.

title: Chile  cenbank to expand  currency intervention  program as peso plummets
text:
SANTIAGO, March 12 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank said on Thursday it would expand an intervention program aimed at ensuring liquidity and stabilizing the peso as markets globally were routed and regional currencies plummeted over the worsening coronavirus outbreak.

The bank in November said it would sell as much as $20 billion in foreign currency interventions after the peso nose-dived amid riots over inequality in the South American nation.

That plan was initially slated to run through May 29, 2020, but the bank said in a statement Thursday that the "worsening financial condition of international markets" had prompted it to extend the program through January 2021.

The Chilean peso plunged again to an historic low on Thursday over coronavirus concerns. Chile's main stock index fell 5.9% to a four-year low.

The bank said it would re-initiate foreign currency interventions beginning Monday, March 16.

(Reporting by Dave Sherwood; editing by Richard Pullin)

text:
By Marc Jones

LONDON, 22 Jan (Reuters) - Chile's central bank will intervene strongly if violent protests again threaten the local currency, the peso, though it hopes the relative calm of recent weeks will be enough to keep the country out of a recession, he said the body's vice president, Joaquín Vial.

In an interview with Reuters, Vial said the biggest protests since Chile's 1990 return to democracy had caused serious damage to the economy.

However, he believes the situation will not be worse than what the Central Bank feared in December when it cut its growth forecast for 2020 to a range of 0.5%-1.5% from an earlier 2.75%-3.75%.

"It seems to me that the estimate we made last quarter is very much in line with what happened," Vial said.

Asked if there was still the risk of a "technical" recession, defined as consecutive quarterly contractions in the economy, he added that "if you look at the graph, we're probably going to avoid it because the worst figures were in October and November."

title: Chilean  central bank  hopeful of no recession, will prevent peso panic - deputy governor
text:
* Violent protests in Chile did major damage to economy

* Deputy central bank chief sees demonstrations continuing

* Bank still ready to intervene in FX markets if needed

* Central bank "not uncomfortable" with current peso level

* Hopeful no need to cut growth forecasts further

* Chart of peso's troubles https://tmsnrt.rs/2ujYthh("https://tmsnrt.rs/2ujYthh")

*

By Marc Jones

LONDON, Jan 22 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank will intervene forcefully if violent protests threaten its peso currency again, though it hopes the relative calm in recent weeks will be enough to keep the country out of recession, its deputy governor Joaquin Vial said.

Vial told Reuters in an interview that Chile's most widespread protests since its return to democracy in 1990 had done serious damage to the economy.

He is hopeful though that it will not be worse than the central bank feared in December when its slashed its 2020 growth forecast to a range of 0.5% to 1.5% from 2.75% to 3.75% previously.

"It looks to me that the estimate (for the economy) we made last quarter is very much in line with what happened," Vial said.

Asked if there was still a risk of a "technical" recession, defined as back-to-back quarterly contractions in the economy, he added: "If you look at the chart we are probably going to avoid that because the worst figures were from October and November."

"December is going to be very bad also, but we have seen some normalisation and the first quarter will most likely be somewhat better...But we have to see how fast confidence is going to restore."

The protests initially erupted in October after metro ticket prices were raised, but quickly escalated to subway stations being set alight and riots on the streets that left 26 dead and upwards of $1.5 billion in losses for businesses.

Vial warned that March and April could get rough again, with more student protests expected and then a referendum on replacing Chile's dictorship-era constitution.

If tensions do flair again though the central bank is prepared after last year's troubles saw the peso plunge 15%.

Vial said it had looked like getting "out of control" at one point, but the central bank stepped in, putting $10 billion of its roughly $40 billion of currency reserves on the table to stem the rout.

It required a number of emergency meetings but it worked. It ended up using about $2 billion of its reserves and the peso made back some ground, but the bank is still on alert.

"We have signalled very clearly that we may intervene again in the foreign exchange market if there is disruption again."

At the same time, Vial stressed that the central bank does not want to change the "trend" of the exchange rate.

"Among other things we think this is part of the normal reaction to the new reality of the Chilean economy," he said referring to the sharp shock to growth. It could be argued that is should be lower, but "we don't feel uncomfortable with this level of the exchange rate," he added.

On interest rates, which did not change during the protests, there are opposing forces. The economy is under stress, but the sharp drop in the peso means inflation will soon be nearly 4%, well above the central bank's preferred level of 3%.

"We don't feel the depreciation has created the pressure to raise rates," Vial said.

However, with the risk of more peso weakness if demonstrations become violent again, he added: "from my personal point of view, (a rate cut) is less likely that the opposite option."

(Reporting by Marc Jones; Editing by Angus MacSwan)

title: Chile 's  central bank  suspends sale of spot market of  intervention  program
text:
The Central Bank of Chile reported that from next Monday it will not sell dollars in the spot market under the current foreign exchange intervention program, although it will renew the current forwards stock, equivalent to US$ 4.5 billion. Already this week the institution had suspended spot sales.

Since the current program was announced on November 28, the dollar has fallen nearly $56, to trade today at around $773.

"Any increase in such a level, or restart of spot sales, will be communicated in a timely manner by the Council and decided on the basis of market conditions considering the volatility and liquidity prevailing," the statement said in a statement.

"The daily forward renewal schedule will continue to be reported every Friday, along with funding measures in pesos and dollars," he added.

The intervention program began on December 2 and provided for the sale of spot dollars for up to US$10 billion from reserves and the sale of foreign exchange hedging instruments for up to $10 billion. The Central Bank currently holds reserves of more than US$40 billion.

The last time the Central Bank had intervened directly on the market was in 2011 and is the largest operation of this size since 1999.

title: Foreign betting against Chilean peso consolidates upward trend in early 2020
text:
For several months now, foreign investors' bets on the Chilean peso have been carriers unusually.

This, because, contrary to the logic, when the dollar began to rise due to the social crisis the anti-local currency bets were falling, while since the exchange rate began its bearish streak - at the end of November - the positions of the foreigners were steadily rising.

This under what is called carry trade, which consists of a strategy used in the foreign exchange trading market where an investor sells a certain currency with a relatively low interest rate and buys a different interest rate with an interest rate higher.

Beyond this dynamic, the upward trend of foreign weight positions continues to extend until the early days of 2020. Thus, between December 2, 2019, when they began to reverse the downturn, until January 3 of this year, the last available data on the Central Bank website, they disarmed carry trade positions of US$3.912 million.

"There is no clarity on these latest movements of foreigners, it may be related to the vision of emerging economies in general – the one that has so far deteriorated - and, on the other hand, more so in particular, to a local economy that should internalize negative effects that arose after the crisis and should be reflected in the next figures," explains Martina Ogaz, EuroAmerica economist.

For his part, the head of Capitaria Trading Studies, Ricardo Bustamante, states that "Chile's weak macroeconomic figures and projections are likely to be supporting less confidence in the local currency, especially after activity data economic that they strongly disappointed in recent months, coupled with the lack of clarity about the text of the agreement in its phase one, which created uncertainty in investors."

Exchange rateIn parallel, since geopolitical tensions between the United States and Iran broke out last Friday, after an attack by the former killed the Iranian military chief, the dollar has strengthened globally and felt strongly at the local level.

This Monday closed at $772.4, implying a $21.3 hike in just two days, which was also influenced by the Central Bank's announcement that the foreign exchange market will not intervene this week.

"Due to the brakes of the Central Bank of Chile's exchange rate intervention this week, coupled with increased uncertainty over the escalation of tensions between Iran and the United States, the dollar could continue to rise in the short term, considering that the most risky and linked to the economic cycle, such as emerging currencies and copper, should continue to be weakened," Bustamante said.

In that sense, it indicates that the next levels to consider are $780-788.

Ogaz, meanwhile, notes that "our scenario envisages a moderate depreciation of parity, all in line with an economy that over the coming months should begin to reflect the already more real effects of the impact of the crisis. In the meantime, there is added the uncertainty that the discussion and constituent process would cause, which would ultimately also impact the exchange rate."

For this reason, it anticipates parity would be $750 in a month, $755 in three months, and $770 by the end of the year.

title: Two months of social crisis, financial indicators show signs of recovery, but productive sectors remain lagging behind
text:
The main local stock index, IPSA, rose 1.7% in 2019 to October 18. The outbreak of the social crisis left that performance behind and dyed the local market uncertainly.Thus, ipSA fell 13.58% in the year and on November 13 reached a two-and-a-half-year low by closing by 4,412.25 points. That day was the turning point for the local stock market, as it has shown an uptick from there, although it is still 7.3% below the pre-crisis level. Yesterday it closed at 4,814.68 points.Since the social outburst, the most affected IPSA shares are Salfacorp, which has declined by 38.78%; Ripley, who is down 34.52%, and Entel, who has fallen 27.72%.

 Despite these casualties, analysts note that local stocks have had a recovery in recent weeks, given greater local stability and a decrease in violence."The situation of violence and instability has tended to decline in the country; Chileans' lives return to the pre-social outburst routine, which normalizes economic activity in the country," says MBI equities analyst Sébastien Fresard.This has been accompanied, according to experts, by a political environment that seeks to clear uncertainty, reaching agreements around the main demands of the public.However, Pablo Solís, head of institutional equities at Tanner Investments, notes that "agreements on sensitive issues for citizens are still lacking. If strong consensus is reached this summer, we should expect to have more visibility into domestic economic behavior and how that performance will affect corporate performance by 2020."After peaking at $829, the dollar has fallen and the Chilean peso is the currency that most appreciates against the dollar in DecemberIt has been 61 days since the social outburst and the markets have suffered its effects. Uncertainty that has been generated regarding the economy and new regulations led investors to seek the dollar as a safe asset, causing it to climb to all-time highs of $829 in late November.However, in recent weeks it has recovered. In December it has fallen $53.4 and the Chilean peso is the most appreciated emerging currency against the dollar with an advance of 7.17%. Despite this drop, the exchange rate is still far from the $712 levels it was in prior to the social outburst.Yesterday, the exchange rate dropped $5.8 and closed at $756.6 since November 8 when it ended at $747.5.According to analysts, several events have led to the fall of the dollar. These include the central bank's exchange rate intervention, the decrease in violence alongside the progress in legislative agreements in pursuit of the social agenda announced by the Government and, most recently, the increase in the price of copper under the agreement of the "phase one" between the United States and China.Felipe Bravo, strategy and studies manager of Sartor Finance Group, comments that "the intervention of the Central Bank together with the legislative-political progress and the decrease in events of extreme violence are elements that underpin the strengthening of the weight."On the international level, Banmerchant Capital General Manager Luis Mendez notes that it influenced "the rise in the price of copper after the signing of phase 1 of the China-U.S. trade agreement."Moving forward, analysts predict that the exchange rate will continue to fall below the current level to stabilize at around $750.Sébastien Fresard, MBI's equity analyst, says "should stabilize at these levels, between $750 and $760. We also believe that at these prices the Central Bank will begin to withdraw some of its intervention (as it has done every Friday). This should stopto fall and keep it stable around these levels."While expectations are positive and some recovery of the local currency is shown, Banmerchant's Mendez says that uncertainty levels will remain high in the face of the new Constitution.Country risk downgraded by political agreementsAlmost 60 points came the country risk measured by the CDS to 5 years in the context of social and political crisis that the country is going through. Thus, since 18 October, this indicator has risen 22%, but so far in 2019 it has a decrease of 35.86%. Yesterday it dropped 6.13% and closed by 40.18 points, away from the 57.43 peak points that marked November 29 along with the dollar rising to historic levels and ended with the exchange rate intervention of the Central Bank.Pablo Solís, head of institutional equities at Tanner Investments, points out that country risk is an indicator that has tended to stabilize. "We consider that it is unlikely to see an additional deterioration to solvency in the country. With an autonomous central bank and a well-functioning financial market, the likelihood of seeing a structural change in the rules of the game is low," says Solís.The fall in the country's risk is due, according to Felipe Bravo, strategy and studies manager of Sartor Finance Group, to "actions in foreign exchange policy, political agreements and reduction of violence along with better prospects for emerging countries and exporters of raw materials".Rising and recovering financing costsA significant milestone marked on Tuesday the long-term local financing costs measured by one of the market benchmarks: 10-year Central Bank bonds in UF (BCU 10). Their rates fell sharply 24 basis points, to 0.25%, below the 0.26% they were marking on October 18 last year, when the social outburst was exposed."Overall, the mood is calming down and this social explosion has been falling down: it looks more governance and that has stuck not only to the rates, but also to the stock market," says Milenko Mitrovic, fixed income manager at Octogone Chile. "Add to that the intervention of the Central Bank in both the foreign exchange and fixed income markets," he says.In the market they believe that the key lies in the intervention of the Central Bank, which has led the dollar to fall $72.4 from its all-time high ($829). As of this Tuesday (when the currency dropped $5.8 to $756.6), the monetary body had injected $1.95 billion in spot reserves and $2.85 billion in forward hedges in nearly two and a half weeks of intervention. In addition, the entity had purchased $2,758 million in its own bonds from the market as of last Thursday. It is the so-called Creole QE, or Central's debt-buying program, which is intended to contain financing costs.The leak from Chilean stock fundsThe first economic signs of the social crisis had a rapid impact on the market: small investors quickly reduced assets - both bonds and shares - in their cards. This was evident in mutual funds, instruments whose flows capture changes in small investors' preferences. During the eight weeks following October 18, funds investing in local stocks saw many bailouts and very few contributions. This led to persistent net uninvestments. The amounts of these weekly sales, which totaled almost US$ 250 million, reached a peak in mid-November, after which they were regressing, until last week: the first since the beginning of the crisis that Chilean stock funds managed to capture more contributions that ransoms, which gave them their first positive balance. It's a timid $859 million, but it could be the basis for new advances.Exports20%, but is attenuated in DecemberThe performance of foreign trade has been impacted by the social crisis that is going through the country, both by the instability of the exchange rate and by the partial work that was recorded a few days in ports and transport Terrestrial. Between the week ended October 23 and December 7, exports fell 20% compared to the same period in 2018.In the first post-crisis week, local exports fell 39%, while imports fell 33%. However, these setbacks have tended to slow, especially in the case of shipments. According to Central Bank statistics, exports of goods between 1 and 7 this month fell 6.6% compared to the same week last year, while imports fell 29.4% over the same period.On the export side, one of the products that has helped mitigate the decline is fruit shipments, explains Banchile chief economist Carolina Grunwald. "Cherry season, for example," explains the economist.He adds that, in general, foreign trade had been slowing down before. "Decisions to ask for things are made from the before," he points out.It analyses that November came with foreign trade information with "the crisis" so that the commissions of that month were affected by the uncertainty it generates, in addition to the likely less need for products.Employment impact: Dismissals for the needs of the company reach 110 thousand since the beginning of the crisisOne of the most sensitive blows that economists have anticipated by the social crisis is the one that has received the job. Between 18 October and 13 December, dismissals for Article 161(1) of the Labour Code, which refers to the causal "needs of the undertaking", reach 110,630 jobs.Although there are some indicators that have tended to recover in recent weeks, it still does not show an improvement. In fact, in the first 13 days of December alone, dismissals for the company's needs amounted to 35,836, very close to the monthly average of 40,313 this year between the months of January and September before the social outburst.The Undersecretary of Labour, Fernando Arab, comments that "in the first fortnight of December we already reached the average layoffs for the needs of the company of a normal month. It is therefore unfair for workers to suffer the effects of the crisis by losing their jobs. That is why it is so important, on the one hand, to curb violence, as many of the jobs lost respond to employers who were vandalized and, on the other hand, it is key to move rapidly on the agenda of economic revival and employment protection."Since the social outburst on 18 October, November is the month that has had the most layoffs for this cause, ranking at 62,049 compared to 33,628 that he scored the same month in 2018.In its last Monetary Policy Report (IPoM) in early December, the Central Bank estimated that given the country's crisis, unemployment will record a sharp increase, and could reach 10% early next year. In the August-October mobile quarter, the last available data, the unemployment was 7%.Commerce begins to normalize its operations and active demolition of burning rooms after relocating its workersEven as the economic sector most affected by the social crisis, two months after the events have started - which have involved stinging, damage and even fires in its buildings, its main players have already begun, as far as possible, to normalize its operations throughout the country.This is the case of the Sodimac home improvement chain, linked to the soa-wingFalabella, who said that of the 89 stores it operates in Chile, at this time of year "almost all of it are operational (only a Homecenter, a Builder and a store of the Imperial subsidiary are closed, as they were affected by fires)", he said.Regarding the future of the burned enclosures, which were located on leased land, the company said that "we have not yet defined the investment plan", so its reconstruction is still being evaluated. However, he explained that "we have relocated all the workers in the stores that were burned."In the case of the Tottus supermarket chain, which is also part of Falabella, they indicated that 12 of its 69 premises were significantly affected. The firm even stated that "there are two supermarkets where the damage was significant and of great severity, which has involved making the decision to keep them closed."These are located in Llolleo, in the town of San Antonio and Pedro Fontova, in the commune of Huechuraba, Santiago.All of the above affected 2,000 workers of the company, of which 90% were relocated to other rooms.In the case of SMU, Unimarc's parent, Wholesale 10, Alvi and OK Market, stated that "95% of our premises are operating to date. In relation to burning premises, we are initiating demolition processes in those that require it. The company has not made any other decisions."Pharmacies Ahumada has also begun to normalize its functions. Of the 341 premises operating in Chile, 305 are already operational, while 36 remain closed.Even with this process of reactivation of operations, the Santiago Chamber of Commerce (CCS) analyzed that "the holiday season has been very weak, despite the fact that in recent weeks there is a moderate improvement in demand". Thus, he predicted "a drop of around 1% in sales this year, as a result of the last quarter crisis, and for now a flat 2020 year."On employment, according to a recent CCS survey, 18% of those over the age of 18 said that at least one person in their household has lost their jobs since the social crisis erupted.Construction continues with braking plans and notes that "it is far from saying that tranquility has returned"One of the most obvious reactions of the social outburst in the construction and real estate sector was the freezing of the start of investments whose works were about to begin. Added to this was the industry's recognition of a decline in sales, which has affected 70% of companies, according to a recent survey by the Chilean Chamber of Construction that adds that more than a third of firms admit that they have cancelled contracts and that their dot has been reduced.Productivity in the ongoing work has also declined, especially in completion work and in the first weeks after 18 October. Meanwhile, coarse-work activities will be resented in a few months when the crews that are now in these activities see the labor supply reduced because of a shortage of new projects, they indicate in the sector.Regarding the vision of the item two months after the social outburst, the executive director of the Association of Real Estate Developers (ADI), Vicente Domínguez, notes that "my appreciation is that after the worst moments of the social upheacon, the situation is not appreciates as critically as a few weeks ago; however, it is far from saying still that the tranquility has returned. As we know, the investment will return if calm returns and the state manages to take back control of public order, which has lost it. If this does not happen, the fall in investment will continue."Dominguez adds that "there are sensitive lows in real estate sales, which are approaching 50%. But, for example,on the other hand, it is clear that a significant housing deficit is still being maintained and needs to be built, which should lead to steps in the way of taking steps to make this possible."The constitutional debate and within that the social role of housing also concerns the sector. "The discussion around the role of social housing is handled more by ideological convictions than by technical evidence. Ordinarily, experiences in other countries are known in a twisted way to justify positions," says Dominguez.He admits that "there is, of course, concern for constitutional discussion, but the central themes of the debate are not yet seen; for example, whether it will be a more presidential or parliamentary government, whether the independence of the Central Bank will be maintained, whether or not there will be a Constitutional Court, and so on."In tourism they have not managed to revive the demandA critical outlook. This is how the executive vice president of the Federation of Tourism Companies (Fedetur), Helen Kouyoumdjian, described the situation in tourism. The sector has been one of the main areas resentful of the effects of the social crisis, which two months after its start, fails to rebound.According to the latest figures from the Undersecretariat of Tourism, 292,215 foreign visitors arrived in November, 37% less than in the same month of 2018. It is the largest year-on-year low recorded since the coming of international tourists."We still don't see an uptick in bookings. Initially there was a nearly 50% cancellation of bookings and a significant drop in demand, that has not improved at all," Kouyoumdjian said.On what is expected for December, the executive of Fedetur pointed out that the fall will not be so pronounced, mainly because last year there was a lower tourist arrival explained by the decline of Argentinians. "But even few people are going to get there, it will be a figure well below the historical ranges of the month of December," he said."We wanted to have a hope, campaigning various lycampaigns, but from an economic point of view we are still in the critical state of a month ago," he added.Fedetur estimated that 2019 will close with a 23% drop in the influx of foreign tourists. This means that a total of 4,390,000 people from other countries will visit the country, compared to 5,722,928 who arrived in 2018.Kouyoumdjian projected that the sector could return to normal in about four to six months more. "It will all depend on how the security conditions are provided, if there are no longer disturbances where the tourist infrastructure is. That's where we should be able to reactivate," he said.Demand for energy recovers and grows 0.4%An improvement presented demand for energy as of November, according to data revealed yesterday by the National Electricity Coordinator. This, after the social outburst that has affected the country.According to the end of November, electricity consumption in both the industrial and residential sectors rebounded and showed a slight growth of 0.4% compared to the same month of the previous year, reaching 6,286 GWh in gross energy demand. title: Latin American  currencies  are no longer on the brink of collapse
text:
We can say it in a very low voice, but the worst may have already happened for Latin America's foreign exchange markets.

Currencies in Brazil, Chile and Colombia are reducing losses in December after falling to historic lows last month, following a wave of violent protests that threatened to depress already slow growth in the region.

Chile's weight rose 3.3%, Colombia's weight rose 1.8% and Brazil's real gained 0.5% in the first four days of the month. It may not seem like much, but it's Chile's longest winning streak since June and Colombia since September. The central bank's intervention in Chile and Brazil has played an important role, while Colombia is relieved as the protests did not get out of hand as many feared.

Of course, not all currencies have left their problems behind. The Argentine peso remains close to an all-time low amid strict monetary controls as Alberto Fernandez prepares to take over the presidency on December 10.

"There is a possibility that Latin America's foreign exchange market will continue to rebound to close this gap" between the rest of the currencies of developing countries, which surpassed the region in November, said Ilya Gofshteyn, senior macro market strategist Standard Chartered Bank in New York. "Lower liquidity at the end of the year creates unfavourable seasonal dynamics, but I would expect the BRL, MXN, COP and CLP currencies to start in 2020 with a stronger tone."

The entry Currencies of Latin America are no longer on the brink of collapse was first published in La Tercera.

title: Chile 's historic  central bank intervention  fails to curb peso volatility
text:
A day after Chile's central bank announced a historic intervention to contain the depreciation of the peso, the local currency on Friday suffered a day of heavy volatility. The $20 billion injected by the autonomous body on Thursday has not calmed the markets, but there has been some recovery from the peso to the dollar. If the record of 828 pesos per greenback was reached on Thursday, it closed at 809 today. During the day the depreciation left him at times in 797 with peaks of up to 826. And it was precisely the movements of the peso against the dollar that caused the central bank to take the action.

"The origin of this increased uncertainty is a growing and persistent degree of crispness in the country, expressed in public security issues, in political conflicts, in questioning and weakening of the institutions," the president of the central bank, Mario Marcel.

The economist said they aspire to reduce volatility—in fact, he has announced that he will inject 2,000 of the $20 billion between Monday and Friday—but that the central bank's measures will not be able to influence the origins of uncertainty: "It is clear that when we see in the economy a growing degree of uncertainty that influences certain markets, particularly those that are more sensitive to it, as in this case the exchange market, of course we can through measures like this reduce volatility, contain some of that uncertainty, but we have no ability to influence the origins of it."

For Economy Minister Lucas Palacios, "the dollar continues with volatility because markets remain very speculative regarding the economic situation in our country." On the injection of $20 billion, he indicated that it is a "very significant amount, corresponding to roughly half of the international reserves held by the Central Bank."

The depreciation of the local currency has been on the rise since the start of demonstrations on 18 October in Chile, which in addition to peaceful protests has caused violent altercations in different cities of the country. At the moment, there is no clear way out of the conflict. Neither social measures nor the possibility of changing the Constitution seem sufficient to calm the street, and the political crisis has already spread the economy to high levels of uncertainty. If on 18 October the dollar was changed to 712 Chilean pesos, in mid-November it exceeded the barrier of 800, marking unprecedented levels.

The last time the Chilean autonomous body had intervened directly in the exchange rate market was in 2011, however, it is the largest such operation since the flexible exchange rate system debuted in Chile in 1999. The new and historic injection will be applied from next Monday until May 29. The agency will report every Friday the amount, terms and conditions of the auctions.

title: Chile 's  central bank  will  intervene foreign exchange  market in the face of weakness in weight
text:
28 Nov (Reuters) - The Central Bank of Chile said Thursday that the foreign exchange market will intervene with asset sales of up to $20 billion, amid the recent currency crash over the country's social uncertainty.

The Chilean peso closed Thursday in its second consecutive all-time low, in a volatile session in the face of the wave of protests shaking the country more than 40 days ago. The intervention will take place from Monday and will be extended until May next year.

"The events in our country in recent weeks have affected the normal functioning of the economy," the central bank said in a statement.

The program will consist of a possible sale of $10 billion in the spot forex market and up to another $10 billion in sales of "exchange hedging instruments".

"This exceptional measure is consistent with the monetary policy scheme, based on an inflationary goal and exchange rate flexibility," the central bank's statement added.

At least 26 people have been killed, more than 13,000 injured and 25,000 have been arrested in Chile amid demonstrations, rants and incendiary attacks on supermarkets, metro stations, hotels and churches.

The bank is expected to cut its benchmark interest rate to 1.5% in December, according to a monthly analyst survey published on November 12, at a time when the riots are affecting the copper-producing country's growth.

(Report of Fabian Cambero. Edited by Rodrigo Charme)

title: Chile 's  Central Bank  announces historic  intervention  to contain peso depreciation
text:
The Central Bank of Chile has announced a historic intervention in the foreign exchange market of up to $20 billion from next Monday until May 2020. The decision has come after a further rise in the dollar against the Chilean peso, which changed to 828 pesos for each U.S. currency setting new records. Six weeks after the social outburst, which has installed uncertainty in the Andean country from different fronts, the injection of the autonomous body responds to high volatility and seeks to stop the violent escalation of the US currency in front of the Chilean one. In the last two days it's gone up 30 pesos. Since October 18, the day the protests began, 116 pesos (a 16.7% increase).

"Beyond the level reached by the exchange rate, which partly importantly reflects greater uncertainty, the speed and succession of movements in the same direction have generated volatility that is deemed excessive," Chile's Central Bank said in a statement. "Given the fundamentals of the Chilean economy, including low indexation to the dollar, exchange rate changes do not have an immediate impact on households, businesses and the public sector, and their move to inflation is generally moderate. Even so, excessive exchange rate volatility makes it difficult to form prices, and spending and production decisions for individuals and businesses. It also affects the healthy economy's adjustment and creates market unease," the bank added.

The last time the Central Bank had intervened directly in the foreign exchange market was in 2011, however, it is the largest operation of its kind since the flexible exchange rate system debuted in Chile in 1999. The new and historic injection will be made through two modalities: spot dollar sales of up to $10 billion and sales of foreign exchange hedging instruments, also for up to $10 billion. The intervention will apply from 2 December until 29 May. The agency will report every Friday the amount, terms and conditions of the auctions.

The market has reacted to the uncertainty that has been in Chile for six weeks. Protests and violence, which has failed to contain itself despite social ad measures and a new constitution that will have a plebiscite next April, have the country running at half-machine. The Treasury has not ruled out a technical recession in 2020 and an estimated 300,000 new unemployed people as of the end of December. The destruction of public and private infrastructure is still unquantifiable. According to guild calculations, some 20,000 small and medium-sized enterprises could file for bankruptcy due to the consequences of the social outburst. Large companies have also suffered: Walmart has accounted for 1,300 events - between shears and fires - that have left 35 supermarkets burned, 18 completely destroyed and 97 currently closed. "They have put the labor source of about 5,000 people at risk," Walmart said in a newsletter. After the announcement of foreign exchange intervention, in after market transactions the dollar dropped by about 23 Chilean pesos, to 805.

title: Currencies  from Chile, Colombia and Brazil touch historic lows against the dollar
text:
The currencies of Chile, Colombia and Brazil hit all-time lows against the dollar this week due to political instability, outstanding reforms, popular demands for social equity and growing war-on-account uncertainty non-trepy.

"The dollar has been strengthened by a nervousness in the face of the possible contagion of political instability in the region," announced on Thursday in an interview with Efe, Latin America's chief analyst at OANDA, Alfonso Esparza, who believes that "inequality has crawling in the slow progress of the economy" leading to these social manifestations.

According to the spokesman for the foreign exchange and "commodities" firm, the devaluation also comes to "the attractiveness of the dollar" as a refuge from the uncertainty of the trade war and "a solid advance" of the US economy "when most developed and emerging economies remain stagnant."

The Brazilian real, the Colombian peso and the Chilean peso hit new all-time lows against the dollar this week.

A scenario in which Latin America's central banks could cut rates even further to boost economic growth in the face of low inflationary pressures.

These are the keys to the movement of the U.S. currency in the region.

1.BAD DAYS FOR THE CHILEAN PESO

The weakening of Latin American currencies peaked in Chile, where the peso depreciated on Thursday by 1.1% and closed at 828.36 units per dollar, its lowest value in history.

This slip of the Chilean currency coincides with the 42 days since the beginning of the violent social outburst in the country that still shows no signs of a nearby exit.

Chile's Central Bank today announced an intervention in the foreign exchange market that will consist of the sale of dollars in the amount of up to 10 billion spot and exchange hedging instruments for another 10 billion.

The issuer also lowered its growth forecast for 2019 from 2.5 to 1.9%. The Government estimates that up to 300,000 jobs could be lost by the end of the year, which would raise the unemployment rate from 7% to 10%.

2. MEASURES THAT DO NOT CONVENCE

Colombia has been facing a wave of protests since November 21 against President Ivan Duque's economic and social policies.

According to analysts, the demonstrations are beginning to have an impact on the foreign exchange market, and in fact this week the US currency hit all-time highs in that country.

The dollar valued a little over 1% against the Colombian peso on Wednesday and hit a new all-time high by achieving a trading cap of 3,524.

And in today's session the U.S. currency hit 3,520 per unit, but it eventually closed at 3,508.

A report released on Thursday by OANDA notes that "investor nervousness is rising the longer unemployment is," which does not seem to be diminishing in the face of the disconnect between the Colombian government and the leaders of the demonstrations that have already expressed to the what their conditions for negotiating are.

3.AFTERTHE STORM...After three consecutive record-breaking slamming, the dollar relinquished 1% in Brazil and was posted to 4,215 reais on Thursday thanks to a new intervention from the Central Bank.

This fall comes after the Brazilian issuer auctioned $1 billion on the market to contain the greenback hike.

Alfonso Esparza states that "the risk of contagion of protest movements" in Brazil "has forced the government of Jair Bolsonaro" to curb "the reforms planned to avoid triggering a confrontation with groups opposed to the measures".

Yesterday the US dollar hit a new all-time high in Brazil, after it appreciated 0.45% against the Brazilian real and ended the day sold at R$4,258 in the trade exchange rate.

4.A WEEK WITHOUT MAJOR UPS

In Argentina, despite the relentless devaluation of the last year, the dollar remained stable on Thursday for the second consecutive day and stood at 57.75 pesos for the purchase and 62.25 pesos for sale at the state-owned Banco Nación.

Argentine economist Gustavo Ber explains that one of the market concerns has to do with Argentina's debt restructuring, following the urgency of the "bulging" maturities of the coming months.

By 2020, the South American country faces debts to private creditors and multilateral agencies of about $39.3 billion.

5.A DOLLAR THAT IS STRENGTHENED

During today's day, the US dollar appreciated 0.05% against the Mexican peso and was exchanged at 19.56 per unit after "solid data" in the U.S. economy and "an increase in turbulence" in the possible U.S.-China trade treaty, according to OANDA.

"The Mexican currency has been depreciating all week with a strong dollar, on the one hand, and on the other the growth revision that remains stagnant. (...) The Mexican peso depreciated 1.83% in November and continues to press down for the same factors that have led to all-time highs in other Latin American currencies," he says.
