title: Dollar climbing ignites debate over whether  Central Bank  of  Chile  should  intervene
text:
The violent rise of the dollar today, the biggest since being recorded in an exchange rate free float scheme and leading the currency to surpass the $800 mark during the session, ignited the debate among economists as to whether it is time for the Central Bank to oversee market to slow the progress and how it should.

Since the foreign exchange band was eliminated in September 1999, there has been a flexible exchange rate system in Chile where the value of the currency is determined by the interaction of market players. However, he has left himself the power to intervene when he believes that exchange rate movements are not in line with the long-term fundamentals.

The last time the Central Bank intervened in the market was in 2011, when it had to go out and buy dollars at a time when it was trading at $465.

The situation, now, went to the other end: a hike that reached $40 intraday shortly before noon.

The central bank has influenced the price of the dollar through statements - known as "verbal invention" -, paper tenders or purchases or direct foreign exchange sales.

Should he intervene or not now?

"Exchange rate reaches $800, levels unimaginable a few weeks ago. Inaction of the Central Bank only ends up feeding perception of risk and short-term macroeconomic deterioration," Jorge Selaive, chief economist at Scotiabank, said in a tweet and who earlier exceeded $780 had indicated that a "containment action of the Central Bank seems necessary very soon."

Nathan Pincheira, Fynsa's chief economist, said: "An intervention through foreign exchange sales seems unlikely to me at the moment. Short-term dollar swap tenders seem highly likely to do so, to maintain dollar liquidity in the face of significant rate increases in that currency over the past few days. Verbal intervention may be in conversation now."

title: No sign of  Chile central bank intervention  seen despite peso fall
text:
SANTIAGO, Aug 21 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank is nowhere near intervening in the foreign exchange market, economists said, despite the peso's fall to a 12-year low against the U.S. dollar.

The peso weakened sharply against the greenback this week, extending its year-to-date decline to 12.5 percent. It came close to breaching the 700 peso to the dollar mark for the first time since 2003, as fears over the Chinese economy have led down the price of copper, Chile's key export.

Out of nine economists and analysts surveyed by Reuters, three thought the central bank might decide to intervene if the peso were to hit 750 per dollar, but others did not see an intervention likely at all.

"I don't see any kinds of signs they are ready or inclined to intervene in the FX," said Tiago Severo, economist at Goldman Sachs.

"When we look at the language of the central bank's communications it seems that they see this adjustment of the currency as part of a natural rebalancing of the market," he added.

The bank has made no attempt to talk down the peso but has expressed concern that risks from the Chinese economy and U.S. monetary policy could increase volatility and have a knock-on effect on inflation.

Of the world's 36 most-traded currencies, the Chilean peso has posted the 6th biggest fall versus the dollar in 2015, trading at 696.70 on Friday, much weaker than prior forecasts.

FANNING INFLATION

Many of Latin America's central banks intervene to a greater or lesser extent in their foreign exchange markets to shore up their currencies.

Colombia's central bank has not intervened so far this year despite a 61 percent depreciation in its peso currency, but analysts say that may change soon because of inflation worries. Policymakers meet to vote on the benchmark interest rate on Friday.

In Chile, the currency's sharp drop has also fanned consumer prices, keeping 12-month inflation at the top end or above the central bank's 2 percent to 4 percent target range since April 2014.

That could lead the central bank to respond by hiking interest rates, the economists said.

"It's possible that the central bank will start to remove its monetary stimulus and hike interest rates by 25 or 50 basis points towards the end of 2015, regardless of weak economic growth," said Diego Colman, analyst with 4Cast. title: UPDATE 1- Chile central bank  says not close to  currency  market  intervention
text:
(Adds central bank's comment on labor market, background)

SANTIAGO, Dec 18 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank has no plans to intervene in the foreign exchange market, the bank's chief said on Thursday, even though Chile's peso has depreciated more than 14 percent versus the U.S. dollar this year, among the steepest declines in emerging markets.

"We have a floating exchange rate policy and as such it isn't part of the central bank's normal policy to intervene in the currency market, and the truth is that we're not even close to thinking about doing it," central bank Governor Rodrigo Vergara said.

Among the world's 36 most-traded currencies, Chile's peso has posted the seventh biggest drop versus the greenback in 2014, according to Reuters data.

"We believe the peso's recent depreciation is a way to adjust to the new international scenario Chile's economy faces," Vergara told journalists.

The economy of the world's top copper producer has been slowing for several quarters, hampered initially by stagnating investment, most notably in the mining sector, with the slowdown compounded by falling consumption.

Growth in 2014 will likely be 1.7 percent, a five-year low, the bank forecast recently. That compares with growth of 4.1 percent in 2013.

Despite cooling economy, the labor market has remained in better shape than many had feared. The jobless rate for the August to October period fell to 6.4 percent from 6.6 percent in September to July.

But Vergara cautioned the labor market could still feel the effects of the slowdown.

"There is a lag between what happens with economic activity and what happens in the labor market ... and so we may see an additional deterioration in the labor market in the coming months due to the lower growth in the economy." title: Barron's Blog:Peru Better Exposure Than Chile: Peruvian Sole Lower Risk
text:
(This story has been posted on Barron's Online's Emerging Markets Daily at http://blogs.barrons.com/emergingmarketsdaily/)

By Shuli Ren

As we have seen last Friday and in Asia today, fear of September QE tapering has driven EM currencies lower. Peruvian sol should be no exception. In a research note published today, Barclays lowered their forecast to 2.85 sol per dollar by 2013 year end, and to 2.95 in 2014. Peruvian sol last traded at 2.8 against the dollar.

But Peruvian sol is seen as a relatively low-risk currency. Its central bank BCRP is more willing to intervene. Earlier this month, BCRP bought its sol in the foreign exchange markets to defend a 2.8 sol-per-dollar ceiling.

In Barclays analysts Alejandro Arreaza, Alejandro Grisanti, and Sebastian Brown's own words:

BCRP is more likely to manage the PEN's volatility than the BCCh [Chile's central bank] is of intervening in the CLP [Chilean peso] market. As a result, we do not think the USD/PEN is likely to go above 2.90. On the other hand, the USD/CLP does not have a ceiling, and while we expect the USD/CLP to only rise by about 3% over the next six months, it could touch levels above 520 in the event of a global shock. In short, the USD/CLP does not have a ceiling.

Foreign exchange risk is a big concern for US investors holding emerging market single-country ETF's. We have two countries: Peru and Chile - both exposed to China and mining and both exhibiting some signs of internal economic strength. The IMF forecast Peru's GDP to grow at 6.1% in 2014 and Chile's to grow at 4.6%. Meanwhile, the two countries' CPI inflation, current account deficits, and unemployment rates forecasts are remarkably comparable. See IMF forecast (table 2.4, p.60) here.

Exchange rate differential can be a main driver of the pricing then, if Peru and Chile have similar fundamentals. Year-to-date, iShares MSCI All Peru Capped ETF ( EPU) lost 22.9%. iShares MSCI Chile Capped ETF ( ECH) lost a comparable 22%.

title: Chile Peso Ends Stronger On Rising Copper Prices, Dollar Sales
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean peso closed stronger versus the dollar Monday on the back of rising international copper prices and institutional dollar sales.

The peso gained to CLP467.20 to the dollar, versus Friday's close of CLP467.80, while trading in a range of CLP466.80 to CLP469.00.

Spot copper prices in London trading rose 1.3% to $4.04060 per pound, according to Chile's state copper commission Cochilco, on bargain-hunting by investors.

Because Chile is the world's largest copper producer, accounting for a third of global output, its currency often takes direction from the industrial metal's prices abroad.

The euro's slip against the dollar, however, tempered the peso's strength. Investors sold euros after Standard & Poor's downgrade of Greece's credit rating.

As Chile's economy is highly export-intensive and almost a third of its exports are bound for European ports, the peso often moves in the same direction as the euro does against the dollar.

"The market was selling dollars today...but if over the coming sessions copper's rebound sputters and the euro stays flat, the peso will be stuck in a tight range," said Osvaldo Molina, currency trader at local brokerage and investment bank LarrainVial.

The local currency will likely see resistance at CLP462-CLP465 and support at CLP470-CLP472 over the coming days, he added.

The Central Bank of Chile, as part of the its $12 billion currency intervention program, purchased $50 million on Monday at an average rate of CLP468.29. The central bank has accumulated $4.4 billion so far this year.

In the bond market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central bank bonds, or BCUs, ended lower on institutional demand for fixed income instruments.

title: ANALYSIS-No pressure from Chile's blue-chips on peso surge
text:
* Strong peso boosts many bottom lines, easing push to act

* Exporters stay profitable with commodities boom

* After intervention, options to tame peso scarce

By Brad Haynes

SANTIAGO, May 5 (Reuters) - Chilean policymakers can hold off aggressive currency measures like those in Brazil as the peso's surge to three-year highs punishes smaller exporters but proves a blessing for major firms riding a consumption-driven boom.

Chile's top-40 IPSA stock index <.IPSA> is dominated by retailers, banks and electric companies that have surged with greater purchasing power and domestic demand. Top exporters, meanwhile, are cashing in on record prices for raw materials.

In the lower-profile fruit sector, where global prices have not offset the waning weight of weak-dollar revenues, some exporters are howling for government measures and elevated central bank intervention -- while the economy's heavyweights stay silent.

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> has rallied 17 percent since mid-2010 and 3 percent in the past six weeks, erasing the impact of a $12 billion 2011 currency intervention program launched in January due to global dollar weakness and the strength of the country's main export, copper.

While regional peer Brazil has implemented a series of unorthodox measures to protect local industry from currency strength, Chilean authorities have repeatedly waved off capital controls, opening the door for an extended rally.

"Chilean authorities haven't succumbed to political pressures," said analyst Eduardo Suarez of RBC Capital Markets, citing one reason he was shorting Brazil's real against Chile's peso. "In Brazil they're getting much more pressure to act." <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ > Chile stocks unfazed by FX rally http://r.reuters.com/vyd49r ("http://r.reuters.com/vyd49r") > Options scarce to tame Chile's peso [ID:nN26276247] > For a TAKE A LOOK on Chile economy [ID:nN26HILEFI] ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

It helps that so many leading Chilean firms see the brighter side of cheaper imports.

"A lower exchange rate is clearly favorable for consumption," said Juan Benavides, chief executive of leading retailer Falabella , Chile's biggest company by bourse capitalization. Benavides noted that a strong peso also helped with higher global prices for inputs like cotton.

Regional airline LAN's cargo and passenger traffic has soared with greater purchasing power in Chile and Brazil, offsetting higher local costs due to currency strength, according to Chief Financial Officer Alejandro de la Fuente.

Meanwhile, state mining giant Codelco, the world's No. 1 copper producer, accepts currency appreciation as a side effect of the boom lifting all of Chile's major commodity exporters.

"It's not a serious problem," Codelco Chairman Gerardo Jofre told Reuters at a business conference this week. "Costs indexed to the local currency are rising, but of course that's counteracted by high copper prices."

Strong wood pulp prices also boosted the bottom line for industrial conglomerate Copec , the IPSA's top-weighted stock, whose profit rose 76 percent last year from 2009, while forestry rival CMPC saw a 144 percent jump.

Raw materials make up about two-thirds of Chilean exports according to UN data, but manufactured goods make up just one-tenth -- compared with more than a third of Brazil's exports and 75 percent of Mexico's.

In Mexico, industries competing with a flood of cheap Chinese goods have begun protesting the local peso's rise even though it remains undervalued by several metrics, according to RBC's Suarez.

Brazilian policymakers have cited the vulnerability of local manufacturers as they beat the currency back from record highs with taxes and reserve requirements on incoming capital. [ID:nN29268075]

Chile's chamber of commerce has remained silent on the peso's appreciation to three-year highs last week.

The Chilean companies hit hardest by the peso's rise, such as fruit and berry farmers, are smaller and less visible in Santiago, the capital. They have seen costs rising in dollar terms while global prices for their goods are flat.

"Our sector doesn't get much attention. There's a political indifference," said Antonio Walker, who runs fruit trade group Fedefruta, as well his orchards in the sparsely populated south. "Chileans have gone from agricultural exporters to a nation of mining, retail and construction."

Fedefruta has adjusted demands accordingly. While some farmers still demand a heavier government hand in currency markets, Walker is asking for more targeted lifelines aimed at farmers' hiring, energy and credit costs.

"Since we have a sector-specific problem, we're asking for sector-specific measures," he said.

The government has responded with programs to help small exporters with currency hedging and cut red tape on customs. But administration and central bank officials continue to express skepticism about capital controls. [ID:nN08100714]

Analysts see the government maintaining more farmer-friendly measures and encouraging capital outflows before turning to more unorthodox currency measures in the case of a severely misaligned peso. For options to tame the peso: [ID:nN26276247]

But Chile's breaking point may be farther off than regional peers'.

The peso closed at 468.50 per U.S. dollar on Thursday. But in 2008, the central bank waited until the exchange rate firmed past 430 per dollar before intervening in the market.

title: IMF: Capital Controls Are Valid Tool, But Unnecessary In Chile
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Although capital controls are a valid tool, implementing them in Chile to fight back the peso's appreciation isn't warranted, Miguel Savastano, the deputy director of the Western Hemisphere Department of the International Monetary Fund, said Wednesday.

Despite the Central Bank of Chile's ongoing $12 billion currency intervention program, the peso has crawled back to a three-year high versus the dollar, having appreciated almost 8% since its low point this year and nearly 12% over the last 52 weeks.

While Chile attracts strong investment flows due to its robust economic growth and tightening monetary policy, the country also sees strong capital outflows, making it unnecessary to "impose more restrictions on capital," said Savastano at the Andean nation's central bank.

According to the most recent data, Chile's private pension fund managers, or AFPs, which are the nation's largest institutional investors, held nearly 46% of their investments abroad.

Late last year, the central bank moved to gradually increase the cap on AFP investments abroad to 80%, from its then 60% limit.

In recent months, the president of the central bank, Jose De Gregorio, has repeated that there's no need to implement capital controls as Chile isn't seeing net capital inflows and will post a small surplus in its current account this year.

In the 1990s, Chile implemented capital controls, through a reserve requirement on foreign investments, which officials have said weren't effective in curbing speculative capital inflows.

Also, despite the IMF's recent warning to the contrary, Savastano said that after the local stock market's fall this year, Chile wasn't currently facing a stock-market bubble.

By mid-February the local blue-chip Ipsa index had slipped over 13% compared to the closing price at the end of 2010. The Ipsa has since pared those losses and is 2.4% lower year-to-date.

If the stock market continues recovering, however, in "about six months or so, it's going to start showing symptoms again of being overvalued," Savastano said.

Late last year, the central bank said the Ipsa index was overpriced, fueling a quick sell-off.

title: Chile  Central Banker: Peso 3%-5% Firmer Without  Intervention  - Paper
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean peso, currently trading at three-year highs against the dollar, would likely be 3% to 5% stronger were it not for the central bank's currency intervention program, bank governor Rodrigo Vergara told Friday's La Segunda evening daily.

Vergara's view coincides with that of other central bank governors and Finance Minister Felipe Larrain.

He said the bank's $12 billion intervention program was sizable and generated significant expenses to the bank.

"The intervention is costly because financing it is more expensive that the returns obtained on reserves," Vergara told the newspaper in an interview.

Vergara, who is seen as a candidate for central bank president when current chief Jose De Gregorio's term ends in December, said the bank wasn't likely to pick up the pace of its current purchases of $50 million a day.

As to capital controls, Vergara said he agreed with De Gregorio's opinion that these measures aren't effective at curbing inflows.

He said Chile isn't seeing massive capital inflows.

"[Capital controls] are available and one can't ever rule them out, but the evidence regarding their effectiveness is debatable," Vergara told the newspaper.

In the 1990s, Chile implemented controls, through a reserve requirement on foreign investment, which De Gregorio and Larrain have often stated didn't stop inflows.

title: Emerging-Market Debt Strengthens Mildly;  Currencies  Mixed
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging-market debt strengthened slightly Thursday, as investors continued to shift to riskier and higher-yielding assets.

Following the U.S. Federal Reserve's signal that its ultraloose policy stance will remain in play for the foreseeable future--along with strong global liquidity conditions--investors placed their bets on riskier assets, though a bit more selectively.

"Risk appetite is probably going to remain strong, and is sort of steady as she goes," said Win Thin, emerging-market strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman. But "markets are still being a little bit discerning in terms of the EM story."

The risk premium on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global tightened by 2 basis points to 302 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms, its index rose 0.37%.

Meanwhile, emerging-market currencies saw mixed performance. Skepticism about central bank policies in Brazil and Turkey weighed on their currencies.

The Turkish lira lost ground, with the dollar up 0.56% to TRY1.5258 late Thursday, according to CQG. The country's inflation will show an upward trend in the short-term due to the late reflections of oil-price rises and base effects, Turkey's central bank said in minutes from its monetary policy committee meeting in April.

Brown Brother Harriman's Thin attributed Thursday's weakness to "some market concerns with central bank credibility" and worries about unconventional monetary policy in Turkey, where the central bank has been avoiding raising interest rates.

On the Embig, Turkey's spread slimmed by 2 basis points to 188 basis points over Treasurys, while its index rose 0.18%.

Against the euro, emerging European currencies did not fare well. Only the Hungarian forint was able to eke out clear gains, strengthening to HUF264.20 against the euro from HUF264.60 late Wednesday. On the Embig, Hungary's spread tightened by 5 basis points to 260 basis points over Treasurys, while its index rose 0.60%.

In Latin America, the Brazilian real underperformed other regional currencies. Possible government intervention in the foreign exchange market during the monthly settlement of the Brazilian real and unclear signs provided by the latest central bank communique unleashed negative sentiment against the real. The dollar was recently up 1.76% at BRL1.5865.

"Brazil has a little more credibility in general, but they're losing it" because they appear to be chasing the curve, Thin said.

On the Embig, Brazil's spread shed 4 basis points to 173 basis points over Treasurys, while its index rose 0.54%.

The Chilean peso hit a fresh three-year high versus the dollar at CLP460.70, despite an ongoing $12 billion currency intervention program, on the back of dollar weakness. Chile's debt, however, weakened mildly, with its spread adding 3 basis points to 124 basis points over Treasurys. Its index rose just 0.10%.

Argentina and Venezuela were solid outperformers on the Embig. Argentina's spread tightened by 10 basis points to 556 basis points over Treasurys, and its index jumped 1.75%. Venezuela's spread shed 5 basis points to 1146 basis points, and its index climbed 0.91%.

Looking ahead, central bank rate decisions will dominate emerging markets on Friday. Colombia's central bank is expected to raise its policy rate by 25 basis points to 3.75%, and Russia's central bank is seen either keeping rates on hold or hiking by 25 basis points, according to RBC Capital Markets. Mexico, meanwhile, will release the minutes from its most recent rate-setting meeting, as well as the second-quarter inflation report.

title: DJ  Chile  Minister: Peso Would Be At CLP450 Without  Intervention
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Without the Chilean central bank's market intervention program and the government's budget cuts, the peso would be trading at around CLP450 to the dollar, Finance Minister Felipe Larrain said Wednesday.

Early Wednesday, the peso was trading at a three-year high of CLP461.90 to the dollar, which is also a level not seen since early January, when the central bank announced its $12 billion intervention program.

In addition to the intervention, the government reduced this year's fiscal budget by $800 million and implemented other measures to keep the peso competitive against the dollar.

The Chilean economy is highly dependent on exports, and a stronger peso makes its products less competitive abroad.

Larrain told reporters the government will continue to monitor the currency market and implement additional measures if these are needed.

Earlier this week, central bank president Jose De Gregorio reiterated the monetary authority wouldn't implement capital controls since there isn't a net dollar inflow.

On previous occasions, both Larrain and De Gregorio have said the capital controls Chile implemented in the 1990s weren't effective at curbing speculative inflows.

title: Chile Stocks Close Lower As Corporate Earnings Fail To Excite
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chile's blue-chip Ipsa index ended lower Wednesday as corporate earnings failed to excite investors.

The Ipsa shed 0.3% to 4754.91 points, while market volume slipped to 88.0 billion Chilean pesos ($190.4 million), from CLP133.4 billion the previous session.

Among companies which recently reported earnings, flagship carrier LAN Airlines (LFL, LAN.SN) lost 1% to CLP12,822.00. Faced with soaring crude oil prices that push fuel costs higher, LAN's first quarter net profit of $97.2 million disappointed investors, while its Ebitda, or earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, of $250.7 million beat them.

Also, the nation's largest power producer, Endesa (EOC, ENDESA.SN), fell 1.3% to CLP865.00, after its first quarter earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization fell 10.8% on the year to CLP201.37 billion.

Its parent company, power holding firm Enersis (ENI, ENERSIS.SN) declined 0.7% to CLP195.02 after its Ebitda slipped 15.5% on the year to CLP434.36 billion.

"In general the earnings reported weren't that exciting," said Rodrigo Arriagada, analyst with local brokerage Molina y Swett.

The local stock market shrugged off U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke's statements that the central bank's policy easing would remain steady after June and that there was no specific timeframe to begin tightening interest-rate policy, traders said.

Among other decliners fuel and forestry conglomerate Copec (COPEC.SN), the Ipsa's heaviest-weighted share, decreased 0.5% to CLP8,797.60 and chemical and specialty fertilizer producer SQM's (SQM) more liquid B-series (SQM-B.SN) fell 1.4% to CLP26,817.00.

In other local markets, the peso strengthened slightly, ending at a fresh three-year high versus the dollar, as institutional investors sold dollars.

The peso strengthened to CLP462.10 to the dollar, versus Tuesday's close of CLP462.30. The currency traded in a range of CLP461.30 to CLP463.75.

As part of its $12 billion currency intervention program, the Central Bank of Chile purchased $50 million at an average rate of CLP462.02. It has accumulated $4 billion so far this year.

In the bond market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central bank bonds, or BCUs, ended mixed as participants anxiously awaited the outcome of the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy meeting and Chairman Ben Bernanke's first-ever post policy meeting press conference.

The yield on five-year BCU bonds ended at 2.53%, from 2.50% on Tuesday, while the yield on 10-year BCUs closed unchanged at 2.85%.

title: Chilean Peso Gains Slightly, Ends At Fresh 3-Year High
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chile's peso strengthened slightly Wednesday, ending at a fresh three-year high versus the dollar, as institutional investors sold dollars.

The peso strengthened to CLP462.10 to the dollar, versus Tuesday's close of CLP462.30. The currency traded in a range of CLP461.30 to CLP463.75.

Despite falling international copper prices and the dollar's recovery against major rivals, the peso firmed on local greenback sales.

As Chile is the world's premier copper producer, accounting for a third of global copper production and because nearly a third of the Andean nation's exports are bound for Europe, the peso often takes trading cues from international copper prices and the euro's movements versus the dollar.

The peso, however, pared back most of its gains during the session after Finance Minister Felipe Larrain told reporters the government will continue to monitor the currency market and implement additional measures if these are needed.

"That verbal intervention rattled investors' nerves and helped to pull the peso back from its earlier highs," said Andrea Lombardi, currency trader with brokerage EuroAmerica.

Despite the peso's stubborn strength, central bank president Jose De Gregorio reiterated earlier this week that the monetary authority wouldn't implement capital controls since there isn't a net dollar inflow.

As part of its $12 billion currency intervention program, the Central Bank of Chile purchased $50 million at an average rate of CLP462.02. It has accumulated $4.00 billion so far this year.

In the bond market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central bank bonds, or BCUs, ended mixed as participants anxiously awaited the outcome of the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy meeting and Chairman Ben Bernanke's first-ever post policy meeting press conference later in the session.

The yield on five-year BCU bonds ended at 2.53%, from 2.50% on Tuesday, while the yield on 10-year BCUs closed unchanged at 2.85%.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Real targets 12-yr high, Chilean peso jumps
text:
* Chile's peso hits 3-year high on cenbank comments

* Bets Fed will keep easy policy stance backs region

* Mexico peso struggles against option barriers

* Brazil real firms 0.57 pct, Mexico peso up 0.28 pct

(Recasts, adds comments, changes dateline, previous SANTIAGO)

By Michael O'Boyle and Jeb Blount

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, April 26 (Reuters) - Brazil's real neared its strongest level in 12 years on Tuesday and Chile's peso hit a three-year high on bets that policymakers would not step up their fight against further gains.

Chile's peso jumped after the central bank chief was seen ruling out capital controls while Brazil's real gained on expectations intervention there would not deter more flows.

Latin America's currencies benefited from bets that the U.S. Federal Reserve will signal its willingness to maintain cheap credit when it ends its policy-setting meeting on Wednesday.

Signs that U.S. rates will remain low through the year could push more investors to seek better returns in Latin America's higher yielding debt.

"As long as the Fed sustains low rates for a longer period, that allows Latin America to absorb more flows seeking higher yield," said Enrique Alvarez, head of Latin America research at IDEAglobal in New York.

Chile's peso got a boost after the head of the country's central bank signaled policymakers will not resort to capital controls to discourage flows. [ID:nN26270395] ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Graphic on Chile peso: http://r.reuters.com/qat29r("http://r.reuters.com/qat29r") ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> bid 1.08 percent firmer at 462.30 per dollar, its strongest since May 2008. The peso erased the impact of a currency intervention launched in January.

Chile and Brazil have been trying to slow currency gains that hurt local manufacturers, but investors are betting policymakers will now allow further strengthening to help fight inflation from high commodity prices.

"This is hitting inflation expectations, and that has propelled central banks to be more tolerant with the exchange rate, which is seen less as an enemy these days as an ally," said Jimena Zuniga, an analyst at Barclays Capital.

The Fed's ultra-loose monetary policy has pushed a tide of investment into Latin America. Brazil's current account deficit ballooned in March as the strong real boosted demand for foreign goods. [ID:nN26216964]

Brazil's real has surged nearly 8 percent since mid-March after the country's authorities were seen putting aside the threat of severe capital controls.

The real <BRBY> bid 0.57 percent firmer at 1.562 per dollar in the local spot market. The currency is just off its strongest levels since it was allowed to float in early 1999.

Brazil's currency was helped by expectations the government will have little success stemming the real's strength with less drastic measures such as taxes on short-term capital flows to Brazil and limits banks' short positions in dollars.

Analysts said movements in the futures market suggest investors think the government's latest measures will have little long-term impact.

The second dollar forward <DOLc2> on the BMFBovespa exchange, which reflects currency exchange expectations for May, fell 0.51 percent to 1.5695 reais to the dollar. By falling it shows market players are betting the real will strengthen more next month.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> firmed 0.28 percent to 11.5755 per dollar. Traders said major foreign banks were buying dollars to defend option positions around 11.57 per dollar and 11.55 per dollar.

The Mexican peso has gained more than 5 percent from a March intraday low to trade at its strongest in 2-1/2 years. The peso has recently hit levels stronger than many expected.

Mexican policymakers have shown the least concerns about currency gains, which could spur even more bets on the peso.

(Additional reporting and writing by Michael O'Boyle in Mexico City; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama)

title: WRAPUP 2-Chile shuns capital controls, peso hits 3-yr peak
text:
* Central bank chief says Chile not facing flood of capital

* His comments push peso to nearly three-year highs

* Chile likely to post a current account surplus in 2011

(Adds comments from De Gregorio, analyst, peso close)

By Brad Haynes and Moises Avila

SANTIAGO, April 26 (Reuters) - Chile's peso surged to three-year highs on Tuesday after the central bank signaled it will not use capital controls to tame the rally, leading some in the market to bet it may ease the pace of rate hikes.

Central Bank President Jose De Gregorio reiterated that unlike some Latin American nations Chile was not facing dollar inflows that merit capital controls. He has repeatedly said the bank will prioritize its fight against inflation over taming the peso.

The peso <CLP=CL> jumped on his remarks, traders said, gaining 1 percent to bid 462.3 per dollar, firming past the 465.5 per dollar rate seen on Jan. 3, which triggered the launch of a $12 billion currency intervention program.

Chile's peso has appreciated to its strongest level since April 2008 as the central bank has aggressively raised interest rates in recent months to fight inflation despite exporters' demands to do more to tame the currency.

Speaking to college students about policies to tame currency strength, De Gregorio said: "A more controversial tool is the use of capital controls, particularly in those countries that are seeing significant net capital inflows. However, this is not the case in Chile."

He said that Chile, the world's top copper producer, will likely post a current account surplus in 2011.

Finance Minister Felipe Larrain has said he is skeptical of capital controls and the government is not considering them.

Foreign bets on the Chilean peso's rally have also eroded the impact of the central bank intervention program, shifting sharply in recent weeks in favor of the peso. [ID:nN25208073]

Chile peso evolution http://r.reuters.com/qat29r("http://r.reuters.com/qat29r")

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

BRAZILIAN MODERATION

"(De Gregorio) is clearly uncomfortable with these levels but does not have many options," said Matias Madrid, chief economist at Banco Penta.

"Maybe you could increase the monetary policy rate by 25 basis points rather than 50 or not even increase at the next meeting, if the bank feels a lot of pressure."

Brazil's central bank raised its benchmark rate last week by 25 basis points rather than 50 in a split decision, backing off the intensity of monetary tightening and easing upward pressure on a rallying real <BRBY>. Brazil has also slapped taxes on some foreigners' investments to try to tame the currency.

Chile's peso is up around 18 percent against the dollar since mid 2010, outpacing the real's 15 percent gain. However year-to-date the real has gained 6 percent, while Chile's peso is broadly flat after erasing the 7 percent drop that followed the intervention announcement.

Brazil's more moderate rate increase sparked market fears that authorities in Latin America's biggest economy are not doing enough to rein in inflation. Brazil's rate now stands at 12 percent, the highest among major economies. [ID:nN20289067]

Chile is also struggling with rising inflation as higher world oil and food prices pushed up consumer prices in March at the fastest pace in 18 months. [ID:nN08178268]

Joining emerging market peers from China to Peru, Chile's central bank has responded by aggressively raising its benchmark rate. It has increased the rate by 100 basis points in the last two months to 4.5 percent, its highest in more than two years.

De Gregorio and other members of the central bank board have not hinted at moderating the pace of rate hikes at their May 12 monetary policy meeting, but the bank's latest monthly poll of analysts forecast the rate at 4.75 percent next month.

In a sign that the bank may stick to hefty rate hikes, De Gregorio said in his speech that interest rate differentials between emerging markets and rich nations are not "astronomical" compared to the early 1990s.

(Additional reporting by Maria Jose Latorre; Writing by Alonso Soto; Editing by Simon Gardner and Kenneth Barry)

title: INSTANT VIEW- Chile  peso at pre- intervention  level near 3-yr high
text:
SANTIAGO, April 26 (Reuters) - Chile's peso hit near three-year highs and returned to pre-intervention levels after Central Bank President Jose De Gregorio on Tuesday reiterated the country was not facing dollar inflows that merit capital controls.

Following are analysts' reactions:

MATIAS MADRID, CHIEF ECONOMIST AT BANCO PENTA

"For the moment, there's not much you can do. Under 460 per dollar they will have to take some sort of measure, speed up the pace of daily dollar purchases if the peso hits 450 per dollar, capital controls ... there aren't many bullets left."

"At these levels, capital controls are completely ruled out, but they could opt for them if it reaches."

"He is clearly uncomfortable with these levels but does not have many options. Maybe you could increase the monetary policy rate by 25 basis points rather than 50 or not even increase at the next meeting, if the bank feels very under pressure."

NATHAN PINCHEIRA, ECONOMIST AT BANCHILE

"The tools the central bank has are extremely limited. The only real option is to increase the amount of daily dollar purchases, but it can only do that from May 6, when there is a new purchase calendar for the month."

"This level of exchange rate works on two levels. On the one hand it limits external inflation because the transfer to the exchange rate by fuels, for example, is lower, but that can also stoke demand, which brings secondary effects, which is precisely what it does not want."

"It could smooth the cycle of rising interest rates to 25 basis points instead of 50 bps. I don't think it's a question of holding them at this point, as it would be a very odd signal to the market given high inflation expectations for this year."

FLAVIA CATTAN-NASLAUSKY, CURRENCY STRATEGIST WITH RBS

"This is a catch-up rally, in the sense that the peso has been an underperformer until last week. This week we had a reinforcement of the weak dollar view, which means no currency is left out."

"The question is do we go lower (firmer). This is a pretty significant level."

"We could go lower still a bit because of the positioning (peso foreign bets) and overall rally triggered by the dollar"

PEDRO TUESTA, ECONOMIST WITH 4CAST

"At this level (of the peso), markets will seek signals from the government before advancing further."

(Reporting by Maria Jose Latorre and Alonso Soto)

title: Chile  Peso Breaks Pre- Intervention  Level, Ends At 3-Year High
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--After breaching pre-intervention levels, Chile's peso ended 1.1% stronger Tuesday at a three-year high versus the dollar, buoyed by broad greenback weakness and the central bank's comments that capital controls aren't needed.

The peso strengthened to CLP462.30 to the dollar, a level not seen since April 2008, versus Monday's close of CLP467.40. The currency traded in a range of CLP462.30 to CLP467.95.

Broad dollar weakness, as the U.S. Federal Reserve lags behind its major counter parts in increasing interest rates, has fueled the peso's strength, despite the Chilean central bank's ongoing $12 billion currency intervention program.

The dollar fell against its major rivals, with the dollar index sliding to its lowest level since August 2008, as participants expected the Federal Reserve to maintain loose monetary policy as the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee begins a two-day meeting.

Also, earlier in the day, central bank president Jose De Gregorio, speaking to university students, said Chile did not require capital controls as it is not seeing net capital inflows and will post a small surplus in its current account this year.

"With the dollar falling abroad and following the central bank's comments regarding capital control's, the peso broke a firm level of resistance and firmed beyond pre-intervention levels," said Rodrigo Sarria, a currency trader with investment bank Celfin Capital.

The central bank president also said that currencies around the world are seeing an adjustment, in part due to the weak dollar, noting that such an adjustment was to be expected and contributed to alleviating international currency tensions.

"There's no currency war going on, it's just currencies having a temper tantrum," he said.

The central bank implemented its intervention program in early January to beat back the local currency's strength and help exporters' competitiveness.

As part of its $12 billion currency intervention program, the Central Bank of Chile purchased $50 million at an average rate of CLP467.66 Monday. It has accumulated $3.95 billion so far this year.

In the bond market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central bank bonds, or BCUs, ended higher as participants continue to await the outcome of the Fed's policy meeting and Chairman Ben Bernanke's first-ever post policy meeting press conference later in the week.

The yield on five-year BCU bonds ended at 2.50%, compared to 2.46% on Monday, while the yield on 10-year BCUs closed at 2.85%, versus 2.84% the prior session.

title: Foreign bets push  Chile  peso to pre- intervention  highs
text:
* Foreign bets shift $2.2 bln in favor of peso in 1 month

* Peso at strongest since Jan. 3 intervention launch

SANTIAGO, April 25 (Reuters) - Foreign bets on the Chilean peso's rally are at their strongest in two months, eroding the impact of a $12 billion central bank intervention and pushing the currency to near three-year highs, central bank data showed on Monday.

On the eve of the bank's dollar-buying program, the foreign position in Chilean non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) <CLPNDF=> represented a net $1.675 billion bet on a stronger peso <CLP=CL>, fueling a rally that squeezed exporters' margins.

Following the Jan. 3 intervention announcement, investors unwound bets and covered themselves against the weakening peso, compounded by conflict in the Arab world, switching positions by mid-March to a net $3 billion bet on a weaker peso.

But from March 17 to April 20, a net $2.2 billion shift in 


NDF contracts back toward a long peso position -- the most
bullish in two months -- suggested rising risk appetite has
emboldened new foreign bets in favor of the peso.

"This is a sign that foreign investors' bets in favor of the peso have increased, putting downward pressure on the dollar locally," said Osvaldo Cruz, a BCI analyst in Santiago.

The shifting tide in the forward market may compound the effects of global dollar weakness, rising interest rates and the strong price of top export copper, which have nearly erased the initial 7 percent impact of the dollar-buying program.

Investment bank Bci said on Monday authorities may turn to micro or macro-prudential measures to tame the peso.

Local authorities have not yet considered capital controls in the top copper producer, although in a newspaper interview published on Monday central bank board member Enrique Marshall said those limits cannot be "completely ruled out."

The peso closed a shade weaker on Monday to bid 467.3 pesos per U.S. dollar after testing a 16-week intraday high of 466.5 per dollar -- a level last seen before the intervention.

title: Chile Stocks Close Mildly Higher As Investors Await Earnings
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chile's blue-chip Ipsa index ended mildly higher Monday as participants were optimistic about the start of the local earnings season.

The Ipsa gained 0.3% to 4751.74 points, while market volume grew to 57.78 billion Chilean pesos ($123.6 million), from CLP48.0 billion the previous session. All markets and government offices were closed Friday in observance of a religious holiday.

Industry analysts expect for a long-standing drought to draw to a close soon, and cheaper hydroelectric power generation to increase, as the Nina weather phenomenon fizzles out.

Also gaining, rival power producer Colbun (COLBUN.SN) rose 1.1% to CLP134.00.

"The end of the Nina [phenomenon] will bode well for power generators and for their bottom lines, which have suffered in recent quarters," said Rodrigo Mujica, analyst with local brokerage BCI Corredor de Bolsa.

In other local markets, the peso ended weaker against the dollar, slipping from a strong level of resistance, after almost breaching pre-intervention levels the prior session.

The peso slipped to CLP467.40 to the dollar, versus Thursday's close of CLP466.50, while trading in tight a range of CLP466.80 to CLP468.30.

As part of its $12 billion currency intervention program, the Central Bank of Chile purchased $50 million at an average rate of CLP467.66 Monday. It has accumulated $3.90 billion so far this year.

In the bond market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central bank bonds, or BCUs, ended higher in thin trading as fixed-income participants awaited the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy meeting and Chairman Ben Bernanke's first-ever post policy meeting press conference later in the week.

The yield on five-year BCU bonds ended at 2.46%, compared to 2.44% on Thursday, while the yield on 10-year BCUs closed at 2.84%, versus 2.83% the prior session.

title: EMERGING MARKETS- Chile  peso climbs to pre- intervention  high
text:
* Strong earnings, risk appetite boosts Latam FX outlook

* Slower Brazil rate hikes not seen stopping real rally

* Mexican peso choppy around 30-month high

* Easter holidays sap trade volumes

By Brad Haynes

SANTIAGO, April 21 (Reuters) - Chile's peso firmed in thin pre-holiday trade and reached its strongest since the January launch of a central bank intervention as robust U.S. and European earnings drove appetite for higher-yielding assets.

The Mexican peso tested new 30-month highs on Thursday as it see-sawed on low volume, settling flat ahead of the Easter holiday.

Brazil's spot currency market was closed for a four-day weekend, but one-month non-deliverable forwards <BRL1MNDFOR=> traded a shade weaker after the central bank slowed the pace of its rate hikes late Wednesday.

The central bank raised its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 12 percent in a split decision, backing off the intensity of monetary tightening and easing upward pressure on a rallying real. [ID:nN20289067]

But with Brazilian interest rates towering over yields in developed economies, analysts see the real continuing its climb past an intraday high of 1.561 per dollar on Wednesday -- its strongest since August 2008.

"The fact that the central bank didn't go with 50 basis points doesn't make a difference," said Kathryn Rooney Vera, an emerging markets strategist with Bulltick Capital Markets.

The real is within 1 percent of its strongest level since the currency was freely floated in 1999, hurting exporters but helping the government's fight with annual inflation nearing its 6.5 percent ceiling.

Brazil has steadily stepped up capital controls against foreign investments, but it may now be slower to fight an exchange rate helping to dampen imported price pressures.

"I think you'll probably see more leniency toward the real's appreciation," Rooney said. "The line in the sand before was 1.65 per dollar, so now it's probably 1.50 per dollar."

Markets will be watching for mention of the currency when the Brazilian central bank releases minutes from Wednesday's meeting early next Thursday.

Mexico reports retail sales on Tuesday. The peso <MXN=> was little changed from Wednesday at 11.6074.

In Chile, where the peso <CLP=CL> closed 0.5 percent firmer, bidding 466.8 per dollar, traders are eyeing industrial output and unemployment data due next week, expecting signs of robust growth driving interest rates to over two-year highs.

The currency could see some consolidation before breaking through to three-year highs past 465 per dollar, however, as its relative strength index is nearing overbought levels.

The peso has almost entirely clawed back from the more than 7 percent drop that followed the launch of a $12 billion currency intervention announced on January 3. [ID:nN04206531]

Chile's bourse wrapped up trading early on Thursday afternoon at its strongest close in two weeks, tracking gains on global bourses boosted by strong earnings.

The blue-chip IPSA stock index <.IPSA> rose 0.5 percent, led by energy utilities Enersis and Endesa and wood pulp giants Copec and CMPC .

Stock markets in Argentina, Brazil, Columbia, Mexico, Panama and Venezuela were closed for Easter holidays.

title: Chile Stocks End Higher, Track US Markets, Await Local Earnings

title: Chile  Peso Ends At Strongest Since  Intervention  On Weak Dollar
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chile's peso ended Thursday at its strongest level versus the dollar since a $12 billion currency intervention program was announced in early January, as the greenback slumped against its rivals and copper prices surged.

The peso strengthened to CLP466.50 to the dollar, versus Wednesday's close of CLP469, while trading in a range of CLP466.50 to CLP469.

The local currency market closed early Thursday ahead of the long Easter weekend when many Chileans go on vacation. All markets and government offices will be closed on Friday.

Broad dollar weakness, on a worsening U.S. fiscal outlook and monetary policy that is expected to remain loose for the foreseeable future, helped boost the Chilean peso.

As Chile's economy is highly export-dependent and nearly a third of its exports are bound for European ports, the peso often moves in the same direction as the euro does against the dollar.

Earlier in the session, the euro jumped to a 16-month high against the dollar.

Also, as Chile is the world's largest copper producer and exporter, currency-market participants usually keep an eye on New York and London copper prices to gauge export revenue inflows and the general health of the Chilean economy.

Spot copper in London trading grew 1.7% to $4.35948 a pound, according to Chile copper commission Cochilco, on the back of a softer dollar.

"All things--copper prices, euro, equity markets--pointed to a stronger peso," said Gloria Soto, head currency trader at FXCM Chile.

The peso, however, still faces strong resistance at current levels before it can strengthen to preintervention levels, Soto said.

As part of its $12 billion currency intervention program, the Central Bank of Chile purchased $50 million at an average rate of CLP467.85 Thursday. It has accumulated $3.85 billion so far this year.

title: UPDATE: Chile  Central Bank  Pres: Inflation Biggest Challenge
text:
(Updates with additional comments from central bank president starting in the fourth paragraph.)

SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Inflation is the biggest challenge the Chilean economy is currently facing, central bank president Jose De Gregorio said Wednesday.

Inflation will likely end this year at 4.3%, above the monetary authority's target of 3%, plus/minus one percentage point.

"Undoubtedly, inflation has been increasing," De Gregorio said in prepared remarks delivered to the Asimet metal industry trade group.

According to the central banker, although inflation won't hit a high anywhere near the 9.9% it saw in October 2008, it still is a risk to the economy.

"High international crude oil and food prices have increased inflationary risks in Chile as well as in the rest of the world," he said.

He added that while the inflation outlook for this year, both locally and abroad, is higher for 2011, next year this outlook should retreat somewhat.

Food prices around the world will likely grow around 4% to 5% this year, so the bulk of the inflationary pressures stem from higher crude prices, he said in his remarks.

De Gregorio reiterated that the central bank will continue normalizing the benchmark overnight interest rate to contain inflationary pressures and avoid the propagation of second round effects.

According to the central bank's most recent survey of analysts expectations, the benchmark overnight rate will likely end the year at around 5.75% to 6%, De Gregorio said.

The survey also shows analysts see the rate holding at around 6%, a rate most consider neutral for the Chilean economy, for most of 2012.

Last week at its monthly monetary policy meeting, the central bank raised the benchmark rate half a percentage point, as expected, to 4.5%.

Regarding the central bank's $12 billion currency market intervention program, De Gregorio reiterated the peso would likely be trading 3% to 4% stronger against the dollar weren't it for the intervention.

He noted, like he has in previous presentations, that Chile isn't receiving net capital inflows and that the peso's strength against the greenback stems from robust domestic growth, strong copper prices and a weak dollar.

"The dollar is at its weakest level in 40 years," De Gregorio told the trade group which represents metallurgical exporters.

He added the peso will likely weaken somewhat as the U.S. economy rebounds.

"At some point, the dollar will strengthen; now, when will that happen? It won't be tomorrow," he said.

title: UPDATE:  Chile  Peso Would Be Stronger Without  Intervention
text:
(updates with additional comments on inflation and the peso intervention.)

SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Central Bank of Chile on Monday reiterated that without its currency market intervention, the peso would be stronger in relation to the dollar.

In early 2011, the bank announced a $12 billion currency intervention program to weaken the currency, which was trading at near three-year highs.

In prepared remarks to Congress, central bank president Jose De Gregorio, added that while the intervention hasn't had "a very large effect" on the peso's trading levels in relation to the dollar, the bank is satified with its daily dollar purchases.

He noted that the peso's trading levels versus the dollar will likely depend on global tensions and events.

"If there's a rebound in industrialized economies, we should see the dollar firm somewhat," he said.

He added that monetary policy currently faces challenges stemming from significant international inflationary pressures as a result of rising international fuel and food prices.

While these imported pressures will push inflation in Chile to end the year at 4.3%, above the central bank's target of 3%, plus/minus one percentage point, core inflation, which factors out fuel and food prices will remain relatively stable.

"Core inflation will hover at around the target level throughout the bank's [24-month] policy horizon," De Gregorio said in his speech.

The central banker added that higher fuel prices account for 70 basis points of the one percentage point increase in the higher headline inflation outlook.

Inflation, at least for two or three quarters, will gain past the higher end of the bank's tolerance range, but these increases will be transitory and limited.

He reiterated the bank will continue withdrawing its monetary stimulus to keep inflation in line.

So far this year, the central bank has increased the benchmark rate a total 75 basis points, bringing it to 4%.

Analysts expect the benchmark rate to end the year around 5.5% to 6%. De Gregorio later noted this rate outlook was incorporated in the bank's baseline scenario for the year.

title: REFILE-Reuters Summit-Chile hopes spending cut slows rate rise
text:

* Tighter public spending to help cap rates

By Simon Gardner and Antonio de la Jara

SANTIAGO, March 29 (Reuters) - Chile's move to tighten fiscal spending for 2011 should help the central bank ease the pace of interest rate hikes as it fends off inflationary oil prices, Finance Minister Felipe Larrain said on Tuesday.

However, Chile's benchmark rate must continue to rise given external pressures on the economy, Larrain told the Reuters Latin American Investment Summit in Santiago. Less spending should help temper inflation and therefore rates.

"We can't think that a nominal rate of 4 percent is the equilibrium rate. The rate needs to keep rising," Larrain told Reuters in an interview.

"If the (lower spending) measures work, we can contribute to how gradually the rate increases and its eventual level," he added.

Larrain said last week the government would cut 2011 spending to a 5 percent increase from last year. Chile passed a 2011 budget designed to grow 5.5 percent from last year, expanding more slowly than the country's estimated 6 percent GDP growth this year. Chile is one of a host of emerging market economies from Brazil to China that have raised rates this year to fight inflation fueled by higher global commodity and food prices.

However Chile has avoided the sort of capital controls that Brazil has opted for to counter inflows of speculative capital -- a move the International Monetary Fund last week said was no substitute for "fundamental measures" such as monetary policy. [ID:nN27133061]

Chile's central bank this month raised its benchmark interest rate <CLINTR=ECI> by a bigger-than-expected 50 basis points and said more hikes will follow as it prioritizes its inflation target over a more competitive exchange rate. [ID:nN17171992]

The bank is seen raising its key rate by an aggressive 50 basis points again in April as it fights price pressures, a fortnightly central bank poll of traders showed last week.

A fresh 50 basis point hike would take the rate to 4.5 percent, adding upward pressure on the peso <CLP=CL>, which rebounded from the initial impact of a $12 billion currency intervention launched in January.

Chile's rates peaked at 8.25 percent in late 2008, before the bank slashed them to a record low of 0.5 percent in mid-2009 and held them there for around a year. Traders see the key rate stable at 6 percent even in two years' time.

Larrain added Chile's government is committed to issuing another sovereign bond by the end of its term in 2014, but has not signed off on issuing one this year.

He said he had also received "promising" signs of interest from foreign institutions keen on issuing peso-denominated "huaso" bonds, which are aimed at countering upward pressure on the peso from capital inflows.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  firm, conviction seen weak
text:
* Mexico peso firms 0.59 pct, Chile peso up 0.33 pct

* Investors seem to rule out deepening EU debt crisis

* Brazil real up 0.18 pct as intervention eyed

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, March 24 (Reuters) - Key Latin American currencies firmed on Thursday, supported by a weaker dollar and rising stock markets, but analysts noted a lack of conviction behind the gains amid a host of global risks.

Brazil's real hit a two-week high, while Mexico and Chile's pesos traded at their strongest in more than a week.

Demand for riskier assets like stocks and emerging market currencies rose despite worries about the ongoing violence in the oil-producing Middle East, fears that Portugal will need a bailout and concerns about Japan's nuclear crisis.

The cascade of the negative global events had slammed Latin American assets this month.

"The market took a breath over the last couple of weeks, the global backdrop deteriorated, but it hasn't changed significantly, so investors are willing to put some money to work," said David Beker, head Latin American

"But I wouldn't say these investors have a strong hand, people are willing to put on short-term positions, but not medium- or long-term positions," he added.

Japan's disasters could end up weighing down global growth, as could a sustained spike in oil prices or the expansion of Europe's debt crisis to a major economy like Spain.

Global investors have been taking advantage of recent declines in Latin American currencies on global jitters to place fresh bets on the region's high-yielding debt.

Latin American currencies could see support from high prices for local commodities, like Chile's copper and Brazil's iron and soy, while expectations of further interest rate hikes will tempt global investors with higher yields.

"Latin America has high commodity prices and these guys are more willing to hike interest rates," said Win Thin, an emerging markets strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York.

Mexico and Colombia are oil exporters while Brazil is energy self-sufficient, so they may be able to better weather higher oil prices than Asia, where most countries import, Thin said.

While intervention in Brazil could limit gains, Mexico and Chile may be poised to advance further.

Mexico's peso <MXN=><MEX01> firmed 0.59 percent to 11.9480, edging past the psychological 11.95 level, which could open the field for a run toward its nearly 2-1/2 year high hit earlier this month at 11.8585.

Local banks exercised $200 million in dollar put options on Thursday, exhausting the last of the $600 million a month sold by the central bank.

Outstanding options can help contain the peso's gains, but with the monthly allotment used up, the currency will find less resistance to advance in the coming sessions.

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> bid 0.33 percent stronger to 479.70 per dollar.

Chile imports most of its crude, but strong copper prices can help offset the impact of higher oil costs, analysts said. Chile is the world's top copper producer.

Brazil's real <BRBY> firmed 0.18 percent to 1.656 per dollar, gaining ground for the fifth straight session and trading at its strongest since March 9.

The real is than 1 percent from a 2-1/2 year high hit earlier this month that stirred concerns of fresh moves by authorities to tame the real's strength, which is hurting local manufacturers.

Traders said the market was cautiously pushing the real stronger amid expectations that new measures could be announced.

title: Chile Peso Ends Flat On Institutional Investor Dollar Buys

SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean peso ended flat against the dollar Thursday, erasing its earlier gains, as institutional investors bought dollars.

The currency ended at CLP486.10 to the dollar, unchanged from Wednesday, while trading in a range of CLP483.80 to CLP487.90.

But "dollar purchases by local banks put downward pressure on the peso," said currency trader Carlos Zamora at local bank Consorcio.

Institutional investors came out buying dollars as the peso reached a strong level of resistance.

"Despite everything going in favor of the peso strengthening, rising copper prices, a stronger euro, etc., participants bought dollars after the peso neared resistance," said Sergio Tricio, head of studies at currency trader Forex Chile.

title: UPDATE 1-Chile seen raising rate 25 bps in March-cbank poll
text:
* Traders see March inflation spiking 0.7 percent

* Three-month peso forecast stronger than pre-intervention

(Updates with March inflation, three0month peso forecasts)

SANTIAGO, March 9 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank is seen raising its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 3.75 percent at its March monetary policy meeting next week, a new fortnightly central bank poll of traders showed on Wednesday.

Consumer prices are seen jumping by 0.7 percent in March, according to the median forecast of more than 40 traders, after a modest 0.2 percent rise in February. [ID:nN08170095]

While most traders forecast a median 25 bps rate increase at its March 17 rate-setting meeting, some respondents saw the bank opting for a more aggressive 50 basis-point increase.

In February, the central bank resumed a cycle of rate increases after a pause in January, prioritizing inflation concerns over worries about a strong peso and lifting the rate by 25 basis points.

The bank is seen raising its key rate to 5.25 percent in 6 months time, the poll showed.

Sustained interest rate increases and record prices of main export copper have strengthened Chile's peso toward nearly three-year highs despite the central bank's $12 billion intervention to tame currency strength. [ID:nN17130996]

Traders' three-month exchange rate forecasts, which jumped to 500 pesos per dollar after the bank launched its intervention in January, have shifted to 470 per dollar in two months -- strengthening past pre-intervention forecasts.

( Reporting by Brad Haynes, Editing by W Simon )

title: Chile  cenbank maintains pace of  forex intervention
text:
SANTIAGO, March 8 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank said on Tuesday it would maintain the pace of a $12 billion foreign exchange intervention to tame the strong peso between March. 9 and April 8, and continue to buy $50 million of U.S. currency daily.

The peso, which weakened sharply after the intervention began in early January, has clawed back most of the 7 percent initially lost due to strong prices for the nation's main export copper and wider dollar weakness, and is again within striking distance of near three-year highs.

The government has ruled out capital controls, but markets are asking what additional steps, if any, the bank will take.

title: Chile Peso Ends Nearly Unchanged On Strong Jan Economic Growth
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean peso closed practically unchanged against the dollar Monday, as stronger-than-expected local economic growth data offset lower international copper prices.

The currency ended at CLP473.50 compared with CLP473.90 on Friday, while trading in a range of CLP472.30 to CLP475.00.

The country's monthly economic activity index, or Imacec, grew 6.8% year-to-year in January, the central bank said Monday. Growth surpassed the 6.0% increase market consensus had been expecting.

The positive figure boosted the peso amid falling copper prices due to the turmoil in the Middle East.

The South American currency often takes direction from copper prices as Chile is the world's largest producer of the metal.

"What he have seen today are opposing forces at work. The Imacec figure was very good and held the peso amid the declines of copper, the U.S. dollar and stock markets abroad," said Ronald Volpi, head currency trader at local brokerage EuroAmerica.

Copper's losses deepened late Monday morning as the equities market fell on higher oil prices. The most actively traded contract, for May delivery, was recently down 3.7%, or 16.75 cents, at $4.3180 per pound on the Comex division of the New York Mercantile Exchange.

On Monday, the central bank, as part of its $12 billion currency market intervention program, purchased $50 million at an average rate of CLP472.70. It has accumulated $2.2 billion so far this year.

On Tuesday, the bank will announce it next round of market intervention. The bank is expected to hold steady with its daily purchases of $50 million, despite the peso firming back to near pre-intervention levels, said Gloria Soto, chief currency trader at FXCM Chile.

In the bond market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central-bank bonds, or BCUs, ended lower as the market awaits consumer price index data to be released before trading starts on Tuesday.

Consensus is for a 0.2% increase in the February CPI from the previous month.

The yield on five-year BCU bonds ended at 2.41%, from 2.47% on Friday, while the yield on 10-year BCUs closed at 2.94%, versus 2.97% on the previous session.

title: WRAPUP 1-Inflation needs decisive attack: Chile cbank chief
text:
* De Gregorio says must attack inflationary pressures

* Chile peso back near pre-intervention levels

* Mexico seen holding rate later on Friday

* Brazil raised interest rates on Wednesday

By Daniel Flynn and Brad Haynes

PARIS/SANTIAGO, March 4 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank must attack inflation to mitigate risks from higher oil and food prices, bank president Jose De Gregorio said on Friday, seen as a signal the bank could opt for steeper interest rate hikes.

De Gregorio's comments in a speech in Paris contrasted with minutes from the central bank's February rate-setting meeting released earlier on Friday, in which board members cautioned against "overreacting" to inflationary expectations, noting core inflation was limited.

The minutes appeared to rule out accelerating the pace of raising its interest rates, saying that it could send the wrong signal about inflation expectations and suggesting more steady, gradual rate hikes like February's unanimous 25 basis point increase are to come.

Several of the board's five members preferred in the minutes from the Feb. 17 rate-setting meeting to be "prudent" and not overreact to rising inflation expectations in light of muted underlying, or core, inflation.

However one unidentified board member said if inflation expectations increased persistently, steeper interest rate increases may be necessary.

Speaking at a global central bankers meeting in Paris, De Gregorio said not acting on inflationary pressures could hit credibility and the ability to rein in prices.

"The risk of propagation towards prices in the wider economy must be mitigated, in particular in economies like Chile's, which are producing close to their potential," De Gregorio said in the speech, a copy of which was released in Santiago.

"Not attacking inflationary pressures could affect credibility, which would have negative consequences for the future capacity to achieve stable inflation with low costs in terms of activity," he added.

The comments were viewed by some as suggesting steeper interest rate increases.

"It (De Gregorio's comments) suggests they're contemplating 


a 50 basis point increase at the next meeting... This points
clearly to the possibility of   steeper rate hikes ahead." said


Matias Madrid, chief economist Banco Penta in Santiago.

The board only considered a 25 basis point increase last month, according to the minutes. A decision to hold rates in January was the first pause since the central bank started raising rates last June.

"Several board members said that while inflation expectations had risen ... it did not seem prudent to overreact at this moment, especially because effective inflation, and in particular core inflation, were limited," the bank said in a statement.

"Accelerating the pace of rate normalization after a pause in January could be confusing because it could be interpreted as an abrupt change in the central bank's inflation forecasts, which is not the case," it added.

Chile's central bank resumed its cycle of rate hikes despite the fact the local peso <CLP=CL> has bounced back to levels that prompted a $12 billion currency intervention in January, hurting exporters and raising questions about what additional steps the bank and government could take. title: Chile Peso Closes Weaker, Erases Early Gains In Thin Session
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean peso closed weaker against the dollar Friday, erasing early gains after testing a significant resistance level.

The currency ended at CLP473.90 compared with CLP472.80 on Thursday, while trading in a range of CLP471.40 to CLP474.20.

The currency firmed when trading got underway on the stronger euro and the gains in London copper prices. It came up against the same resistance level it tested in late February amid near-record high copper prices.

Because Chile produces a third of the world's copper, its currency takes direction from the price of the metal.

"The peso hit resistance around the CLP471-CLP472 mark in early trading, but it didn't have the strength to break it," said Samuel Levy, analyst at ForexChile.

Volume was thinner than usual and the currency shrugged off comments from the central bank president regarding market intervention, traders said.

Central bank head Jose De Gregorio in prepared remarks said the peso would likely be trading 3% to 5% stronger with the central bank's intervention.

In addition, he reiterated that central banks, including Chile's, should subordinate monetary policy to the concerns of the currency market.

On Thursday, the central bank, as part of its $12 billion currency market intervention program, purchased $50 million at an average rate of CLP472.34. It has accumulated $2.15 billion so far this year.

In the bond market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central-bank bonds, or BCUs, ended mixed following the release the central bank's monetary policy meeting minutes.

The minutes show the central bank doesn't rule out speeding up the pace of its rate hikes later on in the year if inflationary pressures increase.

The yield on five-year BCU bonds ended at 2.47%, from 2.44% on Thursday, while the yield on 10-year BCUs closed at 2.97%, unchanged from the previous session.

title: Chile Central Bank  Pres: 2011  Intervention  Different From '08
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean central bank's $12 billion currency market intervention program for this year has had a different effect than the bank's previous intervention in 2008, the head of the central bank said Friday in Paris.

Following the Jan. 3 intervention announcement, the peso initially weakened about 7% from the near three-year highs it was trading at. In recent weeks, however, it's recouped most of its strength.

"This contrasts sharply with the experience of the previous period of reserve accumulation initiated in April 2008," bank president Jose De Gregorio said in prepared remarks delivered at a symposium at the Bank of France.

De Gregorio noted that in the 2008 intervention, the peso depreciated by about 18% through late August and in the current intervention the peso has even firmed to nearly the same levels before the monetary authority intervened.

He attributed the different responses the currency has shown to the dollar's performance abroad and copper prices.

"In 2008, the dollar strengthened and the price of copper fell. Today, the dollar has remained weak and the copper price has reached all-time highs," he said.

Chile is the world's largest copper producer, mining roughly a third of global output, so its currency takes trading cues from the price of the red metal.

De Gregorio, however, said that without the current intervention--which will increase Chile's international reserves to 17% of gross domestic product--the peso would likely be trading 3% to 5% stronger from current levels.

He added than global exchange rate tensions will likely be transitory and will subside once industrialized economies recover from the current financial crisis.

De Gregorio noted that emerging economies are receiving capital inflows as a result of the cyclical differences between these and advanced economies, but that net capital inflows are below those seen in the early 1990s.

He added that Chile has not "seen net capital inflows yet."

Regarding monetary policy in emerging economies, the central bank said the main challenge for these economies is to avoid persistent deviations of inflation from its target, especially in light of rising prices for crude oil and agricultural commodities.

The risk of propagation to other prices has to be mitigated, he noted.

"Monetary policy cannot be subordinated to exchange rate objectives, even in cases where measures to alleviate exchange rate appreciation have been adopted," De Gregorio said.

In Chile's case, the sterilization of the intervention, through bond issues, allows monetary policy to retain its independence to stabilize inflation.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  currencies  stuck in ranges as oil weighs
text:
* Brazil intervention pulls real back from 2-month high

* Chile peso slips as concerns of high oil prices weigh

* Mexico peso firms 0.19 pct, Brazil real 0.06 pct (New throughout, adds comments)

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, (Reuters) - Latin American currencies were trapped in narrow ranges Monday as investors remained cautious about the impact of higher oil prices on global growth and the region's importers, such as Chile.

Concerns that a spike in oil prices could hurt global growth have weighed on the region's currencies in recent weeks, softening a trend of steady appreciation as investors are drawn to Latin America's relatively high interest rates.

Brent crude oil prices rose above $112 a barrel, but the market calmed from last week's jumps as investors weighed a pledge of more supply from Saudi Arabia against the prospect of prolonged disruption to Libya's output.

The currencies of oil producers Mexico and Brazil managed to firm while the peso of Chile, an importer of crude, dipped.

"Mexico's peso has been strengthening since the peak of oil prices last week, so this is just unwinding these extreme scenarios on Middle East oil risk," said Igor Arsenin, head of Latin American fixed-income strategy at Credit Suisse in New York.

"If we have a permanent increase in oil just because of lingering uncertainty in the Middle East, then it becomes actually favorable for oil exporters such as Mexico and less favorable for importers, countries like Chile," he added.

Mexico's peso firmed 0.19 percent to 12.1025 per dollar. Brazil's real bid 0.06 percent stronger on the local spot market to 1.661 per dollar.

Brazil's central bank knocked the currency back from a nearly two-month high hit early in the session by intervening with two auctions to buy dollars in the spot market, a reverse currency swap auction and two dollar forward auctions.

Chile's peso slipped 0.25 percent to 475.70 per dollar.

"Oil prices are more stable ... but the price is still near $112, which is very high for a country like ours that imports almost all of its petroleum," a Chilean trader said.

Investors pushed down yields on Brazilian interest rate futures on bets that government spending cuts may cool the need for an aggressive interest rate hike this week.

Brazil's government said Monday it will slash spending on defense and low-income housing as part of $30 billion in cuts to this year's budget.

Brazilian central bank policymakers meet Wednesday to decide on a possible hike in the country's interest rate.

While some market players were betting last week that they could raise rates by 75 basis points, the market began late last week to unwind those bets.

Yields on Mexican interest rate swaps edged up after the head of the country's central bank expressed worry about crop failures from bad weather and said policymakers may have to raise interest rates if they poison inflation expectations.

Mexico, whose economic recovery has been slower than that of Brazil or Chile, has widely been expected not to raise interest rates until early in 2012.

"Mexico has been spared a significant pick-up in food inflation, but that could change purely because of local conditions," Credit Suisse's Arsenin said. (Additional reporting by Silvio Cascione in Sao Paulo and Froilan Romero in Santiago; Editing by Dan Grebler)
