title: Brazilian Real, Chilean Peso Near Key Pre- Intervention  Levels
text:
-Brazil's central bank more likely to ramp up currency intervention than Chile's

-Central bank interventions could provide trade entry point--money manager


 
   By Erin McCarthy 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Despite ongoing efforts by Brazil's and Chile's central banks to curb currency appreciation, the Brazilian real and Chilean peso are defiantly approaching pre-intervention levels, raising the question of whether these countries will make further efforts to curb them.

If central banks stand back, that could pave the way for more gains, but some strategists warn about the risks of more intense interventions.

Both central banks have argued that their currencies would be significantly stronger had they not intervened at all. But now rising inflation concerns have led both countries to raise interest rates recently, with more hikes expected this year, which only will encourage stronger currencies in the future.

With both currencies nearing major psychological and technical breakthroughs, investors who are already long on either currency should stay in those positions for now, since there is room for further strength, said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, currency strategist with Royal Bank of Scotland.

Though both currencies saw some losses on Tuesday from general risk aversion on Middle East worries, robust copper prices in Chile, the world's largest producer of the red metal, and strong capital inflows in Brazil have been key drivers of the peso's and real's strength in recent months.

For the real, reaching BRL1.65 to the dollar is a key psychological level that it could hit at "any time," while investors should watch for the peso to hit CLP466.70 to the dollar, Cattan-Naslausky said. If the real and peso do surpass those levels, investors could take profits before the currencies are able to stabilize, she added.

John Peta, who manages an emerging-market, local-currency bond fund at Acadian Asset Management, said they remain overweight on the Brazilian real and Chilean peso.

"We're long both currencies because we think the fundamentals are quite positive," he said, adding that the high carry on the Brazilian real still makes it an attractive position. Already-high interest rates in Brazil and expected interest-rate increases in Chile should drive appreciation pressures, he added.

Still, analysts say it's not a good time to enter into these trades, given their already-high valuations and further intervention risks.

Of the two, the real is riskier to buy right now, given Brazil's central bank's ongoing intervention efforts. It regularly intervenes in the spot, forward and futures markets. Most notably, in October, Brazil's central bank stepped up intervention by twice raising its financial operations tax on foreign purchases of local assets, in an effort to curb hot money inflows from abroad. Before that second tax hike, the real was near the BRL1.65 mark, which it is now approaching.

The threat of further measures in Brazil is a serious one, said Alberto Ramos, economist at Goldman Sachs. The Brazilian monetary authority could intensify its current measures or it could also employ more unorthodox capital controls, he said.

The Chilean peso, meanwhile, is more likely to be given some room to appreciate. In Chile, the central bank announced a $12 billion dollar purchasing program for the year in early January, after the peso gained more than 7% in 2010.

But further action from Chile's traditionally conservative central bank is less likely, even though it could increase the amount of its daily dollar purchases.

"They are not ready to go to places that the Brazilians are ready to go," Ramos said.

The Andean nation's hawkish monetary authority has hinted at a shift in priorities, from curbing the peso to focusing on the inflation battle, given its 25-basis-point rate hike last week--making it more likely that the peso will strengthen.

But if the two banks ultimately do intervene, it could provide a buying opportunity for these two currencies, said Adnan Akant, head of foreign exchange and managing director at money manager Fischer Francis Trees & Watts, a New York unit of BNP Paribas.

"Intervention is just a way of cheapening them up for those who really want to be involved in them," he said.

Currently the money manager is not exposed to the Chilean peso or the Brazilian real, after pulling out of a long-real position last year on intervention worries.

Given the recent bout of risk aversion on Middle East concerns, it's "wait-and-see" whether global markets stabilize, but if any new central bank interventions weaken the two currencies, it could provide an advantageous entry point, he said.

-By Erin McCarthy, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2712; erin.mccarthy@dowjones.com [ 02-22-11 1823ET ]

title: Emerging-Market Assets End Week With 'Lifeless' Session
text:
--A lackluster day for emerging-market assets

--Eastern European currencies gave back some recent gains

--Emerging Asian currencies broadly firmer against the dollar


 
   By Cynthia Lin 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Despite lingering uncertainties around the Middle East and continuing inflation concerns, emerging-market debt and currencies were mostly quiet on Friday, heading into a long weekend for the U.S. markets.

"EM markets seem to have gained some breathing space from the concerns that dominated the past few weeks," said analysts at Barclays Capital. "However, we think this relief may be technical and expect rates markets to remain under pressure in the medium term."

Moves on the EM external-debt front were especially muted, as investors continue to gauge various central bank rate decisions. Although mounting inflationary pressure was the prevalent theme across the developing world since the start of the year, EM debt has more recently been in a holding pattern.

"External debt markets are once again lifeless," RBC analysts noted on Friday, with the latest fund flow data showing investors pulling $741 million out of emerging-market bond funds, according to global fund tracker EPFR. Emerging-market equity funds were also hit with another week of redemptions, with $5.45 million withdrawn by global investors.

The risk premium on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global, or Embig, tightened three basis points to 285 basis points over Treasurys, although it lost 0.14% in price terms on the day. Underlying U.S. Treasury yields were higher on Friday after having fallen to a multiweek low in the prior session amid Middle East concerns.

Argentina's spread narrowed 10 basis points to 528 basis points over Treasurys. Its index fell 0.17% on the day. Analysts at RBC said they shifted the nation's external credit back to overweight based on attractive valuations. Brazil, Mexico, and Peru also each saw slightly lower risk premiums.

At the Group of 20 summit, Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega said Brazil would stand firmly opposed to attempts to limit the scope of emerging economies' use of capital control measures to curb the heavy entrance of foreign currency into their economies and the excessive appreciation of local currencies. The Brazilian real was flat against the dollar on Friday.

Other Latin American currencies were generally mixed against the dollar throughout the day, with the Colombian and Chilean peso leading the pack, while others fell slightly.

Chile's central bank on Thursday rose rates by 25 basis points, as was largely expected. Gains in Chile's peso, helped by the rate increase, nudged the currency closer to an almost three-year high despite a continuing $12 billion currency intervention program. On Friday, Chile's central bank purchased $50 million at an average rate of CLP468.71 as part of its dollar-buying program. The peso was recently up 0.26% on the dollar at CLP467.65, according to FactSet.

The usually high-beta Venezuela saw its spread move against the index, up two basis point to 1,127 basis points over Treasurys. Comments from the Venezuelan Oil Minister Rafael Ramirez Thursday confirmed that more dollar debt sales are likely in the pipeline as a measure to control inflation.

Despite being recent emerging-market outperformers, Eastern European currencies broadly weakened against their benchmark on Friday, coming in as some of the day's biggest laggards.

The Turkish lira was weaker against both the U.S. dollar and euro, after having been a recent standout. The euro was up to TRY2.1623 of late from its prior close of TRY2.1434, according to FactSet. The lira was down about 0.2% against the dollar.

Turkey's spread fell six basis points to 204 basis points over the benchmark. The index, however, lost 0.23% on the day. The nation's deputy prime minister said if loan growth exceeds 20% to 25% in February and March, the government may make additional efforts to slow credit expansion. Analysts will be watching next week's credit growth reading.

Early in New York, the Hungarian forint made a sharp turn weaker against the euro, but immediately regained strength. The nation received approval from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission to sell $5 billion of debt in the U.S. With a new government in place, Hungary also has plans to raise EUR4 billion this year. The forint is recently hovering around HUF269 against the euro to be flat on the day, based on FactSet.

The Czech koruna fell more than 0.4% to the euro, recently at CZK24.397, while the Polish zloty lost about 0.3% to the euro at PLN3.9130 of late.

The South African rand, however, managed to continue its ascent against the dollar, recently up 0.6% at ZAR7.1166 on the dollar. The nation's spread narrowed two basis points to 149 basis points over Treasurys, and gained 0.13% in price terms.

Asian currencies took over as the leaders, with the group broadly gaining against the dollar. Early in the day, the Central Bank of China bumped up the nation's bank reserve requirement ratio by 50 basis points as authorities fight to rein in the recent acceleration in headline inflation. That, along with authorities fixing the USD/CNY lower again, set the tone for strong currencies aross the region.

Leading the way were the Korean won, up 0.55% to the dollar, the Indian rupee, up 0.6% to the dollar, and the New Taiwan dollar, up 0.54% to the dollar.

On the Embig, Ghana was one of the few to see its spread expand, up 13 basis points to 393 basis points over benchmark. Its index fell 0.75%. January inflation came in at 9.1% year-over-year, the first increase in nine months. Malaysia was the other notable laggard, with its risk premium increasing eight basis points to 120 basis points over Treasurys. It lost 0.67% on the day. Consumer price data is due out in Malaysia this coming Wednesday.

Gabon also endured a wider spread, up 21 basis points, while losing 1.21% in price terms. The International Monetary Fund is schedule to release its 2010 Article IV Consultation for the unrest-stricken nation on Friday.

Over the weekend, the Group of 20 industrial and developing economies will continue its meeting with the goal of reaching an agreement on setting four indicators as guidelines for measuring global economic imbalances. Also in the week ahead, key emerging-market events include interest rate decisions in Colombia and Hungary, while fourth quarter GDP data is due in Mexico and South Africa.

-By Cynthia Lin, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-4403; cynthia.lin@dowjones.com

title: Chile Stocks End Lower For 4th Straight Day As Investors Sell

title: SCENARIOS-Options to tame  Chile  peso after  intervention
text:
* Widening rates differential attracts dollars

* Peso has nearly recovered from post-intervention drop

* Government reiterates not considering capital controls

By Brad Haynes

SANTIAGO, Feb 17 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank on Thursday reduced options to tame a strong peso hammering exporters when it raised its benchmark rate <CLINTR=ECI> by 25 basis points to 3.5 percent.

(For the main story, see [ID:nN17302923])

The bank made inflation worries a priority and in doing so likely added upward pressure to the peso <CLP=CL>.

The currency is trading near 3-year highs despite a $12 billion central bank currency intervention, boosted by strong prices for main export copper and wider dollar weakness.

(For a graphic, see: http://r.reuters.com/jud77r("http://r.reuters.com/jud77r"))

But Finance Minister Felipe Larrain reiterated earlier on Thursday that Chile is not interested in the sort of secondary measures implemented by Brazil and Peru to address the capital flows behind their currencies' strength.

An aversion to unorthodox currency measures and the mounting costs of the intervention have left Chilean authorities with a sparse second line of defense to bolster their battle against the peso's export-damaging climb.

"They've been burning their boats, bit by bit," said BCI economist Luis Felipe Alarcon.

The following are some possible scenarios:

MORE LIKELY:

* A public commitment to invest the state's dollar revenues in a sovereign wealth fund overseas rather than spending them in the local economy would boost market certainty about the government's commitment to a weaker peso.

Economic growth, forecast at over 5 percent both this year and last, will boost Chile's tax revenue in pesos and let the government rely less on dollars from state miner Codelco's copper exports.

* The government could also allow companies to pay taxes in dollars, relieving demand for pesos from businesses with foreign revenues. Traders said the peso's 0.9 percent rise on Thursday was driven by mining companies selling dollars on the local market to pay monthly taxes denominated in pesos.

* The central bank has left open the chance to increase the volume of its daily $50 million dollar purchases once the second phase of the program ends on March 8. [ID:nSAG002719]

Raising the volume of the daily auctions to $75 million or $100 million would speed up the pace of the intervention and increase market certainty that the central bank will buy the full $12 billion it pledged to accumulate this year.

* Capital market reforms pending congressional approval include a measure giving regulators more discretion to set hedging requirements for pension funds' overseas investments.

The pension funds are currently required by law to hedge at least 50 to 85 percent of their foreign portfolios, diminishing the currency impact of their investments abroad, which make up more than $67 billion of nearly $150 billion under management.

Looser hedging requirements could eventually magnify the effect of the central bank's November decision to let the privately managed pension funds invest more abroad. [ID:nN15266330] [ID:nN10214819]

LESS LIKELY

* Analysts also see the central bank unwilling to increase the total scale of its intervention beyond the record $12 billion in dollar purchases announced on Jan. 3.

Yields on 10-year central bank bonds <CLBCU10Y=RR> have risen nearly 20 basis points to 3.15 percent since the bank announced it would sterilize, or offset, its dollar auctions by issuing debt, magnifying the financial cost of the program.

* Shifting some of the bank's dollar purchases into the derivatives market via non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) would reduce the cost of sterilizing its intervention, but would mean giving up the accumulation of actual reserves.

The central bank said the principal objective of its dollar auctions was to grow its foreign reserves to levels comparable with regional peers, and the bank may be hesitant to undermine its credibility by shifting strategies. (Editing by Simon Gardner; Editing by Andrew Hay)

title: UPDATE 6-Chile raises key rate 25 bps despite strong peso
text:
* Central bank raises key rate by 25 basis points

* Bank suggests more rate hikes are coming

* Quickening inflation is bank's principal concern

* Chile peso nears pre-intervention levels, stocks fall

(Updates with fresh economist comment)

By Simon Gardner and Brad Haynes

SANTIAGO (Reuters) - Chile's central bank Thursday raised its benchmark interest rate and signaled more hikes were on the way as it prioritizes inflation worries over its concerns about a strong peso that is hammering exporters.

The 25-basis-point hike to 3.5 percent, which had been widely expected, will probably put more pressure on the peso, 


which has risen with prices for Chile's main export -- copper
-- and widening dollar weakness.


The peso is trading near three-year highs despite a $12 billion central bank currency intervention.

The central bank surprised the market in January by holding rates steady after seven straight increases to complement the intervention. But investors now see annual inflation at 4.0 


percent in December -- the upper limit of a 2 percent to 4
percent target range -- prompting the central bank to act.


As in regional powerhouse Brazil, inflation in Chile quickened in January, driven partly by rising fuel prices. That put pressure on central bankers to follow the lead of a host of emerging market economies from China to India and Thailand to Peru raising rates.

Widening differentials with near-zero interest rates in economies such as the United States and Japan have prompted investors to seek higher returns in markets like Brazil and Chile.

The central bank cited higher market near-term inflation expectations, but said prices had behaved as expected and core inflation was limited. It also said it would continue to withdraw monetary stimulus in coming months, signaling more hikes to come.

"The strong increase in inflation expectations, due to rising energy and food prices, as well as lower unemployment and the dynamism of internal demand, were the main factors that triggered this decision," said Matias Madrid, chief economist at Banco Penta in Santiago.

"Going forward, we expect the central bank to continue increasing the rate gradually but continually during the first half of the year, and we will only see pauses in the second half," he said.25-basis-point increase, while 16 of 20 analysts polled by Reuters were betting on it.

Chile's peso closed 0.87 percent firmer earlier on Thursday, nearing pre-intervention levels. Chilean stocks closed 1.3 percent lower as investors fled equities for domestic bonds on expectations of a hike. Yields on five-year inflation-indexed central bank bonds have fallen 10 basis points this week.

Chilean consumer prices rose 0.3 percent in January, in line with market forecasts, government data showed last week, boosting bets the central bank would raise its key rate. Core CPI, which strips out prices for fuel, fresh fruit and vegetables, rose 0.1 percent in January.

"Both the central bank and the government are doing all we can to contain inflationary pressures," Finance Minister Felipe Larrain told reporters on Thursday, reiterating that the government was not considering capital controls. "We must be clear that some of those inflationary pressures are coming from international prices."

Exporters, whose revenues have fallen in peso terms as the dollar weakens, have publicly called on the government to take measures to sap the peso's strength.

Central Bank President Jose De Gregorio said Sunday it is vital to control inflation, given rising global oil and food prices. That sent a strong signal that inflation was the bank's overriding focus.

"There are a lot of references to inflation in the bank's rate statement and nothing about the peso," said Erwin Andia, director of Santiago-based brokerage Forex Chile. "The dollar will open weaker (against the peso Friday) and that trend should continue."

"I don't see the central bank intervening again in the very near-term," he added. "It is conscious it can't change the dollar's (downward) trend, because it is an international phenomenon," he said.

The bank said on Wednesday the peso's rise since hitting a trough in late 2008 was "not very different" from currency gains in other commodity exporters and emerging markets where there had been interventions.

Markets are asking what additional steps, if any, the bank and the government will take. De Gregorio on Sunday stressed that any controls to counter currency appreciation should be carefully studied.

The peso weakened sharply after the intervention began in early January, but has been boosted since by strong copper prices and wider dollar weakness, clawing back much of the 7 percent initially lost.

title: Chile Peso Ends Sharply Stronger As Market Bets On Rate Rise
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean peso ended sharply stronger versus the dollar Thursday, as market participants widely expect the central bank will raise interest rates by 25 basis points after market close.

The peso ended at CLP469.70 to the dollar, nearing an almost three-year high despite an ongoing $12 billion currency-intervention program, compared with CLP473.70 on Wednesday. The local currency traded in a range of CLP470.00 to CLP475.00.

Deteriorating inflation expectations, which have in part been fueled by the central bank's intervention program, will likely lead the central bank to more aggressive rate increases this year, analysts said.

In January, the central bank paused its interest-rate increases for the first time since starting to remove its massive monetary stimulus in June 2009. Participants speculated that the bank held the rate in January to support its intervention program.

Central Bank President Jose De Gregorio recently underscored that the bank's main goal is controlling inflation, a message participants interpreted to mean that meeting the inflation target won't be subjugated to the intervention program.

"The market is betting on rates being increased. That would add pressure for the peso to strengthen even more as the gap between U.S. and Chilean rates would be greater," said Guillermo Kautz, head of currency trading at local brokerage BCI Corredor de Bolsa.

Interest-rate increases tend to foster capital inflows, as participants seek better returns.

Dollar sales by Chile's private pension-fund managers, or AFPs, also helped to fuel the peso's strength.

"During the session we saw a lot of institutional dollar sales, especially by AFPs," Kautz said.

On Thursday, Chile's central bank, as part of its intervention program, purchased $50 million at an average rate of CLP474.24. It has accumulated $1.60 billion so far this year.

In the bond market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central-bank bonds, or BCUs, ended lower on strong demand for bonds.

"AFPs have been selling dollars on the local market to buy fixed-income instruments," Kautz said.

The yield on five-year BCU bonds ended at 2.64%, from 2.66% on Wednesday, while the yield on 10-year BCUs closed at 3.14%, from 3.16% the prior session.

title: Chile Peso Ends Weaker On Copper, Institutional Dollar Buys
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chile's peso closed weaker against the dollar Wednesday, as international copper prices retreated and institutional investors bought dollars.

The peso ended at CLP473.70 to the dollar, compared with CLP472.40 on Tuesday, while trading in a range of CLP473.00 to CLP475.00.

As Chile is the world's premier copper producer, accounting for nearly a third of global supply, the peso often takes trading cues from the metal's international prices.

In London trading, spot copper prices fell 1.8% to $4.50191 per pound, according to Chile's state copper commission Cochilco, as inventories of copper stored in London Metal Exchange warehouses rose.

Dollar purchases by banks and Chile's private pension fund managers, helped to weaken the peso, said Felipe Herrera, trader with local brokerage EuroAmerica.

Also, the euro's slip against the dollar after stronger-than-expected U.S. data, helped to push the peso lower.

As Chile's economy is highly export-dependent and about a third of its products are bound for European ports, the peso often moves in the same direction as the euro does against the dollar.

Despite the peso's recent slip, analysts expect the peso will continue gaining to levels it was trading at before the central bank announced in early January a $12 billion currency intervention program if the monetary authority raises interest rates.

Interest rate hikes tend to foster capital inflows, as participants seek better returns.

"The market expects an interest rate hike of 25 basis points, that will help pressure the peso to strengthen a bit, but if the central bank surprises everyone with a 50-basis-points hike, the peso's gains will be much greater," said Nicolas Maqueda, head currency trader at local brokerage Cruz del Sur Corredora de Bolsa.

Over the last several weeks, the peso has pared back most of its post-intervention losses on rising international copper prices, expectations for robust domestic growth and anticipations for continued rate hikes.

On Wednesday, Chile's central bank, as part of its intervention program, purchased $50 million at an average rate of CLP474.40. It has accumulated $1.55 billion so far this year.

In the bond market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central-bank bonds, or BCUs, ended lower as inflation expectations for 2011 have deteriorated in recent days, said Sebastian Ide, head of market making and fixed income at investment bank Santander GBM.

The central bank's latest Monthly Survey of Analysts' Expectations revealed that economists see inflation ending the year at 4%, from a previous 3.6% forecast.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexico peso sinks;  intervention  fears hit  Chile
text:
* Chile currency hurt by concerns of further intervention

* Mexican currency slumps, heavy positioning weighs

* Mexico peso slumps 1 pct, Brazil real 0.06 pct

By Michael O'Boyle and Froilan Romero

MEXICO CITY/SANTIAGO, Feb 15 (Reuters) - Chile's peso slumped by the most in six weeks on Tuesday on falling copper prices and bets authorities may try to limit speculative inflows, while Mexico's peso sank to a two-week low.

Chile's peso slipped back from a six-week high as prices for copper, the country's main export, retreated from a record high. Rising inflation in top copper consumer China raised concerns that tighter borrowing costs there that could hit global demand. [ID:nLDE71E21N]

Traders also cited growing speculation that the government could try again to contain the peso's gains, which are hurting local exporters.

"Banks are taking long-dollar positions to protect themselves from an eventual announcement of measures to brake the peso's gains, this time it could come from the finance ministry," said a trader in Santiago.

The peso <CLP=CL> shed 0.6 percent to 472.30 pesos.

The peso lost ground for the first time in five sessions after surging on bets that Chile's central bank will raise its benchmark interest rate this week.[ID:nN14110508]

Expectations of higher interest rates had helped the currency firm back close to a nearly three-year high and erase most of its losses since the central bank unveiled an intervention program at the beginning of January.

The central bank is not expected to boost its daily dollar purchase program, but the finance ministry could move to tax foreign inflows or it could change regulations governing the market operations of local pension funds, traders said.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> sank 1 percent to 12.17 per dollar, on track to post its biggest one-day loss since violent protests in Egypt rattled global markets at the end of January.

The peso began to weaken after a report on January U.S. retail sales showed they grew less than expected. Mexico sends most of its exports to the United States and it is depending on U.S. demand to fuel economic growth this year.

The Mexican peso weakened past its 20-day moving average, pushing some traders to dump the currency, which then pushed it through other investors' stop-loss levels, deepening the peso's slide.

"There is a complete lack of conviction out there, some people are taking risk off the table and Mexico is vulnerable because everyone is so long," said Paul Biszko, a senior emerging markets strategist at RBC Capital Markets in Toronto.

The Mexican peso has by far the most speculative bets in its favor - or long positions - among the eight major currencies tracked by Reuters. [ID:nN11301566]

Before Tuesday's losses, the Mexican peso gained more than 4 percent since November on the back of a better outlook for the economy of the United States, Mexico's main trading partner.

But the heavy bias in favor of the peso can end up hurting the currency when unforeseen losses, such as Tuesday's, push speculators to run for the door.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> bid 0.06 percent weaker at 1.668 per dollar, likely supported by IPO-related flows into the markets, Biszko noted.

The real's strength would probably be limited by continued central bank intervention in the market, traders said, as Latin America's top economy seeks to limit currency gains that make its exports less competitive.

Yields on Brazilian interest rate futures contracts <0#DIJ:> edged lower after local retail sales volumes stayed unexpectedly flat in December and investors pared their bets for a cycle of interest rate hikes. Brazil's retail sales were expected to rise 0.6 percent, according to Reuters poll. (Additional reporting by Moises Avila in Santiago, Editing by Chizu Nomiyama)

The peso ended at CLP469.30 to the dollar, approaching levels not seen since the central bank announced a $12 billion currency intervention program in early January, compared with CLP472.10 on Friday. It traded in a range of CLP468.80 to CLP473.50.

The risk of propagation to the rest of inflation has to be mitigated. This is most needed in economies, like Chile, that are operating close to full capacity," De Gregorio said in prepared remarks.

He added that the appreciation of emerging-market currencies "is here to stay. Although their effects on the economy can be mitigated for some time, long-term measures must be adopted to foster competitiveness".

The central bank will hold its next monthly monetary policy meeting on Thursday.

On Monday, Chile's central bank, as part of its intervention program, purchased $50 million at an average rate of CLP470.06. It has accumulated $1.45 billion so far this year.

title: MW Mexico unlikely to follow LatAm  currency  controls
text:
By Carla Mozee, MarketWatch

LOS ANGELES (MarketWatch) -- With a newly lowered inflation forecast, and increasing growth in its economy, Mexico is unlike to follow its Latin American neighbors' moves to hike interest rates and impose capital controls, analysts say.

The Mexican peso has begun to test levels not seen since the height of the global financial crisis and recently broke through the psychologically key level of 12 pesos per U.S. dollar for the first time since late October 2008.

Finance Minister Ernesto Cordero has said the country is keeping tabs on the currency's appreciation but has pointedly said Mexico isn't interested in imposing capital controls.

Mexican authorities appear to be content with the peso's rise, according to Marc Chandler, global head of currency strategy at Brown Brothers Harriman "And why shouldn't they be? A small, gradual increase in their currency is slow enough so that they can build up their reserves...and by having a stronger currency, it limits their inflation."

With the slow-growth U.S. as its largest trading partner, Mexico stands in contrast to the rapidly expanding Brazilian economy, Latin America's largest.

Brazil this year extended its battle against currency appreciation by issuing a reserve requirement for local banks and initiating intervention in the futures market, as well as continuing daily auctions to purchase dollars on the spot market. In 2009 Brazil raised taxes on certain foreign investments to cool capital inflows.

"Mexico has maintained a desire to have a free floating exchange rate for many years," said Clyde Wardle, an emerging-market currency strategist at HSBC.

Mexico's only recent intervention was when it sold dollars during the peak of the credit crisis to protest the peso and the economy from certain stresses. "They've indicated that it doesn't make sense to counter one perceived distortion in the market...perhaps the U.S.'s [second quantitative-easing program]...with another distortion such a capital control," said Wardle.

Even with the peso's gains, its advance still lags behind those in other Latin American currencies. Since hitting an all-time low in early March 2009, the peso has risen roughly 20% against the U.S. dollar, trailing the Brazilian real's gain of about 30% during the same period.

Chile's peso also outpaced Mexico's over most of the period. The central bank in Santiago this year adopted its first intervention plan since April 2008, extending through March 8 its plan to make dollar purchases of $50 million a day and the peso has pulled back since the intervention program was launched last month.

While Chile has said it's not looking to implement capital controls the market "sees a non-negligible chance of the government taking further steps to curb peso appreciation," Citigroup analyst Maria Belen Olaiz said in a note to clients this week. However, historically high copper prices will likely make it difficult for the Chilean government to avoid further peso strengthening, she said.

Alfredo Coutino, Moody's Economy.com's director of Latin American research said Mexico's current low-inflation environment puts its policy makers at an advantage over regional counterparts who are facing the prospect that interest-rate hikes to combat inflation will further fuel currency appreciation.

"Mexican authorities have really not been overly defensive in the media with regard to peso appreciation," said Enrique Alvarez, head of Latin American fixed-income research at IDEAGlobal in New York.

He expects the central bank will likely act in a "moderate form" and become "increasingly rhetorically defensive," to hedge against the risk of a quick currency rise if the peso breaks below the 11.80 level.

HSBC's call is for the peso to reach 11.80 by the third quarter of this year, said Wardle.

Coutino also said the country can take a more relaxed stance compared with its regional competitors partially because Mexico has "lower attractiveness to hot money," stemming in part from its ties to slow growth in the U.S. as well as the low level of speculative returns offered by domestic bonds.

Brazil's benchmark interest rate stands at 11.25%, and Argentina's is above 10%. Mexico's benchmark has remained at 4.5% since July of 2009. Coutino said in real terms, the highest return is offered by Brazil, followed by Peru and Chile, and "Mexico at the end."

Mexico has tried "almost all kind of capital controls in the past, with very poor results and extremely high costs for the whole economy," Coutino said. "Policy makers know that the short-term benefits of capital controls are not worth enough to compensate for the sacrifice in the future."

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latin American  currencies  gain on Mubarak exit
text:
* Chile's peso posts 1.4 pct weekly gain

* Peru cenbank swats down sol from 33-month high

* Speculator bets on Mexican peso rise

* Brazil real up 0.24 pct, Mexico peso 0.37 pct (Adds comments, data on Mexican peso CFTC positions)

By Michael O'Boyle and Silvio Cascione

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, Feb 11 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies firmed on Friday after the resignation of Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak eased fears of unrest in the Middle East that had weighed on demand for riskier assets.

Oil and gold prices fell while world stocks rose after Mubarak handed power to the army, curbing concerns that unrest could push up the price of oil and weigh down global growth.

"People came to the conclusion it is not that easy to shut down the Suez Canal," said Dirk Willer, head of Latin America local markets strategy at Citigroup in New York. "If you do not get an oil spike on the back of Egypt developments, since the Suez canal is still open, then it is not a big deal."

Chile's peso closed at its strongest since early January, also helped by the view that the central bank will raise interest rates next week.

Chile's peso <CLP=> bid 0.28 percent firmer at 472.20 per dollar and notched a 1.4 percent gain for the week. The country's central bank is seen raising its benchmark rate to 3.50 percent next week, resuming hikes after pausing last month in part to avoid further appreciation in the peso.

The Chilean peso got a lift earlier this week after the central bank signaled it has no plans to step up dollar purchases. Chile, as well as Brazil and Peru, has been intervening in markets to stem sharp gains in its currency that are hurting local exporters.

Brazil's real <BRBY> bid 0.24 percent firmer at 1.665 per dollar on the local spot market despite two auctions in which the central bank bought dollars. The real firmed 0.54 percent for the week.

SOL INTERVENTION

The new government of President Dilma Rousseff introduced spending cuts this week to bring inflation back under control and minimize the need for aggressive interest rate hikes from the central bank. [ID:nN11131412]

But with Brazil offering among the highest rates in the world, the cuts have not dented appetite for the real.

The Mexican peso <MXN=> firmed 0.33 percent to 12.0325 per dollar, closing the week with a 0.29 percent loss.

Bets by speculators in favor of Mexico's peso edged up to 103,812 contracts in the week ended Feb. 8, according to data from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission in Chicago.

The peso has by far the most bets in its favor of the eight major currencies tracked by Reuters. It is up around 4 percent since November on the back of an improving outlook for the economy of the United States, Mexico's main trading partner.

The large amount of bets on the peso could hurt the currency if U.S. stocks pull back and the hoard of speculators run for the exits, analysts said.

"If the S&P were to have a hiccup, then you could see some pressure on the peso," said Willer.

Mexico is the one major economy in the region not facing worsening inflation pressures and it is not expected to hike interest rates for some time.

Peru's sol <PEN=PE> closed flat after the central bank bought $130 million to knock the currency back from a 33-month high.

The country raised its benchmark interest rate for the second straight month late on Thursday to 3.5 percent, boosting the appeal of the sol to yield-hungry global investors. Peru's central bank bought $367 million so far in 2011 to undermine gains in the sol.

The country is expected to keep hiking interest rates, but it may start to rely on other measures to contain credit growth like raising bank capital ratios.

"Currency concerns should prevent rates from rising (in Peru) to their pre-recession levels and the bulk of further monetary tightening is likely to come through more creative channels," wrote Neil Shearing, an economist at Capital Economics. title: EMERGING MARKETS-Chile peso firms to over 1-mo high, Brazil dips
text:
* Chile bets backed by rate view, lower intervention risks

* Real slumps from more than one-month high

* Mexican finance minister rules out intervention

* Brazil real slumps 0.6 pct, Mexico peso flat

By Michael O'Boyle and Ana Nicolaci da Costa

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO (Reuters) - Chile's peso hit its strongest level in more than a month Thursday after a poll backed bets of higher interest rates and intervention risks were seen receding, while Brazil's currency slumped.

Chile's central bank is seen raising its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 3.50 percent next week, according to a poll.

Chilean policymakers held borrowing costs steady last month to try to discourage yield-hungry investors from pouring into its assets. The pause complemented a currency intervention program introduced at the beginning of the year.

But the move spooked bond investors, who fear the central bank is not doing enough to tame rising inflation. Now policymakers appear to be changing course.

The central bank held back from expanding the intervention program this week despite solid gains in the peso.

"People feel more comfortable that they will tolerate a stronger peso, because they need to worry about inflation," said Igor Arsenin, head of Latin American debt strategy at Credit Suisse in New York.

Seven straight rate hikes last year drove the Chilean peso to a nearly three-year high, pushing the central bank to buy $50 million a day to help protect local exporters.

Chile's peso bid 0.57 percent stronger to 473.50 per dollar, its strongest since early January. The peso has clawed back more than 5 percent from a 7 percent loss spurred by news of the intervention in early January.

Brazil's real shed 0.6 percent to 1.669 per dollar, pulling back sharply after the currency hit a more than one-month high in the previous session.

A broadly stronger dollar and a slump in the euro, a key proxy for gauging demand for riskier assets like emerging market currencies, weighed on the real and Mexico's peso.

NO MEXICAN MEDDLING

Brazil's government unveiled budget cuts of about $30 billion Wednesday in a bid to regain credibility among investors worried that overspending is driving inflation higher and beyond the control of the central bank.

"Yesterday we had a positive economic context here, especially with the announcement of the budget cuts, it makes Brazil seem more trustworthy ... so the day after it is normal that you have an adjustment," said Andre Sacconato, economist at Tendencias consultancy in Sao Paulo.

Brazil has been waging an even more intense battle than Chile to contain the strength of the real, which is considered one of the most overvalued currencies in the world.

Brazil offers among the highest interest rates available, and a relentless flow of funds from global investors continues to bode further strength despite heavy intervention.

The central bank held a reserve currency swap auction Thursday, though the real did not react noticeably to the news.

The Mexican peso reversed steep early losses to trade flat at 12.0765 per dollar after Mexico's finance minister said the country will not intervene in foreign exchange markets, brushing off complaints from exporters who want a weaker peso.

Mexico's peso has lagged the gains in other emerging markets currencies, giving policymakers more room to stay on the sidelines.

But some had begun to bet Mexico could follow suit with greater intervention after the peso gained around 4 percent since November to hit a nearly 2-1/2 year high last month. (Editing by Dan Grebler)

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Feb 8 (Reuters) - Interest rates in Brazil fell sharply on Tuesday as investors bet the new government could soon deliver big spending cuts that would curb the need for steep interest rate hikes.

Yields on longer-term interest rate futures dropped <0#DIJ:> amid market chatter that the new government could deliver cuts close to 50 billion reais ($83.3 billion) later this week, analysts said.

"As we get closer to an announcement, the market thinks that they might actually deliver that positive credibility shock that is necessary to reverse a deterioration in expectations," said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, an analyst at RBS Securities.

By clamping down hard on government stimulus, the country's central bank may not have to raise interest rates as much as the market was expecting in order to contain fears that inflation could spiral out of policymakers' control.

title: Chile  Peso Stays Strong; Views Of Greater  Intervention  Grow
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Faced with a stubbornly strong peso, the Chilean central bank may increase the daily dollar purchases of its currency intervention program to $75 million or $100 million from a current $50 million per day, analysts said.

Following the peso's significant appreciation last year, the central bank announced it would begin intervening in the local market through sterilized dollar purchases totaling $12 billion this year.

While the central bank has already accumulated $1.2 billion during the first phase of its program, which started Jan. 5 and is scheduled to end on Feb. 9, increasing daily dollar purchases should help to stem the peso's continued gains.

"The central bank should consider using bigger bullets," by making more aggressive daily dollar purchases, Felipe Alarcon, deputy head of research at local investment bank BCI, wrote in a note to clients.

The peso weakened some 7% to near CLP500 in the week following the program's announcement. It has since regained most of its losses on the back of record-high copper prices and deteriorating inflation expectations, which likely anticipate more interest rate hikes.

Because Chile is the world's largest copper producer and exporter, currency-market participants usually keep an eye on New York and London copper prices to gauge export revenue inflows and the general health of the economy.

Additionally, deteriorating inflation expectations, in part due to the intervention program itself, are expected to push the central bank to continue hiking interest rates. This will make returns on capital inflows more attractive and tend to appreciate the peso further.

The peso's sizable appreciation last year helped keep inflation benign, absorbing most increases in import prices, but the intervention program has taken that cushion away.

The central bank held the benchmark overnight rate at 3.25% in January, its first pause since it started removing its massive monetary stimulus in June last year.

"The effects [of the peso intervention and depreciation] were still too new to reach conclusions on where the currency would move to and on its inflationary consequences," the minutes of the central bank's January monetary policy meeting said.

Considering that inflation expectations are rising, however, participants anticipate the central bank will continue tightening monetary policy.

"We don't expect the central bank to risk falling behind on the inflation front by turning more dovish to curtail forex appreciation," RBC Capital Markets said in a research note.

Not all participants are convinced that the central bank will increase its daily dollar purchases, however, as the bank's accompanying bond-buying sterilization program has already fueled bond yield increases. Higher yields typically fuel more capital inflows.

"The central bank would have to sterilize the dollar purchases more quickly if it increased [the purchases] to $75 million and that would push bond yields even higher...I'm not sure the bank would want to do that," said Nathan Pincheira, fixed-income analyst with local investment bank Banchile Inversiones.

title: Emerging Mkts Spend Big On  Forex Intervention  Amid Dubious Success
text:
-Emerging-Market Currencies Rising Despite Interventions

-Effectiveness of Interventions Seen As Mixed

-Interventions Bring Costs Of Soaking Up Excess Liquidity


 
   By Erin McCarthy and Anjali Cordeiro 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging-market countries have been undertaking costly interventions to hold down the value of their currencies, but how effective these efforts have been in containing investment inflows is debatable.

Countries from Brazil to South Korea have raised their reserves, taxed outside investments or instituted other types of capital controls to prevent foreign inflows from driving up their currencies. Yet the success in halting currency appreciation remains hard to gauge, with the focus more on slowing the rate of increase rather than on reversing it. At the same time, the interventions have imposed a battery of hidden costs on these countries' central banks and capital markets.

In Brazil, where taxes have been placed on various types of foreign flows and where the central bank has been buying up U.S. dollars on a nearly daily basis, the real has generally stayed on an upward path. It was at BRL1.6722 recently, according to CQG, putting it up roughly 1.7% since increased taxes were announced on outside investments in October.

Still, HSBC strategist Maya Hernandez estimated that the real might have strengthened to as much as BRL1.50 to the dollar, without the policy moves.

"There is a limit to how much [countries] can intervene," she said. "So, going forward, the best intervention can hope for is stability [in the currency] or a slowdown in the pace of appreciation," she said.

In South Korea, policymakers have implemented a cap on banks' foreign-exchange forward positions and imposed a levy against banks' balance of nondeposit foreign-currency debt. Still, the won has been strengthening lately, recently reaching about KRW1115 to the dollar, compared with KRW1165 in mid-December.

"Korea has tried it and it's [apparently] not working but who knows where we'd be without [the policy moves]," said Brown Brothers Harriman strategist Win Thin.

Some argue that these policies can backfire even with regards to the currency's valuation. For instance, Nomura Securities strategist Tony Volpon argued that Brazil's interventions have reduced volatility in its foreign-exchange market and so have made its super high-yielding currency, the real, even more attractive to outside investors.

"This is actually making the currency a better bet and is generating inflows that I don't think would have been there if there had been more actual volatility," he said.

What is more, intervening directly in foreign-exchange markets can be expensive for central banks, which must issue interest-bearing bonds to soak up the excess local currency liquidity that is created in the process.

As Brazil's central bank continues to purchase a mix of euros and dollars, which pay rates of around 1.5% to 2%, it has to offset the added market liquidity by issuing debt at an average local cost of 11%. That 9% shortfall on its reserves amounts to "a very big negative carry," said Nomura's Volpon. "They're really stretching the edge of the envelope by this kind of intervention." He estimated that the costs of sterilization for Brazil may have reached up to 40 billion Brazilian reais in 2010.

Chile in January launched a $12 billion currency-market intervention program. That foreign-exchange intervention has been more successful because it had a "combined coordinated policy response," Volpon said. Chile initiated a large dollar-purchasing program and at the same time held interest rates steady in January. According to CQG, the Chilean peso has weakened to CLP479.05 to the dollar, compared to a close of CLP466.65 on Jan. 3.

As with Chile, Colombia has also made several moves to weaken its currency, including making daily dollar purchases of at least $20 million and placing restrictions on public-sector flows.

Beyond building their reserves, emerging markets in Asia and Latin America have taken other steps. Taiwan last year tightened restrictions on foreign investments in certain short-term local-currency products. In October, Thailand imposed a tax on income that foreign investors could earn on Thai bonds.

While capital controls can be cheaper to implement, they can also have far-reaching effects on investor sentiment. While the jitters that they create among investors might help in keeping speculators away in the short term, the longer-term impact on sentiment is hard to gauge.

"Investors are getting spooked," said Brown Brothers Harriman's Thin. "What if [the restrictions] get out of control? If you prick investor confidence, it's hard to get it back."

Meanwhile, inflation pressure is becoming more of a headache for emerging markets everywhere, a development that will make it even more complicated for policymakers looking to fight price pressures and keep their currencies from rising too much. title: ANALYSIS-Bets on  Chile  peso undercut  intervention  impact
text:
* Foreigners renew forward bets unwound post-intervention

* Derivatives compound fundamentals driving peso strength

* NDF bets diluting impact of central bank intervention

By Moises Avila

SANTIAGO, Feb 4 (Reuters) - Foreign bets on the Chilean peso's appreciation are recovering strength in the local derivatives market, eroding the impact of a $12 billion currency intervention early last month.

The shifting tide in the forward market may compound the effects of global dollar weakness, rising interest rates and the record price of top export copper, which have halved the impact of the central bank intervention in under a month.

On the eve of the bank's dollar-buying program, the foreign position in Chilean non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) <CLPNDF=> represented a net $1.675 billion bet on a stronger peso <CLP=CL>, helping to lift the currency to near 3-year highs.

After the central bank's Jan. 3 announcement, investors quickly unwound bets and covered themselves against the depreciating peso, shifting their positions by Jan. 20 to a net $2.111 billion bet on a weaker peso.

But by Feb. 2, a net $522 million shift in NDF contracts back to a long peso position suggested foreign investors see the currency's downside risk subsiding as the exchange rate erases over one-half of its 7 percent post-intervention swing.

"There's now a recovery (in the forwards market), with new bets coming out in favor of the peso," said analyst Osvaldo Cruz of Chilean bank BCI. "It's complicating the central bank's intervention, essentially producing an appreciative effect and therefore offsetting part of the impact of the intervention." <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ 


  > For a graphic, see            http://r.reuters.com/vuc87r ("http://r.reuters.com/vuc87r")

Central bank data showed the net shift in foreigners' forward positions over the past nine sessions is equivalent to more than 10 of the bank's daily $50 million dollar auctions.

Daily trade in Chile's NDF market averages about $350 million to $400 million, about one-third the size of the country's daily spot market and one-tenth the scale of forwards trade in regional powerhouse Brazil.

NDFs are forward peso derivatives that investors use to hedge other investments against exchange rate risk or to openly speculate on a currency. Derivatives trading can impact the daily exchange rate when local banks cover their forward contracts by buying or selling dollars in the spot market.

In a NDF trade, investors either gain or lose the difference between the spot exchange rate and their bet, without handing over the underlying currency.

"The market is betting with forwards that the local supply of dollars will strengthen the peso, maybe even to pre-intervention levels," said one New York-based NDF trader, asking not to be named in line with company policy.

The peso has also been helped by economic fundamentals as copper export revenues reached record highs and foreign investment helps fuel Chile's bounding economic growth.

Market inflation forecasts have risen to the upper limit of the central bank's annual target, reinforcing expectations the bank will raise its benchmark interest rate next Thursday for the eighth time in nine months. For details, see [ID:nSAG002696]

Chile has ruled out limiting capital inflows that chase higher yields in emerging markets, breaking ranks with regional peers like Brazil and reducing its policy arsenal for confronting the peso's rally. [ID:nN31202514]

Among the central bank's remaining options on the exchange rate is an increase to the volume of its daily dollar auctions after the first phase of the program ends on Feb. 9. [ID:nN03137860] (Reporting by Alonso Soto; writing by Brad Haynes; editing by Simon Gardner and Jeffrey Benkoe)

title: DAVOS-Chile finmin says markets correct to see rate rises
text:
DAVOS, Switzerland, Jan 27 (Reuters) - Chilean Finance Minister Felipe Larrain said on Thursday that markets were right to expect more rate rises from Chile but that the country was not considering capital controls to tame peso appreciation.

"We won't have any surprises in terms of increased intervention" on top of the $12 billion of intervention already announced, Larrain told Reuters at the Davos World Economic Forum annual meeting.

Asked about further measures to rein in the Chilean peso, Larrain said: "We are not considering capital controls."

He emphasised instead keeping a tight rein on spending, using a diversified package of financing and finding different kinds of derivative for small business to cover exchange risk.

Larrain said Chile would stick to its 2-4 percent inflation target. Asked about interest rate rises, he replied:

"You can probably expect more rate increases just because we have now a rate which is 3.25 percent and with three per cent inflation, that is still a very expansionary monetary policy."

Referring to expectations of a gradual rise in interest rates during the year, Larrain said: "That is internalised by the markets, that's what they are expecting and they are expecting correctly.

Chile's central bank began a record $12 billion intervention this year to stop export-damaging strength in the peso.

Much of Latin America is grappling with rising food prices, which have been largely countered in Chile by the strong peso currency.

Seven successive rate hikes have lured foreign investment into local financial markets, one factor that helped propel the peso up 17 percent in the second half of 2010 to its strongest in nearly three years.

The central bank left benchmark interest rates steady at 3.25 percent on Jan 13 after raising it for seven consecutive months, in a move widely seen complementing its currency intervention in curbing the peso's strength.

Consumer prices in Chile rose 3 percent last year, in line with the central bank's inflation target. (Reporting and writing by Michael Stott)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real flat; Fed pledge supports region
text:
* Brazil real flat after latest intervention move

* Mexico peso firms 0.79 pct, Chile peso adds 0.8 pct (Adds comments, updates prices; changes dateline, previous SAO PAULO)

By Samantha Pearson and Walter Brandimarte

SAO PAULO/NEW YORK, Jan 26 (Reuters) - Brazil's real shook off the latest intervention measures deployed by local authorities to end unchanged on Wednesday, while Mexico's and Chile's peso currencies were supported by solid U.S. housing data.

Latin American currencies received further support from a pledge by the U.S. Federal Reserve that it would keep up its bond-buying program, which has boosted higher-risk assets around the world. For details, see [ID:nN25283937]

By underpinning demand for the U.S. bond market to keep yields down, the Fed is pushing investors to seek higher returns in other assets.

"We will continue to have a very large overhang of liquidity," said Enrique Alvarez, head of Latin America research at IDEAglobal in New York. "That continues to point to currency appreciation in Latin America."

The pledge from the Fed after its first meeting of the year was largely anticipated by markets.

Low interest rates in the United States and across the industrialized world have boosted demand for Latin American assets, driving currencies to multiyear highs. Regional policymakers have waded into foreign exchange markets to weaken their respective currencies in an effort to protect the competitiveness of local manufacturers.

Brazil's real <BRBY> bid unchanged at 1.669 per dollar on the local spot market, although it firmed in international trade <BRL=> after the Fed's statement.

Brazil's central bank said late on Tuesday that it could for the first time ever offer currency forwards at auction, adding to its growing toolbox of market mechanisms aimed at cooling the real's gains. [ID:nN25294325]

CLOSING LOOPHOLES

The lack of market reaction to the announcement was blamed on uncertainty about the frequency of such auctions as well as their aim, since the forwards market is tiny compared to Brazil's spot and futures markets.

Analysts said this latest measure is likely an attempt to keep speculators from trying to get around previous measures.

"The decision looks like an effort to close a loophole to capture all sides of the market," said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, a strategist at RBS Securities in New York, in a research note.

Brazil has the highest yields in the region as it hikes interest rates to keep its strong economy from overheating.

The real is expected to keep strengthening until authorities introduce more drastic measures such as widespread quarantines or capital controls, analysts said.

"The next instrument (to be announced) could be some type of restriction on a specific inflow, something like the quarantine," said Jorge Lima, a consultant at Previbank DTVM in Sao Paulo. "But Brazil can't shut itself off from long-term investment, so it would have to be a very specific restriction on speculative transactions."

The Mexican and Chilean pesos both firmed on Wednesday, helped by data showing U.S. single-family home sales in December rose to their highest in eight months.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> strengthened 0.79 percent to 12.0025 per dollar.

"The outlook for the U.S. housing sector could be improving, and that is a good sign for the economy. (The United States) is our biggest trading partner and so this is having a good influence on the peso," said Mario Copca, an analyst at the Vanguardia brokerage in Mexico City.

In Chile, the peso <CLP=CL> firmed 0.8 percent to 489.90 per dollar as the price of copper, the country's main export, was supported by the U.S. economic data.

The Chilean peso closed at its strongest close since the country's central bank announced a $12 billion currency intervention Jan. 3 aimed at keeping the currency in check.

title: *DJ  Chile Central Bank  President De Gregorio: Peso Responding To  Intervention  As Expected
text:
24 Jan 2011 14:36 EDT *DJ  Chile Central Bank President: Capital Controls Not Currently Needed

24 Jan 2011 14:36 EDT *DJ  Chile Central Bank President: Intervention Was Based On Long-Term Outlook

24 Jan 2011 14:36 EDT *DJ  Chile Central Bank President: Global Reserve Increase Helped Intervention Timing

24 Jan 2011 14:36 EDT *DJ  Chile Central Bank President: Economy Already Seeing Intervention Costs

24 Jan 2011 14:47 EDT =DJ  Chile Central Bank Pres De Gregorio: Peso Responding To Intervention As Expected


 
    By Carolina Pica 
    Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean peso has responded as expected to the central bank's market intervention, the bank's president Jose De Gregorio said Monday.

The peso, which for most of the last quarter traded at 32-month highs against the dollar, has depreciated about 5% since the central bank announced its intervention program in early January.

Noting that a central bank could never rule out anything, De Gregorio told Dow Jones Newswires in an interview that capital controls weren't currently needed.

"It's not evident" that Chile would require capital controls in the immediate future as the country is currently a net creditor, he said.

He added that Chile's experience with capital controls in the 1990s shows they weren't very effective as they didn't curb inflows, but just changed the type of inflows.

"They didn't buffer us from the effects of the Asian crisis [in the late 1990s]," he said in reference to the recession into which Chile fell at the end of that decade.

The central banker says capital controls can be effective in certain circumstances, but that for the most part, they produce a dichotomy of sorts.

"Countries say they want long-term capital but not speculative capital. How do you distinguish between the two?" he asked. "They say 'we want capital, but not appreciation,' which in my view is a dichotomous view that can easily become an inconsistency."

As to the bank's currency market intervention, through which it plans to buy a total $12 billion this year to increase reserves to 17% of gross domestic product, De Gregorio said the decision to intervene was based on a long-term outlook, not a specific trading level for the peso.

"It would be a mistake to think that this intervention was contingent on a specific nominal value for the peso," De Gregorio said. "It had to do with the peso's outlook and we couldn't rule out that the peso would remain strong for a prolonged time, and that this could have implications," he said.

Many of Chile's economic sectors, such as agriculture and industry, were losing competitiveness abroad on the peso's strength.

He added that the global context showed many other countries are increasing their reserves, so it made sense for Chile to make the same move.

"To a certain degree, what's happening around the world in terms of reserves pushes us to increase ours in order to improve our safeguards, so the timing for our move was right," he said.

But he reiterated that intervening in the market has its costs, as people are already seeing some import prices, such as gasoline at the pump, increase. Chile imports the vast majority of fuels that it consumes.

While De Gregorio admitted that the intervention could push inflation marginally higher, he doesn't see this modifying the bank's monetary policy.

"The [inflationary] effect is buffered and compensated for," he said.

After applying an unprecedented stimulus which brought the benchmark overnight rate to a record low 0.5% in mid-2009 and included quantitative easing measures, the bank began removing this stimulus in June of 2010.

The benchmark rate is currently at 3.25%. Analysts expect the rate to end the year at 5%, according to the central bank's monthly poll of analysts' expectations.

Regarding the measures his colleagues at the U.S. Federal Reserve have taken, De Gregorio sees the U.S. economy recovering as a result of the strong stimulus.

He downplays the effects that the Fed's quantitative easing has had on emerging markets.

"In the international economic and political scene, the effects of U.S. QE and China's currency policy tend to be overstated. While I don't want to undermine their global impact, they aren't at the heart of matter," he said.

The central banker believes the Chinese yuan, whose strength he says comes from sizable domestic savings, will eventually appreciate, albeit gradually.

"That should come on the back of increased domestic spending in that country and that should ease some of the pressure," he said.

-By Carolina Pica, Dow Jones Newswires; 56-2-715-8919; carolina.pica@dowjones.com

title: Chile  Peso Closes Firmer As  Intervention  Ends, Copper Rises
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chile's peso closed stronger against the dollar Friday, as the central bank's currency market intervention program came to its scheduled end and as international copper prices rose.

The peso ended at CLP517.50 to the dollar, versus Thursday's close of CLP518.20. It traded in a range of CLP516.10 to CLP519.10.

Because Chile is the world's premier copper producer and exporter, accounting for a third of global supply, traders and investors keep track of New York and London copper prices to gauge export revenue inflows and the general health of the Chilean economy.

The most active contract for copper futures, for March delivery, was recently up 5.65 cents, or 1.7%, at $3.3235 a pound on the Comex division of the New York Mercantile Exchange, as some progress was seen on confronting the euro zone's debt crisis.

In addition, rising U.S. markets, as investors digested improving domestic economic data, helped to boost the peso. U.S. markets are often seen as a bellwether for risk aversion.

"In general, today has been a good day for markets, especially considering copper prices rising well above 1%. That's lifting the peso," said Gloria Soto, head currency trader at FXCM Chile.

Chile's central bank, on the last day of its currency-intervention program, purchased $50 million Friday at an average rate of CLP517.59 to the dollar. It accumulated $12.0 billion during the year through the program.

The monetary authority kicked off the intervention program, which sought to increase the bank's foreign-currency reserves to the equivalent of 17% of gross domestic product, in early January when the peso was trading near a three-year high against the dollar.

As exports represent roughly 60% of the country's gross domestic product, a stronger peso cuts into these products' competitiveness abroad.

While the intervention program had the immediate effect of punching the air out of the peso's strength, the local currency gradually climbed back and was trading at three-year highs in July as nervous participants worried about U.S. debt and growth.

Then, as concerns about Europe's sovereign-debt crisis congealed in investors' psyche and international copper prices dropped, the peso weakened to 16-month lows in early October.

In the fixed-income market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central bank bonds, or BCUs, ended mixed in a light trading session.

The yield on five-year BCU bonds ended unchanged at 2.41%, while the yield on 10-year BCUs closed at 2.53%, from 2.52% the prior session. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The head of Chile's central bank said Thursday he isn't ruling out an interest rate reduction, in light of growing international risks, especially in Europe.

In its quarterly Monetary Policy Report released earlier this month, the bank based its baseline scenario on the benchmark rate holding steady through December.

"We aren't married to this baseline scenario," bank head Jose De Gregorio said Thursday.

The bank has held the benchmark overnight lending rate steady at 5.25% for three consecutive months after a series of increases.

Earlier this week, the central bank's bi-weekly poll of traders' expectations showed these market participants see the benchmark rate retreating to 5% by January 2012 and to 4.75% by April of next year.

De Gregorio, speaking at a seminar hosted by the Chilean-American Chamber of Commerce, or Amcham, said the economic outlook in Europe poses the greatest international risk.

According to the central bank, Europe's woes are occurring in "slow motion, like an accident in a tunnel where everyone is driving without headlights," but noted that there won't likely be a crash like there was in 2008 with Lehman Brothers' troubles.

He added that the bank has the policies to act should economic conditions abroad worsen.

Regarding the recent depreciation the peso has posted against the dollar, De Gregorio said the drop was in line with weakening seen in other commodity-related currencies around the world.

"With commodities prices falling, we have to expect some sort of peso depreciation," he said.

As Chile produces a third of the world's copper, its currency takes cues from international copper prices.

In early 2011, when the peso was trading at three-year highs against the dollar, on strong growth expectations and rising copper prices, the bank announced a $12 billion currency market intervention program.

In light of the near 12% drop the peso has seen so far in September, analysts have been speculating the bank could end its intervention program early.

De Gregorio said the bank is always evaluating its intervention.

"But that's the same response I would have had if asked about the intervention three months ago," he told conference participants.

He noted that incentives for carry-trade operations with the Chilean peso had decreased recently on the retreat in the longer-term rate outlook.

The bank's currency intervention is scheduled to end in December.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real gains after  FX  swap; Latam rebounds
text:
* Brazil c. bank swap sale checks real slide, sets 'limit'

* Mexico, Chile pesos rebound from sharp Thursday declines

* Peru intervenes in currency market; sol erases loss

(Updates prices, adds Brazil, Peru, Colombia comment)

By Jeb Blount

RIO DE JANEIRO, Sept 23 (Reuters) - Brazil's real reversed losses to gain more than 3 percent against the dollar on Friday -- its biggest one-day gain in almost 16 months -- after the central bank's move to bolster the currency a day earlier raised expectations it will act again to limit sharp falls.

Thursday's sale of $2.75 billion of currency swaps effectively put a limit on how far the bank will allow the real to slide, said Mario Battistel, head of trading at Fair Corretora, a Sao Paulo currency brokerage. For more see [ID:nS1E78L0PK].

Currency swaps mimic the sale of dollars and provide investors with insurance against future declines in the real.

The real has lost more than 15 percent of its value since the central bank unexpectedly cut its benchmark interest rate by half a percentage point to 12 percent on Aug. 31. The move was based on the bank's expectation that a world economic slowdown would push down Brazil's 7 percent inflation rate. [ID:nE5E7IM05G] and [ID:nL3E7KN1BZ]

"The central bank swap intervention was a pleasant surprise," Battistel said in a telephone interview. "They're clearly worried about inflation and exporters and our other clients weren't about to start moving their large dollar holdings back into Brazil until they had some idea of when the real's plunge would stop."

Brazil's real <BRBY> gained 3.19 percent to 1.8360 to the U.S. dollar, its first gain in six sessions and its biggest one-day gain since May 27, 2010.

The currency had lost more than 1 percent in early trade and still ended the week down about 5.75 percent against the dollar.

The government is ready to intervene more in the currency market to curb wide swings, or volatility, in the market, Finance Minster Guido Mantega told investors in Washington. [ID:nS1E78M134]

Brazil's central bank targets inflation of 4.5 percent plus or minus 2 percentage points and has long said that inflation, now outside the target range, will come under control soon.

A strong real helps control inflation by cutting the cost of dollar-denominated commodities such as food and the cost of essential imports such as machine-tools for Brazil's industry.

Battistel said the central bank, which as recently as August was working to prevent the real from gaining against the dollar, is signaling that it will act any time the real weakens beyond 1.90 to the dollar or strengthens beyond 1.60.

Other traders said the bank is targeting the first dollar futures contract <DOLc1> on the Sao Paulo BM&FBovespa exchange, moving to weaken the real when it firms beyond 2.01 to the dollar and to strengthen the real when it weakens beyond 1.78.

The real-dollar spot exchange rate's close link to the futures market, where bets can be ramped up using loans or "leverage" is one of the reasons the real lost so much in recent weeks, the government said Wednesday.

In first futures trading, which measure expectations for late September, the real shed 2.16 percent to 1.8585.

Bets on a strong real were a key component in the real's nearly 8 percent rise through late July.

Since then the real has reversed all those gains and is now about 9 percent weaker than it was at the end of 2010.
