title: Chile's Pinera: Can't Meet All Demands Of Protesters
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Chilean President Sebastian Pinera, facing protests at home by students seeking higher subsidies among other reforms, said Thursday he sympathizes with the demands but that the government needs to maintain fiscal discipline amid a deteriorating global economic scenario.

"We can accept some of the conditions but not all the conditions," Pinera said in an interview, noting that student demands for a free college education and the elimination of for-profit schools aren't practical.

"We could spend all the money and everyone would be happy for the day, but then what would happen?," Pinera said, referring to funds the government has accumulated thanks to the recovery of Chilean economic growth in recent years.

"We don't want to face the problems Greece and Portugal are facing now, " Pinera said.

Students, who have staged periodic protests over the past four months seeking higher-quality and more-affordable education, took to the streets again Thursday in Chile, with tens of thousands of protesters in the capital Santiago, according to local media reports.

Polls show that the protests have won broad sympathy among older Chileans frustrated by income inequalities in a country long seen as a model of economic stability in Latin America. Unable to allay the students since the protests started in May, Pinera has seen his approval rating plunge over the past several months from the peak of popularity he enjoyed following the daring rescue of trapped miners a year ago. While educational reform was already a priority for his administration, students want quicker and more-aggressive action.

The government in early July committed $4 billion beyond what had been budgeted for education, money that Pinera said would come from the extra revenue that was generated thanks to a recovery in growth since the 2008 financial crisis and increased revenues from rising copper prices. Pinera has pledged to improve the quality of education at all levels and to provide free education for all middle and low income students.

Pinera said he's hopeful a compromise will be reached, but urged those seeking reforms to be pragmatic. "People think we can live as if we were a rich country - we're not," Pinera said. "I am concerned that some people think we have already reached the summit. We are halfway down the path to full development."

Pinera, who took office in March 2010 just after the country was devastated by an earthquake and tsunami, said he's "very concerned" about deteriorating global economic conditions. Chile is a very open economy with numerous free trade agreements, which makes it vulnerable to the global turmoil, Pinera said.

Pinera's hopes for returning the country to economic growth rates of 6% and higher necessary to broadly improve living standards may suffer as a result. His government has already tempered its economic expansion forecasts for this year and next, and Pinera said Europe's process to get over its sovereign debt crisis "will be very slow and it will take a lot of time, and it will face a lot of risks."

Fears about the prospects for Europe and the global economy have caused the price of copper, Chile's main export, to fall to its lowest level in a year. The metal closed trading Thursday in New York at just under $3.50 a pound, down from a high for the year of $4.63 in February. Despite the decline, copper prices remain above the assumptions in the Chilean budget of $3.24 in 2011 and $3.02 in 2012.

Along with the decline in the price of copper, the Chilean peso has fallen to its weakest point against the dollar since July 2010, ending Thursday at CLP521. The peso has now weakened 12% against the U.S. currency since the start of the month.

For Chile, whose central bank has been intervening in currency markets since the start of the year to stem the pace of appreciation of the peso, the weakening of the local currency could be seen as a blessing for the export-reliant economy. But the swiftness of the recent reversal, which reflects heightened risk-aversion among global investors, could be cause for concern.

Pinera downplayed such concerns, noting that Chile views its peso against a basket of currencies, not just the dollar, and against the basket, the peso has been "more stable". He also criticized the so-called currency wars of the past year, in which many countries, including Chile, have sought to stabilize their currencies to protect local industry.

"I think currency wars and protectionist wars are the worst possible answer to this situation and any situation," Pinera said. However, "One of the problems that we have in the world right now is that some countries are not allowing their currencies to float as they should."

By Stephen Wisnefski and Eduardo Kaplan, (212) 416-2191; stephen.wisnefski@dowjones.com [ 22-09-11 2004GMT ]

In early January, the central bank launched the intervention program to beat back the peso as it was trading at three-year highs versus the dollar.

title: *DJ IMF Sees Chilean Peso In Line With Fundamentals
text:
24 Aug 2011 15:03 EDT *DJ  IMF Sees No Need To Extend Central Bank Currency Intervention

24 Aug 2011 15:07 EDT DJ  IMF: Chile Government Should Cut Spending Further

SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean government needs to further reduce spending to ensure macroeconomic stability, the International Monetary Fund said Wednesday.

Chile increased spending in 2009 to combat a recession stemming from the global financial crisis and has since reined in spending to contain inflationary and exchange-rate pressures.

"In the near term, greater fiscal restraint would help guard against upside inflation risks and improve the policy mix, reducing the risk of a surge in capital inflows and easing pressures on the exchange rate," the IMF said after completing the so-called Article IV annual consultation.

As a result of the countercyclical spending, the country in 2009 posted a record-high fiscal deficit of 4.5% of gross domestic product. In 2010, despite reconstruction efforts following an 8.8-magnitude earthquake and tsunami, the fiscal deficit fell to 0.4% of GDP.

The Finance Ministry expects the country to return to a balanced budget in 2014 and has taken steps to simplify the structural surplus rule in place since 2000, which has been credited with contributing to the country's economic stability.

The IMF praised these changes to the structural surplus rule, but warned the country needs to return to a fiscal surplus in the medium-term.

Regarding the peso, which has been trading at near three-year highs against the dollar despite a $12 billion central bank currency intervention program, the IMF found the currency is trading in line with its fundamentals.

It noted it sees no need to extend the intervention program beyond its December end date.

Local exporters have been clamoring for additional government or central bank measures to weaken the currency as their products lose competitiveness abroad.

The relatively strong peso, in relation to the dollar, however, has helped keep import prices low.

While the IMF concurred with local expectations that GDP will grow 6.5% on the back of strong domestic demand, it noted the country's biggest challenge remains boosting productivity.

"Government initiatives to reduce the cost of doing business, increase competition, support research an development, and reform the corporate bankruptcy code are welcome," the IMF said.

title: ANALYSIS-Strong copper, weak dlr to keep Chile peso at highs
text:
* Strong copper, weak dollar maintain peso near 3-yr highs

* Central bank seen out of options to stem surge

By Alexandra Ulmer

SANTIAGO, July 29 (Reuters) - Chile's peso <CLP=CL> is likely to remain around three-year highs, with the central bank seen powerless in the face of soaring prices for copper, the country's main export, and the dollar sagging on U.S. economic and debt woes.

The peso weakened 0.26 percent to close at 457.70 on Friday, just a whisker away from the over-three-year intraday high of 455.40 hit on Thursday.

Copper prices spiked to a three-month high early on Friday, driven up by a strike at Chile's giant Escondida mine, before paring gains. The peso often moves in tandem with prices for copper, which accounts for over half of Chilean exports.

The dollar was under pressure on fears of a looming U.S. debt default, keeping the peso strong after it broke key resistance at 460 per U.S. dollar this week. However, some analysts say weak U.S. economic data will likely drag on the dollar even if a U.S. default is averted.

"It's pretty hard for Chilean authorities to do anything to stop the dollar's fall," said Sergio Tricio, head of research at Forex Chile, a currency brokerage in Santiago.

The currency surge comes despite the central bank holding its key rate steady in July for the first time in six months, seen by some as bid by the bank to weaken it. [ID:nN1E76C231]

It is also defying an ongoing currency intervention program aimed at sapping the peso's strength.

Analysts say that suggests Chile is running out of options to stem a rally that is also hitting most of its regional neighbors. <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ > For a TAKE A LOOK on Chile economy [ID:nN26HILEFI] > Americas indicators graphic http://r.reuters.com/hyt39r ("http://r.reuters.com/hyt39r") ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

Currencies across Latin America are rallying on massive dollar inflows triggered by the widening economic growth and rate differentials with the United States and Europe, though the emerging market nations have responded to the surge differently.

South American nations will work together to fight hot money from abroad that is pressuring their currencies, Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos said on Thursday after a Union of South American Nations (UNASUR) meeting in Lima. [ID:nN1E76R2B8]

But many analysts are skeptical the region has the tools to put the brakes on their strong currencies.

"For all the measures Brazil has adopted, its currency is still reaching maximum heights," said Tricio. "The (Chilean) central bank isn't going to take any measures."

While most analysts do not expect Chile to unveil new measures, many of which are seen as costly and ineffective, some think current tools could be enhanced.

The central bank may for instance increase the amount of its daily dollar purchases from the current $50 million as part of a $12 billion foreign exchange intervention program for 2011 launched in January, said Nathan Pincheira, an analyst with Banchile.

"It's the most probable of the options, but still very unlikely," he said.

Pincheira sees the peso weakening to 470 per dollar by the end of the year as U.S. default fears ease, regardless of whether Chile intervenes.

But others see the peso's appreciation continuing, as fundamentals -- a sinking dollar and high copper prices -- remain constant, potentially boosting it to a record 430 per dollar by the year end, said Cesar Guzman, senior analyst at Inversiones Security.

The peso hit a closing peak of 431.20 in March 2008, the strongest level in the past decade.

"We don't see anything that could reverse the (peso's) direction," Guzman said.

(Writing by Alexandra Ulmer; Editing by Simon Gardner and Dan Grebler)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam  FX  mixed, Brazil real slumps on new tax
text:
* Derivatives tax knocks real from 12-year high

* Chile's peso hits 3-year high, more intervention eyed

* Real sheds 1.33 pct, Mexico's peso dips 0.16 pct

(Recasts, adds comments)

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, July 27 (Reuters) - Brazil's government surprised the market with new capital controls on Wednesday, knocking the real off a 12-year high, but the measures are unlikely to keep the currency from regaining its strength.

Chile's peso hit a three-year high, raising concerns of more intervention there, while Mexico's peso weakened as investors grew increasingly nervous about the political stalemate over raising the U.S. debt limit.

Brazil's government imposed a 1 percent tax on currency derivatives, while allowing for a tax of up to 25 percent in the future. For details, see [ID:nN1E76Q01I]

Brazil's finance minister, Guido Mantega, said the government stood ready to take further actions to curb the real's strength, which is hurting domestic industries by curbing export profits and cheapening rival imports.

"A lot of people thought the government was not going to take further measures," said Roberto Padovani, a strategist at West LB in Sao Paulo.

"The fact that this same rule allows for further tax hikes means that risk in the local foreign exchange market has dramatically increased," he added.

The real <BRBY> bid 1.33 percent weaker at 1.5585 per dollar, heading for its steepest one-day loss in nearly three months. The currency pared losses of nearly 2 percent.

The new rules are the latest in a series of measures that Brazil has taken to discourage banks and speculators from gaming the global financial system in the so-called "carry trade," in which investors borrow low-interest rate currencies and invest in higher-yielding ones.

Analysts said the new measures would likely end up reducing the yield that investors can earn on non-deliverable forward contracts <BRLNDFOR=>, which is a favored vehicle for foreign investors.

RBS Securities strategist Flavia Cattan-Naslausky said the measures would reduce liquidity in the local market, which may increase the effectiveness of the central bank's dollar purchases in taming the real's gains.

The market had shrugged off recent threats of new measures, pushing the real past 1.55 per dollar this week -- a level that many saw the government closely eyeing.

The country's capital controls and intervention strategy have occasionally spurred steep, short-term losses in the real. But the currency has maintained an appreciation trend since 2009 as investors are drawn to Brazil's double-digit interest rates and strong domestic growth.

"Ultimately, the new measures will not likely be very effective to stem the real's appreciation," said Igor Arsenin, head of Latin American fixed-income strategy at Credit Suisse in New York.

"You have foreign direct investment flows and you have the overall global dollar weakness. People will still be looking to acquire Brazilian assets, but this will make it more complicated," he said.

Chile's peso <CLP=CL> firmed to a three-year high, bidding 0.24 percent stronger at 456.50 per dollar.

The Chilean peso has strengthened despite a pause in interest rate hikes this month after a string of increases took the benchmark rate to 5.25 percent. The peso's gains have raised concerns that the country's central bank could step up its dollar purchases, or try some other measure.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> slipped 0.16 percent to 11.6574 per dollar.

If U.S. politicians fail to raise the debt ceiling, U.S. interest rates could rise sharply and crimp the economic recovery in the United States, Mexico's top trading partner.

If the debt limit is raised without spending cuts, ratings agencies could still downgrade the United States' debt rating, which could also push up interest rates.

Also hurting the Mexican peso, a report from the U.S. Federal Reserve showed economic growth slowed in much of the United States in June and early July, which bodes poorly for Mexican exports. [ID:nN1E76Q1G2]

"The Fed's report and the impasse in the U.S. debt talks are hurting the peso," said a trader in Mexico City. "If there is no deal by Friday, the peso could weaken to 11.85 or 11.90."

(Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: Chile's Peso, Other Emerging  Currencies  Prepare To Go Global
text:
--Moves in bond markets seen as early steps to make Chile's peso deliverable

--Chile's currency market seen becoming more liquid

--Other emerging market countries also opening up bond markets


 
   By Anjali Cordeiro 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Chile is preparing to gate-crash the small club of emerging-market countries whose currencies are fully accessible to international investors anywhere.

The drive to make the peso deliverable, or easy to trade and access offshore, has begun. In an early step, the country recently said Euroclear, a global provider of cross-border settlement services, will begin operating in Chile to help foreign investors access the local fixed-income market. In another step to make the peso deliverable, Chile's government recently eased restrictions on peso-denominated bonds issued by foreigners.

Among a growing field of emerging-market nations that are liberalizing their bond markets and setting their currencies on the path to full, international convertibility, Chile is seen as a leader. That step is expected to assure it of financing gains as the added market liquidity in its markets are expected to narrow interest rate spreads and reduce execution costs for investors. But Chile will also have to live with a potentially more volatile currency during periods of global turmoil.

Chile, which currently intervenes aggressively in currency markets to manage the peso's value, may have to intervene less as its currency becomes convertible, says RBC strategist Eduardo Suarez. The local currency market would be deeper and it would be harder for the central bank, or any one player, to influence the market. Suarez says, though, that the added liquidity will be a "long-term tailwind" for the peso.

Currency convertibility might also help Chile, a big copper producer, solidify its base in international trade, says IDEAGlobal strategist Enrique Alvarez.

International investors currently have restricted access to most emerging market currencies and trade them via derivatives called nondeliverable forwards. If these currencies become deliverable, international banks could hold them as assets offshore and the market for these currencies would become more liquid.

The experiences of the other three freely accessible emerging-market currencies--the Mexican peso, the South African rand and the Turkish lira--suggest it may take a few years for Chile to join them. RBC's Suarez says Mexico's peso took three or four years to be deliverable from the time Euroclear started operating there.

Even countries with a history of strict capital controls such as India have started loosening bond market restrictions, with implications for their currencies. The rupee isn't expected to be fully convertible anytime soon, but Ravi Chachra, chief investment officer of Eight Capital, an India-focused credit fund, points to India's moves to increase the limits for foreign investors investing in local bonds.

As India's bond market grows "the money is going to be flowing in and out in dollars," says Chachra, adding that could imply a "ten-fold boost" in trading in the rupee.

Adrian Lee, president of currency management firm Lee Overlay Partners says currencies like the Russian ruble are also on the path to become deliverable currencies. Of course, the elephant in the room remains China's yuan, still a tightly controlled currency. If China allows the yuan to become convertible, other Asian currencies like the Indian rupee might follow suit, Lee says. That may still be some way off.

-By Anjali Cordeiro; Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2200; anjali.cordeiro@dowjones.com [ 06-22-11 1255ET ]

Strong domestic demand continues to fuel economic growth, though the pace of expansion has slowed.

title: SURVEY: Chile  Central Bank  Seen Raising Benchmark Rate 25BPs
text:
TPM Rate History (annual percentage): 
   Apr  Mar  Feb  Jan   Dec 
   4.5% 4.0% 3.5% 3.25% 3.25% 
 

By Carolina Pica

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--As inflationary pressures and expectations show incipient signs of subsiding, the Chilean central bank will likely revert to a slower pace of interest-rate increases.

At its monthly monetary-policy meeting Thursday afternoon, the central bank will probably raise the benchmark overnight rate 25 basis points to 4.75%, according to 12 of the 16 analysts Dow Jones Newswires polled. The four dissenters expect a larger, 50-basis-point increase.

At its March and April meetings, the bank surprised markets by putting its foot on the gas pedal and raising the benchmark rate, known locally as the TPM, 50 basis points at each meeting.

The recently released April consumer price index data tempered some analysts outlook for an extended brisk rate-rise pace as headline annualized inflation was 3.2% and core inflation was 2.4%.

In addition, the narrower core inflation the central bank also looks at, known locally as IPCX1 which not only factors fuels and perishables but regulated services as well, only grew 0.7% on the year.

The three different measures of inflation are in line with the central bank's target of 3%, plus/minus one percentage point and below the bank's outlook of 4.3% inflation at the end of 2011.

"The IPCX1 was low enough to give the central bank room to slow down the rate increases," said Guillermo Kautz, head currency and bond trader at local brokerage BCI.

In addition to the mild April data, the strength of the peso in relation to the dollar, despite a $12 billion currency-market-intervention program, is also easing some inflationary pressures, analysts say.

With the peso trading at near three-year highs and pre-intervention levels against the dollar, imports are less expensive.

As Chile imports 98% of the fuels it consumes and isn't self-sufficient in its food production, higher import prices pressure local inflation.

"The inflationary pressures we're seeing today aren't the result of the economy overheating. They are imported inflationary pressures from oil and food," Finance Minister Felipe Larrain said in prepared remarks Tuesday.

Analysts add that the correction in the prices of commodities, including crude oil, have also relieved some of the imported inflationary pressures.

"We've recently seen a sharp retreat in oil prices which could quickly impact inflation readings in the next few months," said Matias Madrid, chief economist at Banco Penta.

Private-sector inflation expectations improved slightly in recent days, as the bank's most recent Monthly Survey of Analysts' Expectations show year-end 2011 and 2012 expectations fell 10 basis points to 4.3% and 3.4%, respectively.

The central bank will release its post-meeting communique after 2200 GMT Thursday.

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Dec 13 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies firmed on Monday after China held back from raising interest rates over the weekend, easing concerns that one of the region's top trading partners could put the brakes on growth.

Global equity markets rose and the dollar broadly weakened after China's central bank extended an increase in reserve requirements for top banks rather than raise benchmark interest rates. For details, see [ID:nL3E6ND0F6]

Some had feared China could hike interest rates, which could slow growth and curb demand for Latin American commodities such as Chilean copper and Brazil's iron ore.

"The climate in global markets has improved. The majority of stock markets are up and this is also an indication of risk appetite. Because of this the real is stronger," said Reginaldo Galhardo, head of currency trading at the Treviso brokerage in Sao Paulo.

Brazil's real <BRBY> currency pierced the closely-watched level of 1.70 per dollar and last bid 0.82 percent stronger at 1.699 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market.

Some think the level could spur the country's central bank to step up intervention efforts to keep the real's strength from hurting local companies, whose exports are becoming more expensive abroad as they compete with cheapening imports.

"The hanging sword of intervention is very much alive in the country, and investors must not downplay this risk," analysts at BNP Paribas wrote in a research note.

Traders across the region noted that volume was dropping as most clients were winding down business ahead of the holiday season.

Brazil has tripled a tax on capital inflows into local bonds and regularly bought dollars in the foreign exchange market in recent months to curb the real's rally.

TAX RELIEF RALLY

The Mexican peso currency <MXN=> strengthened 0.47 percent to 12.3917 per dollar, helped by signs that U.S. President Barack Obama's tax deal with Republicans to extend cuts will likely win grudging passage in the Congress. [ID:nN12152826]

Some think the tax cut extension could help fuel growth next year in the United States, Mexico's top trading partner.

"The market is seeing this as good for the economy," said Roberto Melzi, a strategist at Barclays Capital in New York.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> hit a fresh 30-month high early on Monday, but later pared some gains to trade 0.25 percent stronger at 474.8 per dollar.

Chile's peso was boosted by the price of copper, which hit a new high after China's decision to eschew an interest rate hike lifted optimism about demand for the red metal.

Unlike Brazilian authorities, Chile has held back from intervening heavily in financial markets.

"All the fundamentals keep playing in favor of the peso, with markets mostly positive, the price of copper again hit a record prices and the dollar is weak around the globe," said a trader in Santiago.

SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Inflation in Chile will likely end this year at 3% as inflationary pressures have subsided, central bank governor Rodrigo Vergara said Friday.

The monetary authority currently expects inflation to end at 3.9% in 2010, but that outlook will likely be revised to 3% when it releases its quarterly Monetary Policy Report later this month.

A strong peso in relation to the dollar has contributed to easing inflationary pressures as imports have become cheaper. In recent months, the peso has been trading at around 31-month highs against the dollar.

Vergara, in prepared remarks delivered at a seminar, said the peso's strength had moderated the pace at which the central bank is withdrawing its significant monetary stimulus.

After holding the benchmark overnight rate at a record low 0.5% since July 2009, in June 2010 the bank began increase the rate.

The central bank initially began increasing the rate at a pace of 50 basis points a month, but decelerated this pace at its October meeting, when it only increased the benchmark rate a quarter of a percentage point.

In November, it increased the rate another 25 basis points to 3.0%, but according to the minutes of that meeting, it considered taking a temporary pause amid reduced inflationary pressures and a strong peso.

Higher local interest rates put pressure on the currency to post further gains, which is damaging to the country's export sector. Chile is highly dependent on its exports, especially of natural resources such as copper, fertilizers, wood pulp, fresh fruits and wines.

title: Stiglitz: US Should Consider Implementing 2nd Stimulus Package
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The U.S. should consider a second stimulus package to prop up its struggling economy, Nobel laureate economist Joseph Stiglitz said Friday.

U.S. gross domestic product will likely increase between 3.0% and 3.6% in 2011 year-on-year, after rising by around 2.5% this year.

"The first stimulus package had too much emphasis on tax cuts. Those were relatively ineffective and not enough aid for the states," Stiglitz told reporters on the sidelines of a seminar in Chile's capital.

A new stimulus package should include a revenue-sharing program to make up for a shortfall in state revenue and should pick up the states' investments that had to be stalled. Also, there should be a special focus on human capital, in particular on education and training, he said.

"We have to believe that the economy will eventually recover...[W]hat kinds of jobs will we want to have in five years...[W]e need to have people trained for that," Stiglitz said.

Additionally, Stiglitz argued the U.S. Federal Reserve's quantitative easing bond-purchasing program is creating an excess of liquidity, which is flowing into emerging-market nations.

Emerging-market economies such as Chile's are growing at a much faster pace than the U.S. and have comparatively higher interest rates, making them attractive destinations for investors looking for higher returns.

According to Stiglitz, the $600 billion bond-purchasing program has created a large amount of "liquidity looking for relatively safe high returns" that aren't found in the U.S. but can be found in many emerging-market nations.

As many emerging markets are trying to discourage capital inflows, "the liquidity goes to the places where they haven't yet put barriers for the inflows," Stiglitz told reporters.

As the Columbia University professor and 2001 co-winner of the Nobel price for Economics sees it, this increasing pressure will likely lead those countries that haven't yet intervened their currency markets or imposed capital controls to eventually do so.

"These countries that are open would be better advised to set up a framework of controls with a willingness to adjust the intensity [of inflows] depending on the pressure they feel," he said.

Chile, one of the remaining Latin American nations that hasn't intervened this year in its currency market, has recently seen its currency surge to 31-month highs against the dollar as international copper prices, a bellwether for the nation's economy, surged to record highs.

The Andean nation "should be ready to do a whole portfolio [of measures], because none of them are perfectly effective...They should be ready to intervene directly in exchange rates," said Stiglitz.

Chile's former reserve requirement, which effectively "was a tax on short-term flows, but encouraged long-term flows...was a pretty good system," he said.

The Chilean central bank has maintained that intervention is a tool that's always available, but it will only use it if the exchange rate, in real terms, moves out of line with its long-term fundamentals. The central bank says that despite the peso's recent appreciation, the local currency is still in line with fundamentals.

Exporters in the South American nation have clamored for currency market intervention, arguing the peso's strength is eating away at the competitiveness of their products.

-By Anthony Esposito, Dow Jones Newswires; 56-2-715-8929; anthony.esposito@dowjones.com [ 10-12-10 1756GMT ]

text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Despite Chilean exporters' pleas for currency market intervention as the peso hovers near a 30-month high versus the dollar, a move by the central bank in that direction likely isn't imminent.

As the U.S. economy limps along and the U.S. Federal Reserve pursues aggressive monetary easing, the dollar has swooned as investors seek better returns in emerging markets, including Chile.

The Andean nation's peso has also gained as the country's central bank tightens monetary conditions, investments pour in as part of recovery efforts from a devastating February earthquake and as international copper prices shoot higher.

Chile is the world's largest copper producer and exporter, so repatriated receipts from copper sales abroad have a major influence on the peso.

In response to the peso's appreciation, which reduces exporters' competitiveness overseas, Chile's government cut red tape for their products and state-owned bank BancoEstado will offer up to a $200 million dollar-denominated credit line to small and medium-size companies.

Exporters, however, contend that more can be done to combat the peso's strength. "Those measures just aren't enough because the exchange rate weighs so much on the ability to remain competitive in this business," said Antonio Walker, president of the Fedefruta fruit exporters trade group.

Over the last decade, the central bank has only intervened in the local currency market three times, and the last time it intervened, in April 2008, the peso was trading at 10-year highs against the dollar.

When the peso was trading at CLP488.90 to the dollar in late October, central bank President Jose De Gregorio said, "if an intervention were justified today, we'd already be intervening," although he added then that an intervention was more likely than it had been even three months ago. The peso closed at CLP483.40 on Wednesday.

The central bank has room to increase its international reserves by around $5 billion to $8 billion, which would push the local currency down by about CLP20, said Sergio Tricio, head of studies with local currency trader Forex Chile.

RBC Capital Markets senior emerging-markets analyst Eduardo Suarez argues, however, that Chile's push to become a regional financial hub and its intention to make the peso a deliverable currency--so it can be bought and sold everywhere--will lead the government to seek more market-friendly measures that decrease the likelihood of direct intervention.

Exporters, though, are pointing to other countries, such as Brazil, that have implemented measures to stanch their currencies' growth. Brazil last month raised its financial operations tax on fixed-income securities and some equities, while its central bank is purchasing dollars.

"The fact is the Chilean peso ... has not appreciated as much as (the Brazilian real), hence it does give Chile some room to maneuver for now," Standard Chartered Bank's Mike Moran said.

If the peso breaks the CLP475 barrier and gains to levels around CLP450-CLP460, traders see an increased risk of currency market intervention.

Although traders argue that a central bank intervention would in all likelihood have only a transitory effect as copper prices remain high, interest-rate differences continue to make Chile an attractive market and the dollar remains soft internationally, exporters say a short-term reprieve from the peso's strength would be welcome.

title: Chile's Peso Closes Weaker On Falling Euro, Copper Prices
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean peso closed weaker against the dollar Monday as the euro lost versus the dollar on flaring concerns about euro-zone debt and as international copper prices slipped on fears China will again tighten its monetary policy to slow its surging economy.

The peso ended at CLP482.40 to the dollar, versus Friday's close of CLP481.20, while trading in a range of CLP481.70 to CLP485.10.

As Chile's economy is highly export-dependent and a third of its exports are bound for Europe, the peso often moves in the same direction the euro does against the dollar. The common currency dropped against the dollar as worries about the region's crisis of sovereign debt grew on speculation Ireland might soon request a European Union lifeline.

Also, as Chile is the world's premier copper producer, accounting for roughly a third of global supply, the peso often takes trading cues from the metal's international prices. Spot copper in London fell 1.4% to $3.90 a pound, according to Chile's state copper commission Cochilco, as a move by China to further tighten monetary policy could hurt demand for the metal from the world's largest consumer.

Meanwhile, exporters in Chile have clamored for currency-market intervention as the peso, recently near a 30-month high, hurts the competitiveness of their products.

"The competitiveness of our non-copper exports is at risk. Especially in the case of manufactured [products], whose main export destination is the U.S.," said Eduardo Moyano, president of Chile's Asexma exporters trade group

In the bond market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central bank bonds, or BCUs, ended mixed after heavy buying of the shorter bonds by the nation's private pension fund managers.

The yield on five-year BCU bonds ended at 2.66%, from 2.68% on Friday, while the yield on 10-year BCUs closed at 3.06%, from 3.05% the previous session.

title: Chile FinMin would prefer 'somewhat' weaker peso
text:
* Finance minister wants weaker peso

* Central Bank has been weighing intervention

* Peso near 2-1/2 year highs

SANTIAGO (Reuters) - Finance Minister Felipe Larrain would like Chile's peso, which has sharply appreciated in recent weeks to near 2-1/2 year highs, to weaken, hinting in an interview published on Sunday he believed central bank intervention was a possibility.

Chile's peso has soared around 14 percent since the end of June, prompting intervention warnings from Chilean authorities concerned about the competitiveness of local exporters.

"If you ask my opinion, I would prefer the exchange rate to be somewhat higher (peso to be somewhat weaker) than it is today," Larrain told La Tercera newspaper's Sunday edition, reiterating the peso's gains were cause for worry.

"I have to respect what the central bank decides (on intervention) -- they have the last word," he added. "But no-one ever said that in a floating exchange rate regime that intervention was impossible."

Larrain said the upward pressure on Chile's peso would last as long as the United States' economy remained weak.

"There is no increase in U.S. rates looming a reasonable horizon to make financial flows towards the U.S. economy attractive, and as long as China does not move its currency, we will have this pressure," he added.

Chile's central bank said Thursday it would gradually raise foreign investment limits for pension funds to 80 percent from 60 percent as it seeks to counter the recent sharp gains of the peso.

The bank said the limits on the pension system, which manages more than $138 billion, would begin rising in December, with three more increases coming in the following nine months. Greater investment abroad would increase demand for dollars, helping to weaken the peso or at least offset capital inflows.

The Federal Reserve's unveiling of new monetary stimulus on Wednesday had added pressure on the currency, Larrain said.

Chile has so far held off on buying dollars in the local market, like Colombia, or raising taxes on foreign investment in local assets, as Brazil did twice last month.

The central bank has said it constantly weighs direct intervention in the foreign exchange market, but fundamentals do not justify action at the peso's current levels.

The bank cited the peso's strength when it slowed the pace of increases to its benchmark interest rate last month. Higher interest rates have attracted foreign investors in recent months, adding to the peso's appreciation.

Chile's last market intervention came in 2008, when the peso was trading around 430 per dollar and the central bank began a program of dollar purchases to increase international reserves and weaken the peso. The peso closed on Friday at 477.30/477.80 per dollar. (Writing by Simon Gardner, editing by Maureen Bavdek)

title: UPDATE 3-Chile ups fund investment limit to stem peso rally
text:
* Central bank move follows sharp peso appreciation

* Gradual rise to 80 pct from 60 pct to begin in December

* President said last month he is eyeing capital account (Adds graphic, factbox links, quotes, international context)

By Antonio de la Jara

SANTIAGO, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank said on Thursday it would gradually raise foreign investment limits for pension funds to 80 percent from 60 percent as it seeks to counter the recent sharp appreciation of the peso <CLP=CL>.

The bank said the limits on the pension system, which manages more than $138 billion, would begin rising in December, with three more increases coming in the following nine months. Greater investment abroad would increase demand for dollars, helping to weaken the peso or at least offset capital inflows.

Chile's peso has soared nearly 14 percent since the end of June, prompting intervention warnings from Chilean authorities concerned about the competitiveness of local exporters.

The peso was broadly stable after the announcement, closing up 1.9 percent at 479.90/480.40 per dollar following the Federal Reserve's unveiling of new monetary stimulus after the local market close on Wednesday.

After the Fed announcement, policymakers from the world's economic powerhouses in Latin America and Asia said they would consider fresh capital controls.For more, see: [ID:nTOE6A300V]

Chile's pension fund announcement appeared to be the first concrete foreign exchange measure adopted after the Fed announcement, which involves massive debt purchases to lower long-term interest rates. That makes emerging market investments more attractive.

Santiago-based Banchile economist Fernando Soto said the impact of the new pension policy would not be immediate, as the local market remains attractive for many investors.

"This establishes a cap for the exchange rate to some degree, although not in the short-term, given that authorities are taking measures focused on the currency it means we are already near that cap," Soto said.

Chile has held off so far on buying dollars in the local market, like Colombia, or raising taxes on foreign investment in local assets, as Brazil did twice last month.

"We view the measure as not particularly aggressive," said Jimena Zuniga, with Barclays Capital in New York. "Despite the government's concern about ... appreciation pressures, it seems inclined to concentrate all the efforts on market-friendly measures at this stage."

President Sebastian Pinera said last month that he is not planning capital controls, and he would like to stem the peso's appreciation by encouraging more Chilean investment abroad.

Finance Minister Felipe Larrain told reporters after the announcement that he had asked the central bank to revise the pension funds' investment limits.

The central bank has said it constantly weighs direct intervention in the foreign exchange market, but fundamentals do not justify action at the peso's current levels.

The bank cited the peso's strength when it slowed the pace of increases to its benchmark interest rate last month. Higher interest rates have attracted foreign investors in recent months, adding to the peso's appreciation. [ID:nN14173354]

Chile's last market intervention came in 2008, when the peso was trading around 430 per dollar and the central bank began a program of dollar purchases to increase international reserves and weaken the peso.

The bank previously lifted the limits on investment abroad for Chile's privately administered pension funds beginning in October 2008, from 45 percent to 60 percent.

At that point, amid the global financial crisis, fund administrators were slow to take advantage of the new freedom. But within 18 months the pension system's most aggressive funds had expanded their foreign portfolios by more than 12 percentage points.

Now as then, few of the funds in the privately managed pension system are investing in foreign assets to the maximum extent allowable. But the new limits may open possibilities, as the highest-risk funds will soon be able to invest entirely overseas.

title: Chile's Peso Closes 1.9% Stronger On Reaction To US Fed Decision
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chile's peso ended 1.9% stronger against the dollar Thursday as market participants reacted to the Federal Reserve's decision to pump $600 billion into the ailing U.S. economy between now and the middle of next year.

The Fed's decision was announced after the local currency market closed Wednesday.

The peso ended at CLP479.90 to the dollar, nearing a 30-month high, versus CLP489.10 a session earlier. It traded in a wide range of CLP479.20 to CLP484.50.

As Chile's economy is highly export-dependent and a third of its exports go to Europe, the peso often moves in the same direction as the common currency does against the dollar. Investors fled the dollar, sending it sharply lower versus the common currency in the wake of the Fed's bond-buying plan.

Since Chile is the world's premier copper producer, accounting for a third of global supply, the peso also often takes trading cues from the metal's international prices. Copper futures in New York rallied 3% as the dollar weakened internationally.

Meanwhile, the Chilean central bank's move to gradually increase the cap on private pension fund managers' investments abroad to 80% from the current 60% -- which was announced earlier in the day and is seen as part of an effort to weaken the peso -- had a limited effect on the local currency.

The pension fund managers, known locally as AFPs, are the nation's largest institutional investors and had the equivalent of 45.6% of their total assets invested abroad --despite the 60% cap-- as of Sept. 30, according to the quarterly data released by the SAFP pension fund regulator.

"The effect on the exchange rate will be limited, because the AFPs already had plenty of room to invest abroad before reaching their current investment limit," said Patricio Roncagliolo, director at currency trader FXCM Chile.

Exporters have been clamoring for market intervention as the local currency's strength eats away at the competitiveness of their products.

"The move shows, however, that the authorities are keeping a watch on the exchange rate," he added.

For his part, Finance Minister Felipe Larrain noted the measure will "balance capital flows and that will tend to impact the exchange rate in the medium term," according to local newswire Valor Futuro.

In the bond market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central bank bonds, or BCUs, ended lower as the local fixed-income market took cues from yields on U.S. Treasurys, which also fell following the Fed's announcement.

The yield on five-year BCU bonds ended at 2.65%, from 2.68% on Wednesday, while the yield on 10-year BCUs closed at 3.06%, from 3.13% the previous session.

title: UPDATE:  Chile Central Bank  Head:  Intervention  Not Yet Merited
text:
(updates with additional comment from the president of the central bank.)

SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--If the Chilean currency merited an intervention, the central bank would have already intervened in the market, central bank President Jose De Gregorio told Friday's Diario Financiero newspaper.

With the peso trading at around 29-month highs against the dollar, exporters who've lost competitiveness abroad have called for market intervention in order to weaken the local currency.

"If an intervention were justified today, we'd already be intervening," De Gregorio told the newspaper.

He noted, however, that an intervention is more likely now than it was three months ago, "because the exchange rate in real terms has appreciated and the occurrence of more complex phenomena can't be ruled out."

The central bank monitors the peso's real, not nominal, exchange rate, which factors in inflation, trade flows and other parameters.

Agricultural sector exporters have been the hardest hit by the peso's appreciation, especially as the southern hemisphere summer harvest season is about to begin.

The central banker said that the central bank couldn't make decisions based on sectorial problems, such as those the agricultural sector faces.

"For sectorial problems, you have to use sectorial tools; when the problems are aggregated, the decisions must be macroeconomic," he said, noting that the central bank doesn't make sectorial decisions.

He told the newspaper the central bank doesn't have a steadfast rule regarding when to intervene.

"We don't follow a dogma regarding free-floating or intervention, because the latter isn't always the solution each time the peso strengthens," he said.

In the past 10 years, the central bank has intervened in three instances.

Regarding capital controls, De Gregorio said the reserve requirement on foreign investment Chile applied in the 1990s is no longer a solution to be used.

"We don't have a massive net inflow of capital, and we have a small current account deficit for this year," he said.

He added that should there be a massive inflow as a result of high interest rates, then the bank could implement some sort of capital control.

title: WRAPUP 1- Chile fx intervention  nearer, peso slows rate-Cbank
text:
* Stronger peso weighed on Oct. rate hike - minutes

* Cenbank says would intervene in peso if justified

* Unemployment rate lowest since early 2009

By Antonio de la Jara and Brad Haynes

SANTIAGO (Reuters) - Chile's appreciating peso has made intervention more likely than it was three months ago and slowed the pace of interest rate hikes, according to an interview with the bank president and bank meeting minutes published Friday.

Chile's surging economic activity would suggest sharper interest rate hikes, but the peso's appreciation, slower inflation and weakness in developed economies point to a more gradual pace of rate hikes, minutes from the bank's October policy meeting showed.

The Chilean currency has appreciated around 12 percent since the end of June. Exporters impacted by the strong peso have called on authorities to step in, but in an interview published on Friday Central Bank President Jose De Gregorio said intervention is not "justified" at the exchange rate's current levels.

"We have to monitor, but undoubtedly intervention is more probable today than it was three months ago," De Gregorio told leading financial newspaper Diario Financiero. "If intervention were justified, we'd be doing it."if capital inflows become heavy, but he said that is not now the case.

"We don't have a massive net inflow of capital. We have a small deficit deficit in the current account this year," De Gregorio said.

The continued appreciation of the peso may also reduce inflationary pressures on Chile's small open economy, Friday's bank minutes suggested.

"Our main takeaway is that the (central bank) is very close to ending the hiking cycle that started in June," said Benito Berber, an economist with Nomura Securities. "In fact, we now believe that the (bank) will increase the policy rate by an additional 25 bps and then it will call it quits."

De Gregorio told Diario Financiero October's 25 basis-point rate hike did not represent a trend, citing the continued dynamism of Chile's economic recovery.

Chile's jobless rate reached its lowest level in a year and a half, government data showed on Friday, as the July-September jobless rate fell to 8.0 percent, below market forecasts and down from 8.3 percent in the June-August period.

Analysts polled by Reuters had forecast an unemployment rate of 8.1 percent for July to September, as the economy consolidates its recovery from the global economic crisis and a massive February earthquake.

The central bank cut its benchmark interest rate to a record low 0.5 percent amid the financial crisis and kept it there following the devastating quake, before joining a regional rate tightening cycle in June.

Now the strong peso, bolstered by Chile's surging economy and high prices of top export copper, is contributing to a slower withdrawal of monetary stimulus, according to minutes from the bank's last meeting.

The minutes showed all board members voted to raise rates by 25 basis points to 2.75 percent during October's meeting, although the bank also considered raising rates by 50 basis points as it had done the previous four months.

"Under any of the options considered, the benchmark rate would still be expansive, so in future meetings it will probably be necessary to continue withdrawing monetary stimulus," the minutes said. (Editing by Simon Gardner and Andrew Hay)

title: Chile Peso Firmer After G-20; Moderated By  Central Bank  Comment

SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chile's peso ended mildly stronger against the dollar Monday, as major currencies, including the euro, gained sharply on the greenback after the Group of 20 nations agreed over the weekend to avoid "competitive devaluation" of their currencies and as international copper prices firmed.

The peso's gains, however, were mitigated by central bank comments that it couldn't rule out an intervention in the local currency market if the peso continues to firm.

Chile's currency ended at CLP486.20 to the dollar, versus Friday's close of CLP486.90, while trading in a range of CLP483.90 to CLP486.60.

The nonbinding agreement among the G-20 nations freed investors from the fear of governments actively pushing their currencies lower and spurred more dollar selling.

As Europe is one of Chile's main trade partners, the peso often moves in the same direction as the euro does against the dollar. In recent trading, the euro posted strong gains on the dollar, and the ICE Dollar Index, which tracks the greenback against a trade-weighted basket of currencies, traded at lows last seen in January--at 76.962 from 77.494.

Also, as Chile is the world's premier copper producer, accounting for a third of global supply, the peso often takes cues from the metal's international prices. Copper traded at its highest since July 2008 in London, as the weak U.S. currency fueled investment across the commodities sector.

With the central bank reiterating that it can't rule out intervention, though, the peso's gains were limited.

"Chile is one of the few cases, along with advanced nations, where the [currency market] hasn't been intervened or capital controls haven't been applied, although they're tools that we can't rule out may be used," central bank President Jose De Gregorio said earlier Monday at a seminar for agricultural businessmen.

With the peso recently trading at 29-month highs versus the dollar, exporters, particularly the agricultural sector, have clamored for currency market intervention as the strength of the local currency cuts into the competitiveness of their products.

"Continued verbal intervention by the central bank has investors a bit uneasy and they don't want to be caught by surprise. That's what has been keeping the peso trading in a tight range recently," said Eduardo Kutscher, chief currency trader for local investment bank Celfin Capital.

title: Chile  Peso Ends Weaker Reducing Likelihood Of  Forex Intervention
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chile's peso ended weaker against the dollar Friday as investors snapped up greenbacks prior to the weekend, helping to reduce the specter of imminent currency market intervention.

In thin trading, the peso weakened to CLP486.90 to the dollar, versus Thursday's close of CLP485.30, while trading in a range of CLP485.30 to CLP488.10.

With the peso trading recently at 29-month highs versus the dollar, exporters have demanded intervention in the local currency market, as the peso's strength hurts the competitiveness of their products.

The peso, however, has posted a sharp turn around over the last two weeks from its more than two-year high, losing 2.4% versus the dollar over that time.

"The government and central bank are going to avoid direct intervention at all costs. With the peso already losing steam over the last couple of weeks, the possibility of intervention is greatly reduced," said Sebastian Momberg, currency trader with investment bank BCI.

Traders say, though, that if the peso appreciates to CLP450-CLP460, the central bank will likely be prompted to act.

Chile's government announced Thursday that it will cut red tape for exporters in an effort to improve the competitiveness of their products

In the bond market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central bank bonds, or BCUs, ended higher in light over-the-counter trading.

The yield on five-year BCU bonds ended at 2.70%, from 2.65% on Thursday, while the yield on 10-year BCUs closed at 3.10%, from 3.06% the prior session.

title: UPDATE 2-Chile acts to help exporters hit by strong peso
text:
* Finmin says measure key to control currency effects

* Market says measure weak, not see immediate impact

* Gov't to continue analyzing other measures

(Adds analyst comment and background)

By Felipe Iturrieta and Alonso Soto

SANTIAGO, Oct 21 (Reuters) - Chile will cut red tape on customs to help exporters hit by a strong peso as one measure to ease the effects of the currency's rapid appreciation, Finance Minister Felipe Larrain said on Thursday.

"This was one of the main measures that we had planned for this week because this is a measure that takes into consideration the exchange rate problem that we are facing," Larrain told reporters at a customs office in the outskirts of Santiago. "This is not the last measure, we will keep analyzing alternatives."

Larrain said the move, which was not as strong as many analysts expected, added to tight control over fiscal spending, use of copper savings and offering dollar credits to help exporters whose profits have dwindled because of the stronger peso.

"This sort of announcement has no effect," said a currency trader in Santiago. "What the market was awaiting for was concrete measures. This was no good, and that's why the the dollar fell again."

The Chilean peso <CLP=CL> on Thursday pared some early losses triggered by the government announcement of possible foreign exchange measures. The peso was 0.19 percent weaker at 485.30/485.80 per dollar.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real extends rally against Chilean peso
text:
* Traders brush off recent attempt to slow real's gains

* Mexico and Brazil launch new bond sales

* Brazil's real firms 0.8 pct, Mexican peso jumps 0.9 pct

* Colombia and Chile prepare for intervention measures

(Updates prices to afternoon)

By Samantha Pearson and Froilan Romero

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Oct 20 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real hit a two-month high against the Chilean peso on Wednesday, as efforts by both countries to curb damaging rallies in their local currency evoked different reactions from traders.

A broadly weak dollar provided support to Latin America's currencies on Wednesday due to increasing speculation that the Federal Reserve will print more money to boost the struggling U.S. economy. An influential report gave investors clues on Wednesday about how big the stimulus package could be, a source told Reuters [ID:nN20129482]

But that support hasn't been felt equally across the region's currency markets, in part due to the different approaches that individual governments are taking to slow their currency's gains.

A strong currency makes exports more expensive and difficult to sell, potentially endangering long-term growth.

The Brazilian real gained as much as 1.1 percent against the Chilean peso <BRLCLP=R> on Wednesday -- its strongest level against the Andean currency since Aug. 10 according to the international reference rate.

Brazil has taken aggressive action to curb a recent rally in the real, which is now the world's most overvalued major currency, according to Goldman Sachs.

The central bank has bought more dollars in the market, while the government has increased its tax on foreign purchases of bonds, which it raised again on Monday. But investors have largely brushed off the measures. That is due to Brazil's compelling economic fundamentals, including a high benchmark interest rate widely expected to be held at 10.75 percent at the central bank's meeting later on Wednesday.

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said on Wednesday the government will take as many measures as necessary to curb the real's rally. [ID:nSAQ002514]

Meanwhile, mere hints at possible intervention by Chile's Finance Minister Felipe Larrain on Tuesday were enough to keep traders nervous. [ID:nN19122042]

"Up until now investors have largely assumed that Chile's central bank wouldn't intervene but in Brazil there has been a certain expectation built in that they would continue to introduce more measures and intervene more aggressively," said Nick Chamie of RBC Capital Markets.

"That mind shift is now slowly being priced in so that's why you're seeing a heightened sense of sensitivity to any mention of it."

BONDS BONANZA

Latin American currencies have enjoyed a multi-week rally as traders have bet that U.S. stimulus measures will keep yields on U.S. Treasuries near to record lows, encouraging more investors to buy the region's higher-yielding debt.

That trend was briefly interrupted on Tuesday due to a surprise interest rate increase from China, which boosted the dollar and caused sharp losses among the region's currencies.

But the dollar resumed its decline on Wednesday.

After losing more than 1 percent on Tuesday, the real strengthened 0.77 percent to 1.672 on the local spot market <BRBY>, not far from a two-year high against the dollar.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> firmed 0.91 percent to 12.4122 per dollar -- more than 6 percent stronger than it was at the beginning of September.

Both countries also moved to take advantage of this frenzied demand for their debt.

Brazil said it plans to sell more of its 2028 global bonds denominated in reais, while Mexico sold 150 billion yen ($1.84 billion) of Samurai bonds, IFR reported. [ID:nTOE69J013] and [ID:nSPG003094].

Chile's peso <CLP=> gained 0.54 percent to 484.40 per dollar.

"The market is on tenterhooks, waiting for possible measures by the central bank to stop the peso from continuing to appreciate," said one trader in Santiago.

Dollar purchases would be the most likely way of curbing the rally in the peso, which is trading around a 29-month high against the dollar, analysts say.

The Colombian peso <COP=RR>, which has surged around 12 percent against the dollar so far this year, was only 0.4 percent stronger on Wednesday at 1809.10 per dollar as traders also worried about intervention.

President Juan Manuel Santos told a local newspaper this week that a package of measures was on its way. Some analysts have guessed this may include tax relief for exporters.

(Additional reporting by Caroline Stauffer in Mexico City; Editing by Andrew Hay)

title: UPDATE 1- Chile 's c.bank not discussing  FX intervention -deputy
text:
* Miner rescue could boost the economy

* Peso has overstepped boundary of fundamentals

* Central bank not discussion FX intervention at the moment

FRANKFURT, Oct 19 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank is not currently discussing FX intervention despite a view the peso is overvalued, Deputy Governor Manuel Marfan said on Tuesday, while the feel-good factor from last week's mining rescue could boost the economy.

The peso <CLP=CL> has jumped 14 percent against the dollar since June and was cited as one of the reasons for the central bank to slow the pace of interest rate rises last week.

"The (peso) exchange rate has been appreciating and it is at the boundary (of fundamentals) or has even slightly surpassed that," Marfan told reporters on the sidelines of a European Central Bank conference.

On intervention he said: "That's something that I should say officially that we have not discussed at the central bank so far, but the issue is being discussed at the country level."

"Usually when you decide to intervene it is because you think you will be successful."

He added the risk of a global currency war had been overstated, but warned it could not be ruled out and said it could be extremely damaging for Chile.

Economic growth might come in slightly above recent forecasts of 5 to 6 percent, but it would not overly impact the central bank's assessment of the economy, Marfan also said.

Last week's rescue of 33 miners trapped underground for over two months could give the economy a boost, he said, adding it may also carry risks.

"Economy has a lot things that have to do with mood, with perceptions, with expectations and I think when you are successful with something, that's going to give you much more confidence in the rest of the things you do," he said.

"The rest of the world is caring about us, and to be true I don't know whether that is good or bad. It's not good to be the pet."

title: Chile Peso Ends 1.3% Weaker After China Rate Hike, Copper Fall
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean peso weakened sharply against the dollar Tuesday, ending 1.3% weaker, after China caught investors off-guard with an interest rate hike, international copper prices slipped and the Finance Minister reiterated concern on the local currency's strength.

The peso, which was recently trading at 29-month highs, weakened to CLP487.00 to the dollar, versus Monday's close of CLP481.00 to the dollar. It traded in a wide range of CLP482.40 to CLP487.50.

With China's rate hike stoking fears about a possible global slowdown, the safe-harbor dollar jumped sharply against its major rivals, including the euro.

Chile's economy is highly export dependent and a third of its exports are bound for Europe, so the peso takes trading cues from the common currency.

Also, the peso takes direction from international copper prices as the South American nation produces a third of the world's copper.

Copper futures in New York plunged 3% after China's rate hike, as short-term fears about demand from the world's biggest copper consumer overwhelmed a positive longer-term outlook.

Meanwhile, exporters in Chile have been clamoring for market intervention, arguing that the peso's appreciation is eating into the competitiveness of their products.

Earlier in the day, Finance Minister Felipe Larrain said in a seminar that the government was concerned about the peso's strength, especially regarding the impact on agricultural exporters.

He said the government was "studying what alternatives it had [to mitigate the peso's strength] and will likely have something to report on that later in the week."

Only the Chilean central bank, which is autonomous, can intervene in the local currency market. However, the government, through the finance ministry, can take different measures to help moderate the peso's strength.

"Larrain said the government was going to take some measure, that's not exactly intervention, but the market reacted to his comments anyhow," Gloria Soto, head currency trader with FXCM Chile said.

Also, central bank vice governor Manuel Marfan, earlier in the day, didn't rule out future market intervention if justified. Though, he did admit that the monetary authority hasn't yet discussed intervening in the foreign exchange market.

In the bond market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central bank bonds, or BCUs, ended mixed ahead of an auction of central bank sovereign debt scheduled for Wednesday.

The yield on five-year BCU bonds ended at 2.66%, from 2.67% on Monday, while the yield on 10-year BCUs closed at 3.07%, from 3.06% the previous session.

title: UPDATE 3-Chile to hike rate 25 bps in Oct- central bank  poll
text:
* Rate increase seen smallest in latest tightening cycle

* Central bank rate seen at 3.25 percent by year-end

* Peso seen easing to 490 per dollar in December (Recasts with slowed tempo of hikes, adds analyst comment)

SANTIAGO, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank is seen slowing the pace of interest rate hikes, raising its benchmark rate by just 25 basis points later this week, as lower inflation expectations allow it to focus on stemming the peso currency's recent strong rise.

A central bank poll released on Wednesday showed financial analysts expect a 25-basis-point increase to 2.75 percent at the bank's Thursday monetary policy meeting, after four consecutive months of 50-basis-point hikes.

The rate hikes have been aimed at easing monetary stimulus after the economy showed clear signs of recovering from the global financial crisis and a massive Feb. 27 earthquake.

But with foreign capital pouring into the region given low rates elsewhere in the world, which has helped boost the peso nearly 15 percent since late June, the bank is unlikely to want to spur more inflows by boosting rates sharply.

The peso has also been pushed higher by the almost relentless appreciation in the price of copper, Chile's main export, and the weakness of the greenback.

"The fact the inflation expectations for year-end 2011 and longer horizons are relatively well anchored to the 3 percent target midpoint ... offers the central bank extra degrees of freedom to calibrate the rate normalization cycle," Alberto Ramos, a senior economist at Goldman Sachs, wrote in a research note.

Analysts polled by the central bank expected the bank's key rate to reach 3.25 percent in December and saw the peso <CLP=CL> easing 3 percent to 490 by the end of the year.

Chile's central bank has weighed intervening to halt the peso's sharp appreciation for some time. Central bank President Jose De Gregorio said this month the currency was approaching the stronger end of levels justified by economic fundamentals.

The bank's last major foreign exchange intervention was in 2008, after the peso firmed sharply amid a commodity-led boom. It gave the market a clear calendar outlining plans to buy $8 billion via auction.

September's IMACEC indicator of economic activity was seen growing by 7.0 percent from a year prior. (Reporting by Santiago newsroom; Writing by Brad Haynes and Hilary Burke; Editing by James Dalgleish)

title: UPDATE 3- Chile  central banker weighs peso  intervention
text:

* Political pressure rising for intervention

By Brad Haynes

SANTIAGO, Oct 6 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank has weighed intervening to halt a sharp appreciation of the peso, bank President Jose De Gregorio said on Wednesday, noting the currency was approaching the stronger end of levels justified by fundamentals.

The Chilean peso <CLP=CL> has appreciated over 13 percent against the dollar since the beginning of July as rising interest rates attract foreign investment and strengthen the country's currency in a pattern seen around Latin America.

"Decisions on the timing and magnitude of interventions are constantly evaluated by the board, and it has been an issue in our discussions in recent weeks in terms of weighing the benefits and costs," he told the lower house of Congress in a special session about the peso's sharp rise.

De Gregorio earlier told a forum of fruit exporters the exchange rate was pushing the limits of its fundamentals.

"Intervention is a valid and effective tool when it can affect the exchange rate and strengthen the position of the nation," he said. "Frequent and repeated intervention is less effective, so it must be exceptional to give financial markets relevant information."

The peso closed 0.12 percent firmer at 482.20/482.70 to the 


dollar on Wednesday, boosted by stronger prices for copper --
the country's main export -- and widespread dollar weakness.


But traders said De Gregorio's comments did not move the peso.

De Gregorio met with Chile's finance minister and president earlier this week after President Sebastian Pinera said on Sunday that the central bank should do more to slow the peso's rise. title: UPDATE:  Chile Central Bank  President:  Intervention  Can't Be Ruled Out
text:
(Updates with additional comments from De Gregorio)

SANTIAGO -(Dow Jones)- The Chilean central bank can't rule out intervening in the local currency market, but there would be high costs to pay, bank president Jose De Gregorio said Wednesday.

As the peso is trading at two-year highs against the dollar, exporters--whose livelihood depends on a weaker currency--are clamoring for central bank intervention.

In the past 10 years, the central bank has only intervened three times, when it has considered that the peso's exchange rate, in real terms, has deviated from long-term fundamentals.

At a gathering of the Fedefruta fruit exporters trade group, De Gregorio called intervention "a valid tool," adding that the bank's governing council "evaluates the decision [to intervene] and undoubtedly, this is something that's been at the forefront of our recent discussions."

He noted that intervention could be very expensive as it requires sterilizing currency purchases so as to not deviate the effects of monetary policy.

In his prepared remarks, he also said the peso, in real terms, was slightly below the average it had posted in the previous two decades.

Defending the peso's free float adopted in the late 1990s, the central banker said that floating a currency curbed speculation and massive capital inflows.

"We haven't seen any evidence of short-term speculative inflows to arbitrate with other currencies," he said.

De Gregorio later presented the same speech to a special session of the lower house of Congress convened to address the peso's strength.

In his second presentation of the day, he added that the central bank could slow down the pace at which it has been withdrawing its monetary stimulus so as to not put further pressure on the peso.

"We also consider the effects of exchange rate variations on our inflation outlook and our monetary policy," he said.

He noted that a floating exchange rate policy "carried out pragmatically, is the exchange system that's best suited to our reality."

title: Chile Peso Ends 1.1% Weaker As  Central Bank  Doesn't Rule Out  Intervention
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chile's peso ended 1.1% weaker against the dollar Monday, coming off a recent 28-month high, after the central bank didn't rule out intervention in the local currency market.

The peso ended at CLP486.40 to the dollar compared with Friday's close of CLP481.00.

The central bank had maintained in recent weeks that the peso was trading in line with its long-term fundamentals. With the peso continuing to gain, however--having appreciated more than 9% on the dollar since the end of the second quarter--the Chilean currency is closer to straying away from its long-term fundamentals, central bank governor Rodrigo Vergara told daily newspaper La Tercera Sunday.

He said that the bank is keeping a close eye on the strengthening peso, adding "intervention in the currency market is a tool that the central bank doesn't rule out, although it is only used in exceptional circumstances."

As Chile's economy is highly dependent on exports, especially the agricultural and industrial sectors, and the strength of the peso hurts the competitiveness of those products, exporters are demanding intervention in the currency market.

Additionally, Chile's President Sebastian Pinera said he plans to discuss with the central bank shortly how the monetary authority can better coordinate its monetary and exchange-rate policies with the government's fiscal and macroeconomic policies, in order to reach a competitive exchange rate that helps exporters, in particular the agricultural sector. The central bank, however, is an independent body and has complete autonomy over its decisions.

"This verbal intervention by the central bank governor and President Pinera helped tamp down the peso's rise. But, if the market doesn't see concrete action, there's a good chance the peso will again start to strengthen," said Rodrigo Sarria, currency trader with local investment bank Celfin Capital.

Also helping to weaken the peso was the euro's fall against the dollar. As Europe is one of Chile's main trading partners, the peso often moves in the same direction as the euro does against the dollar.

The euro fell against the dollar in the wake of further details on the extent of Ireland's budget deficit and a mixed bag of U.S. economic data.

In the bond market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central bank bonds, or BCUs, ended higher as institutional investors sold bonds, triggering stop-loss orders, a local fixed-income trader said.

The yield on five-year BCU bonds ended at 2.76%, up from 2.72% Friday, while the yield on 10-year BCUs closed at 3.08%, up from 2.99% the previous session.

title: CORRECT: Chile  Peso May Continue Firming But  Intervention  Not Imminent
text:
("=Chile Peso May Continue Firming But Intervention Not Imminent," at 5:01 p.m. Friday and repeated at 7:37 a.m. EDT Monday, misstated the strength of the peso in the second paragraph. The correct version follows:)


 
 
 
 
   By Anthony Esposito 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--With the Chilean peso continuing to rise, and currently at a 28-month high against the dollar, exporters and key political players are increasing pressure for market intervention.

The central bank, however, won't likely intervene as the peso, in real terms, is still considerably weaker than it was the last time the central bank intervened, analysts and traders say.

For the year, the peso has gained 5.1% on the dollar, and a much steeper 9.6% since midyear on a rally in global copper prices to two-year highs and broad international dollar weakness.

Also fueling the peso's gains are expectations for Chile's economy to continue to quickly recover from last year's recession and February's devastating earthquake and growing spread between local and U.S. interest rates. Chile's benchmark rate is currently at 2.5% and expected to reach 5% next year.

As Chile's economy is highly dependent on exports, especially the agricultural and industrial sectors, and the strength of the peso cuts into the competitiveness of those products, exporters have stepped up demands for measures to be taken.

Most recently, Chilean agricultural workers threatened general protests if the central bank doesn't intervene in the peso market, while the conservative UDI political party, which is part of the governing coalition, asked the central bank to intervene because of the negative effect the peso's strength is having on agricultural and industrial sectors.

According to a poll released recently, 80% of exporters belonging to the nations' Asexma exporters trade group feel their business is at risk because of the strength of the peso.

The poll also highlighted that 85% of exporters questioned said the central bank should intervene if the peso firms past the CLP480-mark.

With the peso closing at CLP481.00 Friday, and soon expected to breach the CLP480 barrier, its climb to CLP470 and beyond looks like it's just a matter of time, traders say.

Despite exporters demands for market intervention, traders and analysts alike don't see the central bank signaling its willingness to intervene unless the peso strengthens to CLP460-470. Some analysts even say the range is closer to CLP445-CLP450.

In recent weeks, central bank President Jose De Gregorio has said the peso, in real terms, is in line with long-term fundamentals and President Sebastian Pinera said the peso was on a "normal path" despite its relative strength to the dollar. However, central bank governor Rodrigo Vergara said in prepared remarks that the central bank can't rule out capital controls, even though the effectiveness of these measures can be disputed.

Over the last decade the central bank has only intervened in the local currency market three times, and the last time it intervened, in April 2008, the peso was trading at 10-year highs against the dollar.

"At some point if the peso continues to strengthen the central bank will take a harder stance and verbalize its willingness to act," said Sergio Tricio, head of studies with local currency trader Forex Chile.

The questionable effectiveness of Brazil's and Japan's recent interventions in their respective currency markets, however, provides fodder for those who argue against intervention.

On Friday, the dollar continued its fall against the yen, hovering around a new post-intervention low of Y83.15 and fell against the Brazilian real to its weakest since Sept. 3, 2008--days before the fall of Lehman Brothers touched off the worst financial crisis in 70 years.

"The way markets are reading this is that market intervention will only provide a short term solution, but it won't be too effective over the medium or long term considering the dollar's overall [international] weakness," said Tricio.

-By Anthony Esposito, Dow Jones Newswires; 56-2-715-8929; anthony.esposito@dowjones.com [ 04-10-10 1621GMT ]
