With Chile producing more than one-third of the world's copper, the peso often takes cues from the metal's international prices. Copper futures in New York vaulted to two-year highs on positive economic data from China and a weaker dollar.

Also, as Europe is one of Chile's main trade partners, the peso often moves in the same direction as the euro does against the dollar. The euro hit a six-month peak against the dollar, after the Federal Reserve said it is almost certain to have to offer fresh support to ensure that already tepid U.S. economic growth does not continue to falter.

Additionally, local market participants digested the Brazilian real's gains to 1.6780 to the dollar despite the Brazilian central bank's action to halt the currency's strengthening. As the strength of the Chilean peso cuts into the competitiveness of the nation's exports and because the local economy is highly dependent on those products, exporters have been clamoring for market intervention.

That Brazil has intervened in its local currency market and the real is still strengthening against the dollar provides an argument for not intervening in Chile.

"Despite Brazil's interventions in the currency market, the real has continued to strengthen because there is broad dollar weakness at the international level. The way markets are reading this is that market intervention will only provide a short term solution, but it won't be too effective over the medium or long term considering the dollar's overall weakness," said Sergio Tricio, head of studies with local currency trader Forex Chile.

In the bond market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central bank bonds, or BCUs, ended lower as the peso's strength fueled expectations that the monetary authority's future interest rate hikes will be less aggressive, traders said.

Chile's central bank raised interest rates by 50 basis points for a fourth consecutive month last month as the country quickly recovers from its first recession in a decade last year and a devastating February earthquake.

   By Anthony Esposito 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean peso ended at a 27-month high against the dollar Thursday as international copper prices held at a two-year high, sparking a new round of exporters' demands for intervention in the foreign-exchange market.

The peso finished at CLP483.50 to the dollar, compared with CLP485.50 the prior session, while trading in a range of CLP482.70 to CLP485.00.

With Chile producing more than one-third of the world's copper, the peso often takes cues from the metal's international prices. Copper prices held at the two-year high reached following a four-month rally driven by improving industrial demand and concerns about supply.

As the strength of the peso cuts into the competitiveness of Chilean exports and because the local economy is highly dependent on its exports, exporters are turning up the heat as they demand market intervention.

Earlier in the day, Chilean agricultural workers threatened general protests if the central bank doesn't intervene in the peso market.

During the third quarter, the peso gained 8.8% on the dollar while, for the year, it has strengthened a milder 4.6% against the U.S. currency.

Although in Latin America, Brazil, Colombia and Peru have already intervened to tamp down their currencies due to the dollar's broad international weakness, the Chilean monetary authority isn't expected to intervene in the local currency market unless the peso strengthens past CLP460 or CLP470.

"While in nominal terms the exchange rate is concerning exporters, the real exchange rate is still considerably above levels that would merit intervention," said a local currency trader.

The last time the central bank intervened in the currency market, in April 2008, the peso was trading at 10-year highs against the dollar.

In the bond market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central bank bonds, or BCUs, ended mixed as institutional investors sold bonds, triggering stop-loss orders, a local fixed-income trader said.

The yield on five-year BCU bonds ended unchanged at 2.73%, while the yield on 10-year BCUs closed higher at 3.08%, from 3.03% the previous session.

title: Chile exporters urge cenbank to curb strong peso
text:
* Exporters says stronger peso eats away profits

* Firms see intervention after 480 pesos/dlr - poll

* Cenbank has signaled no immediate intervention

SANTIAGO, Sept 28 (Reuters) - Exporters in Chile, a major producer of fruit, wine and wood pulp, on Tuesday urged the central bank to step into the forex market and curb a rapidly appreciating peso that has hurt profits.

The peso <CLP=CL> <CLP=> is trading at over 2-year highs of 480.50 per dollar as the economy of the world's top copper producer picks up steam amid a sluggish global recovery.

A stronger peso has weighed on the revenues of local exporters that are paid in dollars for their sales abroad.

The Manufacturing and Services Exporters Association, or Asexma, said exporters are quickly losing ground against competitors abroad due to a stronger currency.

A poll released by the trade group showed that more than 85 percent of the firms surveyed believe the bank should intervene when the peso passes 480 per dollar. The survey included executives at 112 companies within the trade group during August and September.

<^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

TAKE-A-LOOK on Chile's economic recovery [ID:nN30113748]

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

The central bank has so far brushed aside talks of an immediate intervention in the currency after it reiterated late last week that the peso is in line with long-term fundamentals.

Still, bank President Jose de Gregorio has said future rate hikes would be faster without a strong peso, hinting of smaller rate increases that could take away some of the peso momentum.

A growing differential between rates in Chile and those in the United States and Europe has lured droves of investors looking for a quick profit, exponentially increasing dollar inflows and strengthening the peso.

Bank board member Rodrigo Vergara said in a speech published on Monday that emerging countries cannot rule out capital controls to ease currencies, but acknowledge its "effectiveness is even more disputed" than intervention.

The government of President Sebastian Pinera has said it plans to slow public spending, which could in turn help stem the sharp appreciation of the peso. (Reporting by Alonso Soto; Editing by Richard Chang)

Prior to Wednesday's drop, CorpBanca, which is owned by the local Saieh family, had risen 10.3% over the last week on speculation Banco do Brasil could acquire part or all of its shares.

Holding company Hipermarc (HIPERMARC.SN), which is also owned by the Saieh family and holds the Unimarc supermarket chain, surged 59.3% to CLP27.08. Participants hoped the Corpbanca stake sale would give Hipermarc's owners cash in hand for new investments. Hipermarc isn't on the Ipsa, but is listed on the general stock index.

As the strength of the peso cuts into the competitiveness of Chilean exports and the local economy is highly dependent on its exports, exporters' demands for market intervention have become louder.

Traders think the central bank could intervene in the local currency market if the peso strengthens past CLP470.

title: WRAPUP 1-Chile rate hikes faster without strong peso-cenbank
text:
* De Gregorio hints at slower rate hikes- analysts

* Peso trades at over two-year highs to the dollar

By Antonio de la Jara and Brad Haynes

SANTIAGO, Sept 24 (Reuters) Chile's central bank would hike its benchmark interest rate faster if it were not for the strengthening of the local currency, according to a speech by Central Bank President Jose De Gregorio.

De Gregorio, who spoke at a banking conference held by the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, said the peso <CLP=CL> had appreciated "significantly" in recent weeks due to the increase of capital inflows.

His comments could signal a slowdown in future rate hikes after the bank started an aggressive upcycle in June to preempt inflationary pressures amid a rapid economic recovery.

"Although in our latest Monetary Policy Report we said that the bank will keep withdrawing the significant monetary stimulus, without the strengthening of the currency the withdrawal would certainly be faster," according to the text of the speech delivered on Friday.

Chile's peso is trading at over two-year highs against the U.S. currency as the economy of the world's top copper producer picks up and the greenback has weakened across the board.

The peso's sharp appreciation has prompted analysts and traders to talk of possible central bank intervention to weaken the Chilean currency. <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ TAKE-A-LOOK Chile's economy recovery [ID:nN30113748] ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

De Gregorio said in his speech that exchange rate intervention cannot be ruled out when there is a misalignment of the exchange rate plus huge capital inflows that "may be the prelude of problems, in the extreme a currency or financial meltdown."

He added that capital inflows may be a source of bubbles in the domestic asset prices in the emerging countries, many of which are growing faster than developed nations amid a slow global recovery.

Juan Pablo Castro, an economist with Santander GBM in Santiago, said it was too soon to say if the central bank would slow its rate hikes from the 50 basis-point pace of the past four months but De Gregorio has raised the possibility.

"Clearly if this appreciation of the peso continues and the consumer price index for September comes in below expectations, there we could see a 25 basis-point hike," Castro said.

Central bank board member Enrique Marshall said in a presentation released earlier on Friday that the peso <CLP=CL> <CLP=> when compared to a basket of currencies in real terms is in line with long-term fundamentals.

The peso ended 0.41 percent higher on Friday at 486.50/487.00 per dollar, extending a two-day rally.

Interest rate futures show the market expects Chile's central bank to raise its benchmark rate by 50 basis points for a fifth straight month in October to 3.0 percent, attracting more inflows of foreign capital and strengthening the peso.

President Sebastian Pinera said on Wednesday the exchange rate between the peso and the dollar was at normal levels and there was no immediate need for government intervention. [ID:nN22256063]

The wider weakness of the dollar is driving much of the peso's rally as the dollar index <.DXY>, which tracks the performance of the greenback against a basket of currencies, has dropped nearly 8 percent in the last eight months.

22 Sep 2010 14:38 EDT DJ  Chile's Pinera: Peso On 'Normal Path'; Sees 6% 2010 GDP Growth

By Riva Froymovich

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Chile's strengthening peso remains on a "normal path," although the central bank has the tools to intervene in markets if necessary, said Chilean President Sebastian Pinera on Wednesday.

The peso has been fast appreciating against the U.S. dollar as U.S. interest rates remain low, leading investors to chase higher yields in emerging markets. Chile's economy is also growing faster, providing an alternative to the stagnant developed world.

"If you grow faster than the rest of the world your currency has to appreciate," said Pinera, particularly given the price of copper, the country's top export, is at elevated levels.

He was speaking at an Americas Society and Council of the Americas event in New York.

Pinera said strong fiscal policy will protect the economy from the effects of a rising peso, but the central bank has the tools to intervene if necessary.

The peso was recently near a 35-week high at CLP493.70 to the dollar, versus Tuesday's close at CLP497.20, according to Valor Futuro newswire.

Pinera also repeated forecasts for Chile's gross domestic product to grow 6% this year, and said the country may even surprise economists to the upside. He said inflation isn't a concern, and the country's growth rates are sustainable.

Due to the country's high savings, Pinera doesn't expect the government to issue much more in global bonds after selling debt to international markets for the first time in six years this past July.

Chile issued the notes to provide guidance for its private sector, he said.

Pinera said, however, that Chile could again issue debt before the end of his government's term. He added that the country will be active in capital markets to "add value" to its massive raw material exports.

Chile is among the top global copper exports.

Those resources have attracted huge investment and trade with China, which receives about 25% of Chile's exports, said Pinera.

He said Chile's growth strategy relies on open and competitive trade. Pinera added that he would like to see the U.S. move faster on furthering those principles through free-trade agreements with other Latin American nations, such as Colombia and Panama.

Pinera repeated the goals of his administration for the next four years and for the next decade. He aims to defeat poverty, double investment in education, reform the health-care system, and create 1 million jobs.

"We are very confident we can achieve our goals," he said.

Separately, Pinera said 33 workers trapped in a mine since August may be rescued earlier than expected, in the beginning of November.

Pinera took office in March, after a massive magnitude 8.8 earthquake and ensuing tsunami that killed hundreds, left tens of thousands homeless and caused damages upwards of $30 billion, roughly 18% of GDP.

text:

* Chile's peso gains 0.2 pct, Mexican peso adds 0.3 pct

By Samantha Pearson and Jean Luis Arce

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Sept 14 (Reuters) - The Brazilian real hit a fresh 2010 high on Tuesday as investors bet on massive future investment in Latin America's biggest economy.

Strong U.S. retail data also helped to boost the region's currencies, allowing the Mexican peso to shrug off early losses. For details, see [ID:nN14247794]

Brazil's central bank has stepped up intervention efforts to weaken the currency in a bid to protect exporters, but so far it has failed to halt the real's rally.

The Brazilian real <BRL=> was bid 0.32 percent stronger at 1.7041 reais per U.S. dollar, according to the international reference rate. It was trading at 1.703 on the local spot market <BRBY>, its strongest level since Dec. 4, 2009.

"The market is testing the government's willingness, and they will continue to take the currency lower," said one head currency trader in New York.

Brazil plans to sell $500 million more of its 2041 global bonds, underscoring a growing foreign interest in the country's markets.

Investors are also optimistic about huge foreign investment in an upcoming fundraising deal by state-owned oil company Petrobras and a wave of other local corporate deals.

But if the real breaks the closely watched 1.70-per-dollar level, the central bank could be forced to be more aggressive in the market, analysts said.

Authorities have already been increasing dollar purchases in the spot market, calling multiple auctions each day, but some believe they may also start intervening in the futures market via derivatives called "reverse swaps."

MEXICAN PESO REVERSES GAINS

The Mexican currency <MXN=> gained 0.25 percent to 12.8215 per dollar for a three-week high after the strong U.S. data raised hopes about the global economic recovery.

The currency had weakened earlier in the session as investors remained cautious after a rally in the region Monday.

Mexico's fragile recovery from a deep recession is dependent on U.S. growth because it sends about 80 percent of its exports to its northern neighbor.

"The good data in the United States prompted another round of risk-taking," said Daniela Blancas, currency strategist at Scotia Capital in Mexico City.

But she said volume was relatively low due to an upcoming public holiday in the country.

title: Chile Peso Ends Stronger On US Econ Data,  Central Bank  Comments
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chile's peso ended slightly stronger against the dollar Thursday on encouraging U.S. jobs and trade deficit data as well as the Chilean central bank's comments that it isn't likely to intervene in the local currency market.

After paring back some of its earlier gains, the peso ended stronger at CLP496.00 to the dollar, compared to Wednesday's close of CLP496.50. The currency traded in a range of CLP493.40 and CLP496.50.

Currencies closely tied to the pace of global growth gained after better-than-expected U.S. data painted a brighter picture of the economic recovery.

As Europe is one of Chile's main trade partners, the peso often moves in the same direction as the euro does against the dollar. The euro posted a small gain against the greenback.

Chile's central bank tempered speculation about intervention in the local currency market. With exporters clamouring that the peso's relative strength versus the dollar is hurting the competitiveness of their products, central bank President Jose De Gregorio said Wednesday that Chile's currency is in line with its fundamentals.

Although analysts see the peso moving toward CLP492 in the short term, the peso again bounced back, giving up most of its gains, after hitting a key level of resistance located around CLP493-CLP494.

"If the peso doesn't manage to break resistance we'll probably see the peso stuck trading in a short range of CLP494 to CLP498," said Gloria Soto, head currency trader with FXCM Chile.

In the bond market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central bank bonds, or BCUs, ended higher after banks placed stop-loss orders.

The yield on five-year BCU bonds ended higher at 2.45%, from 2.37% Wednesday, while the yield on 10-year BCUs ended higher at 2.81% from 2.72% the prior session.

title: SNAP ANALYSIS- Chile  peso to firm but no  intervention  seen
text:
SANTIAGO, Sept 1 (Reuters) - Chile's peso <CLP=CL> <CLP=> will likely continue to rise in the short-term after hitting new 7-month highs on Wednesday, but gains are seen limited and are not expected to trigger central bank intervention. <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

For a TAKE-A-LOOK on Chile economy, peso [ID:nN30113748] ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

VOLATILITY AHEAD

Stronger global stocks, high copper prices and rising domestic rates will likely boost the peso in the short term, but fears of a double-dip global recession that pushes investors to take refuge in the dollar could keep a lid on the currency's gains.

Uncertainty over copper demand in top consumer China also signals more volatility ahead for prices of copper, by far the main export of world No.1 producer Chile.

Analysts say positive local economic data and expected further interest rate hikes have already been factored in by the market as the country steadily recovers from the global downturn and a massive Feb. 27 earthquake.

Traders and analysts point to wider dollar strength, global bourses and copper demand as the key drivers for the peso in the coming months.

INTERVENTION UNLIKELY

Analysts see the central bank intervening to stem the peso's rise if the currency rises to a range of 480 to 465 per dollar, but expect further gains to fall short of that.

Central Bank President Jose De Gregorio has not ruled out an intervention, but has said the peso is in line with long-term fundamentals in real terms -- which markets took as a signal there would be no imminent bank action.

The peso has appreciated 2.7 percent against the dollar so far this year, with most of the gains posted since July. Last year, the local currency appreciated 26.4 percent after depreciating 22.4 percent in 2008.

ABOVE 500/DLR BY YR-END

Fears of a slowing global recovery are seen ultimately exerting downward pressure on the peso later this year.

title: UPDATE 2- Chile central bank  doesn't rule out peso  intervention
text:
* Peso in line with longer-term fundamentals-De Gregorio

* Central bank does not rule out intervention

* Peso has retreated slightly from seven-month highs (Updates with fresh De Gregorio comment, details)

By Ignacio Badal

SANTIAGO, Aug 24 (Reuters) - Chile's peso is in line with longer-term fundamentals in real terms, Central Bank President Jose De Gregorio said on Tuesday, while warning the bank can intervene in currency markets in exceptional circumstances.

The peso <CLP=CL> recently surged to seven-month highs, boosted by strong prices for copper, Chile's top export, and higher interest rates that have lured investment. The rising currency prompted warnings from President Sebastian Pinera and Finance Minister Felipe Larrain.

"The floating exchange rate allows for foreign exchange intervention in exceptional cases, as we have done on previous occasions," De Gregorio said in a presentation uploaded to the bank's Web site.

"A floating exchange rate regime can bring with it exchange rate volatility and uncertainty, at least in the short-term," he added. "However, those costs do not counter the benefits of floating."

When the central bank announced its last major intervention in 2008, after the peso appreciated sharply amid a commodity boom, it gave the market a clear calendar outlining plans to buy $8 billion dollars via auction.

"The central bank will not renounce the use of its instruments, but their use will depend on the board's evaluation that their benefits and effectiveness outweigh their cost," De Gregorio said.

The peso has eased back in recent sessions and was weaker on Tuesday, little moved after De Gregorio spoke.

Larrain on Thursday warned investors that authorities could intervene to stem a sharp appreciation of the local peso. For more, see [ID:nN19246318].

Some analysts believe the central bank would only move if the peso firmed beyond 480 per dollar.

Analysts expect South American policy makers to step up intervention to stem surging currencies but caution that doing so risks stoking inflation and say it could ultimately put the brakes on a regional interest rate up-cycle. [ID:N17270580]

Peru has aggressively intervened this year to counter sharp gains by its sol currency <PEN=PE>, which is around two-year highs, while Colombia is looking at measures to give businesses relief from currency strength. [ID:nN18206932] (With reporting by Antonio de la Jara and Molly Rosbach; Writing by Simon Gardner; Editing by Paul Simao)

title: SCENARIOS- Chile  peso rally may prompt  intervention
text:
SANTIAGO, Aug 19 (Reuters) - Chile stepped up warnings to investors on Thursday that financial authorities could intervene to curb the peso, which has sharply appreciated.

The peso has gained more than 6 percent since July as investors snapped up the local currency to cash in on rising central bank interest rates.

Fresh warnings from Finance Minister Felipe Larrain on Thursday helped weaken the peso by 0.7 percent to 505.20/502.70 to the dollar.

President Sebastian Pinera has also warned his government will use every macroeconomic tool at its disposal to make the peso more competitive. A stronger peso increases costs for exporters in the world's top copper producer.

The following are some of the possible scenarios in the short term as the peso continues to appreciate:

CLIMB TO NEAR 480/DOLLAR - VERBAL WARNINGS

The government is already stepping up verbal warnings to ease the peso's upward trend.

Now, if the peso keeps appreciating to near 480-per-dollar levels, the central bank could join in the verbal exchange to temper the currency's rise.

Central Bank President Jose De Gregorio repeatedly warned of intervention in late 2009 and early 2010 after the peso surged. His warnings helped the peso slide back later in 2010.

The bank and central government may issue debt to absorb excess liquidity and exert more influence over the exchange rate.

The government could also slow repatriation of dollars from copper-boom savings held abroad and an international debt sale aimed at helping fund reconstruction after a massive Feb. 27 earthquake, to ease upward pressure on the peso.

A stronger-than-expected economic recovery could give the government some breathing room.

BELOW 480/DOLLAR, CENBANK SEEN STEPPING IN

If the peso firms to below 480 per dollar, the central bank will likely intervene.

The local market expects any intervention to be similar to that seen in 2008, when the central bank built up reserves through a dollar purchase program after the peso hit 430 to the dollar.

That intervention reversed gains in the peso, which rose to the highest level in over a decade in 2008, driven by strong prices for key export, copper.

This month De Gregorio voiced concerns about foreign capital flows following rising rates in emerging economies, saying countries should be "alert and thinking what implications that has for monetary policy."

The central bank could impose capital controls by boosting banks' dollar reserve requirements, although analysts see that as a more unlikely choice.

The central bank could also slow the pace of future rate hikes to make the peso less attractive to foreign investors, though this is also seen as less probable.

The government could change hedging limits or investment requirements for local pension funds, big players in the local currency market, to increase their dollar holdings and temper the peso's gains.

PESO SLIDES ON EXTERNAL FACTORS

A stronger dollar driven by fears of a double-dip recession in the United States as well as volatility in copper prices could again weaken the peso and prevent direct intervention.

In early 2010, the peso slid from around 488 per dollar to 550 in just over two weeks. Wider dollar strength and the expiration of a central bank global crisis-driven liquidity measure helped ease the peso in late January. (Reporting by Maria Jose Latorre and Alonso Soto; Editing by Simon Gardner and Todd Eastham)

"The government is doing what it can on its part to avoid additional appreciation," Larrain told state television, referring to the fact the government has not repatriated hundreds of millions of dollars raised by an international bond issue.

"If the price of copper rises strongly, if the U.S. economy is growing weakly and there are no expectations of a rise in (U.S.) rates, it is very difficult to battle against that," he said. <------------------------------------------------------ For Chile peso scenarios, see [ID:nN19249922] For a Chile peso graphic, see http://link.reuters.com/wex55n For a Latam forex graphic, see http://link.reuters.com/ged55n("http://link.reuters.com/ged55n") ------------------------------------------------------->

Benchmark interest rates in the United States remain near zero percent and are not seen rising anytime soon. By contrast, Chile's central bank has raised its benchmark rate three times since June to 2.0 percent currently, and the market is betting on another rise of 50 basis points next month.

A continuing surge in the peso would make Chile's exports less competitive, which could put the brakes on the economy's recovery from the February earthquake and from the global financial crisis.

Larrain cited examples of past central bank interventions.

"In the past, there have been exchange rate interventions in cases which were considered extreme," he said. "Those interventions are never announced beforehand, only after they happen."

However, when the central bank announced its last major intervention in 2008 after the peso appreciated sharply amid a commodity boom, it gave the market a clear calendar outlining plans to buy $8 billion dollars via auction.

The peso eased after Larrain spoke, deepening losses on the back of poor U.S. jobs data.

The peso closed 1.1 percent weaker at 507.30/507.80 per dollar compared with Wednesday's close. The currency is up around 8 percent since the end of June. [ID:nN19267404]

Traders are betting the peso will appreciate by a miniscule 0.01 percent over the next month, according to the non-deliverable forwards market <CLPNDF=>, a form of derivatives trading popular outside Chile due to the country's currency controls.

But the peso is expected to then erase those gains and gradually weaken against the U.S. dollar in the months ahead. The NDF market indicates the peso will depreciate 0.06 percent in two months' time and trade 0.18 percent weaker in three months' time, compared with the current level.

Larrain had voiced similar concerns about the strong peso on Wednesday, which followed on the heels of comments by President Sebastian Pinera about the exchange rate last week.

Market players suspect the central bank could intervene if the peso's rally continues much further.

"Below 500 pesos per dollar, the authorities will get nervous and could intervene, but so far these are just warning shots," said one foreign exchange dealer.

"The market tends to react to this sort of comment, but if it does not see concrete action, things resume their course, and so far, we have just seen words," he added.

Some analysts believe the bank would only move if the peso firmed beyond 480 per dollar.

Analysts expect South American policy makers to step up intervention to stem surging currencies, but caution that doing so risks stoking inflation and say it could ultimately put the brakes on a regional interest rate up-cycle. [ID:N17270580]

Peru has aggressively intervened this year to counter sharp gains by its sol currency <PEN=PE>, which is around two-year highs, while Colombia is looking at measures to give businesses relief from currency strength. [ID:nN18206932]

And some analysts believe Brazil could intervene aggressively to counter strength in its real <BRBY> currency if the psychologically important 1.75 per dollar level is broken for a sustained period. [ID:nN19252564] (Additional reporting by Froilan Romero and Samantha Pearson in Sao Paulo; Editing by Leslie Adler)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Chile, Brazil  currencies  break key levels
text:
* Bond flows support region's currencies

* Brazil's real firms 0.3 pct, Mexican peso flat

* Chilean peso pares gains after new government warning (Adds comments, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Maria Jose Latorre

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Aug 18 (Reuters) - Chile's peso and the Brazilian real broke through key levels on Wednesday, putting pressure on the countries' central banks to follow through on threats to intervene in the market.

Chile's currency <CLP=CL><CLP=> broke through the 500 peso-per-dollar level for the first time since January.

The region's currencies were boosted by strong demand for a German government bond auction, increasing demand for some higher-risk assets.

Concerns over U.S. economic growth, which are expected to keep returns on U.S. Treasuries near record lows, have also prompted investors to pour money into Latin America's higher-yielding debt, lifting the region's currencies.

But the sharp rise in Chile's peso prompted the government to issue another warning to the market Wednesday, saying it is closely monitoring the peso's appreciation and wants a competitive exchange rate.

After firming to 498.20 per dollar, the peso pared gains but still traded 0.1 percent stronger at 501.60 per dollar.

"The market has already factored in strong growth for the country, and is foreseeing further interest rate hikes, which in turn strengthens the peso," one trader in Santiago said.

Chile's GDP expanded 4.3 percent in the second quarter compared with the first quarter, data Wednesday showed, the fastest pace since at least the mid-1990s. For details, see [ID:nN18182427]

Chile's economy has recovered much faster than expected from the effects of a devastating earthquake in February, boosting the currency to seven-month highs.

The government might decide to slow its repatriation of dollars from copper revenues as a way to curb the currency's rise, analysts said. [ID:nN17124678]

BRAZIL'S REAL BACKS OFF

Brazil's real <BRBY> also firmed past the psychologically important level of 1.75 real-per-dollar but struggled to remain there.

The currency toyed with the level throughout the session, and traded 0.28 percent stronger at 1.748 against the U.S. dollar.

"The economy is growing and rates are high, so inflows are inevitable," said Doug Smith, head of Latin American research at Standard Chartered.

"Brazil has allowed the currency to absorb a great deal of appreciation pressure, unlike the Chinese, and so have a legitimate argument that Brazil has carried much of the global appreciation pressure in the region."

If the real remains stronger than the 1.75 level for an extended period, analysts expect the central bank to act via verbal warnings, bigger or multiple dollar purchases in the spot market or intervention in the futures market.

But analysts at Brazil's Prosper brokerage said the currency could strengthen to 1.70 per dollar because of huge inflows, partly due to the upcoming capital-raising plan by state-run oil company Petrobras .

"Besides this, we expect additional foreign inflows (excluding investment in Petrobras) via bonds and/or shares of $5-6 billion in the short term."

Mexico's peso <MXN=><MEX01> closely tracked the performance of the U.S. stock market throughout the day, trading flat at 12.5990 in the afternoon session. U.S. stocks were slightly higher in afternoon trade.

The performance of U.S. assets is closely watched by investors in Mexico due to the countries' strong trade links.

Juan Carlos Lopez, head of trading at brokerage Intercam in Mexico City, said the peso would be stuck between 12.58 and 12.63 per dollar during the session due to the lack of important economic data in Mexico or the United States. (Additional reporting by Jean Luis Arce and Michael O'Boyle in Mexico City and Molly Rasbach in Santiago; editing by Jeffrey Benkoe)

title: EMERGING MARKETS- Chile  peso firms, but  intervention  talk crimps
text:
* Strong second-quarter growth in Chile boosts currency

* Chilean peso pares gains after new government warning

* Brazil's real firms 0.11 pct, Mexican peso slips

* Bond flows support region's currencies (New throughout, adds comments)

By Froilan Romero and Michael O'Boyle

SANTIAGO/MEXICO CITY, Aug 18 (Reuters) - Chile's peso firmed to a seven-month high on Wednesday after stronger-than-expected growth in the second quarter raised bets the country's central bank will keep hiking interest rates.

However, the currency pared intraday gains after the Chilean finance minister said the government wanted a competitive peso, stoking concerns about intervention.

Brazil's real and Colombia's peso were also hemmed in by the looming threat that authorities could enter currency markets to stem sharp gains that are hurting exporters.

Data showed Chile's economy expanded at the fastest pace since the mid-1990s in the second quarter from the previous quarter as the country bounces back from an earthquake earlier this year. For details, see [ID:nN18182427]

"The Chilean economy stands out in the region for having strong growth ahead of it while in other places we have begun to see moderation," said Jimena Zuniga, an analyst at Barclays Capital in New York.

"This is consistent with a significant increase in the level of interest rates, so that combination is boosting the currency," she added. Earlier this month Chile's central bank tightened borrowing costs for the third month in a row, bringing its key rate to 2 percent.

Weak U.S. growth is expected to keep yields on U.S. Treasuries near record lows for some time. That has boosted the appeal of Latin America's higher-yielding debt and lifted the region's currencies.

TALKING TOUGH

The Chilean peso has surged almost 9 percent since the end of June. While pressure is building on the central bank to stem the gains, Zuniga said policymakers would not want to jeopardize their credibility.

"The central bank does not want to intervene at a level that later on proves to be sustainable," she said.

The government could curb its sale of dollars from copper exports, but that would not outweigh the larger draw to local assets due to the government's reconstruction efforts that are boosting growth, analysts said. [ID:nN17124678]

Colombia's government said on Wednesday it was looking at ways to improve productivity to give businesses short-term relief from the strong local currency, which has surged on inflows into the country's energy and mining sectors. [ID:nN18206932]

The Colombia peso <COP=STFX> bid 0.17 percent weaker 1,1810.60 per dollar a day after jumping by the most in three months.

Colombia's central bank is widely expected to detail new efforts to curb the currency's strength at its policy meeting on Friday. Analysts think the central bank could reinstate a dollar-purchase program that expired in June. [ID:nN18197601]

Brazil's real <BRBY> bid 0.11 percent stronger at 1.751 per U.S. dollar, touching the psychological level of 1.75 and adding to concerns that country's central bank could soon step up efforts to weaken the real.

The government may test other measures before intervening directly in the market, said Luiz Antonio Abdo, the head of currency trading at the Souza Barros brokerage in Sao Paulo.

"Before acting directly in the currency market, it could carry out less direct measures such as offering incentives to exporters or taxing imports. As such, it would be acting in more of a fiscal way, closing the door to more speculators," Abdo said.

Mexico's peso <MXN=> lagged the region's currencies, slipping 0.25 percent to 12.63 per U.S. dollar.

Traders said the peso traded a range due to a lack of U.S. data that could either ease or reinforce concerns about a slowing economy in the United States, Mexico's top trading partner.

Early in the session, the Mexican peso hit a one-week high. (Additional reporting by Samantha Pearson in Sao Paulo; Editing by Kenneth Barry)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Colombia and  Chile 's pesos soar, c.banks eyed
text:
* Traders test out intervention threats across region

* Colombia's peso jumps by most in three months

* Chile's peso at strongest in seven months

* Brazil's real firms 0.11 pct; Mexican peso adds 0.62 pct (Adds comments, updates prices)

By Nelson Bocanegra and Michael O'Boyle

BOGOTA/MEXICO CITY (Reuters) - Latin American currencies strengthened Tuesday after data suggested the U.S. economy will keep growing, while solid debt auctions in Europe supported bids for riskier assets.

Colombia's peso jumped by the most in three months and Chile's peso hit a seven-month high, while the currencies of Mexico and Brazil firmed to one-week highs.

A 1 percent rise in U.S. industrial output for July suggested the economy of the United States had enough strength to support economic expansion in the region. U.S. producer prices also rose last month, calming fears of deflation.

"The fact that U.S. industrial production continues to advance is good news since this is the sector behind Mexico's recovery," said Luis Flores, an economist at brokerage IXE in Mexico City.

Mexico's rebound last year from deep recession was fueled by manufacturing exports. Many of Mexico's factories supply U.S. plants.

Mexico's peso gained 0.62 percent to 12.59 per dollar, gaining ground for the fourth straight session.

The United States is also Colombia's top trading partner, and Colombia's peso bid 1.52 percent stronger at 1807.00 per dollar. The currency is heading back toward a two-year high hit last week.

One trader in New York said that the Colombian peso had been boosted in early trading by a huge inflow from a dealer based in the city.

Also lifting demand for emerging market assets, Irish and Spanish bond auctions yielded solid results, easing concerns about Europe's debt troubles.

INTERVENTION LOOMS

Investors are buying Colombian bonds based on expectations that the country will soon regain its investment grade credit rating under an ambitious reform agenda set by the country's new president, Juan Manuel Santos.

Investors have flocked to Latin America's higher-yielding debt, strengthening currencies, due to expectations that slow U.S. growth will keep returns on U.S. Treasuries at record lows.

But that is raising the specter of intervention across the region as policy-makers look to protect exporters and prevent the formation of bubbles in the market.

The Brazilian real bid 0.11 percent stronger at 1.753, paring gains after hitting the psychologically important level of 1.75 reais per U.S. dollar. Analysts think the central bank could aggressively step up intervention if this level is broken for an extended period.

"There is a certain apprehension in the market about betting against the U.S. dollar at this level, which is lending very strong support to the American currency," said Luciano Rostagno, chief strategist for CM Capital Markets in Sao Paulo.

One way that this level might be broken, he said, is if a mass of dollars flows into the country. Weekly central bank reports on dollar flows -- the latest of which is due on Wednesday -- have shown dollars starting to flow back into Brazil after flowing out during June and most of July.

Chile's government has also threatened to intervene in markets last week following a rapid rise in the country's peso, but traders have continued to test the resolve of the authorities.

Chile's peso was bid 0.66 percent firmer at 502.00 per dollar, hitting a fresh seven-month high. (Additional reporting by Samantha Pearson and Silvio Cascione in Sao Paulo, Jean Luis Arce in Mexico City; editing by Todd Eastham)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Colombia,  Chile  peso dip on  intervention  talk
text:
Chilean peso hits five-month high after rate hike

* Colombian peso hurt by intervention talk

* Rise in early August U.S. consumer confidence supports

* Mexican peso firms 0.06 pct, Brazil's real up 0.17 pct

By Michael O'Boyle

MEXICO CITY, Aug 13 (Reuters) - Colombia's peso weakened sharply on Friday on fears of government market intervention, while Chile's peso reversed early gains one day after an interest rate hike.

Colombia's peso sank for a second straight session on concerns local authorities will intervene in the foreign exchange markets to cool sharp currency gains that are hurting local exporters. The peso <COP=STFX> shed 0.51 percent to 1,835.70 per dollar.

The currency pulled back about 1.6 percent after hitting a two-year intraday high in the previous session after Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos met with central bank officials to discuss the peso's strong appreciation.

"The official rhetorical intervention finally pushed the Colombian peso into defensive mode," wrote Enrique Alvarez, head of research at consultancy IDEAglobal in New York.

The Colombian currency has gained about 11 percent since early May, boosted by investment flows into the country's oil and mining industries -- also drawing speculative traders.

Analysts think Colombia could reinstate daily dollar purchases that expired in June, but that would do little more than slow the pace of gains.

Chile's peso hit a five-month high Friday, a day after the country's central bank raised interest rates, but the currency gave up ground as traders locked in gains ahead of the expected rate hike.

Late Thursday, Chile's central bank raised its benchmark interest rate to 2 percent, in line with expectations as the economy bounces back from a devastating earthquake. For more, see [ID:nN12145806]

Chile's peso's <CLP=CL> opened at its strongest level since early March, but reversed early gains to bid flat at 509.50 per dollar.

The country's currency has firmed about 7 percent since the end of June. Chilean President Sebastian Pinera hinted Thursday the government could cash in less dollar revenues from copper sales to offset the flows into Chilean assets. [ID:nN12124343]

But analysts looked for the currency to firm further on expectations of more interest rate hikes by the central bank, which is seen taking its benchmark rate to 3.75 percent by year-end. [ID:nN12129420]

BOND DEMAND

U.S. consumer sentiment inched up in early August from July, providing support to Mexico's peso and Brazil's real [ID:N13180040]

The data came after another report showed retail sales rebounded in July and eased concerns about the slowdown in the United States, Mexico's top trading partner and a major influence on the region.

But analysts said the Mexican peso would be far more sensitive to any negative data, given concerns of renewed recession after more signs of a slowdown in U.S. growth.

"Private consumption is a very important issue," said Daniela Blancas, a strategist at Scotia Capital in Mexico City. "This is the main worry about economies, above all in the United States."

Flows into Mexican peso bonds have also been boosting the currency, following a decision by the U.S. Federal Reserve to continue buying Treasury bonds and hold down its benchmark interest rate at its near-zero level for an extended period.

Mexico's benchmark 10-year peso bond <MX10YT=RR> bid down 1 basis point to 6.32 percent trading close to a record low hit in the previous session. Mexican bonds have been posting record lows since May.

The meager yields on U.S. Treasuries are giving investors more reason to buy higher-yielding emerging market debt.

The Mexican peso <MXN=> hit a session high of 12.6825 per U.S. dollar after the U.S. consumer confidence data, but pulled back to trade at 12.7235 per U.S. dollar, 0.06 percent firmer.

Brazil's real <BRBY> bid 0.17 percent stronger at 1.769 per dollar. (Additional reporting by Simon Gardner in Santiago and Jean Luis Arce in Mexico City; editing by Jeffrey Benkoe)

title: UPDATE 2-Chile president warns will keep peso competitive
text:
* Pinera says to use every tool to keep peso competitive

* Taming peso a challenge-analysts

* Peru gov't moves to ease sol currency (Updates with peso close, adds analyst quote)

By Antonio de la Jara and Brad Haynes

SANTIAGO, Aug 12 (Reuters) - Chilean President Sebastian Pinera said on Thursday he was worried about the recent sharp appreciation of the country's peso <CLP=CL> currency and warned his government would use all macroeconomic tools to keep it competitive.

Chile's peso closed on Thursday at a new 5-month high versus the U.S. dollar of 509.50. Even though the peso has depreciated 0.5 percent against the dollar so far this year, in recent weeks it has seen sharp gains from strength in global bourses, higher prices for the country's main export of copper and expectations the central bank will continue to raise rates.

The peso approached 7-month intraday highs before Pinera spoke but later eased.

Analysts say Chile's central bank could intervene if the currency appreciates toward the 470/480 level. Neighboring Peru is also seeking to tame its sol currency <PEN=PE> as its economy surges, while Colombia's peso is at two-year highs. For more, see [ID:nN12111152] [ID:nN12112796]

"We have lots of problems and one of them is the exchange rate, which worries us," Pinera told a local radio station. "We will do everything we can with our macroeconomic policies; fiscal spending, debt policy to ensure that Chile continues to have a competitive currency."

A stronger peso adds costs to exports in the world's top copper producer, which is also a key exporter of wood pulp, fruit, salmon and wine.

TAMING PESO A CHALLENGE

Some analysts say Pinera and the central bank will have a hard time to rein in the peso as the economy rebounds from a massive Feb. 27 earthquake and from the global crisis.

The central bank is expected to raise its benchmark rate by 50 basis points to 2 percent later on Thursday, marking a third aggressive rate increase in as many months as domestic demand remains strong. For a preview, see [ID:nN0965183]

"The problem with Chile is that they're currently hiking rates. It doesn't make too much sense to be hiking rates and intervening," said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, a strategist at RBS Securities in Stamford, Connecticut.

She added that the government's move to repatriate copper savings in dollars for post-quake reconstruction would also complicate efforts to tame the peso.

Joseph Ramos, an economist at the Universidad de Chile, said authorities would likely need to go beyond verbal intervention.

"I don't think verbal warnings are enough," he said, saying the bank could opt for additional dollar purchases to boost reserves, but said the bank would be unlikely to act unless the peso appreciated to around 470 per dollar.

"There are other options. One is a tax on capital inflows," Ramos added. "There are other instruments, like not selling as many dollars now to fund (post-quake) reconstruction."

Investors expect Chile's peso to hold onto gains by the year end if copper prices remain high and the central bank continues to aggressively raise rates, but do not rule out swings in the interim. [ID:nN11234503]

Top financial players predict the peso will trade at 510 per dollar by year-end, a central bank poll showed on Wednesday. [ID:nN11245410]

Analysts say government plans to regulate taxation of derivatives to encourage currency hedging by smaller companies as part of wider capital market reforms, could add upward pressure to the peso by boosting currency liquidity, clearing uncertainty and luring investment. title: EMERGING MARKETS- Chile 's peso firms despite  intervention  talk
text:
* Region's main currencies shrug off euro zone concerns

* Brazil's real flat, Mexican peso firms 0.45 pct

* Colombia peso dips after Santos hints at intervention (Adds comments, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Froilan Romero

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Aug 12 (Reuters) - The Chilean peso <CLP=CL> climbed to its strongest level in five months on Thursday in spite of government talk of intervention, while the region's other major currencies shook off early losses.

Chilean President Sebastian Pinera said on Thursday he was worried about sharp appreciation of the peso and said his government would use all macroeconomic tools available to keep it competitive.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> pared gains slightly after the comments but was still 0.59 percent firmer at 509.20 per dollar, trading at its strongest level since March 8.

Chile's central bank is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate by 50 basis points to 2 percent later on Thursday as the country's economy bounces back from a devastating earthquake in February more quickly than expected. For details, see [ID:nN0965183]

"Projections for the interest rate are still around 3.75 percent by year-end, with a 50 basis point increase in August, although we're not ruling out the option that at this meeting we could see a 75 point hike, in accordance with what the swap rates are showing," one trader in Santiago said.

"From a technical point of view, there are a lot of dollars coming in," said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, a strategist at RBS Securities in Stamford, Connecticut.

The recent rise in the peso was initially triggered by the revelation by the Chilean government about a month ago that it had started to cash in its copper revenues to help rebuild the country after the earthquake, said Cattan-Naslausky.

Chile's peso has strengthened about 6 percent since the beginning of July, outperforming the region.

But she said intervention in the market could be difficult.

The fact that Chile is " selling dollars for pesos in the market (as part of cashing in copper windfalls) means it would be counter-intuitive that they would come back into the market to buy those dollars," she said. "But it's possible."

Colombia's peso also firmed in early trading to a fresh two-year high, a further sign the performance of Latin American currencies is beginning to diverge.

Meanwhile, currencies in Brazil and Mexico suffered early losses on fears that a sharp slowdown in the United States and Europe could reduce demand for the region's exports.

Mexico's peso hit a three-week low after an unexpected rise in new claims for unemployment in the U.S., Mexico's top trading partner.

But the currency <MXN=> recovered to trade 0.45 percent stronger at 12.718 per dollar, helped by flows into Mexico's peso bonds, traders in Mexico City said.

In separate economic reports, industrial production in the euro zone also dropped unexpectedly in June, and Greece's economy shrank more than forecast in the second quarter. [ID:nLDE67B0S3] and [ID:nLDE67B0TH].

On the local spot market, the bid quote for the Brazilian real <BRBY> was flat at 1.768 against the U.S. dollar after paring early losses.

COLOMBIA ALSO SIGNALS INTERVENTION

Colombia's peso <COP=STFX> firmed to its strongest level since August 2008 in early trading but was later 1.1 percent weaker at 1,822 per dollar.

Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos has said that he will ask the central bank to be "creative" in dealing with the Andean country's appreciating peso currency at a meeting on Thursday. [ID:nN12110755]

The lack of a threat of intervention in the market had been one of the main reasons for the outperformance of the peso, according to a note released earlier on Thursday by analysts at HSBC.

The Colombian currency has been boosted by the re-establishment of diplomatic ties between Colombia and Venezuela.

The country is also expected to see a rush of about $10 billion in direct foreign investment in its oil and mining industries this year, and the government estimates that exports will reach a record $40 billion.

"In contrast the Brazilian real looks vulnerable from the perspective of strong official intervention and positioning," HSBC analysts wrote. "The Mexican peso, despite being cheap from a historical REER (Real Effective Exchange Rate) valuation perspective, carries vulnerability from worsening U.S. sentiment and growth."

The REER is a weighted average of a country's currency, relative to a basket of other major currencies, adjusted for inflation.

(Additional reporting by Molly Rosbach in Santiago and Michael O'Boyle in Mexico City) (Editing by Theodore d'Afflisio)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Mexican peso leads region's losses on US data
text:
* Brazil's real dips 0.4 pct, Mexican peso loses 1.4 pct

* Chile outperforms region over week on growth optimism

* Investors eye intervention by Brazil's central bank

(Adds comments, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Michael O'Boyle

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Aug 6 (Reuters) - The Mexican peso headed for its biggest daily loss in more than two months on Friday, leading the region's losses, after data showed twice as many U.S. jobs were lost last month than economists had forecast.

The report added to concerns that the United States is facing a sharp slowdown, which would reduce demand for Latin American exports and make jittery investors less likely to buy the region's higher-risk assets.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> lost 1.44 percent to 12.7409 per dollar, hitting its weakest level for a week and was set to record its steepest daily percentage decline since June 4.

"The peso's weakness is due to the perception of a slowdown in the United States and the impact this could have on economic activity in Mexico," said Salvador Orozco, a debt and currency strategist at Santander in Mexico City.

Mexico's fragile economic recovery from the financial crisis is particularly dependent on U.S. growth, since the country sends most of its exports across its northern border.

Slowing U.S. activity would also reduce the amount of money that Mexican workers in the United States send to their families back home.

The Mexican peso was also set to record the region's deepest weekly loss of 0.75 percent.

The Brazilian real <BRBY> weakened 0.4 percent to 1.759 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market on Friday, and was heading for a weekly loss of 0.28 percent.

Implicit warnings from Brazilian officials that they will prevent the real from strengthening much past its current value have kept investors cautious around the 1.75 real-per dollar level.

Brazil's finance minister, Guido Mantega, said on Friday that the government was "concerned" about the real's strength. "The central bank and the Finance Ministry don't want (the real) to strengthen further," he said.

ANDEAN REGION STORMS AHEAD

While the Chilean peso was flat at 514.50 on Friday, the currency was set to gain 1.26 percent over the week.

The South American country's economy is recovering much faster than expected from the effects of a devastating earthquake earlier this year, recent data has shown.

Booming growth could also put more pressure on its central bank to sharply raise the cost of borrowing.

Analysts have widely been expecting the central bank to opt for a third straight monthly rate increase of 50 basis points when it meets on August 12, but interest rate futures show market expectations for the year-end are rising.

Higher interest rates would help boost the Chilean peso by attracting more yield-hungry foreign investors.

"What we have is an economy that's growing in an important way, and at the same time, we don't have any significant inflationary pressures," said Francisco Hazbun, a trader with the Tanner brokerage in Santiago.

The Colombian peso <COP=STFX> settled at its strongest closing level in two years on Friday, as investors continued to bet on inflows into the country's mining and energy sectors.

Peru's currency <PEN=PE>hit a fresh two-year intraday low on Friday.

The Peruvian economy grew more than 9 percent in the second quarter, central bank officials said on Friday, a day after raising interest rates by more than expected to avert inflationary pressures. [ID:nN06260729]

title: EMERGING MARKETS-LatAm  currencies  post strong July gains
text:
* Chile peso posts best month in eight months

* Brazil real, Mexico peso see best month since March

* U.S. Midwest business survey eases double dip fears (Adds comments, updates prices)

By Michael O'Boyle and Samantha Pearson

MEXICO CITY/SAO PAULO, July 30 (Reuters) - Latin American currencies strengthened on Friday after a surprisingly strong survey on business activity in the U.S. Midwest eased fears the slowing U.S. economy could fall back into recession.

Friday's gains capped the best month for Brazil's real and Mexico's peso since March, while Chile's peso surged by the most in eight months.

Solid corporate earnings reports in the region and in the United States during July helped offset concerns that the U.S. recovery is losing steam. On Friday, a report showed business activity in the U.S. Midwest grew more than expected. For details, see [ID:nN30265688]

"This data dissolved a bit the doubts about the pace of recovery," said Ramon Cordova, a trader at brokerage BASE in Monterrey, Mexico.

Mexico, whose factories operate in lockstep with its northern neighbor, saw its peso <MXN=> gain the most, firming 0.67 percent to 12.6455 per dollar.

title: Chile stocks, peso tumble on global bourse rout
text:
* Stocks close 2 pct lower, in line with global bourses

* Global bourses drag Chilean stocks off life highs

* Peso falls 1 pct to new 14-week low (Updates with bourse close, adds fresh quote, background)

By Aaron Nelsen and Maria Jose Latorre

SANTIAGO, Feb 4 (Reuters) - Chile's blue chip IPSA index <.IPSA> tumbled 2 percent on Thursday and the peso fell to a fresh 14-week low, tracking a rout on global bourses on fears of sovereign debt problems in Europe.

Global bourses fell sharply, with Brazil's Bovespa <.BVSP> down 4.73 percent and the Dow Jones industrial average <.DJI> down 2.4 percent. [ID:nN04194705]

The IPSA closed 2 percent lower at 3,774.20 points, but ended off the day's lows, retreating from a new life closing high of 3,853.58 set on Tuesday. The all-market IGPA <.IGPA> fell 1.62 percent to 17,499.33 points.

Sovereign debt "risks in Spain, Portugal and Greece, dragged European stocks lower and infected world markets. There was also negative employment data in the United States. Both caused Chile's bourse to fall," said Francisco Hazbun, a trader with Tanner brokerage in Santiago.

"There was also some profit-taking," he added.

Shares of industrial conglomerate Copec fell 2.06 percent to 8,200 pesos per share, while rival forestry group CMPC closed 2.53 percent lower at 22,150 pesos.

Shares of Soquimich , Chile's leading exporter of fertilizer and the world's biggest producer of iodine and lithium, tumbled 3.1 percent to 19,500 pesos per share, while shares of Chile's leading electricity generator, Endesa , ended 1.59 percent lower at 910 pesos.

Regional airline LAN fell 1.52 percent to 8,760.1 pesos. President-elect Sebastian Pinera is set to sell his major stake worth around $1.5 billion on Friday.

The IPSA is still trading about 5.4 percent higher year-to-date and is seen ending 2010 around 15 percent higher.

Earlier in the day Chile's peso <CLP=CL> closed 1 percent lower to a new 14-week low, extending a sharp sell-off a day earlier on wider dollar strength and global stock losses.

The peso fell to 543.50/544.00 per U.S. dollar compared with Wednesday's close of 538.00/538.50, but ended off the day's lows. The peso is now down 6.7 percent against the dollar year-to-date.

The local currency sank as much as 2 percent on Wednesday due to bank dollar buying related to a central bank liquidity measure.

Analysts said ongoing uncertainty spawned by modifications to rules governing pension fund hedging was also weighing on the peso, but said the market was overreacting.

"We are witnessing the effects of the changes in norms regarding pension fund hedging, which is having an impact that goes beyond their implications," the BCI brokerage said in a research note.

"Reallocations in pension fund portfolios means that they are not renewing forward sales contracts, which are pressuring the exchange rate," it added. "We should see worry at the central bank over the transitory impact of this rise (in the dollar) given it could hit inflationary expectations."

Christian Vidal, director of FXCM Chile, does not expect the central bank to intervene unless the peso depreciates to around 600 per dollar.

On Wednesday, analysts said banks snapped up dollars to prepare for a Feb. 8 expiry of a central bank measure that allowed banks to use pesos instead of dollars for reserve requirements on foreign exchange deposits.

title: Chile stocks hit new life high, peso at 19-mo peak
text:
* Stocks at new life high led by commodity shares

* Peso hits 19-month high on copper and weak dlr

By Aaron Nelsen

SANTIAGO, Jan 11 (Reuters) - Chile's bourse closed at a record high on Monday, led by demand for commodity stocks, while the peso strengthened on wider dollar weakness and rising prices for main export copper.

The IPSA blue-chip share index <.IPSA> rose 0.47 percent to close at 3,744.17 points, while the all-share IGPA <.IGPA> index closed 0.41 percent higher at 17,264.89. The IPSA has hit a string of 11 consecutive life highs in recent sessions.

The bourse gained nearly 51 percent last year as utility, retail and commodity stocks fueled the biggest annual rise in 16 years. Analysts expect the bourse to continue to forge ahead in coming months.

"Commodities lifted the bourse last week and lifted the bourse again today," said Alexis Olivares, senior analyst with BBVA Research. "Market sentiment is extremely positive and that's reflected in commodity prices."

Investor optimism about the recovery of the Chilean economy after the global financial crisis hit key exports such as copper and has also driven recent bourse gains.

Shares in Soquimich , Chile's leading exporter of fertilizer and the world's biggest producer of iodine and lithium, surged 1.36 percent to close at 21,350 pesos.

Shares of forestry group CMPC closed 1.54 percent higher at 21,910 pesos per share. Chilean iron and steel producer CAP closed 1.72 percent higher at 16,250 pesos.

Energy stocks also gained, led by Chile-based regional group Enersis . They rose 0.50 percent to 231 pesos, while electricity generator Endesa Chile closed 0.71 percent higher at 885 pesos.

Profit taking in the banking sector limited bourse gains, led by a 1.18 percent fall in shares of Santander Chile , the nation's largest private sector bank. Santander stocks ended 1.18 percent weaker at 32.7 pesos per share.

Earlier in the day Chile's peso <CLP=CL> closed up 0.78 percent, hitting a 19-month high on wider dollar weakness and higher copper prices.

The peso rose to 489.50/490.00 per dollar, compared with Friday's close of 493.30/493.80.

Chile's peso has appreciated sharply in recent months, prompting Central Bank President Jose De Gregorio to warn of possible intervention to tame the currency rally in the world's top copper producer.

However, in an apparent shift, De Gregorio warned in an interview published on Sunday that "addiction" to intervention was dangerous. He said Chile's flexible exchange rate has helped the country cope with the global financial crisis and any attempt to fix it would also be "extremely dangerous."

"The dollar is weakening against other major currencies abroad. Add to that higher copper prices and positive global bourses. In other words all the fundamentals favor peso appreciation," said one local trader.

Strong demand for copper in China drove prices higher on Monday.

The peso rose more than 26 percent against the dollar in 2009 on dollar weakness, the closing out of carry trades and a sharp rise in prices for copper, Chile's main export.

The peso, which fell 22.3 percent in 2008, has climbed 3.58 percent so far in January.

(Additional reporting by Carlos Romero and Maria Jose Latorre; Editing by Simon Gardner and Andrew Hay)

title: Chile  cbank warns  intervention  'addiction' dangerous
text:
SANTIAGO, Jan 10 (Reuters) - Chile's flexible exchange rate has helped the country cope with the global financial crisis, and any attempt to fix it is "extremely dangerous," Chile's Central Bank President Jose De Gregorio said in an interview published on Sunday.

De Gregorio told daily El Mercurio's Sunday edition that "addiction" to intervention was also dangerous. His comments contrast with repeated verbal intervention warnings in recent months amid a sharp appreciation of the local peso <CLP=CL>, which is near 18-month highs on dollar sales and high prices of No. 1 export, copper.

Chile's peso appreciated 26 percent against the dollar in 2009, after a 22.3 percent depreciation in 2008, and the central bank had warned repeatedly it reserved the right to intervene in exceptional circumstances.

"Often there is temptation to try to fix the exchange rate, and that is an extremely dangerous path," De Gregorio told the paper.

"The worst risk is what I call intervention addiction," he added. "In the end, they are ineffective and the first step towards rigidities, and are very harmful in the medium term."

The last time the central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market was in 2008, when the peso hit levels of 430 per dollar. It intervened through a program of dollar purchases to boost international reserves and weaken the peso.

De Gregorio warned as recently as mid-December that the bank was closely monitoring the peso and did not rule out intervening if it saw significant imbalances. (Reporting by Rodrigo Martinez; Writing by Simon Gardner; Editing by Maureen Bavdek)

text:

LONDON, Dec 17 (Reuters) - Chile is keeping a close eye on the fundamentals that may be affecting the peso, Chile's finance minister said on Thursday, as the country battles with a near 30 percent rise in its currency this year.

"Underlying fundamentals matter. We keep a very close watch on those fundamentals," Andres Velasco told a news briefing.

"The level of the exchange rate and competitiveness of our exports is a key element in the country's performance and economic growth."

The peso <CLP=> has surged as foreign investors return to a pre-crisis hunt for yield, and there is an upturn in demand for copper, Chile's no. 1 export.

Other countries, including Brazil, have imposed capital controls to curb rise in their currencies which hurts the competitiveness of exporters.

Velasco declined to say at what level he would like the peso to trade, or whether he would like to see intervention to limit the currency's strength.

"The central bank has said that they do not rule out intervening under extraordinary circumstances, I am not adding anything."

Chile's central bank this week maintained its outlook for 2010 economic growth in Chile of 4.5 to 5.5 percent, as the economy bounces back from its first recession in a decade.

The bank also forecast an economic contraction of 1.9 percent in 2009, compared with a previous outlook for a drop of 1.5 to 2.0 percent.

Velasco said the finance ministry's own 2009 growth prediction, in the budget submitted in September, was for a contraction of 1.6 percent, with a growth forecast for 2010 of 5 percent.

"Yesterday the central bank forecast -1.9 percent (for 2009), it's only slightly worse than we had forecast," Velasco said.

"We have had four consecutive months of month-on-month expansion -- we are expecting a fourth quarter of even more rigorous growth."

Chile was invited this week to join the Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development as its 31st member, the first country from South America to join the club of mostly wealthy free-market democracies.

title: ANALYSIS- Chile central bank  may  intervene  in peso rally
text:
* Intervention seen if 30 percent rally continues

* Any intervention seen slowing rally, not stopping it

* Dollar abroad, copper prices to determine direction

By Maria Jose Latorre

SANTIAGO, Nov 27 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank may make good on threats to intervene in the foreign exchange market to curb a peso rally of around 30 percent against the dollar if it continues much longer, analysts say.

Chile's peso has been one of the best performing emerging market currencies against the U.S. dollar this year, rallying to 16-month highs despite the central bank's warnings about a rapid appreciation so far this year that is hurting exporters.

The peso closed flat on Friday at 493.00/493.50 per dollar, clawing back after tumbling to around 500 pesos per dollar in early trade as investors cut risk exposure on Dubai debt woes and pile into the dollar.

But the peso has steadily advanced in recent months, and some analysts say the central bank could opt to intervene if it hits 480 per dollar, while others think the bank could wait until it hits 450 per dollar.

The local market expects any intervention to be similar to that of 2008 when the central bank built up reserves through a dollar purchase program after the peso rose to 430 per dollar.

The peso ultimately closed 2008 down 22.3 percent against the dollar, battered by global financial crisis.

"(Intervention) might be seen sooner rather than later due to continued peso strength over the past several sessions," said Alfredo Coutino, Latin America director for Moody's Economy.com.

The peso has gained in the wake of wider dollar weakness against other global currencies, gains in prices for Chile's No. 1 export, copper, and as investors who borrowed pesos at low interest rates to buy dollars to invest in Brazil closed positions.

Central Bank President Jose De Gregorio has said Chile's free-floating system allows for possible intervention in extreme cases and has warned the bank has not ruled out doing so in future.

"Central banks usually issue a verbal warning first," said Alejandro Puente, head economist with Banco BBVA Chile. "So it's possible it could move to the next phase and eventually decide to intervene in the currency market."

SWIMMING AGAINST THE TIDE?

However, analysts say intervention may only give short-term relief given the dollar's wider depreciation and rising copper prices. Chile's peso tends to gain in tandem with prices of copper, which have rebounded sharply from a slump during global crisis.

"You have to see where the peso is headed compared with what's happening to copper prices and what's happening to the dollar internationally," said Alberto Ramos, senior economist with Goldman Sachs in New York.

"What the central bank has done in the past is simply to announce a dollar purchase program, something very transparent and characteristic of this central bank," he added.

The central bank is keeping a close eye on the sharp appreciation of the peso and its inflationary implications, according to minutes of the bank's November monetary policy meeting published on Friday.

"You can't go thinking the central bank can change the trend. However, it can help slow an appreciation of the peso which is out of line with fundamentals," said Guillermo Pattillo, an economist at the University of Santiago.

Some analysts also wonder if the finance ministry could take measures to help sap peso strength, though Finance Minister Andres Velasco has said the government will do its part by raising the ceiling for peso debt issuance in 2010. title: UPDATE: Chile Peso Closes Weaker On Dollar Rally Against Euro
text:
(Updates with details of daily central bank dollar sale.) 
 

By Carolina Pica

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean peso ended slightly weaker against the U.S. dollar Friday on the greenback's rally against the euro in international markets.

The peso ended at CLP501.30 to the dollar compared with CLP500.70 the previous session, after moving in a broad range of CLP500.60 to CLP507.60.

The dollar held on to its gains against the euro and other higher-yielding currencies Friday morning as revived concerns about how fast the global economy will rebound prompted investors to shun riskier assets. The peso often moves in the same direction the euro does against the dollar.

Losses in U.S. stock markets and lower London copper prices also contributed to the peso's tumble, traders said.

Earlier in the week, the Chilean currency had been trading at 16-month highs against the dollar, but the dollar's recent gains and comments from the head of the Central Bank of Chile that the bank couldn't rule out intervening in the market pulled the currency below the CLP500-mark.

The peso is trading about 22% stronger against the dollar from where it began the year, fueling exporters and farmers to ask for central bank intervention in the market to weaken the currency. Exporters say their products are losing competitiveness abroad, while farmers say they'll lose money this season on the stronger peso.

In its daily sales on behalf of the Finance Ministry, the central bank sold $40 million at a weighted average of CLP506.16 to the dollar. The monetary authority doesn't provide information on which banks bid for dollar sales.

Earlier in the year, the Finance Ministry began a $4 billion sale, repatriated from one of its sovereign-wealth funds, in the local market. The ministry is selling the $4 billion to finance this year's expected fiscal deficit, at a rate of $40 million a day.

Traders said a fresh central bank warning on Thursday of possible intervention to curb peso appreciation of around 27 percent against the dollar year-to-date added only marginal pressure to the currency.

The dollar rose abroad on Friday, extending gains from the previous session as investors shied away from riskier assets, while murmurs of capital controls weighed on some emerging markets.

Russia's rouble continued to retreat from 2009 highs on central bank rhetoric about possible measures and rate cuts to stem speculative capital flows, while Brazil's real continued to depreciate a day after weakening on concerns over a new government tax aimed at curbing the currency's sharp appreciation.

SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chile's Central Bank doesn't rule out more intervention in the foreign exchange market to weaken the local currency, Central Bank President Jose De Gregorio said Thursday.

The Chilean peso has been trading at a 16-month high against the U.S. dollar, prompting exporters to call for market intervention to weaken the currency as their products lose competitiveness abroad.

Higher international copper prices and the euro's gains against the dollar have been contributing forces in the peso's gains.

In prepared remarks at a central bank conference, De Gregorio said the bank intervened in April 2008 when the exchange rate was "over appreciated" and "strengthening international liquidity by way of accumulating reserves made sense."

The intervention was suspended in September 2008 because of the lack of liquidity in the market caused by the international financial crisis.

"In the future, we won't rule out intervening again," De Gregorio said.

The currency reacted to the central banker's comments, and to the dollar's gains against the euro on international markets, and closed 1.6% weaker from the previous session.
