title: UPDATE 2- Chile  cenbank does not rule out peso  intervention
text:
* Central bank renews intervention warning

* Peso up almost 30 percent vs US dollar year-to-date (Updates with peso close, regional comparisons)

By Alonso Soto

SANTIAGO, Nov 19 (Reuters) - Chilean Central Bank President Jose De Gregorio said on Thursday that he is not ruling out intervening in the country's foreign currency market, which has seen the Chilean peso <CLP=CL>, soar 28 percent against the U.S. dollar this year.

"We do not rule out intervening again in the future," De Gregorio said at the bank's annual conference in Santiago, reiterating a warning he made last week.

The peso has been one of the highest-performing emerging market currencies this year against a weaker dollar and is trading around 16-month highs. Some analysts expect the central bank to intervene if the peso reaches 480 per dollar.

Chile's peso slid more than 1.6 percent on Thursday, its biggest one-day percentage fall in nearly 7 months, easing on broad-based dollar strength, global stock losses and lower prices for copper, the country's No. 1 export.

Traders said the peso, which was already down around 1 percent before De Gregorio's comments, was unfazed by the fresh threat of central bank intervention and even firmed initially after he spoke, though his comments were seen underpinning a continued slide later in the session.

Traders said the fall was not influenced by weakness in the Brazilian real after that country announced a new, 1.5 percent tax when overseas investors convert U.S.-listed shares of Brazilian companies into local shares. That move drove other emerging market currencies lower as investors worried about the introduction of capital controls to stem speculative flows.

"In economies with inflation targets, the first line of defense is monetary policy," De Gregorio said. "If there is a persistent appreciation, with deflationary consequences, the apt response would be a relaxation of monetary policy, reducing pressure on the appreciation," De Gregorio said.

"However, this is not always enough, and for that reason you can also use sterilized interventions in the foreign exchange market," he added.

De Gregorio had warned last week that the bank was monitoring the exchange rate very closely and that Chile's free-float system left room for intervention in extreme circumstances.

FRESH INTERVENTION ON CARDS?

Last year, the central bank intervened in the currency market through a dollar purchase program to build up its reserves, after the peso rose to 430 per dollar.

The bank held its benchmark overnight lending rate steady at 0.50 percent last week, saying that the rate would remain at that level until at least the second quarter. The bank also said it would relax complementary stimulus measures but hinted at a more gradual recovery in the economy of the world's top copper producer.

The bank said it would gradually reduce the term of a liquidity facility for banks, unveiled in July in a bid to help fend off the global crisis, and end the facility in May 2010.

Chile's central bank is targeting inflation of 3 percent over a two-year horizon, and has slashed its key rate by 775 basis points since the beginning of the year, leading the charge to cut rates in Latin America.

Beyond verbal warnings to the market, analysts say the central bank's options included buying dollars and issuing bonds to absorb the extra peso liquidity.

Another option would be for a non-sterilized intervention, whereby the central bank buys dollars to inject peso liquidity while unwinding credit facilities at a stepped-up rate to mitigate the affects of the intervention.

Third quarter gross domestic product data released on Wednesday showed Chile's economy was turning the corner on global crisis.

On an annual basis, Chile's third-quarter GDP shrank 1.6 percent from the year-earlier quarter, slowing the pace of decline from a revised 4.7 percent drop in the second quarter.

But GDP in the third quarter grew 1.1 percent from the second quarter, as calculated on a seasonally adjusted basis.

The central bank forecast Chile's economy will contract 1.5 percent to 2 percent this year after the global slowdown curbed international copper demand but sees growth next year of 4.5 percent to 5.5 percent. (Writing by Simon Gardner; Editing by Padraic Cassidy)

title: Chile peso rallies past 500/dlr, nears 16-mo high
text:
* Chile peso breaks 500/dlr psychological barrier

* Firm copper prices, end of carry trades boost peso

* Gov't again warns to keep close eye on currency

* Cenbank seen heightening warnings before intervention

By Froilan Romero

SANTIAGO, Nov 16 (Reuters) - Chile's peso <CLP=CL> rose to a near 16-month high on Monday, breaking the psychological 500 per dollar level on carry trade closures and higher copper prices, despite warnings of possible central bank intervention.

The peso firmed 1.1 percent to close at 496.30/496.80 per dollar, slightly off the day's highs. The peso closed at 501.80/502.10 per U.S. dollar on Friday.

Finance Minister Andres Velasco on Monday again signaled that the government was keeping a close eye on the country's peso after the central bank warned it could intervene to stem a sharp appreciation of the local currency.

"The government is closely watching the exchange rate," Velasco said, repeating a warning he had made on Thursday.

"Last week, we took measures during the passage of the budget, when we practically doubled the ceiling for debt issuance so the next government has an alternative and can avoid selling dollars and instead issue peso bonds if it wishes," he added.

Goldman Sachs senior economist, Alberto Ramos, said the central bank would likely refrain from an outright intervention and keep warning the market if the peso keeps gaining ground.

"It is still too early to talk about intervention. Certainly you can see some verbal intervention because the appreciation is still a recent phenomenon, and it's not disassociated from a global weak dollar," Ramos said.

"They will probably wait until the peso crosses 475 or 450 (per dollar), in territory were the overvaluation is very clear."

He said the bank intervention could entail direct purchases of U.S. dollar in the market.

FIRM COPPER BOOSTS PESO

Traders said the peso was propelled by firm prices for No.1 export copper, which hit its highest level in more than 13 months on the London Metal Exchange on Monday <MCU3> at around $6,830 a tonne, boosted by a weak dollar, and bad weather in major metals consumer China and improving Japanese growth data.

"The fundamentals are very positive. Copper prices are at new highs in London and the markets have firmed significantly," said one trader, asking not to be named.

"At a local level, we continue to see inflows of dollars as investors end carry trades," he added.

Until recently, many carry trade investors borrowed in Chilean pesos at low interest rates and used the proceeds to buy dollars on the Chilean market to invest in Brazil, where rates are higher.

In closing these trades, the investors must buy Chilean pesos to repay those peso-denominated loans.

Copper is Chile's No.1 export and strong copper prices tend to underpin the local currency.

Traders said a 24 percent rise in Chile's copper export revenues to $2.48 billion in October compared with $2.0 billion in the same month a year ago, also helped buoy the peso.

The currency has gained around 28 percent so far this year, making it one of the world's best-performing emerging market currencies. (With reporting by Maria Jose Latorre. Writing by Alonso Soto, Editing by Chizu Nomiyama)

title: LATIN AMERICAN MARKETS: Brazil Stocks Drop; Chile Rate Decision On Tap
text:
A broad-based sell-off hit Brazilian equities Thursday, with investors taking gains from a three-session winning streak off the table as a downturn in prices for resources pressured commodity-related heavyweights.

Brazil's Bovespa equity index fell 3% to 64,447.93 as shares in consumer staple companies, home builders, telecommunication-services provider and miners were the worst performers of the session.

Meatpacker JBS (JBSAY) dropped 6.5% and air carrier TAM (TAM) fell 6%, pacing decliners.

Mining giant Vale (RIO) shares dropped 4.1%, Gerdau (GGB) fell 4.3% and MMX Mineracao lost 4.7%. The steel producer reported a third-quarter net loss of 27.2 million reals, narrower than its loss in the year-ago period.

Shares of Petrobras (PBR), the most heavily weighted on the Bovespa index, slumped 2% as crude-oil futures slid 3% to below $76.94 a barrel. Crude prices fell after U.S. government data showed weak demand and higher inventories.

Separately, Petrobras' third-quarter results are due late Friday.

Prices for crude, as well as for silver, copper and platinum, were also pressured on Thursday because of rise in the U.S. dollar against its key rivals. The greenback found support after U.S. Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner said the government's borrowing needs would be less than it had anticipated. The dollar index (DXY) rose 0.6%.

But back in Sao Paulo, shares of Lojas Renner climbed 2.3% after MSCI Barra said the department-store operator will be added to its MSCI Emerging Markets Index.

Shares of Banco do Brasil were one of the few advancers on Thursday, rising 0.2% after the state-run bank said third-quarter earnings rose 6%.

In Santiago, Chile's IPSA fell 0.9% ahead of the central bank's decision on interest rates. The central bank is widely expected to hold its key rate at the ultra-low level of 0.5%.

The key issue for investors will be what the central bank will do with its liquidity facility, according to RBS Securities. Policymakers in late October outlined gradual phasing of 28-day repo operations with flexible collateral and foreign-exchange swap operations.

"The strength of the [Chilean peso] has triggered some rumors that the [central bank] will not only phase out the FX swaps quickly but that it could even start intervening in the market to curb the appreciating trend," wrote RBS Securities economist Benito Berber in a note to clients Thursday.

According to media reports Wednesday, Jose de Gregorio, the president of Chile's central bank, said the bank is considering a possible intervention aimed at cooling the peso's rise.

Chile's peso recently reached a 15-month high against the U.S. dollar.

MSCI bulks up Brazil's index presence

Index provider MSCI Barra late Wednesday, as part of its semiannual review, said that 11 Brazilian companies will be added to its MSCI Emerging Markets Index. The additions are the most for one country, followed by China, which will see seven issues added and one deleted. The index tracks issues from 22

Brazil's PDG Realty and Lojas Renner will be the largest additions to the index. The changes will be in effect as of the close of Nov. 30.

The heftier representation of Brazilian companies on the index arrives as Brazil's Bovespa has surged 72% this year as investors seek exposure to Latin America's largest economy. The country was the first in the region to emerge out of recession.

At the same time, Brazil has been working to curb a surge in its currency and "can only see its challenges exacerbated by the MSCI decision," in part because not all of the new companies being added to the EM index have U.S.-listed shares or dual listings, said Marc Chandler, global head of currency strategy at Brown Brothers Harriman, in a note to clients Thursday.

Brazilian officials have reportedly been considering extending measures to pull back the currency's rise. Last month, Brazil levied a 2% tax on all foreign purchases of stocks and fixed-income assets.

More than $3 trillion are benchmarked against its indexes worldwide, estimates MSCI. [ 11-12-09 1915ET ]

Analysts say the central bank's options included so-called sterilized intervention, whereby the central bank buys dollars and issues bonds to absorb the extra peso liquidity.

title: Chile ups public sector wages, peso seen easing
text:
SANTIAGO, Nov 12 (Reuters) - Chile's Senate approved a 4.5 percent salary hike for around 500,000 public sector employees late on Wednesday, a move analysts said should help ease pressure on a sharply appreciating peso.

Public sector employees have staged a series of strikes and protests in recent weeks to demand higher wages.

Local media reported the 4.5 percent hike ranks as the largest increase in two decades, after factoring inflation data.

On an annual basis, the consumer price index fell 1.9 percent in the 12 months through October, the National Statistics Institute said last week.

The civil servants' wage hike comes as Chile's peso is trading at 15 month highs after surging around 26 percent year-to-date, and as the central bank has warned it could intervene to weaken the local currency.

"In Chile's case, there have been no red lights or anything to suggest there is fiscal disorder," said Pedro Tuesta, senior analyst with market research company 4CAST in Washington D.C.

"Increased government spending usually generates greater aggregate demand, and that generates more demand for imports," he added. "We know the government and central bank are worried about the exchange rate and an increase in aggregate demand will always help halt the appreciation of a currency."

The peso <CLP=CL> closed at 507.00/507.50 per U.S. dollar on Wednesday, the strongest close since August 2008, though was slightly weaker in early Thursday trade.

SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean central bank doesn't rule out intervening in the peso market if the local currency were to show a significant fluctuation, the bank's president told a group of manufacturing sector exporters Wednesday.

Chile, whose economy is largely dependent on commodity-related and other types of exports, has seen its currency firm around 15% so far this year.

Exporters blame the Finance Ministry's decision to repatriate a total of $7 billion from one of its sovereign wealth funds.

Chile switched to a free-floating exchange rate from a central bank-set trading band in the late 1990s, a change which the central banker praised.

"All of the financial crises since the 1960s have all been linked to the defense of the peso," bank president Jose De Gregorio told exporters linked to the Asexma trade group.

He added that the central bank would only intervene in light of unusual market circumstances.

In 2008, when the peso strengthened to 10-year highs against the dollar, the central bank took market-intervening measures, including daily dollar sales on the local market.

"Last year we intervened because we saw that the peso was affecting [the economy] at the aggregate level," De Gregorio said.

With regards to gross domestic product growth, De Gregorio reiterated previous comments that the economy will likely recover in the second half of the year.

Third-quarter GDP results will likely be worse than the same quarter last year, but will likely be up from the second quarter of this year, he said.

"Market expectations show an outlook for increased dynamism in the second half of the year," he said in prepared remarks.

First-quarter GDP fell 2.1% on the year. Second-quarter GDP will likely contract about 4%, according to preliminary data. The central bank will release second-quarter GDP data in August.

title: Chile Banking Regulator: Financial System Liquidity Normal
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Liquidity in Chile's financial system is at normal levels, and the system "is functioning with normal parameters," Chile's SBIF banking regulator said Friday.

In the past two weeks, the central bank has adopted several measures to maintain dollar liquidity in the local market. In addition, the Finance Ministry placed a total $1 billion in local dollar-denominated certificates of deposit, which also eased greenback liquidity.

"Banking institutions have sufficient liquidity both in local and foreign currency," the SBIF said in a statement, adding that the central bank and Finance Ministry moves helped with dollar liquidity.

The regulator said that Chile's financial system is obviously a part of the globalized economy and that it's still part of international economic cycles.

"We can affirm, however, that the fundamentals that support our banking industry allow us to calmly observe its capacity to resist the negative moments of the cycle," the regulator said.

The SBIF will continue to closely monitor any international events or moves for their repercussions on the local system, it said.

Analysts say Chile's banks are on more solid ground than banks in other countries as banking regulation was tightened after a banking crisis in the 1980s, when several failing banks were intervened.

Chile's central bank still holds a small stake in Banco de Chile (BCH), the country's second-largest bank in terms of loans, as part of the 1980s bailout.

TPM Rate History (annual percentage): 
Jan    Dec    Nov   Oct    Sep   Aug   July  June  May 
3.25%  3.25%  3.0%  2.75%  2.5%  2.0%  1.5%  1.0%  0.5% 
 
 
  By Anthony Esposito 
  Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Following a recently announced $12 billion currency-market intervention program for 2011, the Chilean central bank held its benchmark interest rate steady on Thursday.

At its monthly monetary policy meeting Thursday, the bank kept the benchmark overnight rate, known locally as the TPM, at 3.25%, the bank's first pause since it started withdrawing its monetary stimulus in June last year following the massive stimulus that began in 2009.

Only half of the 10 analysts polled earlier in the week by Dow Jones Newswires saw the bank pausing its rate increases, while the other half expected the central bank to raise the TPM 25 basis points to 3.5%.

The monetary authority pointed out that its program to increase its foreign currency reserves by $12 billion this year has weakened the peso versus the dollar.

In the first days following the announcement of the currency-market intervention on Jan. 3, the peso lost over 7% against the dollar, although it has regained some territory in recent sessions as international copper prices rise.

The central bank said that private expectations for inflation have risen, particularly in the short term.

Earlier this week, the central bank released its monthly analysts' survey of economic expectations and its bi-weekly traders' survey. Both surveys showed private-sector inflation expectations have increased, with analysts seeing 3.6% inflation by the end of the year.

The outlook is higher than the central bank's 3.3% year-end inflation expectations.

Core inflation remains limited, though, the central bank's post-meeting communique said.

The core consumer price index gained 0.3% in December from the previous month. For the year, core CPI, which factors out volatile fresh produce and fuel prices, rose 2.5% on the year.

The central bank reiterated that it will be necessary to continue removing the monetary stimulus in coming months, although the "rhythm will depend on domestic and external macroeconomic conditions."

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Chile's peso up on rate move, Mexican peso dips
text:
* Brazil's real and Chilean peso both gain 0.5 pct

* Mexican peso dips 0.2 pct after U.S. jobs data

(Adds comments, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Maria Jose Latorre

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Jan 13 (Reuters) - Chile's currency firmed on Thursday, helped by bets the central bank would hike interest rates, drawing in yield-hungry investors even as policymakers intervene to weaken the currency.

Chile and Brazil's currencies were also supported by successful bond auctions in Spain and Italy that helped to ease euro zone fiscal concerns, while Mexico's peso dipped on a rise in U.S. jobless claims.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> firmed 0.47 percent to 488.20 per dollar as some investors in a divided market bet that Chile's central bank will hike its benchmark interest rate for the eighth consecutive time later on Thursday. [ID:nN13261867c]

"There should be an increase of 25 points," said Rodrigo Sarria, a trader at Celfin Capital in Santiago. "And we should keep seeing increases from here onward, especially because of the inflation pressures," he added.

Others think policymakers will leave borrowing costs steady so as not to lure even more hot money to the country and undermine the $12 billion intervention plan launched last week that knocked the peso off a nearly three year high.

Broadly supporting bids for riskier assets, Spain sold 3 billion euros of five-year bonds, raising the maximum amount targeted. Italy's auction of 5- and 15-year government bonds also went well. [ID:nLDE70C0IA].

The Brazilian real <BRBY> was bid 0.48 percent stronger at 1.667 reais per U.S. dollar on the local spot market.

"The worries over Europe are diminishing a little... I'm not seeing any real difference to yesterday, we're continuing on the same track," said Alfredo Barbutti, an economist at the BGC Liquidez brokerage in Sao Paulo.

However, investors were reluctant to push the currency much higher in case it triggered more aggressive government intervention in the market, he said.

MEXICAN PESO RETREATS FROM 2-YR HIGH

The Mexican currency <MXN=> slipped 0.21 percent to 12.0965 per dollar after jobless claims in the United States, Mexico's main trading partner, jumped to their highest level since October. [ID:nN13271305]

The news helped weaken the peso after the currency hit its strongest level since Oct. 2008 in the previous session. But overall, U.S. data was mixed, with higher producer prices and a jump in U.S. exports.

"The fact that there was inflation in the United States tells you the economy is recovering and it is not all bad," said Antonio Magana, head of currency trading at brokerage Interacciones.

The peso has won favor among investors since it is one of the few currencies in the region which is not at risk from intervention.

However, Mexico's free-market orthodoxy has not been challenged too much with the peso barely clawing back from pre-crisis levels.

If the peso reaches 11.50 per dollar, the Mexican central bank could take measures similar to Chile's dollar-buying plan, said Benito Berber, an economist at Nomura in New York.

title: UPDATE:OppenheimerFunds Cuts Brazil, Mexico Sovereign-Debt Exposure
text:
(Updates with firm's complete name in first paragraph.)


 
   By Anjali Cordeiro 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--OppenheimerFunds's emerging-market bond funds have sold all their Mexican and Brazilian sovereign-debt holdings, and are paring exposure to currencies of countries intervening in foreign-exchange markets, a senior portfolio manager for the firm said in an interview.

Sara Zervos--who oversees about $11 billion in emerging-market debt for OppenheimerFunds and is among the biggest emerging-market portfolio managers in the U.S.--said her funds have reduced their exposure to Chile's peso and Brazil's real as central bankers in these countries take steps to prevent their currencies from appreciating.

The funds she manages cut their exposure to Brazil and Mexico sovereign bonds at the end of last year because they see little room for substantial returns on these assets, whose spreads with Treasurys are already narrow. In search of higher returns in emerging markets, her emerging-market teams are moving more money to higher yielding emerging-market corporate debt. For exposure to Brazil and Mexico, her funds now own only corporate debt from those countries.

Zervos's funds can also invest in local currency bonds to get exposure to a country's currency and benefit from any potential appreciation. Her funds are increasing their exposure to the South African rand, partly because it stands to benefit from increased demand for commodities.

Zervos's comments highlight the changing landscape that emerging-market fund managers are facing as money rushes into these fast-growing regions. As more money has moved to the developing world, spreads between emerging-market sovereign bonds and Treasurys have tightened significantly, making it harder to project big returns on such investments. Meanwhile, the surge in capital flows to developing countries has driven up their currencies, pushing local policymakers in countries from Brazil to Chile to intervene in foreign-exchange markets. That is making emerging-market investing more challenging.

"Last year was a pure rebound year, extending from 2009. We got through the double-dip fear and then it was all ships ahead," she said. "But this year we are worried about intervention, we are worried about central banks being behind the curve and it makes the outlook much trickier."

Earlier in January, Chile's central bank announced that it would intervene in the local currency market with plans to increase its foreign currency reserves by $12 billion in 2011 in an effort to hold down the peso and assuage the worries of Chile's exporters.

Zervos, who is based in New York, said her funds had a small exposure to Chile's peso, which she completely erased right after the intervention was announced, even though she has a strong fundamental outlook for the Chilean peso. Along similar lines she has cut back exposure her funds have to the Brazilian real via local currency bonds, bringing down that allocation to marketweight from overweight.

Brazil's central bank recently moved to reduce the size of banks' bets in the foreign-exchange market to protect the financial system and investors have grown more concerned that the government will be more aggressive in halting the currency's gain.

"There might be every macro reason in the world to love the Brazilian currency, but the randomness of policy to try and stop appreciation makes us want to have a smaller position," Zervos said.

Zervos, an emerging-markets veteran, is portfolio manager of the Oppenheimer International Bond Fund, Oppenheimer Emerging Markets Debt Fund, and Oppenheimer Global Strategic Income Fund. Her comments underscore how countries risk pushing even longer term investors away when they intervene in foreign-exchange markets.

"I tend to be more overweight stories with good fundamentals plus lack of intervention," she said. She is bullish on the Mexican peso on expectations that the U.S. economy will keep recovering and pull Mexico with it. Also, Mexican authorities don't interfere with the currency.

Zervos says despite her more cautious tone on Brazilian sovereign bonds, she is bullish on corporate debt from the country. "That's where the best bang for the buck is," she said, referring to high yield emerging-market corporate bonds.

-By Anjali Cordeiro, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2200; anjali.cordeiro@dowjones.com [ 12-01-11 1852GMT ]

title: Chile  Peso Ends 1.2% Stronger Despite  Intervention , As Copper Rises
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chile's peso ended 1.2% stronger against the dollar Wednesday, despite the central bank's ongoing currency market intervention program, as international copper prices jumped.

The peso ended at CLP490.20 to the dollar, compared with Tuesday's close of CLP496.30, while trading in a range of CLP490.20 to CLP495.10.

As Chile is the world's premier copper producer, accounting for nearly a third of global supply, the peso often takes cues from the metal's international prices. Spot copper prices in London jumped 1.5% to $4.36583 per pound, according to Chile's state copper commission Cochilco, after an encouraging Portuguese bond auction bolstered the demand outlook for the metal.

Also, the chief executive of Chilean state copper giant Corporacion Nacional del Cobre's expectation that copper will average $4 a pound this year helped to boost the peso.

"His forecast likely helped to support the peso's rise," said a local currency trader.

With the peso recently trading at 32-month highs against the dollar and exporters demanding help as the local currency's strength puts their competitiveness at risk, the central bank stepped in to increase its foreign currency reserves by $12 billion this year.

Before the peso rose Tuesday, it had lost 7.1% against the dollar since Jan. 3, when the central bank announced the program.

During the first phase of the intervention program, the central bank will make daily purchases of $50 million between Jan. 5 and Feb. 9.

On Wednesday, the central bank purchased $50 million on the local market at an average rate of CLP494.77 to the dollar, on the sixth day of the bank's intervention program.

So far the monetary authority has purchased $300 million through its program.

Over the coming weeks, traders see the peso trading in a narrow range of CLP490 to CLP500.

"Participants are looking for levels to buy dollars, which will bring the exchange rate to around CLP500 in the short to medium term," the currency trader said.

In the bond market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central bank bonds, or BCUs, ended lower in light over-the-counter trading.

The yield on five-year BCU bonds ended at 2.80%, from 2.82% on Tuesday, while the yield on 10-year BCUs closed at 3.19%, from 3.24% the prior session.

title: UPDATE 2- Chile  peso extends post- intervention  rebound
text:
* Peso seen stabilizing below 490 per dollar

* A fresh central bank rate hike would boost rally (Updates with peso close, adds byline)

By Froilan Romero

SANTIAGO, Jan 12 (Reuters) - Chile's peso <CLP=CL> rose more than 1 percent on Wednesday, extending a post-intervention rebound from four-month lows hit this week, driven by strong prices for main export copper.

The peso on Tuesday broke a five-day slide that followed a $12 billion currency intervention plan introduced last week as the peso neared three-year highs. The peso firmed 1.2 percent on Wednesday to close at 490.40/490.90 per dollar.

Chile, the world's No. 1 copper producer, has followed Brazil, Peru and Colombia in moving to rein in its currency as investments pour into the fast-growing emerging markets.

"With all the markets positive and the dollar weak abroad, demand for dollars dried up and now it's expected to stabilize under 490 pesos per dollar," said one currency trader.

The peso has depreciated around 5 percent against the dollar since the intervention began.

A central bank poll released on Wednesday showed a majority of traders expect the bank to raise its benchmark interest rate <CLINTR=ECI> by 25 basis points to 3.5 percent at Thursday's rate-setting meeting. For details, see [ID:nSAG002686]

title: RPT-EMERGING MARKETS-Mexican peso hits 8-month high, Brazil lags
text:
(Repeats to additional subscribers)

* Mexican peso gains 0.6 pct, Chilean peso up 0.6 pct

* Brazil's real dips 0.06 pct as intervention fears weigh (Adds comments, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Michael O'Boyle

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Jan 11 (Reuters) - Mexico's peso jumped to an 8-month high on Tuesday, helped by surprisingly strong local industrial output data.

Chile's currency firmed after rising copper prices helped reverse some of the recent losses from a central bank intervention launched last week, while Brazil's currency was held back by concerns of further meddling in markets.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> strengthened 0.6 percent to 12.1400 per dollar, hitting its strongest level since April of last year, helped by data that showed local factories were gaining momentum at the end of 2010 as U.S. demand picked up. [ID:nN11130858]

"It seems that industrial production continues to do well and domestic consumption is picking up," said Benito Berber, an economist at Nomura in New York.

The Mexican currency was poised to post an over two-year high if it firms a bit past 12.13 per dollar.

Berber said the peso could have some trouble breaking past option barriers around 12.10 per dollar. However, if the currency pierces that level, the peso could quickly firm past 12 per dollar.

"The forecasts that are calling for the peso to trade below 12 per dollar are likely to be reached in the first quarter," Berber said.

In the short term, other analysts said that too many investors may have piled into the Mexican peso trade, too quickly, leaving the currency open to profit-taking in the short term.

"The Mexican trade is pretty crowded," said Flavia Cattan-Naslausky, a strategist at RBS Securities in New York. "We need to take a breather here before we take another move."

INTERVENTION LOOMS

Brazil's real underperformed Latin American currencies on Tuesday as the threat of more aggressive intervention in the Brazilian market weighed on the real <BRBY>, which bid only 0.06 percent stronger at 1.685 per dollar.

Brazil's finance minister, Guido Mantega, said Monday he was sure the country's currency would not strengthen further, adding that intervention via so-called reverse swaps in the futures market would carry little financial risk. [ID:nN10282474]

If reverse swaps are used, the real could weaken to 1.75-1.77 per dollar, according to one New York-based head currency trader.

The government has taken a number of measures to try to put the brakes on the real's recent gains, including a new reserve requirement on banks' short U.S. dollar positions.

"Mantega's threats went largely ignored by the market, though he is making it quite clear that policymakers will fight very hard against any further BRL appreciation," said Nick Chamie of RBC in a research note.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> firmed 0.6 percent to 496.50 per dollar, helped by higher prices for copper, the country's main export.

"The peso's performance here is mainly following what is going on abroad," said Rodrigo Sarria, a trader at Celfin Capital in Santiago.

"We have copper going up, so we should see the market here trying to test new levels. We could see corrections between 15 and 18 pesos in the next few days, which would be half of how much the peso fell following intervention," he added.

Chile's peso slumped last week after the central bank announced a massive dollar-buying plan to curb its strength. For more, see: [ID:nN1124735]. (Additional reporting by Maria Jose Latorre in Santiago; Editing by Dan Grebler)

title: Chile Central Bank :  Currency Intervention  Program Working
text:
BASEL, Switzerland (Dow Jones)--Capital controls and currency interventions undertaken by a number of emerging nations are a by-product of the two-tier growth of the global economy, but they won't change the long-term course of these currencies, the governor of the central bank of Chile said Monday.

"There is so much tension in the foreign-exchange market that what we are doing in a way is to stabilize the sharp appreciation of the currency. But we won't change the long-term fundamentals...the adjustments will take place," Jose de Gregorio told reporters on the sidelines of a gathering of central bankers in Basel at the Bank for International Settlements.

Several emerging countries have imposed capital controls at their borders or intervened on foreign-exchange markets in order to curb the value of their currencies, pushed up by a surge in foreign capital inflows in search of higher remuneration against a backdrop of record low interest rates in the developed world.

At their meeting in Basel, central bankers agreed that these sharp inflows of capital are an issue for emerging markets. De Gregorio said they are a reflection of the "world's dual recovery," with emerging economies experiencing buoyant growth, while more mature ones are only witnessing a subdued pickup in activity.

The central Bank of Chile last week launched a $12 billion currency market intervention program in order to tame the peso's appreciation and prevent exports from being stifled.

De Gregorio said the program, which will beef up the country's foreign-exchange reserves, will help make Chile more resilient in the event of an external shock and is also giving the Chilean economy some breathing space to improve its competitiveness.

"The program is currently working," he said, adding that the Chilean central bank isn't targeting a specific level for the peso through the intervention.

France, which currently heads the Group of 20 industrialized and emerging economies, argues erratic capital flows can create currency volatility and disrupt the monetary policies of emerging countries. It wants the group to explore ways to better regulate them.

While De Gregorio said the central bank would consider any measure to further help stabilizing the Chilean economy, he stressed there was no need at the moment to expand the market intervention program or to use any other policy tools. He added that the currency intervention program will be assessed on an ongoing basis, and vowed it won't compromise the central bank's inflation target.

The program is designed in such a way "that we feel independent to move our interest rates as needed to fulfil our inflation objectives," De Gregorio told reporters.

-By Nathalie Boschat, Dow Jones Newswires; +33 (0) 1 40 17 17 45; nathalie.boschat@dowjones.com [ 01-10-11 1155ET ]

title: Chile  c.bank chief: no plan to up peso  intervention
text:
BASEL, Jan 10 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank has no plans to increase the size of its $12 billion programme aimed at curbing the rise of the peso but the intervention will not solve the problem of underlying appreciation pressure, its governor said on Monday.

Jose de Gregorio said recent interventions had had the intended impact but added that currency tensions were likely to remain as the country's economy improves at a faster rate than those in more developed regions.

"The programme has two components: one is the objective of reserve accumulation and we have stated that 12 billion is an appropriate figure. That's what we are planning to do as interventions and no further plans of changing that amount," he told reporters on the sidelines of a meeting of central bankers.

"We have been very clear that this has no permanent effect. As long as the world remains in the state as it is now we need some domestic adjustment because the tensions will persist." (Reporting by Marc Jones and Sven Egenter; editing by Patrick Graham)

title: Emerging-Mkt Debt Move Little Against Tsys;  Currencies  Mixed
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging-market debt saw little change on Monday against Treasurys, which continued to rise on the euro zone's sovereign-debt concerns, while key Latin American currencies saw mixed results after initial losses.

On Monday afternoon, the risk premium, or spread, on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global, or Embig, widened just three basis points to 285 basis points over U.S. Treasurys. In price terms, the index slipped 0.16% on the day.

Worries that Portugal's debt woes could spread to larger economies in the euro zone drove investors toward U.S. Treasurys and made them more cautious about riskier assets in emerging markets.

Investors are still holding long positions on emerging-market debt, said Paul Biszko, analyst with RBC Capital Markets.

"There's some hesitation or caution to add to those positions in recent weeks ... given the uncertainties on the euro-zone front," he added.

Mexico was in focus as its National Statistics Institute, or Inegi, reported Monday that its global economic activity indicator rose 4.3% on the year in October. The increase, however, marked a slowdown from the previous months as the rebound in industrial production lost steam, while growth in services picked up.

Analysts still expect Mexico to have a good growth year in 2011, nonetheless.

"Only major accidents around the world will keep Mexico's economy growing below trend," said Bulltick Research in a note.

On the Embig, Mexico's spread barely changed, tightening just one basis point to 154 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms, its index was flat.

Mexico's peso, meanwhile, pared back earlier losses, as it stood nearly flat at MXN12.2145 against the dollar Monday afternoon.

Brazil's debt also saw little change on the Embig; its spread widened a modest two basis points over Treasurys. Its index was flat.

Brazil's real, however, weakened significantly on expectations of further currency interventions. The real slid 0.32% to BRL1.6878 Monday afternoon, from BRL1.6825 the previous day.

On Monday, the Brazilian government authorized the use of the sovereign fund to take on a role in both the spot market and the futures market for the real, raising speculation the government may start using reverse swap auctions to try to stem the appreciation of the real.

A reverse swap auction is a form of intervention in the foreign exchange futures market. At the auction, the central bank swaps futures contracts linked to foreign-exchange positions to contracts indexed to interest rates.

A Deutsche Bank report cited Moody's analyst Mauro Leos on Monday as saying Brazil's rating could be considered for an upgrade in April, "as long as the government curbs spending to meet its fiscal target and acts against inflation."

Chile's currency intervention efforts also continue, with the central bank purchasing $50 million on the local market Monday as part of its program to increase its foreign currency reserves by $12 billion this year.

The Chilean peso ended at CLP498.60 to the dollar, compared with Friday's close of CLP497.60. It was the first session the peso weakened in intraday trading to the CLP500 level since early September.

On the Embig, Chile's spread widened by seven basis points to 121 basis points over Treasurys. Its index dropped 0.33%.

Venezuela's spread also changed by slightly wider margins, by seven basis points to 1142 basis points over Treasurys. Its index declined 0.15%.

Venezuela ended 2010 with an inflation rate of 27.2%, higher than the 25.1% rate of 2009, according to statistics the Central Bank of Venezuela released last week.

-By Erin McCarthy, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2712; erin.mccarthy@dowjones.com

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Chile peso slumps 6 pct in week, Mexico peso up
text:
* Chilean intervention hammers peso to 4-month low

* Brazil real slides 1.2 percent in week

* Mexican peso gains 1 percent on U.S. outlook (Adds comments, updates prices, changes dateline, previous SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY)

By Brad Haynes and Michael O'Boyle

SANTIAGO/MEXICO CITY, Jan 7 (Reuters) - The currencies of Chile and Brazil posted steep losses this week after officials stepped up efforts to sap those units' strength, while Mexico's peso rose on the improving outlook for the U.S. economy.

The Chilean peso ended Friday at a 4-month low after policymakers threw their muscle into the foreign exchange market with daily dollar purchases, knocking the currency down 6 percent in its worst weekly slide in almost 2 years. For details see [ID:nN30113748].

The market is divided about whether Chile's central bank could hike interest rates next week to cool rising inflation or if it could leave borrowing costs steady so as not to boost the attraction of its debt to yield hungry investors.

"We think they will pause because they want to give credibility to the intervention," said Roberto Melzi, an analyst at Barclays Capital in New York.

Others are betting higher inflation, pushed up by rising food prices, could push the central bank to hike. [ID:nN07198777]

The Chilean peso <CLP=> shed 0.44 percent to 497.50 per U.S. dollar on Friday.

After surging to a nearly three-year high before the central bank's move this week, analysts expect the currency to be range-bound between 470 and 510 or so as attraction to Chile's strong economy is tempered by intervention risks.

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ Graphic on region's currencies: http://r.reuters.com/cat64r("http://r.reuters.com/cat64r") ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The Brazilian real <BRBY> bid 0.12 percent weaker to 1.684 per dollar, capping a 1.2 percent loss for the week after the latest measure to stem the real's strength by authorities, who have been intervening since 2009.

The central bank said on Thursday it will impose an unremunerated reserve requirement of 60 percent on U.S. dollar short positions when certain limits are exceeded. [ID:nN0697246]

"Regardless of whether the latest measures prove effective or not, one thing is clear: regulatory uncertainty is rising, and investors are asking, 'What next'? " wrote analysts at BNP Paribas in a research note.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> was little changed on Friday, dipping 0.02 percent to 12.2324 per dollar and on track to post a gain of around 1 percent for the week.

Mexico's peso firmed this week on signs the U.S. economy may grow more than expected this year, and it has also been supported by intervention in Chile and Brazil as they boost the attraction to Mexico's free-floating market.

"You can make a pretty bullish case for Mexico," said Win Thin, an emerging markets strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York.

The peso touched an 8-month high on Thursday and it may be poised to soon hit its highest levels in more than two years, Thin said. (Additional reporting by Jean Luis Arce in Mexico City and Samantha Pearson in Sao Paulo; Editing by James Dalgleish)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil real hit by  FX  rule, Chile stabilizes
text:
* Brazil's cenbank imposes new rule on banks' FX positions

* Real drops 0.78 pct, Mexican peso loses 0.4 pct

* Chile's peso stabilizes after huge losses (Updates prices, adds comments)

By Samantha Pearson and Nathalia Ferreira

SAO PAULO, Jan 6 (Reuters) - Brazil's real sank on Thursday after officials said they would make it more expensive for banks to continue to bet on the fast-rising currency, while Chile's peso stabilized after this week's government intervention.

Brazil's central bank imposed a reserve requirement on banks' short positions on the U.S. dollar, turning up the heat on speculators authorities blame for overvaluing the real. For details, see [ID:nLDE7050Z6] and [ID:nN06102054].

"It is not the most powerful measure, but it is one more, and the threat is there that they could do even more," said Roberto Melzi, a strategist at Barclay's Capital in New York.

The country has been buying dollars in daily auctions and also raised taxes on foreign investments.

Like many emerging Latin and Asian economies, Brazil has struggled with currency appreciation that has made its exports more difficult to sell abroad and flooded the country with cheap imports.

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Graphic on region's currencies: http://r.reuters.com/cat64r("http://r.reuters.com/cat64r")

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Banks have 90 days to get ready for the new rules, meaning there was not a mad rush to reduce positions.

"It won't necessarily change the trend -- it could hold the market back a little," said Jose Carlos Amado, a currency trader at the Renascenca brokerage in Sao Paulo.

The real <BRBY> was bid 0.78 percent weaker at 1.686 per dollar, extending losses as investors broadly bet in favor of the greenback ahead of Friday's U.S. monthly payrolls data for December.

The jobs report could support the view that the U.S. economy is growing faster than expected.

Expectations of better U.S. growth have pushed up U.S. bond yields, making dollar investments more attractive compared to higher-yielding, but riskier, emerging market assets.

CHILE'S PESO STABILIZES

The Chilean peso <CLP=> stabilized after two days of sharp drops, shedding 0.04 percent to 495.20, its weakest close in more than three months. The currency has lost 6 percent of its value against the dollar and suffered its worst one-day plunge in a quarter century since Chile unveiled its plan to intervene in the currency late Tuesday. [ID:nN30113748]

"The market has calmed, and we're not seeing the exuberance of the first days," said one trader in Santiago.

Some analysts expect the Chilean currency to be range-bound between around 510 and 470 per dollar for now as investors are drawn to the Chile's strong economy but also worry about further intervention.

The Mexican peso <MXN=> hit an eight-month high early in the session but then fell as the dollar broadly gained. The peso weakened 0.4 percent to 12.2340 per dollar.

Analysts at some banks see the Mexican peso soon firming to a more than two-year high and then breaking past the 12-per dollar per level.

Even with such gains, the peso remains below the levels it traded at before the 2008 financial crisis, easing concerns that officials could intervene any time soon. (Additional reporting by Michael O'Boyle in Mexico City and Frolin Romero and Brad Haynes in Santiago; Editing by Padraic Cassidy)

title: UPDATE 2- Chile  peso takes breather after  intervention  plunge
text:
* Peso trades shade stronger after dropping 6 pct

* Cenbank conducts 2nd auction in $12 bln intervention (Updates with peso close, monetary policy implications)

By Froilan Romero and Brad Haynes

SANTIAGO, Jan 6 (Reuters) - The Chilean currency closed broadly flat on Thursday, taking a breather after falling about 6 percent in two days following a $12 billion central bank intervention in foreign exchange markets.

The world's No. 1 copper producer followed Brazil, Peru and Colombia in drafting measures to rein in its currency as so-called hot money poured into the fast-growing emerging market countries. The Chilean peso <CLP=CL> soared 17 percent against the dollar in the second half of 2010.

Chile's central bank conducted its second $50 million auction to buy dollars on Thursday, paying an average of 493.84 pesos per dollar. The first phase of the auctions will last until Feb. 9.

"The market has calmed and we're not seeing the exuberance of the first days," said one trader. "I think after that first wave, where the market was moving on capital flows, now it will be looking to foreign markets."

The peso gained as much as 0.5 percent before settling to close flat on Thursday, bidding 495.3 per dollar. The bank announced its intervention plan after the currency hit a near three-year high of 465.5 per dollar on Monday. ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

> For a TAKE-A-LOOK, see [ID:nN30113748]

> For a graphic, see http://r.reuters.com/cat64r("http://r.reuters.com/cat64r") ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

Meanwhile, the Brazilian real <BRBY> weakened sharply on Thursday after its central bank made its boldest move so far to curb currency gains, imposing reserve requirements on banks' short positions on U.S. dollars. For details, see [ID:nLDE7050Z6]

Chile's peso sank 4.5 percent on Tuesday, its biggest daily drop in more than 25 years, in the first day of trading after the central bank announced plans to buy $12 billion in greenbacks in installments to help exporters. [ID:nN04206531]

The central bank said the intervention's effect would be transitory as the currencies of the world's commodity exporters continue to appreciate.

Analysts see the exchange rate slipping as far as 510 pesos per dollar in the coming months before reverting to an equilibrium closer to 470 per dollar.

Long-term local debt yields rose after the central bank announced it would sterilize, or offset, the intervention by issuing new debt. The market's implicit inflation expectations also jumped as investors bet that the rising effective cost of imports would hit consumer prices.

The central bank cited the peso's appreciation as a factor containing inflation last year amid a robust recovery, allowing the bank to slow the pace of its interest rate hikes.

But Finance Minister Felipe Larrain said on Wednesday he didn't expect the weaker exchange rate to boost inflation.

"The firming exchange rate wasn't entirely reflected in prices, so the weakening of the exchange rate after the intervention announcement won't be reflected in prices either," said Larrain.

Central bank chief Jose de Gregorio also said this week that the bank would continue managing monetary policy to target inflation "without restrictions."

The central bank's last market poll showed traders closely divided on whether the bank will opt for a pause or an eighth consecutive rate raise at its Jan. 13 rate-setting meeting.

Some analysts believe the central bank is more likely to hold its benchmark rate in order to bolster the intervention. Others see the dollar purchase program adequately addressing the peso's strength, giving the bank room to continue raising rates after the economy grew faster than expected in November.

The central bank weighed holding the rate in December, according to bank minutes, though market rate futures point to another 25 basis point increase to 3.5 percent.

title: =DJ Emerging-Market  Currencies  Seen Facing More Appreciation Pressure
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--The upward pressure on currencies of emerging-market countries is expected to linger this year, causing headaches for policymakers in those countries, even though recent data point to an improving economic outlook for the U.S. and the prospect of a more dollar-supportive policy mix in Washington.

Despite strong economic news--such as the gains shown in a U.S. payrolls report Wednesday--analysts still expect the Federal Reserve to stick with its plans to buy $600 billion in government bonds. Liquidity from the Fed's easing is still seen flowing through to emerging markets and seen putting pressure on those currencies to appreciate.

And, in any case, the strengthening U.S. economy is seen as helping emerging-market economies as well, and ultimately boosting their currencies.

Brown Brothers Harriman's global head of emerging markets strategy, Win Thin, said he still expects emerging-market currencies to outperform in 2011. Strong U.S. growth ultimately encourages investors to take more risk, and so could drive more flows to emerging-market assets, he noted.

"A strong U.S. is great for emerging markets. EM still needs the developed world. That's where they are shipping a lot of their goods," he said.

On Wednesday, a national employment report published by payroll giant Automatic Data Processing Inc. (ADP) and consultancy Macroeconomic Advisers showed that private-sector jobs in the U.S. rose by 297,000 last month. Meanwhile, a report from the Institute for Supply Management showed improvement in the U.S. service sector.

Most analysts don't expect these data to shift the Fed's plans on quantitative easing--not unless they are backed up by a series of very strong jobs reports in the more closely watched Bureau of Labor Statistics' nonfarm payrolls series.

"There are no clear indications that the Fed at this juncture is likely to change its course," said Guillermo Mondino, Latin America research strategist at Barclays Capital. "If that is the case, then we have a favorable cocktail for emerging markets, liquidity remains abundant and emerging-market currencies are likely to be under [appreciation] pressure."

Continued strength in emerging-market currencies is likely to push their policymakers to keep intervening in foreign-exchange markets or to introduce capital controls, both to try to hold back potentially volatile "hot money" inflows and to prevent currency appreciation from undermining local producers' competitiveness.

Earlier this week, Chile's central bank said it would intervene in the local currency market, increasing its foreign-currency reserves by $12 billion in 2011. That intervention came after the peso traded at a 32-month high and local exporters protested that the peso's strength was hurting their competitiveness.

On Tuesday, Brazil Finance Minister Guido Mantega said his government is ready to take measures against the strengthening local currency, the real, and its negative effects on the country's exports. Brazilian foreign exchange, or policy, intervention remains a high risk, RBC analysts wrote in a note this week.

-By Anjali Cordeiro, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-2200; anjali.cordeiro@dowjones.com

* Mexico's currency near 8-week high on U.S. optimism (Adds comments, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Brad Haynes

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Jan 5 (Reuters) - Chile's peso and Brazil's real weakened on Wednesday as investors fretted over official meddling in the countries' markets.

But Mexico's currency, which is not seen to be at risk from intervention, firmed to just below a eight-week high touched in the previous session on encouraging U.S. labor data.

Chile's market was still reeling from Monday's news that the central bank will buy $50 million daily to curb the peso's rise -- a program that kicks off on Wednesday.

After suffering its biggest one-day loss in more than 25 years in the previous session, the Chilean peso <CLP=> weakened 1.5 percent more to a three-month low of 495 per dollar.

The effect of the central bank's intervention could be magnified as the price of Chile's main export -- copper -- slips from record highs, but analysts are not expecting another drop as dramatic as Tuesday's plunge. For details, see [ID:nN05260728]

"The currency will remain rangebound with a bias to appreciate for the coming months," said Bertrand Delgado, an economist at Roubini Global Economics in New York, who sees the currency trading between 480 and 510 per dollar.

"The (Chilean) economy will continue to grow above potential and the central bank is likely to keep hiking interest rates, so it is still positive story, but now there is the risk of intervention," Delgado said.

Chile's peso had surged nearly 18 percent in the second half of 2010, as investors were drawn to the country's strong local economy and rising interest rates. The peso hit a nearly three-year high before the Chilean central bank announced its dollar buying program on Tuesday.

Meanwhile, investors in the Brazilian market were cautious after the government issued fresh warnings on Tuesday that it was ready to take tougher action if the real firms further.

Brazilian "Finance Minister (Guido) Mantega keeps repeating his mantra that the government has tools to prevent excessive appreciation, including further measures to restrain capital flows," Zeina Latif, chief Brazil economist at RBS in Sao Paulo, said in a research note. "We should expect more verbal intervention with (the real) below 1.65, but not meaningful currency measures," she added.

Analysts at some banks see the Mexican peso breaking past the 12 per dollar per level this year.

text:

1219 GMT [Dow Jones] After losing nearly 5% versus the dollar Tuesday, the Chilean peso weakened further Wednesday morning as the central bank's intervention was set to begin. The central bank will increase its foreign-currency reserves by $12 billion this year, starting with daily purchases of $50 million on the local market between Jan. 5 and end Feb. 9. Prior to the intervention announcement late Monday the peso was trading at a 32-month highs versus the dollar, prompting exporters to clamor for a lifeline as the local currency's strength eats away at the competitiveness of their products abroad. In recent trading the peso was weaker at CLP491.40 to the dollar, versus Tuesday's close of CLP487.80, according to data provided by Valor Futuro newswire. (anthony.esposito@dowjones.com)

1215 GMT [Dow Jones] Brazil's government is likely to continue to jawbone the market if the real moves below BRL1.65 per dollar, but its options for halting the appreciation are limited, says RBS. "We should expect more verbal intervention with BRL below 1.65, but not meaningful currency measures," it says in a note. There might be "few options remaining without crossing over to more heterodox measures," it says. President Dilma Rousseff seems to be expressing a more moderate forex policy stance, it says. Rousseff wants to "spur the competitiveness of the economy in order to protect the private sector from excessive BRL strength, maybe as a tacit recognition on the limits on effectively altering the BRL trend." (matthew.cowley@dowjones.com)

1214 GMT [Dow Jones] Greece/10-year bund spreads on Wednesday rise 10 bps to reach a notional historic high of 975 bps, but with no transactions taking place at that level. Trading is subdued with just EUR2 billion in trades on the local HDAT and European trading platform, traders saying that the spread reflects a rally in German bunds rather than a sell-off in GGBs. "There has been no trading in the 10-year bond so far today. The market is very quiet," says a local bond trader. "We saw a rally in the bunds today but the peripherals failed to follow." (alkman.granitsas@dowjones.com)

1142 GMT [Dow Jones] AUD/USD has stabilized during the European session after falling below parity in Asia Wednesday. Citi says that move came as the retracement in commodities and worries about the economic impact of the Queensland floods weighed. AUD/USD now trades at 1.0003, the bank says there is chatter of stops around 0.9980. (gary.stride@dowjones.com)

1127 GMT [Dow Jones] The downtrend in EUR/SEK is embarking on another bear wave towards the key support cluster around the 8.8500 level, extending the long-term decline off the March 2009 peak at 11.7861. See Wednesday's Charting Europe column by Francis Bray. (francis.bray@dowjones.com)

1119 GMT [Dow Jones] The euro falls to the day's lows across the board, with stops triggered in EUR/USD and EUR/JPY, says a UK bank trader. EUR/USD slides to 1.3212, EUR/JPY 108.51, EUR/GBP 0.8483 and EUR/CHF 1.2570. (gary.stride@dowjones.com)

1112 GMT [Dow Jones] Poland's Monetary Policy Council, or MPC, is likely to raise key rate by 25 basis points, to 3.75%, on January 19, BNP Paribas says, commenting on the central bank governor's warning that policy tightening will be delivered soon. "Overall, we expect the MPC to deliver tightening of 50-75 bps, raising the policy rate to 4.00%-4.25% by end of 2Q," BNP says. But adds "rate hikes will prove to be a policy mistake, given softening GDP growth and the lack of underlying inflationary pressure." BNPP adds "Policy tightening in early 2011 might need to be reversed as soon as 4Q or early 2012." (malgorzata.halaba@dowjones.com)

1108 GMT [Dow Jones] Portugal's EUR500 million six-month Treasury bill sale Wednesday brings "no particular surprise," says Barclays Capital strategist Giuseppe Maraffino. As expected, Portugal issued the amount announced but with a huge concession of around 15 basis points versus Tuesday's close, he says. He adds that there was no particular interest before the auction and this has favored the cheapening of the t-bill on auction. "Overall, the auction was good as it was bid and they issued the amount announced but at a cost of huge concession in terms of pricing," Maraffino adds. (emese.bartha@dowjones.com)

1103 GMT [Dow Jones] The USD/INR forward premia is lower after the increase in the spot USD/INR rates and receiving interest on improved liquidity among banks, a senior trader with a privately-run bank says. The one-year forward premia is at 2.43 from 2.5250 late Tuesday. The trader adds, some profit-booking in premia had been spotted, while data showing a major reduction in banks' daily borrowing from the RBI helps forward premia ease. Banks borrowed INR370.70 billion from the RBI Wednesday, compared with a INR1 trillion daily average last week. "If the spot keeps inching up to trade between 45.50 and 45.70, we could see the forward premia move in a band of 2.40 to 2.60 this week," the trader says. The USD/INR is at 45.29. (khushita.vasant@dowjones.com)

title: DJ UPDATE: Chile  Fin Min: $12B  Intervention  Is Biggest In Local History
text:
(Updates to add comments from the Finance Minister)

SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean central bank's announced $12 billion local currency market intervention won't pressure inflation upwards as most local prices weren't adjusted to the strength the peso was showing against the dollar, Finance Minister Felipe Larrain said Tuesday.

Late Monday, the central bank announced it would begin intervening in the local market through sterilized dollar purchases throughout the year for a total $12 billion.

For most of the final two quarters of 2010, the peso traded at 31-month highs against the dollar, prompting calls for intervention as exporters lost competitiveness abroad.

The Chilean economy is highly dependent on its exports of natural resources such as copper, fertilizers, molybdenum, wood pulp, fresh fruit and wines.

Larrain noted that this was the biggest local intervention and that "massive" interventions such as this one tended to be successful.

"We've seen that for an intervention to have a real effect on the currency, it has to be massive and this one is the largest in Chilean history," Larrain told reporters.

He added that the government "supported and appreciated the move," noting that the ministry and the autonomous central bank closely coordinate their measures.

As Finance Minister, Larrain by law sits in on the central bank's monetary policy meetings but doesn't vote on the bank's decisions.

The official declined to estimate just how much the peso could gain on the central bank's dollar purchases, which are scheduled to begin Wednesday.

In the Monday session, the peso firmed to close at a 32-month high against the dollar. In early Tuesday trading, the peso slid 4% versus the dollar in reaction to the intervention announcement.

Larrain added that several key sectors of the domestic economy were losing competitiveness as a result of the strong peso.

"While copper exporters are protected by high copper prices, the agricultural sector needed support," he said.

He added the government would continue with its own measures aimed at contributing to keeping the peso at competitive levels against other currencies.

These measures include curbing fiscal spending, keeping dollar financing at a minimum, improving financial legislation, and streamlining and modernizing certain areas of government.

"We have to generate long-term tools to support the peso's competitiveness," he said.

Recently, the ministry announced it would issue most of its 2011 debt on the local market. The 2011 fiscal budget set a $7.8-billion cap on sovereign debt this year and the Finance Ministry last week announced it would issue $6 billion in sovereign debt domestically.

Local debt issues, denominated in pesos, cut down dollar inflows and ease some of the pressure rising interest rates and robust economic growth put on the peso.

"We left a $1.8-billion margin for other issues like we did in 2010," Larrain said.

Last year, for the first time in nearly a decade, Chile issued sovereign debt on international markets. Of the total $1.5 billion it issued abroad, $500 million was placed in peso-denominated debt to take some pressure off of the strong local currency.

Foreign investors have poured money into the region's attractive economies, shunning markets in developed countries still struggling to recover from the global financial crisis.

Below are the main steps Latin American countries have taken to curb the strength of their local currencies:

CHILE ANNOUNCES LONG-AWAITED FOREX INTERVENTION

BRAZIL BUYS DOLLARS, FIGHTS INFLOWS, LOOKS TO TAX BREAKS

* Central bank resumed daily dollar purchases soon after the financial crisis, recently buying as much as $1 billion a day via double auctions.

* Sovereign wealth fund authorized to buy dollars on spot market but has yet to act.

* Government triples tax on foreign purchases of bonds to 6 percent to curb inflows into fixed income market.

* Government increases tax on derivatives margins to dissuade short-term investors.

* Raises bank reserve requirements to cool a credit boom and ease the currency situation by paving the way for lower interest rates.

title: BUY OR SELL-Which Chilean assets to hold after  FX  action?
text:
* Inflation expectations on the rise after FX intervention

* Investors buying inflation protection, stocks

* Peso, government bonds to sell off

By Walter Brandimarte

NEW YORK, Jan 4 (Reuters) - Chilean assets offering protection against inflation have become a favorite among investors after the government said on Monday it will intervene in the currency market to curb the strength of the peso.

The outlook for stocks remains positive, especially for exporters which should benefit from a weaker currency in the short term.

Meanwhile, the peso is poised to weaken a little further but it could resume its appreciation trend later in the year if commodity prices remain on the rise.

Chile's central bank said late on Monday it would buy $12 billion this year to tame the peso, which has gained more than 17 percent against the U.S. dollar since the end of June.

Here is a compilation of the main trade ideas floated by analysts following the announcement:

BUY

* Protection against inflation

Inflation expectations are on the rise as a weaker peso will translate into higher prices of imported goods in the short term. In the longer run, investors are also likely to demand a higher inflation premium on government bonds if expectations of a pause in the cycle of monetary tightening are confirmed next week.

"If you interrupted your rate hike cycle, and you interrupted your peso FX appreciation, clearly the markets are going to demand a higher policy risk on the (country's yield) curve," said Siobhan Morden, head of Latin America research and strategy at RBS Securities.

Morden says her favorite investment in Chile is the long two-year break-even inflation trade. Break-even inflation is the difference between the nominal yield on a fixed-rate investment and the real yield on an inflation-linked investment of similar maturity and credit quality.

Rates on that trade jumped to around 3.65 percent on Tuesday from 3.55 percent in the previous session and are poised to rise further, Morden said.

* Stocks

Chilean stocks in general should benefit from an expected pause in the central bank monetary tightening cycle, which analysts see as a complementary measure to stem the currency appreciation.

Miners should post a good performance as the global outlook for commodities remains positive.

"Companies related to the exporting sector and with regional exposure should boost the local stock market," Santiago-based brokerage BCI said in a report.

Chile's blue-chip IPSA index <.IPSA> rose 0.9 percent on Tuesday while the broader IGPA index <.IGPA> gained about 0.8 percent.

SELL

* Peso

The peso <CLP=> sank about 4.5 percent on Tuesday, to 487.60 per U.S. dollar, following the intervention announcement. It is poised to weaken a little further before stabilizing at weaker levels and eventually resuming its appreciation trend, especially if commodity prices remain strong.

Most analysts say the peso could weaken to near 500.00 per dollar in the short term. Many see attractive entry points around that level, however.

"JP Morgan house view is bullish on commodities and copper in particular. If that outlook proves to be right, sellers of USD/CLP may surface if the currency trades above the 500 level," JP Morgan analyst Felipe Q. Pianetti wrote in a research note.

* LONG-DATED BONDS

Chile's domestic yield curve is expected to become steeper as inflation expectations rise and the central bank sells more bonds to sterilize its dollar purchases.

Yields on Chile's peso-denominated bonds maturing in 2020 <CL00001265=RRPS> rose 36 basis points to 6.458 percent, according to Reuters data. (Additional reporting by Brad Haynes in Santiago; Editing by Leslie Adler)

title: TEXT-Chile  central bank  to buy $12 bln to help tame peso
text:
SANTIAGO, Jan 3 (Reuters) - The Chilean Central Bank said on Monday it would intervene in the foreign exchange market and purchase $12 billion in 2011 to tame the strong peso's impact on the local economy.

Following is the text of the announcement:

"The board of the Central Bank of Chile has decided to initiate a program to buy foreign currency to strengthen its international liquidity position. The aim of this initiative is to raise international reserves to a level compatible with those in economies similar to Chile's. Moreover, this intervention should soften the impact of exchange rate adjustment in our economy.

"Global risks are heightened. The international economy is in an unusual position, characterized by high commodity prices, low interest rates, a slow recovery in developed economies and the depreciation of the U.S. dollar. Meanwhile, emerging economies are growing strongly and their currencies are appreciating. Significant risks include an escalation of financial tensions in Europe, sustained high rates of unemployment in developed economies and severe adjustments in emerging economies facing inflationary pressures. The availability of additional reserves will allow a better handling of any major deterioration of the global outlook."

"Currency markets are under stress and currency adjustments occur asymmetrically. There is also the risk that the uncoupling of global growth could continue beyond expectations, which could intensify currency tensions. Therefore the effects of this measure, although transitory, should provide room to allow real adjustments in the national economy."

"To implement this program, the Central Bank of Chile will accumulate additional international reserves worth $12 billion in 2011 through regular dollar purchases from Jan. 5 until the end of December 2011. This program will bring the international liquidity position of the Central Bank to 17 percent of GDP."

"The monetary effects of this measure will be offset in order to maintain peso liquidity at levels consistent with current monetary policy. This sterilization will be achieved with a combination of short-term liquidity instruments and long-term debt issuance, according to the annual calendar that will be announced promptly. The first phase of this program, effective from Jan. 5 to Feb. 9, will consist of daily purchases of $50 million through competitive auctions. The Central Bank of Chile will promptly communicate the next steps, which may be revised depending on market conditions."

"The accumulation of international reserves implies significant financial costs associated with the difference between the return on investment and the cost of financing. The proposed level of international reserves is consistent with the long-term financial sustainability of the Central Bank, although there is limited room in this regard."

"The Central Bank board reiterates its commitment to conducting monetary policy based on an inflation target and floating exchange rate. For a country like Chile, which may face significant changes in foreign financial conditions and terms of trade, exchange rate flexibility is an essential ingredient of macroeconomic and financial stability. On the contrary, rigid exchange rate arrangements may have undesirable costs on the volatility of growth, credit, interest rates and inflation. In a volatile environment as seen in recent years, an inflation targeting and floating exchange rate regime has shown its benefits in allowing a more stable evolution of the Chilean economy. Furthermore, our floating regime allows interventions in emergency situations, such as the one announced in this press release."

title: EMERGING MARKETS- Chile  peso slumps on  intervention ;real recovers
text:
(Repeats to additional subscribers)

* Chile's peso closes down 4.5 pct at 9-week low

* Brazilian real pares losses after press conference

* Finance Minister Guido Mantega announces no new measures

* Mexico eschews intervention, benefiting peso (Adds comments from Mexico, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Brad Haynes

SAO PAULO/SANTIAGO, Jan 4 (Reuters) - Chile's peso suffered its biggest daily drop in more than 25 years on Tuesday on tough new intervention plans while the Brazilian real recovered after Brasilia stopped short of introducing further measures.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> slumped as much as 4.9 percent to 489.60 per dollar. It later closed 4.5 percent down at a 9-week low of 487.60 -- its biggest daily loss since February 1985, according to daily central bank data.

Brazil's real <BRBY> also weakened sharply after the government announced it would hold a news conference in the afternoon to tackle foreign exchange issues, prompting speculation fresh measures could be announced.

But Finance Minister Guido Mantega said very little and only reiterated that the government was ready to act, causing the real immediately to pare losses.

Chile has taken one of the most hands-off approaches in Latin America to its foreign exchange market. But it surprised investors late on Monday with a massive dollar-buying plan.

The central bank announced it will buy $12 billion to tame the peso, which has appreciated more than 17 percent against the greenback since the end of June. For details, see [ID:nN03137860].

Like many attractive emerging economies across Latin America and Asia, Chile has struggled with currency appreciation that has made its exports more difficult to sell abroad and flooded the country with cheap imports. <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ Graphic on region's currencies: http://r.reuters.com/cat64r("http://r.reuters.com/cat64r") ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

Chile's surprise move added to existing concerns about intervention across the region as it could give countries such as Brazil an excuse to implement more currency measures.

"If the pretty conservative Chilean central bank intervenes, what can you expect of the Brazilian central bank!" said Pedro Tuesta, senior Latin America economist at research firm 4Cast Inc in Washington.

However, others played down a possible regional impact.

"Chile is just the last domino to fall into intervention. I don't think it changes others' attitudes as they are already intervening," said Tony Volpon, head of emerging markets research for the Americas at Nomura in New York.

BRAZIL: KING OF INTERVENTION

The Brazilian real pared its losses to close 0.79 percent weaker at 1.662 per dollar on the local spot market, after closing at its strongest level since Sept. 1 2008 in the previous session.

Brazil's trade and industry minister said on Monday the country would not remain "passive" while the real continues to strengthen.

Latin America's biggest economy has already taken the lead in the region when it comes to intervention, buying vast amounts of dollars on a daily basis and raising taxes on inflows. But investors worry the government could increase those levies even further and take other measures, such as intervening in the futures market. For possible measures, see [ID:nN01117570].

Mexico is now the only major Latin American country that is not heavily intervening in its currency market, partly because the peso is fully convertible and thus more widely traded and harder to control.

The country has also suffered more from the financial crisis, which means it has not seen the flood of currency-boosting investment experienced by Chile and Brazil.

The Mexican peso <MXN=> gained 0.14 percent to 12.2318 per dollar, even as U.S. stocks were mixed.

"If you believe that intervention in Mexico is pretty moderate and subtle, then the peso become more attractive in the eyes of investors," said Luis Flores, an economist at brokerage IXE in Mexico City. (Additional reporting by Jean Luis Arce in Mexico City; Editing by Dan Grebler)
