title: Chile Central Bank  Says  Intervention  Exceptional; Peso Weakens
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean central bank's $12 billion currency market intervention program is an "exceptional measure" and as such carries credibility, the bank's president, Jose De Gregorio, said Tuesday.

The market evidently agreed, knocking the peso down nearly 5% against the U.S. dollar by the end of the first full trading session following the program's announcement late Monday. The plan to accumulate $12 billion in additional international reserves is the largest since the peso's free float was adopted in the late 1990s, De Gregorio noted.

The peso has been trading at 32-month highs against the dollar in recent months, prompting exporters to demand a lifeline as the strong local currency cuts into the competitiveness of their products. Yet the Central Bank of Chile has resisted far longer than peers in emerging markets from South Korea to Thailand, Taiwan, Colombia and Brazil in purchasing dollars, applying capital controls, or increasing local banks' reserve requirements in bids to cool red-hot local currencies and heated domestic demand.

"We haven't fallen into the addiction of repetitive intervention," De Gregorio told reporters. He predicted that the size of the intervention will make it effective "in softening the pressures on the peso."

The peso ended local trade Tuesday 4.8% weaker at CLP487.80 to the dollar.

"We now finally have some breathing room," said Antonio Walker, president of the Fedefruta fruit exporters trade group. The strong peso had "paralyzed" exporters, he said, noting that it reduced their incomes and made it difficult to cover their costs and invest.

At least in the short-term, economists said, the central bank's plan should prove effective.

"We expect a meaningful impact on the currency market. The bank has gained a lot of credibility over the past decade regarding its commitment to a free-floating exchange regime... and we think this has enhanced the effectiveness of intervention as a policy tool," Barclays Capital said in a research note.

This is the fourth time the central bank has intervened in the exchange market since eliminating the peso's trading bands in 1999 and letting the currency float freely, and the first time since 2008.

This bout of dollar buying won't affect Chile's long-term competitiveness, nor its long-term real exchange rate, De Gregorio insisted.

Much, however, depends on the global backdrop.

"The bigger picture is that emerging markets have relatively good fundamentals [and have to deal] with domestic inflation pressures against a backdrop of strong capital inflows, which push up the values of the currencies," said Neil Shearing, Latin American economist at Capital Economics in London.

De Gregorio pointed out that Chile hasn't seen net capital inflows. "Today the problem isn't a massive inflow of capital," he said.

Still, record-high copper prices, the wide differentials between interest rates in Chile and rock-bottom rates across the developed world, and a rapidly expanding Chilean economy suggest the central bank's intervention program can't guarantee the peso won't resume appreciation.

Chile is the world's biggest copper exporter, so sustained high demand out of China and other high-growth emerging markets implies continued high prices for the red metal, and more pressure on Chile's peso.

"If the terms of trade continue to improve, the U.S. dollar continues to weaken in global markets, and the Chilean economy's cyclical position remains markedly strong vis-a-vis the trading partners, we sense the central bank will not lean excessively against the wind of further moderate Chilean peso strength," Goldman Sachs economist Alberto Ramos said.

But given the size of the intervention program, which involves an initial $50 million in daily "very predictable non-discretionary" dollar purchases, Ramos said it "stands a good chance of being effective."

Moreover, the central bank can also continue with interest rate increases, reining in domestic demand and inflationary pressures. That, in turn, should help ease pressure on the peso.

De Gregorio said the bank remains committed to a target of 3% inflation in a two-year policy horizon. January-November inflation for 2010 stood at 2.9%.

title: Chile  Exporters Applaud  Intervention , Request Govt Measures
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chile's exporters applauded the central bank's decision to intervene in the local currency market, but asked for the government to follow up with other measures to help boost the competitiveness of their sector.

With the peso trading at or near a 32-month high against the dollar in recent months, exporters clamored for a lifeline as the strength of the local currency hurt the competitiveness of their products abroad.

Chile's export-dependent economy is among the world leaders in the production of natural resources such as copper, fertilizers, molybdenum, wood pulp, fresh fruit and wines.

"[The exchange rate] paralyzed us. It reduced our income, made it difficult to pay our business costs and froze our investments, creating debt [in the sector]. We now finally have some breathing room," said Antonio Walker, president of the Fedefruta fruit exporters trade group.

The breathing room created by the central bank's program to increase foreign currency reserves by $12 billion in 2011, however, may be short-lived if the government doesn't follow up with measures of its own, exporters argue.

The government needs to "take long-term complementary measures to protect products made in Chile, so that the intervention's impact isn't diluted over time by factors such as increasing copper prices," said Roberto Fantuzzi, the president of Chile's Asexma exporters trade group.

As Chile is the world's premier copper producer, accounting for nearly a third of global supply, the peso often takes trading cues from the metal's international prices. Record-high copper prices, on strong fundamentals, helped to fuel the peso's rise in recent months.

Among other initiatives, Asexma is calling for long-term foreign exchange hedging programs "for investment projects in the non-commodities export sector."

Earlier in the day, Finance Minister Felipe Larrain said that the government "supported and appreciated" the central bank's move, pointing out that the ministry and the autonomous central bank closely coordinate their measures.

According to Larrain, the government will continue with its own measures to help stem the peso's strength. These include limiting fiscal spending, holding dollar financing at a minimum, improving financial legislation and cutting red tape for exporters.

-By Anthony Esposito, Dow Jones Newswires; 56-2-715-8929; anthony.esposito@dowjones.com [ 04-01-11 1926GMT ]

SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean peso ended 4.8% weaker versus the dollar Tuesday as the market digested the central bank's plans to intervene in the local currency market by increasing its foreign currency reserves by $12 billion this year.

The peso ended at CLP487.80 to the dollar, versus Monday's close of CLP465.40, which was a 32-month high. The local currency traded in a range of CLP482.70 to CLP490.50

Exporters had demanded a lifeline in recent months, as the strength of the peso hurt the competitiveness of their products abroad.

Many analysts, however, question the mid-to-long-term effectiveness of the intervention considering historically high copper prices, the wide interest rate differential between Chile and the U.S. and a rapidly recovering Chilean economy versus sluggish growth in the U.S.

Over the next several sessions it is likely that the peso will weaken to levels near CLP500, "at which point the market will again look at fundamentals such as [international] copper prices, economic activity, interest rates and how the dollar evolves against its [major rivals], to get direction for the future of the Chilean peso," said local currency trader Forex Chile.

As Chile is the world's premier copper producer accounting for nearly a third of global supply, the peso often takes trading cues from the metal's international prices.

In the bond market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central bank bonds, or BCUs, ended vastly higher after the central bank detailed plans to use $2 billion in short-term instruments and facilities and $10 billion in both peso-denominated and inflation-indexed bonds to "sterilize" its $12 billion dollar purchasing program.

title: INSTANT VIEW 3- Chile  to  intervene  to curb peso gains
text:
NEW YORK, Jan 3 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank announced on Monday a plan to purchase as much as $12 billion in 2011 to stem the appreciation of its currency, the peso.

The peso <CLP=> on Monday firmed almost 0.5 percent to 465.5 per dollar to close at its strongest level since May 2008.

For a story, see [ID:nN03137860].

Following are comments from analysts:

MARJORIE HERNANDEZ, LATIN AMERICA CURRENCY ANALYST, HSBC, NEW YORK:

"I think the market was anticipating some sort of reaction. The question was at what level. There was a little bit of a divergence in views as to whether it should come below the 460 or 465 level. But clearly this was entering a danger zone.

"When you look at the press release, clearly it is more a medium-term concern that the underlying pressures that have been driving emerging market currencies stronger are here to stay for 2011. They do talk about a divergence between emerging markets and developed markets and they do allude to higher commodity prices.

"A lot of commodity currencies were rallying and Chile was among them. Now that the announcement has been made I think that you can start to look at Chile underperforming the rest of the commodity currencies.

"Volumes in Chile are OK, they are not as high and I think $50 million does make a difference."

MATIAS MADRID, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANCO PENTA, SANTIAGO:

"This was definitely a surprise. It was expected around 460 pesos per dollar, so this came a little early.

"Obviously, this will have an immediate impact on the exchange rate, which should rise to around 480 pesos per dollar.

"This is quite an aggressive measure, a strong play by the central bank. The most important thing is the volume of the purchases, which is quite high."

"It won't be enough to entirely settle the issue. If copper keeps advancing toward $4.50 per pound we can expect it to come back. But this should have a short-term effect."

ALBERTO RAMOS, SENIOR ECONOMIST, GOLDMAN SACHS, NEW YORK:

"I think it will have some impact, but not a major one because even the central bank admits that part of the currency pressure stems from fundamental factors, such as a world with asymmetrical growth levels between emerging markets and developed economies.

"We'll have some impact, but (it won't be that large) if we continue to see commodity prices rallying and a weak dollar in the global economy. The idea is not to reverse the trend (of peso appreciation), but probably to smooth it a little bit."

EDUARDO SUAREZ, EMERGING MARKETS ANALYST, RBC CAPITAL MARKETS

"Although the announcement could present some short-term headwinds, we believe fundamentals are still supportive for the Chilean peso." (Reporting by Walter Brandimarte and Daniel Bases in New York, Brad Haynes in Santiago)

text:
* Brazil's real, Mexican peso gain 0.9 pct

* Chilean peso firms to strongest since May 2008

* Chile's central bank unveils intervention plan

(Adds comments, updates prices)

By Samantha Pearson and Michael O'Boyle

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Jan 3 (Reuters) - Strong reports on global manufacturing drove Brazil's real and Chile's peso to more than 2 year highs on Monday and Chilean authorities said they would start buying dollars to curb the peso's strength.

Mexico's peso hit a six-week high after data showed the manufacturing sector in the United States grew for a 17th straight month in December, boding well for Mexican factories that are closely tied to U.S. output. For details, see [ID:nN03175600]

European factory data was also solid as was an output survey in China, Brazil's top trading partner. Slower growth and cooling inflation seen in the Chinese data eased concerns of an interest rate hike by the world's second biggest economy. [ID:nTOE6BU02S]

"This implies that Chinese authorities will refrain from taking aggressive measures and not slow down their economy too much," said Emilio Diez De Sollano, an analyst at brokerage Monex in Mexico City.

Investors are concerned that Chinese rate hikes could weigh on Latin American growth. Asian countries, especially China, have been consuming Latin American commodities such as Brazilian soybeans and Chilean copper.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> firmed almost 0.5 percent to 465.5 per dollar to close at its strongest since May 2008.

Chile's central bank said late on Monday it would take similar measures to control the peso's strength as countries like Brazil and Colombia have implemented to protect local exporters from sharp gains in their currencies.

After the local market had closed, Chile's central bank said it would start buying $50 million a day in dollars in a bid to slow peso appreciation.

The Mexican currency <MXN=> strengthened 0.9 percent to 12.2551 per dollar in its biggest one-day percentage gain since Oct. 20.

The central bank said it had soaked up 592 million dollars by exercising dollar put options that Mexico implemented early in 2010 to build up its foreign currency reserves.

title: Chile  Peso Ends At 32-Mo High On Record Copper; Intervention  Seen Nearer
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chile's peso ended at a 32-month high against the dollar as international copper prices hit a new record, bringing the local currency closer to levels expected to prompt central bank intervention.

The peso finished stronger at CLP465.40 to the dollar compared with Thursday's close of CLP467.30, while trading in a range of CLP465.10 to CLP467.00.

Markets and banks in Chile were closed Friday for the New Year's Eve holiday.

After appreciating 7.8% in 2010 versus the dollar, the peso continued to strengthen in the new year as international copper prices rose to a record high.

As Chile is the world's premier copper producer, accounting for nearly 35% of global output, the peso often takes cues from the metal's international prices.

In New York trading, the most actively traded contact, for March delivery, was recently up 0.5% at $4.4670 a pound, after setting a fresh intraday record at $4.4980, on strong fundamentals and declining inventories.

With the peso's sharp appreciation in recent months, exporters have demanded currency-market intervention as the strength of the local currency hurts their competitiveness abroad.

The central bank recently said it doesn't rule out increasing its foreign-currency reserves as a way to limit the peso's recent strength.

Traders see an increased risk of intervention if the peso appreciates to CLP450-CLP460. Some traders, however, feel an intervention may have limited effects because of historically high copper prices, broad international dollar weakness and strong economic growth in Chile compared to the sluggish U.S. recovery.

"A central bank intervention may happen, there's political pressure for them to act, to help exporters. But market forces and fundamentals, such as record-high copper and robust growth in Chile, may well erase the effect of an intervention in very little time," said Ronald Volpi, head currency trader with local brokerage EuroAmerica.

In the bond market, yields on inflation-indexed Chilean central bank bonds, or BCUs, ended higher in light over-the-counter trading.

The yield on five-year BCU bonds ended at 2.67%, from 2.65% on Thursday, while the yield on 10-year BCUs closed at 2.95%, from 2.89% the previous session.

(Peso and bond quotes provided by Valor Futuro newswire.)

title: ANALYSIS-Strong copper puts off  Chile  peso  intervention
text:
* Bank to intervene only if strong peso lacks support

* Record copper prices bolster fundamentals of peso rally

By Brad Haynes

SANTIAGO, Dec 17 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank is unlikely to intervene to rein in a sharply appreciating peso as long as record prices of the country's top export, copper, continue underpinning the currency's rally.

This week surging copper prices have pushed the peso <CLP=CL> to new 30-month highs below 475 pesos per dollar for the first time since Oct. 13, renewing calls for central bank action from lawmakers and businessmen.

But bank president Jose De Gregorio reiterated to Congress on Tuesday that intervention would be effective only if the peso were unmoored from long-term drivers, citing ineffective recent interventions by other central banks. For more see [ID:nN14274122].

Chile's currency is the best performer in Latin America this year, gaining 15 percent since June as the price of copper <HGH1> has climbed over 30 percent to hit new records above $4/lb on strong Chinese demand, boosting dollar revenues. The peso is tracking the weekly movement of copper prices closer than it has for two years, according to Thomson Reuters data.

"When the price of copper was at $3.50 (per pound), the level for intervention would probably have been 470 pesos (per dollar), because past that we would be getting away from fundamentals," said BBVA Chile economist Alejandro Puente.

"But with a much higher price of copper now, I see the central bank probably intervening at a stronger exchange rate, for example 450 pesos (per dollar)." <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ 


TAKE-A-LOOK at Chile's economic recovery      [ID:nN30113748]
For a graphic on the peso rally:   http://r.reuters.com/mux99q ("http://r.reuters.com/mux99q")

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

Central banks from Brazil to Thailand have carried out costly dollar purchases to stem their rallying currencies, which have risen this year as investors pour money into higher-yielding emerging markets. Few of those attempts, however, have achieved lasting results.

De Gregorio has said repeatedly that the central bank does not rule out entering the foreign exchange market if it were justified by a temporary misalignment of the peso, but the effect of the bank chief's verbal intervention is diminishing.

The peso's strength has helped contain inflation in recent months by keeping down the effective cost of imports. This has allowed the central bank to slow the pace of its interest rate hikes from 50 basis points to 25 basis points and to consider a brief pause in its monetary tightening cycle.

The central bank raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 3.25 percent on Thursday, its seventh consecutive rate increase, to keep up with an economy expected to grow over 5 percent this year.

COPPER ALIGNMENT

The central bank's last direct currency intervention came in early 2008 when the peso strengthened past 430 per dollar, trading 9 percent stronger than today's nominal exchange rate at a time when copper was 5 percent weaker.

That intervention came within weeks of the fall of Bear Stearns, which precipitated a nearly 70 percent collapse in copper prices and compounded the depreciation of the peso, which lost more than a third of its value by the end of 2008.

The greatest risk of direct intervention in Chile today may be a sharp drop in copper prices without a corresponding depreciation of the peso, suggesting a disconnection from fundamentals.

If the central bank eventually intervenes, it is likely to announce a calendar of dollar purchases as it did in 2008 rather than set a target exchange rate.

But copper is not the only long-term fundamental supporting the peso's bullish trend. Chile's economy is now growing far more vigorously than two years ago while more developed economies are mired in a slow recovery, further underpinning peso strength.

Meanwhile De Gregorio told lawmakers the current account is near neutral this year, meaning the peso's rally is not driven by speculative capital flows seen in other emerging economies.

Still, several analysts argue that a peso approaching 460 per dollar, whatever the cause, is the strongest level acceptable to the central bank in the short term.

But Chilean authorities have a limited arsenal to battle the currency appreciation. After cutting red tape and boosting hedging operations for small exporters hurting from the stronger peso, Finance Minister Felipe Larrain acknowledged that taming the peso is a daunting task.

"The exchange rate is a topic of concern for the government, but the dollar's weakness is a global problem," he said in an interview with state television on Friday. (Editing by Alonso Soto and Chizu Nomiyama)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Brazil rates dip, Latam  FX  firms on US data
text:
* Investors pare Brazil rate hike bets after retail data

* Chile invokes intervention as peso hits 30-mo high

* Brazil's real firms 0.35 pct, Mexico peso adds 0.13 pct (Adds comments, changes byline, updates prices)

By Jose de Castro and Michael O'Boyle

SAO PAULO/MEXICO CITY, Dec 14 (Reuters) - Yields on Brazilian interest rate futures fell on Tuesday after weaker than expected retail sales prompted bets the central bank will be under less pressure to raise borrowing costs.

Brazilian retail sales rose only 0.4 percent in October from the prior month, which pushed market players to rethink widely-held expectations that Brazil's central bank will raise its benchmark interest rate - called the Selic - early next year to cool inflation pressures. For details, see [ID:nN14196422]

"Now there is some doubt over if, in fact, the Selic will go up and, if it goes up, by how much." said Jason Vieira, an analyst at the Cruzeiro do Sul brokerage.

The yield on the interest rate contract due January 2012 <DIJF2>, one of the most heavily-traded of the session, fell 5 basis points to 11.85 percent.

A head trader at a bank in New York noted that the drop in rates on Tuesday showed the market is now pricing in a rate hike of only about 30 basis points at the central bank's next meeting in January. Last week, the market had been betting on a 50-basis-point increase.

Currencies across Latin America firmed after surprisingly strong November U.S. retail sales boosted optimism about consumer spending in one of the region's top trading partners.

Brazil's currency <BRBY> bid 0.35 percent stronger at 1.693 per dollar. Traders were buying up the currency after the real pierced the key 1.70 level without without prompting additional intervention measures, traders said.

CHILE JAWBONES

Chile's peso surged to a 30-month high on the back of record prices for the country's main export, copper, and despite warnings from officials that they could intervene in the market.

The Chilean peso <CLP=> firmed 0.44 percent to 472.70 per dollar even after the country's central bank chief said policymakers were continuing to evaluate the possibility of intervening to slow the peso's gains. [ID:nN14274122]

Mexico's peso initially firmed the U.S. retail sales data, which boosted the outlook for Mexican exports to its top trading partner.

But the Mexican currency gave up gains late in the session after the U.S. Federal Reserve showed no signs of curtailing its economic stimulus measures, raising the prospect of accelerating U.S. economic growth and also inflation.

The Fed's statement sparked steep losses in the price of U.S. bonds, driving up yields.

That pushed investors to dump riskier Mexican debt in favor of the rising yields on safer U.S. bonds, undermining the peso currency as investors bought dollars to sink into U.S. government debt.

The yield on the government's 10-year peso bond <MX10YT=RR> jumped 13 basis points to bid at 7.17 percent.

"People are expecting a possible boom now in the U.S. economy, and with that pushing up returns on U.S. bonds, it is more attractive to be in Treasuries," said an analyst at a foreign bank in Mexico who does not have permission to speak to media. (Additional reporting by Samantha Pearson in Sao Paulo)

title: Chile  Peso Ends Weaker Despite End Of Ctrl Bk  Intervention
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean peso closed slightly weaker against the U.S. dollar Tuesday, falling to a fresh three-year low, despite the central bank's announcement that it ended its currency market intervention program.

A sharp tumble in spot copper prices on the London Metal Exchange and uncertainty over the outcome of the U.S. government's $700 billion financial bailout plan, which the U.S. House of Representatives rejected Monday afternoon, pulled the peso down, trader said.

The peso ended the session at CLP552.00 to the dollar, compared with CLP551.40 at Monday's close. The peso moved in a broad range of CLP548.00 to CLP556.30 during the session.

State copper commission Cochilco reported that LME spot copper fell 2.6% from Monday's close to a year-to-date low of $2.91161 a pound. As Chile is the world's largest copper producer, market participants and analysts look at copper prices to gauge the general health of the economy. Cochilco estimates the mining industry represents 22% of the country's gross domestic product.

Late Monday, the central bank announced it ended its $8 billion program to beef up its foreign reserves through the end of the year. The bank, which had been making daily $50 million purchases on the local currency market, said it ended the purchases in light of international market conditions.

The central bank began its forex intervention program in mid-April, after the peso firmed to 10-year highs in March as a result of sky-high copper prices. It began daily $50 million purchases on the local currency market with the aim of building up foreign reserves by $8 billion at the end of 2008.

In recent weeks, the bank's daily dollar purchases came under fire, as some analysts said the intervention program had weakened the peso too much, which in turn caused inflation to rise.

In addition, the bank on Monday said that to ease the normal functioning of the forex market and interbank dollar liquidity it would resume its currency swap tender offers starting Tuesday.

Before trading ended Tuesday, the central bank offered local banks up to $500 million in dollar swaps to increase greenback liquidity on the local market. The swaps were offered at a premium of 3.49% over the London Interbank Offered Rate, the monetary authority said on its Web site.

The total amount banks tendered reached 214.36 billion Chilean pesos at a fixed exchange rate of CLP552.47 to the dollar, or $389 million.

The peso could test a significant support level at CLP558 in coming sessions if copper prices continue to tumble and markets remain uncertain as to how the U.S. government will navigate the ratification of its bailout plan through congress, analysts said.

On the bond market, Chilean central bank bonds ended considerably lower on the central bank's decision to end its intervention program ahead of schedule. The program included the neutralization of the daily dollar purchases through auctions of five- and 10-year bond. These auctions also ended Monday.

In addition, a higher September inflation outlook, in light of current crude oil prices, also brought yields down. Chile is a net crude importer.

Bonds are indexed for inflation so that a higher inflation outlook makes them a more attractive investment.

The yield on inflation-indexed five-year BCUs ended at 3.10%, down from 3.28% Tuesday, while the yield on the 10-year BCUs ended at 3.20%, down from 3.34% Tuesday.

title: UPDATE 1- Chile 's  central bank  ends  forex intervention
text:
(Updates with fresh quotes, peso data)

SANTIAGO, Sept 29 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank on Monday called an early halt to an $8 billion foreign-exchange intervention plan that has seen the peso depreciate 22 percent since April, citing international financial turmoil.

The central bank said the program, under which it bought $50 million worth of greenbacks daily, was 70 percent complete. The plan was originally introduced in April to reverse a sharp appreciation of the peso <CLP=CL> <CHILJ> earlier in the year.

"In recent days, there has been a significant deterioration in international financial markets. Due to this, the board has decided today to end its program to accumulate reserves," the bank said in a statement.

The central bank said it had increased international reserves to the tune of $5.75 billion under the program.

"The Chilean economy remains prepared to adequately face turbulence in international markets," it added.

The bank also said it would resume a program of currency swaps from Tuesday, which were replaced by the intervention program.

The peso skidded on Monday to a three-year low as prices for copper -- Chile's main export -- fell below $3 a pound and investors worried that a global financial crisis could deepen.

The peso closed 2.23 percent lower at 551.50/552.00 pesos per dollar, compared with its close at 539.20/539.70 on Friday. It was the peso's weakest close since August 2005.

The peso fell to 558.7 pesos per dollar in after-hours trade following rejection of a U.S. financial sector rescue plan.

The peso has now depreciated over 10 percent in the year-to-date.

The central bank said it would continue to use all instruments at its disposal to ensure financial stability and the normal flow of payments.

The central bank has raised its policy interest rates to their highest levels in around a decade in recent months in a bid to curb inflation which is running at its quickest since 1994.

Annual inflation is currently over 9.0 percent, or three times the bank's target. (Writing by Simon Gardner; editing by Gary Crosse)

title: Analysts see Chile peso settling by year end
text:
SANTIAGO, July 10 (Reuters) - Most analysts see the Chilean peso converging at about 500 per dollar at year end, as a currency intervention program expires and the central bank re-establishes its inflation-fighting credentials by raising rates.

The greenback started the year at near 500 pesos, slumped to 430 pesos in March, but after the central bank kicked off an $8 billion currency intervention in April to curb the strength of the peso the dollar scaled to a high of 529 pesos in June.

Six currency analysts and economists estimated the value of the dollar at year-end would be between 485 pesos and 530 pesos, but said the level would be influenced by several factors, including the intervention, oil and food prices, interest rates, inflation and the policies of the central bank.

Bertrand Delgado, senior economist and currency strategist with IDEAglobal in New York, said the intervention has complicated projections.

He sees the peso at about 506 per dollar at the end of the year, as the central bank fights inflation, but said it could strengthen to 485 depending on the bank's decisions.

"A few months ago the bank practically subordinated its monetary policy to the exchange rate policy. That's why the peso weakened so much," Delgado said. "That gives me a certain degree of assurance that they're going to raise rates and focus on inflation now."

Pedro Tuesta a senior Latam analyst with 4CAST in Washington sees the peso at 530 per dollar, given a reduction in the central bank currency intervention and moderately aggressive interest rate increases to 7.5 percent by year end.

"(The problem is) the intervention is temporary, it will change over time, and it's taking place in a highly inflationary context, so it's working against the bank's monetary policy."

Analysts say that while exporters benefit from a cheaper domestic currency, the rest of the economy is getting walloped with even higher inflation.

INFLATION PRESSURES AND INTERVENTION

Chile's consumer price index rose 1.5 percent in June, bringing 12-month inflation to 9.5 percent, its highest level since 1994.

The figure reinforced expectations the bank would hike its key rate by 50 basis points for a second month in a row to 7.25 percent on Thursday to control runaway inflation, which has helped the peso to appreciate to 504 per dollar despite the continued intervention.

"They're depreciating the currency at a time when inflationary pressures keep rising. That's very dangerous," said Delgado.

Barclays Capital Research does not see the bank suspending the intervention despite the problems it may be creating with inflation and sees the peso at 485 per dollar at year end.

"We do not expect an interruption of the intervention program, as the rules-based Chilean central bank will be very reluctant to modify it," Barclays said in a report. "We think the intervention program is largely priced in at this point."

Tomas Flores, a local economist with the Instituto de Libertad y Desarrollo also thinks the bank is unlikely to change course on its intervention.

"Our view is that they never should have started, but now that they have, its not easy to get out of it. They're stuck." (Additional Reporting by Maria Jose Latorre; Editing by Tom Hals)

title: GLOBAL YIELD: Emerging Mkt  Currencies  Steal Bonds' Thunder
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Bond investors, be aware: if you want to boost returns in emerging markets, stay away from government debt and go for pure plays in currencies.

Surging food, energy and raw material prices have spurred rising inflation worldwide, forcing central banks from Asia and Europe to Latin America to raise interest rates, while allowing local currencies to appreciate to keep price pressures from running out of control.

The policies have prompted a switch in investment strategies as rising interest rates push up bond yields, reducing the value of fixed income securities. Bond prices fall when yields rise. Bonds are also less attractive amid concerns over inflation, which eats into their fixed interest payments over time.

"A strengthening currency probably is one of the more popular policy tools central banks are going to utilize, along with higher interest rates, over the next year or two," said Nick Chamie, head of emerging markets at RBC Capital Markets in Toronto.

Chamie said some of the best destinations for currency bets are Brazil, Russia, Mexico and Colombia where economic fundamentals are sound, central banks are hawkish and expected to rapidly tackle inflation. On the other hand, he recommended investors shun currencies in South Africa, South Korea, India and Argentina.

Brazil stands out as a popular choice. The local central bank has tightened interest rates by 100 basis points this year, pushing up its key rate to 12.25%, among the highest in the world. Brazil began to hike rates in April, after being on hold since September.

The rate increases came as inflation in May stood at 5.58%, well above the central bank's target of 4.5%. There is growing concern that food-led price pressures will spill over into wages and other sectors if left unattended.

"Brazil's real is still attractive," said Igor Arsenin, an emerging-market fixed-income strategist at Credit Suisse Group in New York. "I expect interest rates to rise significantly further in Brazil."


 
   Rising Ruble 
 

Arsenin said he expected Brazil's central bank to boost the key rate to 14.25% by the end of the year and the Brazil real, which traded at BRL1.6151 to the dollar Monday, to strengthen below BRL1.6 against the dollar over the same period.

The real has risen 9.35% against the dollar so far this year, while the Mexican peso, Russian ruble and the Colombian peso have gained 5.96%, 4.05%, and 18.1%, respectively, over the same period.

Monday, Brazil's 10-year government debt yielded 5.578%, higher than the 4.16% on offer on 10-year Treasurys.

Dario Pedrajo, who manages $100 million at Kapax Investment Advisers LLC in Miami, targeted the Russian ruble, whose value has been artificially held back by the local government.

With the Russian government shifting its attention to the fight against inflation, it may allow greater appreciation in the ruble against the dollar, making this a good time to bet on the currency's gains, he said. The ruble was trading at RUB23.6607 to the dollar Monday.

Pedrajo also noted that the Russian ruble is a better bet than the Chinese yuan because he doesn't expect a significant appreciation in the yuan in the foreseeable future.

The yuan, which traded at CNY6.8740 to the dollar Monday, has gained 5.05% this year and has risen more than 20% since a dollar peg was removed in July 2005.


 
   Risks 
 

Still, such currency bets aren't without risks - as seen in the past month with the dollar's rebound against its major rivals amid the shifting interest rate outlook.

The market is now betting on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates by the end of the year, a sharp reversal from several months ago when rate futures markets were discounting additional rate cuts.

Bets on higher rates, however, were moderated last week after The Wall Street Journal and the Financial Times reported that Fed officials were divided on tightening and a rate hike may not be a sure thing.

The swings in Fed rate expectations fueled fluctuations in bonds and currency markets, adding to the risks of currency bets.

"Investors need to be aware of the fact that markets remain extremely nervous," said Chamie. "Currency bets need to be a very selective process."

Investors also need to be mindful that some emerging market governments may intervene to limit the appreciation of their currencies to protect their exporters. Rising currencies make local products less competitive in international markets.

In Latin America, governments in Chile and Colombia are looking to contain gains in their currencies by intervening in foreign exchange markets. Since April, Chile has been buying $50 million a day to reverse the Chilean peso's appreciation. Colombia Friday said it plans to buy $20 million a day in currency markets.

(Min Zeng writes about Treasurys markets for Dow Jones Newswires.)

title: ANALYSIS- Chile central bank  seen clipping  currency intervention
text:
SANTIAGO, June 13 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank may have to scrap its $8 billion currency intervention only two months after its launch, as rising oil prices and a weaker peso are pushing up inflation, making it counterproductive.

The intervention, implemented in April after the peso appreciated some 16 percent year-to-date against the beleaguered U.S. dollar, achieved its goal of curbing the peso's strength, but a rebound in the dollar has now undermined the need for intervention.

"At the time it was a good decision, but the situation changed," said Rodrigo Aravena, an economist with the Banchile brokerage . "The plan was probably to take the level to about 460 to 470 pesos, but they hadn't considered that oil prices would rise so much."

After ending last year at 498 pesos, the dollar fell to 430 pesos in March and since the intervention has recovered, ending at 497 pesos on Thursday.

In early April, when the intervention was announced, prices for oil were at just above $100 per barrel and the dollar was in a global slump.

The intervention included buying $50 million dollars daily on the local currency exchange until the end of the year, a commitment the bank has continued to honor despite high inflation.

CONTROLLING INFLATION

Chile imports nearly all of the fuel it consumes and the intervention to curb the peso's strength, on top of the effect of soaring oil prices, and a stronger dollar, hit Chile with even higher than expected inflation in May of 1.2 percent.

The Bank's response this week was to raise the benchmark interest rate an aggressive 50 basis points to 6.75 percent, its first increase since January.

The decision underscored the change in focus from the exchange rate to inflation, and called into question the effects of the currency intervention.

"The problem is if the peso depreciates too fast it tends to pressure inflation... and this is getting too fast." said Pedro Tuesta, a currency strategist with 4CAST in Washington.

"They probably won't stop (the intervention) right away, because they are committed month to month," he said. "But it doesn't make sense any more."

The peso has depreciated nearly 13 percent since just before the intervention was announced in April.

Aravena also said the bank would avoid any sudden changes after this week's rate surprise, but said he did not see the intervention continuing as it has.

"Having two surprises together could be costly. It would be more prudent to wait a bit and then reduce the amount of dollars they are buying or eliminate it," he said.

"We might have a few more months of intervention, but I really doubt it will last the year."

The central bank is not giving any indication it is thinking of pruning back the measure.

The bank, in its third monthly phase of the intervention, should announce its plans for the next phase before July 8. (Additional reporting by Froilan Romero)

title: POLL-Chile market expects  central bank  rate hike of 25 bps
text:
* What: Chilean Central Bank benchmark rate decision

* When: 6 p.m. (2200 GMT) Tuesday, June 10

* Forecast: Most expect rate hike to 6.50 percent

By Maria Jose Latorre

SANTIAGO, June 9 (Reuters) - A Reuters poll on Monday showed a majority of market watchers expect Chile's central bank to raise its key interest rate a quarter of a percentage point at its monthly monetary policy meeting on Tuesday.

Of 26 traders and analysts polled, 21 said they expected the bank to raise the monetary policy rate <CLTPM=> to 6.50 percent in the first rate hike since January, on recent higher-than-expected inflation and growth data.

May inflation of 1.2 percent and April economic growth of 4.8 percent released last week exceeded market expectations and reinforced views the bank might raise rates to control inflation, a move it had shunned given a weaker dollar and cooling growth.

"We think the bank is going to raise the rate 25 basis points because of the positive surprise in growth and the negative surprise in inflation. On top of that, trade balance data is showing that consumer demand is healthy, that it's strong enough to pull the wagon," said Bertrand Delgado, an economist with IDEAglobal in New York.

June trade figures released on Monday showed Chile's consumer imports up about 25 percent and foreign investment surging near 50 percent above the same month last year.

DOLLAR EXCHANGE RATE

Another factor in Chile's monetary policy has been a weaker dollar, which started the year at about 498 pesos and then tumbled to 430 pesos, leading Chile's central bank to institute an $8 billion currency intervention program in April to curb the appreciation of the peso <CLP=>.

The peso's relative strength against the dollar left the bank reluctant to raise interest rates, which would strengthen the peso further, but on Monday the greenback was trading above 480 pesos per dollar.

Not all agreed that the bank should raise the rate.

"There's still the possibility they could hold the rate. The main factors behind rising inflation are external, such as oil prices, and they'll continue to rise," one trader said.

Chile, which imports nearly all of the fuel it consumes, has seen energy costs rocket amid short supplies of natural gas from Argentina and lower hydroelectric reservoir levels after last year's scant rainfall.

Last year annual inflation soared to 7.8 percent from only 2.6 percent in 2006, leading the bank to hike rates five times between July 2007 and January 2008.

According to a central bank poll released on Monday, analysts predicted annual inflation at 5.5 percent, up from the prior estimate of 4.7 percent, and above the bank's 12- to 24-month target rate of 3 percent.

Economic growth for 2008 was seen at 4 percent in the survey, lower than the rate of 5.1 percent posted last year. (Reporting by Maria Jose Latorre and Lisa Yulkowski; Editing by James Dalgleish; )

title: UPDATE:  Chile  Ctrl Bk Pres: Satisfied With  Forex Intervention
text:
(Updates with more comments from central bank president and executive)

SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chilean central bank president Jose De Gregorio said Friday the monetary authority is "satisfied" with its announced intervention in the local foreign exchange market.

Last month, in a bid to weaken the peso - which was trading at 10-year highs - the central bank announced it would increase its international reserves by $8 billion by the end of the year through daily purchases of $50 million.

Since the bank began its daily purchases on the local forex market in mid-April, the peso has weakened nearly 8%.

"We are very satisfied with the intervention program and it's coherent with our inflationary objective," De Gregorio told reporters.

He added that the bank currently has no plans to increase its purchases and if it did, it would announce it in due course, just like it announced this intervention before it began its daily purchases.

To prevent an inflationary expansion in money supply, the central bank is sterilizing the dollar purchases by issuing short-term debt during the first month of the intervention.

Last week, the central bank announced it would increase by $3.0 billion its local debt offerings during the next three months to sterilize the intervention.

The announcement of the additional $3 billion sent long-term central-bank bond yields shooting up 40 basis points and analysts fear that these yield increases will spill over into higher mortgage rates.

The yields on inflation-indexed 10-year bonds have risen nearly 40 basis points in the past few sessions, reaching 3.4%-3.42% earlier this week. By Friday, they saw a correction to 3.19%-3.21%.

De Gregorio said he couldn't rule out that the fixed-income market had overreacted to the bond issue announcement. He said he expects central-bank bond yields to continue correcting downwards in coming sessions.

"These (yield hikes) should normalize in the short-term and these (corrections) will be the ones that will have repercutions on long-term home and corporate financing; mortage rates won't be reacting to what's happening in yield rates within the short span of a week," De Gregorio said.

Early this week, Chilean central bank cut its 2008 gross domestic product estimate to 4%-5% with a downside risk, from a previous 4.5%-5.5% estimate. Analysts, meanwhile, expect 4% GDP growth this year.

In the first quarter of 2008, the Imacec economic growth index, a GDP proxy, posted a 3.3% on-year gain. The bank will release the first-quarter GDP later this month.

The central bank expects growth to pick up in the second half of the year.

"Just on the effects of the basis of comparison, second-half growth should be higher than in the first half of the year," the bank's head of research, Pablo Garcia, told reporters.

Chile's GDP grew 5.1% in 2007, up from 4.3% in 2006. GDP in the first six months of 2007 grew 6.2% on the year, but decelerated to a 4% on-year gain in the second half.

title: ANALYSIS- Chile central bank intervention  impact seen limited
text:
SANTIAGO, April 17 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank has followed in Mexico and Brazil's footsteps by intervening to curb the strength of its currency versus the dollar, but the move is seen having limited impact and stoking inflation.

The U.S. dollar ended last year at 497.80 pesos and then slumped to 430 pesos in March, the peso's strongest level in over a decade, by which time it had appreciated 15 percent for the year-to-date.

Chile's peso has been appreciating on strong trade surpluses fueled by high world commodities prices, particularly copper, and by robust economic growth. But exporters have been complaining the cheap U.S. dollar hurts their profits and their ability to be compete in world markets.

After its monetary policy meeting last Thursday, the bank surprised markets with a currency intervention program that included buying an additional $8 billion worth of reserves in dollars by the year-end to erode the strength of the peso.

"The end result is that it probably does slow down domestic currency appreciation, but it doesn't completely curtail it. It won't affect market fluctuations day-to-day," said Greg Anderson, a currency strategist with ABN AMRO in Chicago.

The day following the announcement, the peso <CHILJ> <CLP=CL> fell 2.86 percent. The bank implemented its plan on Monday with the first daily $50 million dollar purchase on the forex market. The peso fell slightly on Monday and Tuesday, but held at 456.30 pesos per dollar for the subsequent two days.

"The biggest impact is the announcement effect. The shock of the announcement is a very strong signal to the market that the central bank and government authorities don't want the peso to appreciate nearly as fast as it has been," said Anderson, who left his year-end forecast for the dollar at 450 pesos.

RATE SIGNALS AND INFLATION

With the intervention, the bank is sending a message that it will not raise rates despite high current inflation. The message was not lost on the local stock market which rose for five consecutive days.

"You're not going to intervene if you're planning on hiking. That would be counterproductive," said Pedro Tuesta, senior analyst with 4CAST in Washington.

"They're even indicating that they may cut rates. That reduces the interest rate differential and means the (peso) currency should weaken."

While Chile has raised its benchmark rate to 6.25 percent to rein in inflation, the U.S. federal Reserve has slashed its fed funds rate to 2.25 percent to stave off recession, which has made the peso a more attractive investment.

Following the central bank intervention, Tuesta said he adjusted his year-end forecast upward to 495 pesos per dollar.

A side effect of the intervention is higher inflation.

"What's happening is the bank is borrowing pesos and if they're borrowing pesos, they're increasing the money supply and that causes inflation," said Anderson, who mentioned China's and Argentina's big inflation problems.

"It can work for a little while but it doesn't work for periods of much longer than a year. Inflation gets away from you real quick," he added.

Chile's relatively strong economic growth should give it room to raise rates to control inflation, but the bank is less likely to exercise that option with the intervention.

"The central bank seems to have forgotten about inflation. If you can't increase rates when you have inflation, then you shouldn't intervene, because if you do you're defeating yourself," said Tuesta.

While emerging markets are trying desperately to curb the strength of their currencies against dollar because of their dependence on foreign trade, there is little they can do.

"At the end of the day, the movements we see in foreign exchange rates are going to depend on the United States," said Rodrigo Aravena, economist with the Banchile brokerage, who has held his year-end forecast to 480 pesos per dollar.

The problem is not the Chilean peso but the dollar.

"Take the dollar out of the equation and the Chilean peso really hasn't changed much relative to the euro or the yen. It's only changed relative to the dollar," Anderson said. (Editing by Clive McKeef)

Chile's central bank has raised its benchmark rate five times since July in a bid to control accelerating inflation, while the U.S. Federal Reserve has slashed its key rate to 2.25 percent to stave off recession.

The Chilean central bank kept its benchmark rate steady at 6.25 percent this month for a third month in a row.

"According to the latest data available, our view is that it is equally likely the rate will rise or fall in the future," he said in a speech to the Chilean-American Chamber of Commerce in Washington.

"The recent decisions of the central bank do not rule out future increases in policy rates, but it is equally likely there could be reductions."

Comparatively higher interest rates in Chile than in the United States make the peso an attractive investment, and sky-high copper prices are contributing to strong trade surpluses.

That has sparked a sharp appreciation of the peso, creating another headache.

The central bank last week announced an $8 billion foreign-exchange intervention program aimed at weakening the peso, and on Monday bought the first daily installment of $50 million worth of greenbacks.

It was the first time the bank has intervened in the foreign exchange market since 2002.

The peso hit a decade high of 431.20/431.50 on March 18 to trade around 15 percent higher for the year-to-date, the strongest level since late 1997.

The peso stayed close to that level, sparking a cry from Chilean exporters who fear the loss of their competitive edge worldwide. On Friday, however, the peso fell 2.8 percent on news of the intervention plan.

"It is an exceptional measure," De Gregorio said. "There is an explicit commitment not to try to fix the value, or range, of the exchange rate, thus reducing the space for speculation."

Inflation is also an obstacle.

Chile's consumer price index rose a milder-than-expected 0.8 percent in March, but the reading still pushed annual inflation to a 14-year high of 8.5 percent from 8.1 percent the prior month.

"What we are signaling with this (intervention) measure is that our inflation targets and current monetary policy framework can accommodate a depreciation of the peso, something we could not have been sure of a couple of months back," De Gregorio said. text:
(Updates with peso close)

SANTIAGO, April 11 (Reuters) - The Chilean peso fell 2.8 percent on Friday after the central bank said it would buy $8 billion worth of greenbacks this year to curb the sharp appreciation of the country's currency.

The peso <CHILJ> <CLP=CL> fell as much as 3.7 percent earlier in the session, but recovered some ground later in the day amid profit-taking to close at 446.30/446.80 per dollar.

At Thursday's close of 433.80/434.10, the currency was up nearly 15 percent against the dollar in 2008, making it one of the strongest performers worldwide against the U.S. currency.

The peso is now 11.6 percent firmer against the dollar for the year to date.

To stem the rise, the central bank said Thursday night it would step into the foreign exchange market for the first time since 2002 and purchase $50 million a day in competitive auctions, starting on Monday.

As reasons for stepping into the market, it cited risks of fallout from the U.S. subprime crisis, wider global market turbulence, the weak dollar and the need to boost liquidity in the local market. For details, see [ID;nN10415307].

Central Bank President Jose De Gregorio reaffirmed market dynamics would determine the peso's value.

"We are not looking for either a floor or a ceiling... The market determines the exchange rate," he told a news conference.

"We are not considering capital controls."

The peso hit a decade-high of 431.20/431.50 on March 18, the strongest level since late 1997, and stayed close to that level since, sparking a cry from Chilean exporters fearing the loss of their competitive edge worldwide.

On Friday, Chile's center-left government welcomed the intervention by the central bank, which has autonomous status.

"The government values the decision ... taken by the central bank to accumulate international reserves," Finance Minister Andres Velasco told a news conference after the central bank said the dollar purchases will boost reserves by around 40 percent from March levels of $17.9 billion.

He added: "I am convinced the decision adopted by the central bank will contribute to the competitiveness of the economy and correct this (exchange rate) misalignment."

But some analysts were not convinced the central bank policy would have a profound effect.

HSBC noted the daily auction size looked relatively small.

"Fifty million dollars a day is a relatively small sum compared to daily volumes of between $1.5 billion to $2 billion, so the purchases can at best have a psychological effect on the market," it said.

But Goldman Sachs said the size of the intervention was "not trivial" and expected it to contribute to peso weakening.

Like some other Wall Street banks, it expressed puzzlement that the central bank did not introduce the intervention as part of a broader monetary policy package that would have included a central bank rate hike on Thursday night to control inflation. For details, see [IDn:N10230653].

title: TEXT- Chile  cenbank to  intervene  in  currency  market
text:
SANTIAGO, April 10 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank said on Thursday it will intervene in the foreign exchange market to boost liquidity in the economy and in response to the local peso's <CLP=CL> <CHILJ> sharp appreciation against the dollar.

The central bank said in a statement the "exceptional measure" aims to boost foreign reserves by $8 billion by buying dollars on the currency market, in the period from April 14 to Dec. 12.

Following is the text of the statement.

The complex scenario that financial markets in developed economies are going through, triggered by the crisis in the United States real estate market, has increased the risk of severe disruptions that could negatively impact the external financial conditions faced by the Chilean economy.

The macroeconomic framework based on a floating exchange rate, inflation targeting, a fiscal rule and prudential financial supervision puts the Chilean economy in a favorable position to weather these turbulences. Nevertheless, the depth and consequences of an international financial crisis remain highly uncertain.

With these concerns in mind, the Board of the Central Bank of Chile today decided to intervene in the foreign exchange market so as to strengthen the external liquidity position of the Chilean economy.

This increase in the stock of international reserves will leave the Chilean economy better prepared to face the eventuality of an additional, severe and abrupt deterioration of the external environment.

In the inflation targeting and exchange rate flexibility framework put in in September 2nd 1999, this exceptional measure is justified by the unusual degree of uncertainty regarding events in international financial markets.

It is also coherent with the evaluation that the real exchange rate is currently below the level that would prevail once real and financial conditions in the world economy return to normal.

The Board of the Central Bank of Chile has adopted the following measure:

To increase the stock of international reserves by US$ 8000 million, by purchasing foreign currency over the period extending from April 14th to December 12th 2008.

The Central Bank of Chile will, in due course, announce the specific purchase programs, which could be modified according to market conditions. The first program, which will run from April 14th to May 9th will consist of daily purchases of around US$ 50 million via competitive auctions.

The monetary effects of this measure will be offset so that liquidity provision is consistent with the monetary policy rate. During the period comprising the first program mentioned above this will be done with short term operations.

This exceptional measure is coherent with the overall conduct of monetary policy, which aims to keep inflation at 3% most of the time, with a tolerance range of +/- 1%.

The current monetary policy rate allows the convergence of the current high current inflation rates to 3% over the policy horizon. Monetary policy actions, in one direction or the other, cannot be ruled out in response to future changes in inflation prospects.

The Central Bank of Chile will continue to use all of the tools at its disposal in pursuit of the objectives assigned to it by law. (Editing by Carol Bishopric)

title: Chilean farmers protest strong peso, want action
text:
REQUINOA, Chile, March 27 (Reuters) - Hundreds of farmers and farmhands protested in Chile's agricultural heartland on Thursday to demand authorities take measures to boost their profits in a sector hammered by the strengthening peso.   

 Farmers say production costs have doubled in the past five years due to a nearly 45 percent appreciation of the peso against the U.S. dollar and sharp rises in fuel, labor and other expenses.   

 Sector leaders and businessmen joined workers carrying placards and black flags in the farming town of Requinoa, 60 miles (100 km) south of the capital Santiago, vowing more demonstrations to press for government and central bank action.   

 "We have seen a certain insensitivity on the part of the economic authorities," said Luis Schmidt, president of the National Agricultural Society union. "What we need is a political decision to face up to the issue."   

 The orderly protest was held by a motorway. Two donkeys stood by the roadside, wearing banners that read "Finance Ministry" and "Central Bank."   

 Exporters have appealed to the Central Bank, which is autonomous, to intervene in the foreign exchange market to weaken the peso to bring down their overheads like labor costs and to make their dollar revenues worth more in peso terms.   

Central Bank President Jose de Gregorio has warned the bank has not ruled out intervention and has warned currency speculators not to look for a bailout. But so far the bank has not intervened -- and has not done so for almost a decade.   

Chile's peso, which trades in a free-float exchange rate, is now worth about 443 to the dollar.   

 The Finance Ministry has decreed measures to help exporters, such as simplifying taxes, but has deferred to the central bank on the issue of the currency.   

 Chile, the world's top copper producer, has seen a boom in global commodities prices boost its trade surplus. Its main agricultural exports are fruit and farmed fish.   

 RUNAWAY PESO   

 Chile's peso has strengthened nearly 14 percent against the dollar so far this year to its highest levels in more than a decade on the back of strong copper prices and a widening gap between domestic and U.S. interest rates.   

 Chile's central bank has raised its benchmark rate to 6.25 percent to control inflation.   

 By contrast, the U.S. Federal Reserve slashed its benchmark federal funds rate last week by three-quarters of a point to 2.25 percent, the lowest since February 2005, to try to jump-start the weak U.S. economy and ease a mortgage crisis.   

 "We share the need to be very alert to what happens with economic competitiveness and in particular the exchange rate," Finance Minister Andres Velasco said in Santiago, adding the government was considering new economic measures.   

 Fuel prices, which have shot up amid a drought that has dried up reservoirs and hit hydroelectric power generation, are also hurting the farm sector.   

 Union leader Schmidt said 45,000 farm workers were fired in 2006 and another 12,000 in 2007 due to falling profitability.   

 The sector employs about 800,000 people on a permanent basis and 500,000 part time in the country of around 16 million people.   

 "I came to support my company because, given the fall of the dollar, we risk our company being closed down and losing our jobs," said Maria Castillo, who works at a plant that exports lemons, cherries, pears and apples.  (Editing by Simon Gardner and John O'Callaghan)

With the weaker dollar, the revenues don't go as far as they once did in paying peso-denominated costs like labor.   

The currency <CHILJ><CLP=CL> extended its rally on Wednesday, gaining 1.17 percent to 445.40/445.90 by 1139 local (1439 gmt).   

Chile's central bank has raised its benchmark rate to 6.25 percent to control inflation, while the Fed has lowered rates to try to jump-start the weak U.S. economy.   

By contrast, the U.S. Federal Reserve slashed U.S. interest rates last week by three-quarters of a percentage point, taking the benchmark overnight rate down to 2.25 percent, the lowest since February 2005.   

De Gregorio said there was no evidence to suggest that carry trades were behind the peso's appreciation.

title: UPDATE 3-Chile  central bank  chief says no haste on peso
text:
(Adds further central bank comment on speculators)

SANTIAGO, March 18 (Reuters) - Chilean Central Bank President Jose De Gregorio said on Tuesday the institution would avoid hasty action to combat the rapid appreciation of the peso against the dollar, but did not discard future intervention.

"Not acting is in itself a monetary policy decision that is justified under present conditions and which can change as local and global economic conditions evolve," De Gregorio told Chile's Lower House, or Chamber of Deputies.

Chile's peso is close to an 11-year high against the dollar, buoyed by extended, soaring copper prices and a widening differential between interest rates in Chile and the United States.

"We cannot discard an intervention in the exchange rate in the event that there is a disalignment that threatens the stability of the economy, in the event where we feel an intervention would be effective," De Gregorio told legislators, who are demanding relief for Chileans suffering from the strong peso.

With the currency one of the fastest rising against the dollar this year, legislators demanded action on Tuesday from the central bank chief and warned that no action could be harmful.

"Where is the pilot here," one legislator said ahead of De Gregorio's speech to federal deputies. "We have a serious problem here ... We need a flight plan."

The peso has gained more than 14 percent against the dollar this year, among the strongest gains of any Latin American currency this year against the greenback.

Hardest hit by Chile's powerful currency have been farmers, who export most of their fruits and vegetables to buyers who pay in dollars.

With the weaker dollar, the revenues don't go as far as they once did in paying peso-denominated costs like labor.

The currency <CHILJ><CLP=CL> strengthened 0.60 percent on Tuesday to close at 431.20/431.50 per dollar, compared with the prior session's close at 433.80/434.10.

Chile's central bank has raised its benchmark rate to 6.25 percent to control inflation, while the Fed has lowered rates to try to jump-start the weak economy.

The U.S. Federal Reserve slashed U.S. interest rates on Tuesday by three-quarters of a percentage point, taking the benchmark overnight rate down to 2.25 percent, the lowest since February 2005.

After nearly three hours of debate with congressmen, De Gregorio said the monetary policy scenario was extremely complex, involving fundamental local and global factors.

"We have not discounted any measure, but neither will we encourage speculation among those who are taking positions thinking that in the end the central bank is going to rescue them, that the central bank will intervene," he said in a rebuttal. title: UPDATE 4-Chile  central bank  sees lower growth,higher prices
text:
(Recasts lead, adds comment on non-currency intervention, paragraph 12)   

SANTIAGO/VALPARAISO, Jan 16 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank on Wednesday cut its 2008 economic growth estimates to between 4.5 and 5.5 percent, and signaled higher interest rates were on the horizon as the inflation outlook climbed.   

In a speech to Chile's Congress in the port city of Valparaiso, central bank governor Jose de Gregorio said the bank was "deeply upset" about Chile's recent inflation trajectory, and said it could raise interest rates again over coming months.   

"This (inflation trajectory), obviously, upsets us deeply, and as such we are adopting monetary policy decisions to ensure that inflation returns to within the policy goal," he said.   

The bank raised its 2008 inflation outlook to 4.5 percent, from a previous estimate of 3.1 percent, which is far higher than its target range and above analysts' expectations.   

Its growth projections, down from a prior outlook for growth of 5.0 percent to 6.0 percent, were in line with the expected increase in gross domestic product for 2007 of 5.2 percent.   

Higher inflation has prompted a gradual rise in the benchmark interest rate to 6.25 percent in January from 4.0 percent a year ago.   

Chile's consumer price index jumped 7.8 percent in 2007, a 12-year high and up from a rate of 2.6 percent in 2006, driven mostly by higher fuel and food prices in the second half of the year.   

The central bank has a 12- to 24-month inflation target of 3 percent, with tolerance of plus or minus 1 percent.   

"The inflation projection ... indicates they're going to have to maintain a restrictive monetary policy in coming months," said Bertrand Delgado, an economist with IDEAglobal in New York.   

STRONG PESO, STRONG COPPER   

The Chilean peso has been trading near nine-year highs against the dollar this month, as rising interest rates in Chile and falling rates in the United States make the peso a more attractive investment option.   

"Even though the peso will be hit by global volatility and a U.S. economic slowdown, it will be supported by the interest rate differential," Delgado said.   

In the past, Chile's exporters have complained the strong peso depresses earnings and makes it difficult to compete in global markets, but De Gregorio said the bank saw no reason to intervene in the exchange rate.   

"When we have intervened, its been precisely because we've seen problems affecting the entire economy," De Gregorio told reporters. "If we haven't done anything, it's because we haven't seen these conditions."   

Average prices for copper, Chile's top export and economic mainstay, are expected to rise to $2.95/lb in 2008 from previous estimates of $2.70/lb.   

Such a rise would support an expected trade surplus of $16.4 billion in 2008, less than the record $24.5 billion surplus posted in 2007.   

"The trade balance is still positive," Delgado said. "And with economic growth at these levels, at around 5 percent, Chile is still pretty stable."   

Exports in 2008 are expected to come in at $68.3 billion, equal to the figure in 2007. (Additional reporting by Lisa Yulkowski; Writing by Pav Jordan; Editing by Diane Craft)

title: China advised to learn from Chile on managing  FX
text:
BEIJING, April 30 (Reuters) - China should learn from Chile how to scale back intervention in the foreign exchange market, a senior government economist said.   

Li Yang, a researcher with the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, the government's top think-tank, said Chile's experience in reducing intervention and making its operations transparent marked a "successful combination of market-oriented mechanisms and appropriate government intervention".   

Whereas the People's Bank of China (PBOC) intervenes heavily to control the yuan <CNY=CFXS>, he said Chile's central bank had greatly reduced its presence in the foreign exchange market since it adopted a floating exchange rate regime in September 1999.   

Li, a former academic member with the central bank's monetary policy committee, was writing in the latest edition of China Finance, a bi-monthly journal affiliated with the PBOC.   

Chile's central bank, according to Li, has intervened in the currency market only 15 times in the last six years to stabilise the Chilean peso <CLP=CL>.   

By contrast, China's excessive intervention -- to keep the yuan from rising too fast or to deter speculation -- would not help Beijing attain its goal of building up a market-oriented exchange rate system, he said.   

Beijing scrapped the yuan's peg to the dollar in July 2005 in favour of a managed float with reference to a basket of currencies, the details of which are secret.   

Chinese officials, including PBOC Governor Zhou Xiaochuan, have pledged to let market forces eventually determine the yuan's exchange rate. However, for now, the central bank still has the ultimate say setting the rate, economists say.

title: UPDATE 2- Chile central bank  has no peso  intervention  plan
text:
(Adds De Gregorio comment on no tax cuts)  

SANTIAGO, May 30 (Reuters) - Chileans can forget about tax cuts in the face of windfall profits from copper, and central bank intervention to weaken the powerful peso currency is unlikely except in extreme cases, officials said.  

Jose De Gregorio, the central bank's vice president, said on Tuesday the institution will stick to a free-floating exchange rate, and urged calm from Chileans who say they are being hurt by the currency's strength.  

Chile's peso, buoyed by soaring prices for No. 1 export copper, has surged in value over the past year -- though it has lost ground recently -- and exporters have said their dollar-denominated profits are being hurt.  

"We must not overreact" on the exchange rate, De Gregorio said at a Santiago seminar on Chile's windfall copper profits.  

Chile is the world's largest copper producer and, with prices soaring to record highs, government income from mining taxes are expected to hit $3.3 billion this year.  

"Not everything is copper-colored," De Gregorio said. "Copper is pretty important, but we mustn't overreact about its impact on the economy."  

At the same seminar, Chile Finance Minister Andres Velasco said the government had no plans to cut income tax, even as surging copper revenue fattens public finances.  

"I don't think that's a path we want to take," Velasco said, adding that the government was already taking other steps to manage the funds.  

The government said in April it would hold some copper profits in a special pension reserve fund and some in a new copper fund to save dollars at home or abroad.  

"Cutting taxes does not seem to me to be the correct macroeconomic response," to high copper revenues, Velasco said.  

The copper profit has helped boost the peso currency by some 9 percent in the past year, although it has weakened recently, in part because of the government's pledges to invest copper funds abroad.  

In the year to date, the peso has lost about 3 percent against the U.S. dollar.  

On the foreign exchange market on Tuesday, the peso <CHILJ> <CLP=CL> fell 1.27 percent in midday trade to 533.20/533.70 per dollar compared with Monday's close at 526.50/527.00.  

"We are in a pretty reasonable situation," said De Gregorio.  

"You can't spend it all, or debit a tax cut. A cut in taxes or rise in spending is practically the same to me."  

On central bank intervention, De Gregorio said such measures were reserved, "for when we are truly convinced of an exchange rate overreaction."  

He also said such measures would only be implemented if they were relatively assured of success.

Chile's government is holding $1.91 billion of its $4.19 billion in foreign reserves in time deposits and certificates of deposit at the New York City branch of state bank BancoEstado, Budget Director Alberto Arenas said Wednesday.  

Chile's government registered a 4.8% of gross domestic product budget surplus, in 2005, followed by a 2.2% surplus in the first quarter, amid surging earnings from state copper holdings and rising tax collections.  

As of April 30, "In consolidated terms, approximately...60% of the resources are invested outside the country," Arenas said.  

The Finance Ministry plans to report foreign investment data every quarter, amid pressure from many exporters to intervene in the foreign exchange market.  

Surging prices for copper - Chile's principal export - and molybdenum have contributed to the peso strengthening against the dollar, to the chagrin of non-metallic exporters who have booked forex-related losses.  

The previous and present governments have argued that they contribute to keeping the currency stable by maintaining government dollar inflows related to the commodities boom off the forex market.  

The holdings include those at BancoEstado in New York and at the central bank, where it has deposited $1.5 billion and thus kept them off the market, according to Arenas.  

Including the latter assets, the government is keeping 81.4% or $3.41 billion in dollar inflows away from currency trading, while $779.44 million, or 18.6% of the assets, are invested in domestic instruments.

Arenas' report comes as the government seeks to move dollar earnings so non-metallic exporters don't suffer the consequences of copper's pull.  

Under the plan - announced Tuesday - budget surpluses above 1% of GDP will flow into an Economic and Social Stabilization Fund and into the government's pension reserve fund, up to certain limits specified in the legislation.  

If approved by congress, those funds in local or foreign currency could be invested in Chile or in foreign countries, in instruments specified by the pension system legislation, except shares.  

Up to 100% of the money could flow outside Chile.  

The flow of funds overseas could help insulate Chile's currency to a greater extent from the volatility of the foreign exchange market, according to supporters of the plan, which emulates Norway's similar efforts to deal with crude oil earnings.  

Chile could also seek third-party management of its foreign portfolio, which would be independently audited.
