title: ANALYSIS- Chile 's peso seen stronger,  intervention  eyed
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, April 12 (Reuters) - At the rate Chile's peso is rising, it could soon reach its strongest against the dollar in more than six years and could even prompt the usually hands-off government to weaken the currency through market interventions.  

Boosted by record high copper prices, Chile's peso briefly hit 510.70 per dollar on Wednesday, a level not seen since December, and traders said that if it crosses the 510 per dollar mark, there was no telling how strong it could get.  

"We feel it could fall below 500 pesos in coming weeks, driven mostly by the price of copper and a good scenario abroad," said Cristian Gardeweg, an economist with the Celfin investment bank.  

The 500 pesos per dollar rate is seen as a key psychological level that could possibly trigger the government to act, economists said.  

Copper prices are soaring as global demand for the metal, which is used in everything from electrical wiring to water piping and as a heat conductor, continues to build, and as investment funds increase exposure to commodities.  

Chile is the world's largest producer of the metal and the government receives tax dollars from the giant foreign mining firms and billions of dollars of profit from No. 1 copper miner, state-owned Codelco.  

U.S. copper futures extended their bull run early Wednesday with benchmark May copper <HGK6> trading at $2.75 a lb, up more than 30 percent this year, and compared with about 60 cents a lb a few years ago.  

The peso, which fell early in the year, has strengthened again in recent weeks and analysts say the momentum it is gathering could lend it a strength not seen since 2000.  

"I believe it is very probable that copper prices will stay high until close to the end of the year," said Ricardo Amorin, head of Latin American research at WestLB in New York.  

"So we see (the currency) touching 500 pesos per dollar, which is very possible because, really, its pretty close already, about 3 percent away."  

And while the high price of copper has fattened miners' profits, the resulting strong peso has hit fruit growers, wine exporters and others who say it makes it hard for them to compete on the global market and have for months been asking the government to intervene.  

Chile has a free-floating currency but the central bank can intervene if it sees speculative bubbles or other dangers in the market.  

"The dollar will be fluctuating in a range between 510 and 530 pesos, depending on the interventions that some political authorities make, trying to maintain the exchange rate," said Franco Parisi, economist with the University of Chile.  

Economists said that the political cost of not intervening could be high, especially since the new government of Michelle Bachelet has promised to help small and medium-sized businesses, such as the exporters who say they are being battered by the super-peso.  

"If the central bank does not do anything and doesn't care, there will be a moment in which the exchange rate will be less than 500 pesos per dollar," said Eduardo Orpis, economist with Finanzas Today consulting firm, who thinks there will be a lot of pressure on the central bank to intervene.  

Other than intervening by buying pesos, economists say the central bank or finance ministry could issue dollar-denominated debt to increase dollar demand, stimulate dollar demand by allowing the country's private pension funds to invest more abroad, or make offshore investments of Codelco's dollar-denominated revenue to keep the dollars out of the Chilean foreign exchange market.  

Up until now officials have limited themselves to occasional verbal messages to the market that have had some effect, and economists said they expect more of that.  

"It's very likely that in the next days and weeks we'll see more than a few verbal interventions or declarations, although the usefulness of that has almost been used up," said Angel Cabrera, economist with Forecast consulting firm in Santiago.  

Chile's record trade surplus of $2.198 billion in March, also pushed up by high copper prices, gives little room for the peso to turn, economists said.  

"We expect something similar in April (for the trade surplus) and the truth is that given the external accounts there is no where the exchange rate can devalue," Orpis said.  

The peso appreciation could also get more fuel on Thursday if the central bank hikes the benchmark interest rate to 5.0 percent, as expected, economists said. (Additional reporting by Maria Jose Latorre and Manuel Farias)

text:

 VALPARAISO, Chile, Jan 3 (Reuters) - Chile's powerful peso fell more than 1 percent on Tuesday as officials met with Congress to discuss exchange rate intervention, but the central bank said after the currency market closed that it will only take measures in "exceptional situations."  

Central Bank governor Vittorio Corbo told Congress the autonomous body would keep an eye on the exchange rate, but reiterated there were no current plans to weaken the local currency.  

 "In such a case where the exchange rate were to evolve toward values which, in the opinion of the central bank, differed significantly from fundamental determinants, be assured that we will use the tools that are at our disposition, particularly interventions in the exchange market," Corbo said.  

 His statements came soon after foreign exchange markets closed in Chile, and will likely disappoint traders who had bet the central bank would announce measures to weaken the peso, which has been free floating since 1999.  

 The Chilean peso <CHILJ> <CLP=CL> fell 1.36 percent against the dollar to 520.30/520.80, its weakest in over a month. On Monday it closed at 513.20/513.70 per dollar.  

 Chilean exporters in particular are calling for official intervention in the strength of the peso after it gained 8.5 percent against the dollar in 2005, touching highs last seen in April 2000.  

 Corbo said during a visit to Congress that the central bank was keeping an eye on the exchange rate and reserved the right to intervene, but had no plans to do so at the moment.  

 "We are reaching (exchange rate) levels where one could worry and as such we are going to be monitoring every day," said Corbo, who also warned that any intervention would not be announced before hand.  

Chile's economy and its currency are powering forward as prices for copper, the nation's top export, surge to new heights that even optimistic analysts had not expected.  

 High copper prices are estimated to have brought in an additional $4 billion to the government in 2005 in profits from state copper miner Codelco, the world's largest producer of the red metal.  

 An industrial group said on Monday that if the peso were to hold a value of 515/dollar in 2006, it would mean some $1 billion in lost revenues to exporters.  

 Finance Minister Nicolas Eyzaguirre, who joined Corbo on Tuesday's visit to the Chilean Congress in Valparaiso, said the peso strength was not yet at worrisome levels.  

 He said the government was taking advantage of the strong peso to boost cheaper dollar assets and pay down debt.

title: Chile  would  intervene  if peso strength dangerous
text:
SANTIAGO, Jan 2 (Reuters) - Chile will take measures if the peso currency, supported by soaring prices for copper, appreciates "dangerously" against the dollar, Finance Minister Nicolas Eyzaguirre said on Monday.  

The peso gained 8.5 percent against the dollar in 2005, touching highs last seen in April 2000, in large part because prices for copper, Chile's chief export, rose even beyond optimistic forecasts.  

Exporters of other goods have asked the government and the autonomous central bank to take measures to weaken the currency.  

"It is necessary to be permanently cautious that the price of the dollar go too much beyond what guarantees sustained growth in the future, for both exporters and for the economy as a whole," Eyzaguirre told reporters.  

"If authorities become convinced that the exchange rate is becoming dangerous, it will take the pertinent measures," he said.  

Chile has had a floating exchange rate policy since 1999.  

High copper prices are seen as having brought in an additional $4 billion to government coffers in 2005 as it received the profits of state copper miner Codelco, the world's largest producer of the red metal.  

On the foreign exchange market, the peso currency <CHILJ> <CLP=CL> closed down 0.27 percent against the dollar to 513.20/513.70, compared with Friday's close at 511.80/512.30.  

An industrial group said on Monday that if the peso were to hold a value of 515/dollar in 2006, it would mean some $1 billion in lost revenues to exporters.  

On the other hand, Eyzaguirre also pointed out that the same exporters who are complaining today were not as quick to do so when the peso was trading at 760 to the dollar.  

"So its not really fair to ask for help when prices are lower and take your winnings when things are going stupendously well and prices are higher."  

Eyzaguirre will join central bank governor Vittorio Corbo in a special meeting with the senate on Tuesday to discuss the strength of the peso against the dollar.

title: Chile stocks edge down as peso rises for a 7th day
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, Dec 6 (Reuters) - Chilean stocks edged down in mixed trade on Tuesday, as the peso shadowed the Brazilian real to rise for a seventh consecutive day to its highest level since April 2000.  

The IPSA blue-chip index <.IPSA> slipped 0.29 percent to 2,035.54 points while the broader IGPA index <.IGPA> was down 0.05 percent at 9,446.94, preliminary closing figures showed.  

"Volume wasn't bad today ... The exchange rate is obviously affecting the market," Euroamerica trader Jose Pablo Aguirre said.  

Analysts said the low dollar is hurting export companies that receive dollar income, such as major wood products manufacturer Masisa.  

Masisa , which sells its products in over 50 countries and has operations in the U.S. and Mexico, was among the session's biggest decliners, as its stock retreated 2.87 percent to 104.90 pesos a share.  

Shipping company Sudamericana de Vapores was down 2.96 percent at 820 pesos a share. Vapores is Chile's largest container shipping firm.  

The retail sector, which imports large quantities of its merchandise, fared better, with leading department store chain Falabella rising 2.55 percent to 1,405 pesos a share and diversified retailer Cencosud jumping 3.0 percent to 1,030 pesos a share.  

"Cencosud has been incredible, it was about a quarter of what we traded today," said Aguirre.  

On the foreign exchange market the Chilean peso <CHILJ> <CLP=CL> rose 0.63 percent to close at 510.30/510.80 per dollar, compared to Monday's close at 513.50/514.00.  

"Market activity is down drastically for year-end, so today's rise in the peso is closely tied to the (Brazilian) real," a trader said.  

The real, rising on increased export sector revenues, continued its advance despite strong sales of dollar indexed currency swap contracts by Brazil's central bank in recent weeks to stop the U.S. currency's fall.  

The peso has risen 12 percent against the dollar in the second half of the year and many exporters complain that the strong peso is taking a bite out of profits. However, the government has said several times that it will not intervene.

title: Chilean stocks retreat, peso rises for 6th session
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, Dec 5 (Reuters) - Chilean stocks retreated on Monday after lower-than-expected economic data, while high copper prices pushed the peso up for a sixth straight session against the dollar to a fresh 5-1/2-year high.  

The IPSA blue-chip index <.IPSA> slipped 0.75 percent to 2,041.44 points while the broader IGPA index <.IGPA> fell 0.60 percent to 9,451.71, preliminary closing figures showed.  

"The economic activity figures are below projections, and the market's interpretation of the data isn't good," said Rodrigo Sarria, deputy manager of the Intervalores brokerage.  

On Monday the central bank issued its monthly economic activity report, showing growth for October at 4.9 percent compared to October 2004, less than the median 5.3 percent median projection of analysts in a Reuters poll.  

Diversified retailer Cencosud led blue-chip declines as its shares slumped 3.71 percent to 999.80 pesos a share, its lowest close in almost five months, in heavy trading.  

Other leading decliners included wood products manufacturer Masisa , which is seeking to raise $160 million in a share offering. Masisa stock fell 3.32 percent to 108 pesos.  

Shares of power generator Colbun were down 2.79 percent to 69.99 pesos a share.  

On the foreign exchange market the Chilean peso <CHILJ> <CLP=CL> inched up 0.1 percent to close at 513.50/514.00 per dollar compared to Friday's close at 514.00/514.50.  

"With copper as high as it is and with the central bank unlikely to intervene to stop the dollar's descent, investors have continued to unload dollars," a trader said.  

Some Chilean exporters have asked the government to intervene to stop the peso's rise against the dollar, but officials have insisted that they will not intervene unless there are signs of market speculation.

title: Chile  Fin Min:Not Opposed To  Intervention  To Boost Dollar
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chile's Finance Minister isn't opposed in principle to an intervention in the foreign exchange market to boost the dollar, he told reporters Wednesday.  

"I'm not opposed to an intervention in cold blood, but I am opposed to an intervention" for a prolonged period, Eyzaguirre said after a meeting with President Ricardo Lagos.  

While the government has some fiscal means at its disposal to intervene, the central bank has greater room to do so, he added.  

The peso set a 66-month record against the dollar earlier, ending at CLP516.00 to the dollar compared with CLP518.85 Tuesday, after trading in a CLP515.35-CLP520.60 range.  

Exporters have pressured authorities - above all the central bank and the finance ministry - to prop up the faltering greenback.  

However, the Chilean peso hasn't lost contact with underlying fundamentals - the record price of copper and the global weakness of the dollar - in continually setting over five-year records against the U.S. currency, Jose de Gregorio, the central bank's vice president said earlier Wednesday.  

The bank has said it will only due so in the event of an imbalance such as major speculation.  

Twice in the past three years, the central bank has threatened to intervene and provided dollar liquidity when the peso weakened sharply against the U.S. currency.  

Both de Gregorio and Eyzaguirre spoke against a foreign exchange rate target for the peso, and both said the peso will likely weaken once copper prices retreat from their current record levels around $2 per pound.  

Chile is the world's number-one copper producer.  

Considering copper prices are expected to drop, the market should adjust the peso's forex rate, not the central bank through intervention, de Gregorio said.  

The last times the independent monetary authority stepped into the forex arena, it announced by how much it would intervene in dollar terms.  

However, Eyzaguirre disagreed with that policy. "The intervention that I think can be done is unpredictable and therefore the central bank should never reveal what it's going to do" in order to weaken speculators' positions, he said.  

Under current conditions, businesses subject to foreign exchange fluctuations need to improve forward coverage, he added.  

"Just as I warned exporters when the dollar was at CLP630 to cover their future exports and not complain later, now I tell importers and those who have debts in dollars that it's a good moment to cover them because I*m not certain this price of copper will last and that the dollar will stay at these levels," he said.

title: Chile central bank  sees no peso  intervention  need
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, Nov 21 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank has not seen the need to intervene in the foreign exchange market despite a major rally in the peso currency, the bank's vice president, Jose de Gregorio, said on Monday.  

The peso is trading at close to five-year highs against the dollar, pumped up by the global copper rally. Non-minerals exporters are pressing the government to intervene in the foreign exchange market to curb the currency's strength, which they contend is eroding their competitiveness abroad.  

Chile has had a free-floating currency system since September 1999 but the bank can intervene in special cases.  

"We have a flexible exchange rate policy whereby under special circumstances we can evaluate whether it is necessary to intervene, but that situation has not occurred," De Gregorio told reporters.  

"Many times interventions are ineffective in the medium term and even in the short term, and a lot of this depends on what is" happening in the market, De Gregorio said.  

Last Thursday, Finance Minister Nicolas Eyzaguirre said that if officials saw signs of speculating in the market, the central bank could intervene, but he said there was no sign of a speculative bubble so far.  

The peso has appreciated in recent weeks due to record high prices for copper, Chile's main export. Voracious Chinese demand for the metal has pumped up prices.  

The peso <CHILJ> <CLP=CL> was trading at 525.70/526.00 per dollar at midday on Monday (1500 GMT). The peso hit a five-year closing high of 523.50 on Nov. 15.

title: Chile  Central Banker Says Not Readying Peso  Intervention
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean peso's rally to its strongest level in five and a half years against the dollar hasn't set the alarm bells ringing at the central bank, the monetary authority's vice president said Monday.  

"We've got a flexible exchange rate policy where under special circumstances we could find an intervention necessary, but that situation hasn't occurred," said Jose de Gregorio at a meeting with business leaders.  

The bank has threatened to intervene twice in the past three years as the peso plunged to all-time lows against the U.S. currency, but in the end provided dollar liquidity in the bond market without intervening directly.  

Since then, the peso has gradually strengthened in line with other commodities-based and Latin American currencies. So far this year, it has strengthened some 6.5% against the greenback to 527.20 pesos to the dollar from CLP561.50 Jan. 3.  

While government officials have said the peso's gains stem from fundamentals, the central bank has limited itself to saying that it could call an intervention in the event of major speculation.  

Some economists say the central bank's foreign reserve holdings, which have dropped in recent months, don't adequately reflect the surge in foreign trade, which has reached record highs.  

De Gregorio said the bank's net position in dollars hasn't changed and that the drop in reserves also reflects the strengthening of the dollar against other major currencies the bank also holds in its foreign exchange portfolio.  

At the same time, the bank in August said it planned to sell assets in dollars and other foreign currencies worth $1.47 billion through the end of the year.  

Wednesday, the bank will report third-quarter gross domestic product growth. Weaker-than-expected mining output limited growth in the third quarter, but overall GDP growth remains on target with the bank's 6.0%-6.5% estimate for the year.  

Last year, GDP growth came in at 6.1%. Last week, the Finance Ministry estimated that GDP grew 5.3% on the year in the third quarter, while domestic demand grew more than 10%.

title: Chile  Peso Ends Stronger But Some Worry About  Intervention
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean peso ended slightly stronger against the dollar Thursday, in line with the euro and Brazilian real, traders said.  

However, some worry that the peso's rally - it has reached its highest level since mid-2000 in recent sessions - could spark central bank intervention if the surge doesn't run out of steam, traders said.  

The peso ended at CLP524.40 to the dollar from CLP524.80 Wednesday, after trading in a CLP522.40-CLP524.90 range.  

According to Chile's Banco Central, the peso traded at CLP523.01 to the dollar around 1500 GMT, about an hour before the market closed.  

The Brazilian real opened marginally stronger Thursday after Finance Minister Antonio Palocci dispelled rumors that he would resign and mounted a spirited defense of the government's austere economic policies in testimony before a senate committee.  

The peso often trades in the same direction as the euro and real. The latter is also a key indicator of short-term confidence in the region.  

The Chilean currency didn't hold on to early gains as the market began to worry the central bank might take action, traders said.  

On two previous occasions in recent years, the bank has threatened multi-billion dollar intervention following plunges in the peso, along with providing dollar-indexed bonds.  

The bank doesn't pursue an exchange-rate target, but says it can intervene in the event of major speculative imbalances.  

The peso still has room to near CLP519 ahead of major technical resistance.  

On the local bond market, rates rose on a rise in supply sparked by a likely slowdown in inflation for next month in line with a drop in fuel prices.  

Bond rates are adjusted for inflation so that a lower inflation outlook makes bonds a less attractive investment.  

The yield on the inflation-indexed eight-year PRCs closed at 3.37%, up from 3.20% Wednesday.  

At the long end of the curve, the yield on the 20-year PRC closed at 3.50%, up from 3.33% Wednesday.

title: Chilean Peso Weakens On Rumor ECB Mulling  Intervention
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chile's peso ended weaker Wednesday, dropping in line with the euro following speculation that the European Central Bank is considering intervening in favor of the dollar, traders said.  

The Andean currency closed at CLP589.40 to the dollar from CLP585.50 after trading in a CLP585.50-590.00 range.  

Traders overseas said the move was triggered in part by a report from the Market News service, which cited unnamed sources from the ECB as saying the bank was prepared to intervene in currency markets in concert with the Bank of Japan to weaken the euro.  

The peso has latched on to the euro in recent weeks, decoupling from copper, Chile's soaring top export product.  

Copper's hold on the peso has lessened after Finance Minister Nicolas Eyzaguirre said the windfall from high copper prices, which have reached eight-year highs and spiked another 3.2% Wednesday, will be used to prepay debt, easing fears of a flood of dollars in the local market, traders said.  

U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's positive comments on the U.S. economy and calmness about foreign Treasurys holdings also undermined the peso, traders added.  

However, the peso may well be headed for turbulence depending on the strength or weakness of the dollar in upcoming trading, they also said. In broad terms, the peso should stay within its CLP569-595 recent range, traders said.

title: UPDATE 2- Chile  Cenbank says to  intervene  on peso if needed.
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, Jan 15 (Reuters) - Chile's Central Bank said on Thursday it was prepared to take measures to halt a sharp appreciation in the peso against the U.S. dollar but was still not convinced this was necessary.   

The peso appreciated 21 percent in 2003 and firmed to 39-month highs last Friday, buoyed by rising prices of its principal export, copper; a good outlook for the domestic and global economies; and the weakness of the dollar against other foreign currencies.   

Central Bank President Vittorio Corbo told a business meeting the peso currency was not "out of its orbit" and was trading within stable margins. He dismissed exporter concerns, saying that the peso was at the same level it was at three years ago.   

"No Central Bank rules out the possibility of intervening in the foreign exchange market. If tomorrow we see the necessity to do it we will," Corbo said.   

"We will act when the Central bank board is convinced this is necessary ... and we're not convinced yet," Corbo said.   

The rise in the peso has caused concern among exporters their profits will be hurt and sparked debate among economists and some government authorities who believe the bank should step in now.   

A special committee of private exporters called on the government on Thursday to begin a discussion about ways to ensure less volatility in the foreign exchange market.   

Though they emphasized they were not lobbying for a fixed or ideal peso value against the dollar, they said the strengthening peso in recent months was affecting potential future investments and job creation for many exporters.   

"We are in a position only to express our concern to the authorities and to public opinion about this process. These abrupt appreciations have worrying consequences," said committee president Andres Concha.   

Seventy-five percent of Chilean exports are directly or indirectly linked to the dollar, the committee said.   

The Central Bank has said it will wait for the market to stabilize the peso.   

After the Central Bank cut interest rates last Thursday to a historic low of 1.75 percent, the currency has depreciated somewhat this week and closed down 0.10 percent at 573.80/574.30 on Thursday.   

But traders said they expect fresh gains in the peso in the next few days.   

"It's most likely that the drop in the peso is a temporary situation that should reverse itself starting tomorrow (Friday), as long as demand subsides," said Patricio Mella, trader at Inversiones J.C. Tour.   

The Central Bank last intervened directly in the foreign currency market in October 2002, when the peso fell to a historic low of 760 per dollar amid political jitters in Brazil.   

The bank on Wednesday raised its forecast for economic growth for 2004 to between 4.5 percent and 5.5 percent from between 4 percent and 5 percent, citing stronger prices for its principal exports, namely copper.

After the Central Bank cut interest rates last Thursday to a historic low of 1.75 percent, the currency has depreciated somewhat this week and closed at 573.80/574.30 on Thursday.   

The bank on Wednesday raised its forecast for economic growth for 2004 to between 4.5 percent and 5.5 percent from between 4 percent and 5 percent, citing stronger prices for its principal exports, namely copper.

title: UPDATE 2-Chile sees faster economic growth, buoyed by copper.
text:
VALPARAISO, Chile, Jan 14 (Reuters) - Chile's Central Bank painted a rosy picture for the economy in 2004, forecasting faster growth and a higher trade surplus, buoyed by an Asia-driven jump in prices of its leading export copper.  

In a presentation to the Senate, Central Bank President Vittorio Corbo raised the forecast range for 2004 economic growth by a half of a percentage point to between 4.5 percent and 5.5 percent. He maintained the bank's estimate of 3.2 percent growth for 2003.  

"Since the last report (in September), there have been significant changes in the international arena and that has consolidated the recovery and our main exports," Corbo said in his quarterly report to the Senate in Valparaiso.  

The bank sees copper prices averaging $1.00 per pound this year, up from a previous estimate of 83 cents per pound, as China leads an upturn in demand for the metal amid a global economic recovery which would help export-oriented Chile overall.  

Chile, the world's No. 1 copper producer and one of the most open economies in Latin America, earns an additional $100 million for every one cent rise in world copper prices.  

The copper rally will help boost the South American nation's trade surplus to $4.6 billion this year, the bank said, up more than 30 percent from its previous trade surplus estimate of $3.5 billion. Copper traditionally accounts for 40 percent of Chile's total exports.  

Exports will also rise due to a bilateral free trade deal between Chile and the United States, its biggest trade partner, that went into effect Jan. 1, dropping duties on 87 percent of all goods. Chile has a similar accord with the European Union.  

FEAR OF DEFLATION  

One soft spot in the economy is a threat of deflation coupled with a 20 percent currency appreciation in 2003 that has sent exporters crying out for Central Bank intervention to stabilize the peso .  

But Corbo, who maintained the bank's 2004 inflation estimate of 2 percent, gave no sign of stepping in to stop the peso's climb.  

"The exchange rate has not gone out of orbit ... it's an international phenomenon," Corbo said.  

Chile has a floating exchange rate but the Central Bank intervenes to sell or buy dollars if it considers the currency to be unstable. Its last intervention was during the financial crisis leading up to the Brazilian presidential elections in 2002.  

After weeks of gains, the peso began sliding this week and after Corbo's remarks, it fell at midsession on Wednesday to 577.00/577.50 per dollar from Tuesday's close of 566.00/566.50.  

Inflation in 2003 was 1.1 percent, the lowest since 1935 after consumer prices dropped in December for the third straight month.  

The undesirably low inflation prompted the bank to slash its benchmark interest rate twice in both December and January to a historic low of 1.75 percent.

title: Chile  Peso Ends Near Support On Ctrl Bk  Intervention  Fear
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chile's peso weakened against the dollar Monday as the market started to worry that the central bank might intervere on behalf of the punished U.S. currency, traders said.  

The peso closed at CLP562.00 to the dollar, near technical support and 0.8% weaker than the CLP557.80 close Friday, after trading in a CLP557.00-562.30 range.  

Technical resistance stands at CLP556.30, traders said.  

Late Thursday, the central bank lopped another 50 basis points off its key interest rate to 1.75% from 2.25%, a previously record-low rate, surprising the market.  

While the peso shrugged off the cut in Friday's trading, dollar demand rose following comments by European Central Bank President Jean-Claude Trichet, who earlier Monday gave the clearest signal yet that euro-zone policymakers are growing increasingly concerned about the strength of the single currency and won't sit on their hands indefinitely.  

Chile's central bank however has so far said it is unconcerned with the strengthening of the peso. In recent history - when the peso swiftly plunged to record lows versus the dollar in late 2001 and 2002 - the central bank fired a warning shot in announcing it was willing to intervene by providing dollar liquidity to the market via dollar-issued bonds.  

The central bank doesn't target the peso as such, but it has left the door open in the event of an emergency, as when the peso plunged to record lows ahead of the Argentina crisis and the Iraq war.  

Analysts have said the bank might soon accelerate buybacks of the bonds to take back the liquidity.  

Along with other commodity-based currencies, the peso has appreciated sharply in recent months, helped primarily by the rise in copper prices and a positive outlook for the Chilean economy. It has also latched onto the euro amid the global weakening of the dollar.

title: Chile Fin Min Worried Peso Could Spark Short-Term Flows
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chilean Finance Minister Nicolas Eyzaguirre Monday said the peso's sharp appreciation against the dollar might spark detrimental short-term speculative currency flows.  

"When the peso strengthens as a result of very good prospects for the economy, there's nothing to be done. But if there's speculative pressure, one has to think where it's coming from, and that can be deactivated if you move on the factors that could be producing the speculation," Eyzaguirre said during a briefing at the finance ministry.  

The peso has appreciated sharply in recent months, helped primarily by the rise in copper prices and a positive outlook for the Chilean economy.  

Chile is the world's largest copper producer, and the peso continued to benefit from high copper prices Monday, traders said, reaching its strongest level in 32 months by closing at CLP596.80 to the dollar. For every cent copper rises in world markets, Chile receives an additional $100 million in dollar inflows.  

As recently as March, the peso traded near record weakness around CLP760 to the dollar.  

There's no evidence yet of a massive entry of speculative capital into the Andean country, but Eyzaguirre called on the financial system to make sure that institutions as well as debtors are duly covered in their dollar and peso positions in order to avoid any future imbalances.  

Traders said the most recent spike - following a surprise central bank rate cut Thursday - has unsettled the market, leading to fewer transactions, they added.  

The peso is, therefore, unlikely to quickly strengthen further and will move in a tight CLP595-CLP600 range in the coming sessions, they also said.  

Still, Eyzaguirre's statements are the first warnings regarding the risks of overshooting on the currency since it started its rally. Chile's central bank, which has a policy of intervening only in the face of severe imbalances, has so far said it's unconcerned by the peso's recovery.  

However, the rally has contributed to a fall in inflation to well below the central bank's minimum 2% target, leading the bank to surprisingly cut its prime interest rate by 50 basis points to 2.25% annually last Thursday.  

The rally has been based on fundamental factors such as exports and an improved outlook for the domestic economy, and the government won't cut back on spending to undermine the peso. That would negatively impact domestic spending which is still recovering from a prolonged slump, Eyzaguirre said.  

He also ruled out increasing spending as that would undermine Chile's investment-grade status, he added.  

Chile is the only investment-grade country in South America.

title: Chile Central Bank  denies  forex intervention .
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Chile's Central Bank said on Thursday it was not intervening in the foreign exchange market even though the peso weakened in reaction to its decision to swap its "exchange-rate" bonds for dollar-denominated ones.  

"The Central Bank is not intervening, it is neutral. The market will gradually digest the information and then we'll see (what happens)," Central Bank President Vittorio Corbo told reporters.  

The bank said late Wednesday it will no longer renew every month all of its so-called exchange-rate bonds, which have a face value in dollars but are paid back in pesos according to the exchange rate at time of maturity.  

The market interpreted the move as a withdrawal of dollars from the market to slow down a sharp appreciation of the peso .  

The peso, which has strengthened by over 12 percent against the dollar this year, lost 0.29 percent in mid-morning trade to 629.80/630.30 per dollar compared with Wednesday's close of 628.00/628.50.  

"The market acts day by day and adjusts itself. The information we announced yesterday is neutral with respect to the foreign exchange market," Corbo added.  

The move aims to reduce the cost of financing central bank debt but would not change its net foreign reserves position or its policy of a free-floating currency, the bank said on Wednesday.  

Markets remained cautious despite remarks by Corbo and analysts that the measure should have no impact on the currency.  

"Even if they've said the measure shouldn't affect the exchange rate, the market is still studying it and its first reaction is to go out and buy dollars as a precautionary measure," said one trader.

title: Chile Central Bank  rules out  forex intervention .
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Chile's Central Bank said on Tuesday it will not intervene in the foreign exchange market to slow down appreciation of the peso currency , which has gained 11.5 percent against the U.S. dollar this year and hit a 27-month high last week.  

Market traders have come to expect some sort of Central Bank action to defend the powerful exporting sector, which complains the strong currency will dig into their returns.  

"Its hard to imagine that we have a fragile exchange rate ... We have a flexible exchange rate and we have intervened in exceptional cases in case of short-term turbulence but today we are very far from that situation," Jose de Gregorio, Central Bank board member who was speaking for the bank, told reporters.  

The Central Bank has floated the peso since 1999, intervening sporadically to bolster the currency during times of turbulence such as the Argentine devaluation and Brazil's financial crisis last year.  

"We have to let the market function adequately in situations that are relatively normal," he said.  

The peso gained 5.5 percent against the dollar in the third quarter and traded at 638.80/639.30 at mid-session on Tuesday.  

De Gregorio said the strong currency favored prices of copper, Chile's top export, and was a natural reaction to an upbeat economic outlook for Chile.  

"The weakness of the dollar is an international phenomenon and responds also to a more auspicious economic outlook internally, especially much better prices for our goods, which we have seen in the price of copper," De Gregorio said.  

De Gregorio estimated that for every 1 percent depreciation of the dollar against major world currencies, copper prices would rise 0.8 percent.  

"The same occurs with prices of all raw materials," he said.

title: Strong  Chile  Peso No Reason To  Intervene -Ctrl Bk Official
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The strength of the Chilean peso is no reason to intervene in the currency market, a central bank official said Wednesday.  

"There are no exceptional conditions that would justify some kind of intervention" in the peso's recent surge against the dollar, said Esteban Jadresic during a conference call with analysts.  

As director of the monetary authority's international division, Jadresic oversees daily currency moves.  

The Banco Central policy on the floating peso is to only intervene under exceptional circumstances, as when the peso weakened sharply against the dollar in late 2001 and again in late 2002.  

This year, it has appreciated more than 10% against the dollar following a weak spell due to the Iraq crisis. Since then, it has recovered, helped by the recovery in world market copper prices to long-term average levels and prospects of faster growth in Chile. Every cent copper gains translates into some $100 million in additional dollar inflows to Chile.  

The peso closed Wednesday at CLP638.70 following copper's rise to above 90 cents per pound on the London Metals Exchange.  

Jadresic didn't say whether the bank would extend its policy of issuing dollar-denominated bonds, which strengthen the peso by adding dollar liquidity in the market.  

He said long-term interest rates are rising in Chile, another factor that supports the peso.  

However, traders said the peso is unlikely to strengthen much in the next few sessions until it's clear whether the bank will continue to issue debt in dollars.

title: Chile  Ctrl Bk Drops  Intervention  Threat Despite Low Peso
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SANTIAGO -(Dow Jones)- Despite the Chilean peso's weakness, the country's Central Bank has given the market a clear signal it won't move to prop it up at this time. 

 In its latest debt calendar, published on its web site over the weekend, the bank sharply cut back its issuance of dollar-denominated debt, or BCDs, to just $60 million a month, from $240 million. Meanwhile, an intervention threat uttered four months ago has run out without being replaced. 

 "Those $2 billion are no longer available," a Central Bank spokeswoman said, referring to the amount that had been earmarked for possible interventions. 

 Initial market response was measured, with a slight drop from the previous session's close. The local currency closed Monday at CLP743.50 per dollar, compared to CLP742.30 on Friday. 

 "While the (dollar) exchange rate is very high, it's fully justifiable due to the Iraq war fear and the rise in crude oil prices. The Central Bank is reconfirming that it will act only when the dollar has an unjustified rise and this is consistent with ... not going out to fight the market," said economist Cristian Gardeweg at Santander Investment. 

 Dollar-denominated central bank bonds provide greenback liquidity to holders, underpinning the peso in the currency market. The peso has suffered since late December, mainly from the rise in crude oil prices brought on by the twin crises in oil-rich Iraq and Venezuela. 

 Early October, the peso hit a record low of CLP760.80 to the dollar, hit by high oil prices in the wake of the U.S.-Iraq crisis and the decline of the Brazilian real, which reflected the loss of investor confidence in Latin American economies. 

 It recovered after the Central Bank called the fall "to some degree a market overreaction" and said it would intervene with up to $2 billion of the country's foreign reserves over four months and offer up to $2 billion in BCDs with two- to five-year maturities. 

 After the announcement, the peso swiftly won back close to 10% from the dollar and traded under CLP700, while Brazil won a honeymoon with the markets and without any direct interventions on the part of the monetary authority. 

 Then the threat of war in Iraq became more acute and Venezuela's general strike erupted on the scene. 

 That pulled the peso back down again to levels around CLP745. It was kept from falling further by fear of Central Bank intervention, traders said. 

 Now, the Central Bank is guarding its hand, while "the market is screaming for a greater amount (of issuance), proven by the last auctions of BCDs in which demand has been far greater than the offer," said trader Cristian Donoso at brokerage Banchile. 

 As the peso recovered, demand for BCDs dropped and the Central Bank cut back supply, but as the oil producers' crises continued, bid levels increased sharply, but retreated slightly at the last auctions Tuesday. 

 In the end, it auctioned only $1.4 billion out of the $2.0 billion it had earmarked. 

 The future monthly $60 million is low considering the peso's rate and the market's hedging needs, "but the market is long on dollars and that could slow peso depreciation," Donoso said. 

 A lot will depend on how successful major companies were in hedging over the past months, traders said. 

 Should they find themselves in need of dollars in the near future, they'll be forced into the market, particularly if they feel the Central Bank isn't worried about a major drop in the peso, they added. 

 That might be the case. In its monetary policy report issued Jan. 15, the Central Bank said any effect from the high oil prices would be transitional, with inflation dropping by the end of the year. Additionally, data released this year has shown headline and core inflation well under control and easily within the Central Bank's 2%-4% target range. 

 As a result of earlier issuance maturing in the last third of this year, the Central Bank will after July begin raising the auction amounts, including two- and five-year bonds, it said Friday. 

 Bondholders from March onward will be able to switch their bonds to new two-year bonds at market conditions six months before maturity, the bank added.

title: Chile Peso Ends Dn In Range Trading As Brazil Real Slumps

title: Chile  peso up, possible  intervention  limits movement.
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, Oct 22 (Reuters) - Chile's peso firmed on Tuesday as brokers, wary of possible Central Bank intervention, offloaded dollars they had hoarded up over recent weeks, while domestic demand remained scarce, traders said. 

 The currency closed at 736.00/736.30, up 0.20 percent compared to 737.50/738.00 on Monday.

 Chile's peso fell to historic lows over recent weeks, pressured by what the Central Bank called "excessive speculation" in the currency. 

 The Central Bank said on Oct. 10, after the peso fell to an all-time low of 760.50/761.00, it would inject up to $2 billion in dollar-denominated bonds over the next four months and sell $2 billion from its reserves to prop up the peso when necessary. 

 The bank began last week selling $120 million in dollar-denominated bonds directly on the market every Tuesday and Thursday and said it will continue until it has sold all $2 billion. 

 "The upside of all this is that without speculation it makes it easier to make decisions as the exchange rate is less volatile," Pina said. 

 Traders said they expect the peso to continue to strengthen in the short term.

title: Chile  peso firms amid talk of CenBank  intervention .

title: Chile Fin Min:To Miss Growth Target Won't Mean Major Debt
text:
SANTIAGO -(Dow Jones)- Chile won't have to resort to major new debt to finance its budget next year if it fails to grow the 4.0% the government expects, Chilean Finance Minister Nicolas Eyzaguirre said Monday. 

 "A missed percentage point in gross domestic product growth will lead to only 0.2% more in debt, so if we grow only 3%, debt will rise to just 0.9% of GDP, and if we grow just 2%, it will rise to just 1.1%, against 0.7%" currently projected, Eyzaguirre said during a press briefing. 

 Chile plans a new bond issuance next year, but Eyzaguirre wouldn't specify an amount of issuance or expected spreads to Treasurys. 

 However, because of the small weight of Chilean debt in overall emerging debt markets, the amount of new bonds will have little impact on current spreads of Chilean sovereign debt, Eyzaguirre said. 

 "In the medium term of 12 to 24 months, I expect spreads to narrow" versus Treasurys, once uncertainty regarding conflict between the U.S. and Iraq and Brazil's public finance ease, he added. 

 While Chilean debt is more expensive than that of its Latin American neighbors, it is cheaper than that of eastern European countries with worse macroeconomic fundamentals than Chile, but more closely tied to the European Union, he also said. 

 Last Friday, Eyzaguirre presented additional debt data to respond to domestic criticism regarding the level of foreign debt owed by the government, the Central Bank, and state-owned companies. 

 Eyzaguirre on Monday said foreign bondholders hadn't sought additional information from Chile on its debt, and that the International Monetary Fund also separately lists central government, central bank and public company debt. 

 Chile has managed to keep its economy growing despite economic depression in neighboring Argentina and crises in several Latin American countries, but growth rates are far below levels seen in the 1990s, and unemployment remains stubbornly high at just under 10%. 

 "This year, Latin America's growth will be around minus 1%, falling for the first time since the early Eighties, while Chile will grow around 2%. There's no crisis symptoms here. Last time around (during the Pinochet military dictatorship), we led the region in falling," Eyzaguirre said. 

 Regarding the likely electoral victory of leftist Brazilian presidential candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, which sparked a financial crisis during the campaign, Eyzaguirre said Chile could be hit by a fall in exports to Brazil and a drop in the value of Chilean assets there. 

 Runoff elections in Brazil will take place Sunday. 

 Most fundamentally, fear of Lula has been reducing foreign direct investment in the region, including Chile. 

 To avoid further problems, a recovery of Brazil is fundamentally necessary, but Lula's team includes respected economists, and he could manage to restore credibility during the "honeymoon" at the beginning of his term, Eyzaguirre said. 

 He added Chile's peso has managed to decouple from the Brazilian real. Both currencies fell to record lows against the dollar during Lula's campaign, but the peso has recovered slightly after Chile's Central Bank threatened to intervene directly in the currency market.

title: Chile 's Peso Recovers From Historic Low On  Intervention
text:

 Uncertainty surrounding Brazil's presidential elections and doubts about that country's ability to meet its debt-financing needs have been affecting markets across the region. The situation is likely to remain volatile as the crisis in confidence affecting Brazil could limit its ability to roll over debt due ahead of the Oct. 27 presidential runoff. 

 Considering the uncertainty, its unlikely the Central Bank will risk intervening below CLP750 to the dollar, traders said. 

 Brazil's political situation has been weighing on markets for months because of the popularity of leftist candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who appears poised to win the presidency. 

 The peso has also been hit by the combination of low copper and high oil prices. 

 While the sluggish global economy has lessened demand for copper, Chile's prime export dollar earner, the U.S.-Iraq crisis has pushed oil prices up, which is detrimental to Chile's terms of trade as the country imports much of its oil. 

 Additionally, the Chilean Central Bank's hesitancy to intervene has undermined the peso, traders have said. The peso has lost nearly 15% of its value this year. 

 The Central Bank had earlier said the peso's fall was justified by economic fundamentals and that it would intervene only under exceptional circumstances. 

 In its statement late Thursday, it said that "Part of the depreciation observed recently reflects movements in a market that has operated with little liquidity and high volatility, and, therefore, overreacting to some degree." 

 Chile's foreign reserves have been relatively stable this year, in the $14.50-15.20 billion range.

title: Chile 's Peso Seen With CLP750/$ Floor On  Intervention
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

 "The BCD auctions provide more liquidity, but alone it won't be enough to put a ceiling on the market. The (dollar's) ceiling will be determined by the Central Bank when it intervenes directly in the market," said Roberto Telias, head trader at Banco de Chile. 

 Thursday, the peso finished at CLP760.50 a dollar versus CLP751.40 Wednesday, falling to an intraday all-time low of CLP760.80. 

 In early trading Friday, it regained some ground, and at 1610 GMT traded at CLP744.80. The local currency had reached an intraday high of CLP738 shortly after trading began. 

 "I think the Central Bank will intervene somewhere near the CLP750 mark," putting a floor under the peso around that level, Donoso said. 

 Uncertainty surrounding Brazil's presidential elections and doubts about that country's ability to meet its debt-financing needs have been affecting markets across the region. The situation is likely to remain volatile as the crisis in confidence affecting Brazil could limit its ability to roll over debt due ahead of the Oct. 27 presidential runoff. 

 Brazil's political situation has been weighing on markets for months because of the popularity of leftist candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who appears poised to win. 

 The peso has also been hit by the combination of low copper and high oil prices. 

 While the sluggish global economy has lessened demand for copper, Chile's prime export dollar earner, the U.S.-Iraq crisis has pushed oil prices up, which is detrimental to Chile's terms of trade as the country imports much of its oil. 

 Additionally, the Chilean Central Bank's hesitancy to intervene has undermined the peso, traders have said. The peso has lost nearly 15% of its value this year. 

 The Central Bank had earlier said the peso's fall was justified by economic fundamentals and that it would intervene only under exceptional circumstances. 

 In its statement late Thursday, it said that "Part of the depreciation observed recently reflects movements in a market that has operated with little liquidity and high volatility, and, therefore, overreacting to some degree." 

 Chile's foreign reserves have been relatively stable this year, in the $14.50-15.20 billion range.

title: Americas Stocks Close Lower on War Fears, Wall Street's Slide
text:
Most major Americas markets closed lower Wednesday as Wall Street's tumble, the increasing chances of war with Iraq and a flurry of profit warnings soured investor sentiment. 

 Selling accelerated on Wall Street late Wednesday as investors pocketed quick profits from the previous session's impressive -- albeit short-lived -- rally. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed down 183.18 points, or 2.3%, while the Nasdaq Composite Index gave back 2.2%. 

 Toronto's S&P/TSX Composite Index fell 117.93 points, or 1.9%, to close at 6100.68. Decliners topped advancers 528 to 443 and trading volume was 145.1 million shares, slightly down from Tuesday's total of 147.3 million shares. The S&P/TSX 60 Index closed down 7.97 points, or 2.29%, to 339.68. 

 Nine of the TSE's 10 stock groups fell. 

 The industrial group was the worst hit, falling 3.4%. 

 Railroads posted steep falls after Burlington Northern Santa Fe issued a profit warning related to the lockout of workers at U.S. West Coast ports. Canadian Pacific Railway closed down 2.15 to 27.10 and Canadian National Railway ended 3.01 lower to 58.94. 

 Air Canada fell 0.22 to 4.63 after UBS Warburg cut the stock to hold from buy. Flight-simulator maker CAE Inc. fell 0.59 to 4.01 following its fiscal 2003 profit warning. Conglomerate Bombardier Inc. slipped 0.20 to 4.36 as the grim outlook for the aerospace sector continued to weigh on the company. 

 Mexican stocks also ended mostly lower, dragged down by losses in U.S. markets on what participants called a technical retreat. 

 Mexico's key IPC index closed down 98.95 points, or 1.7%, at 5827.71. Decliners outnumbered gainers 32 to 19, while 10 issues were unchanged. 

 Industrial conglomerate Desc said Wednesday that economic weakness cut its sales between July and September to $507 million, down from $553 million for the same period one year ago. Exports represent more than 40% of Desc's sales. The company makes auto parts, pretochemicals and processed foods. 

 Desc estimated that third-quarter earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or Ebitda, fell to $60 million from $79 million in the same quarter of 2001, while operating profit fell to $29 million from $46 million. 

 Desc's C shares slid 7% in thin tradem while its B shares fell 8.1%. 

 Guidance has also come in from Cemex, the world's third-largest cement company. Cemex said nearly two weeks ago that it expects Ebitda of $520 million for the quarter, down from $562 million in the same period last year. Weaker currencies in Mexico and Venezuela are in part to blame. 

 The company also warned that cash earnings should be 6% lower than the $421 million reported last year and that majority net income for the third quarter will likely be significantly lower than the same period of 2001. 

 Cemex CPO shares fell 4.2%. 

 Mexican companies are expected to begin reporting official results for the quarter in mid-October. 

 Argentine stocks fell with investors retreating amid little fresh news on the government's bid for an International Monetary Fund debt-rollover program. The Merval blue-chip index fell almost one point, or 0.5%, to 392.06. The broad General Index fell 31.25 points, or 0.1%, to 21035.91 points. Seventeen shares gained and 12 declined. But declines in blue chips offset any broader gains. Another 14 shares were unchanged. 

 Argentine President Eduardo Duhalde is pressing the IMF for an agreement permitting the government to roll over maturing loans through December 2003. But the government has been tightlipped on talks so far this week. 

 Steel maker Acindar fell 3%, while oil company Perez Companc fell 3%. 

 In Brazil, despite early hopes for a continuation of Tuesday's rally, share prices dropped under the weight of the heavy U.S. sell-off. The main Sao Paulo index ended 1.9% lower at 8820. 

 "With all the recent uncertainty, the local market was somewhat directionless and got pulled under by international factors," said a trader in Sao Paulo. 

 Traders said Wednesday's slide came despite attractive local prices that have had local investors forecasting an upturn lately. 

 Brazilian share prices have dropped more than 30% since the beginning of the year amid investor nervousness ahead of the upcoming presidential elections. Monday, shares closed at their lowest since February 1999. 

 Local equities were also hurt Wednesday by a slide in the local currency, which dropped about 1.5% during the day despite central-bank efforts to intervene in its favor. 

 In Chile, blue-chip share prices on the Santiago Stock Exchange ended lower, with institutional investors sidelined, showing how fragile any recovery will be. 

 Chile's 40-share blue-chip IPSA index ended down 1.2% at 78.77, down from 79.72 Tuesday, while the broader-based IGPA index ended down 0.4% at 4695.08 from 4716.20. 

 The most affected shares in the sell-off were highly liquid U.S.-traded stocks, particularly utilities and telecommunications companies.

title: Chile's Peso Ends Higher As Foreign Dollars Come Back
text:
SANTIAGO -(Dow Jones)- Chile's peso closed higher as foreign banks and brokerages put dollars back on to the local market, helped by the recovery in world stock markets and the Brazilian real. 

 The peso ended at CLP745.50 to the dollar, from CLP748.80 Monday, trading in a tight range. 

 "It looks like the market has accepted the CLP750 floor. Whenever the market gets close to it, profit-taking sets in," a Santiago trader said. 

 Monday, the peso set an intraday all-time low of CLP752.20. 

 The peso has fallen to historic lows on international uncertainty, with Brazil in the foreground due to the popularity of a leftist presidential candidate in pre-election polls there. 

 The real's fall has reflected the withdrawal of dollars from the region, including Chile. 

 However, the real recovered Tuesday, helped by central bank auctions and trade data, propping up the peso. 

 Still, in the few days ahead of the Oct. 6 elections in Brazil, the market could cautiously test new lows, traders said. 

 Speaking in New York, Chilean Central Bank President Carlos Massad continued to tread a fine line regarding intervention, reminding the market of Chile's large dollar reserves but saying decoupling of the peso from other regional currencies' moves would be necessary before the central bank steps in. 

 "We are looking closely at what's going on with the peso rate," said Massad, adding that the bank's international reserves, at around $15 billion, are available to intervene in the foreign exchange market if necessary. 

 But he also suggested that he wasn't overly concerned with the current exchange rate, and that intervention would require more than the peso weakening only against the greenback, given the country's diversified export markets. 

 "For intervention to be justified, we have to consider that the situation is extraordinary, that is, that the peso is not moving with the rest of the currencies, but that it has taken a loss by itself," said Massad, adding that this hasn't been the case until now. 

 The peso has also fallen due to higher crude oil prices because of fears of a war between the U.S. and Iraq and low prices for copper, Chile's principal dollar earner.

title: Chile's Massad Warns Of Downside Risk To GDP Forecasts
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 NEW YORK -(Dow Jones)- Chilean Central Bank Governor Carlos Massad said Tuesday there is a downside risk to the country's economic growth forecasts, given the shaky environment globally and in its own backyard. 

 "We judge the bias to be downward," said Massad in a speech at the Council of Americas in New York. 

 The central bank has already revised downward its 2002 economic growth forecast to the 2.0% to 2.5% range, as much of the global economy sputters and financial shock waves emanate from Argentina and Brazil, its two larger South American neighbors. 

 Chile's economy is one of the most outward looking in the world, with exports of goods and services comprising an estimated 36% of gross domestic product. During the 1990s, it routinely booked 5%-plus GDP growth. 

 The central bank is forecasting tentatively that GDP will grow between 3.5% and 4.5% in 2003 and 5% in 2004, but Massad acknowledged he wasn't heartened by the mood at the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund in Washington this past weekend. 

 "As the meetings went on, the question marks were bigger and bigger," he said in reference to the global economic outlook. 

 The IMF is projecting Latin American GDP will contract 0.6% this year, despite pockets of growth in a handful of countries, including Chile. 

 The slowdown in the world and regional economy has pushed prices for copper, Chile's single-largest export, down to around $0.67 a pound, "the lowest we've had since 1934" in real terms, according to the central banker. 

 Regional turmoil isn't helping matters. Massad estimated that the travails of Argentina, where the economy is expected to contract around 15% in the wake of last December's debt default, have probably had a negative impact of half a percentage point on Chile's GDP. 

 Market upheaval in Brazil this year ahead of presidential elections has probably had a negative impact of only around 0.2 or 0.3 percentage point of GDP, according to the central banker, who pointed out that Chilean corporate investments in Brazil are only about half as big as in Argentina. 

 But he admitted that his country is vulnerable to a continued market sell-off in Brazil, which has seen its currency weaken around 40% and bond spreads widen more than 1500 basis points this year amid growing fears that it too may be headed to default. 

 "The main risk," Massad warned, is that a Brazilian crisis might "weaken the capacity of the markets to discriminate the situations of different countries." 

 Chile is South America's last remaining investment-grade credit, after ratings agencies demoted Uruguay to junk status as contagion from Argentina and Brazil overwhelmed the tiny country. 

Forex Intervention Only In `Extraordinary' Case


Chile's markets have been feeling some heat in recent weeks, with the
peso weakening to CLP748.80 to the dollar Monday, a new record closing
low and down 8.3% from the end of June.



"We are looking closely at what's going on with the peso rate," said
Massad, adding that the bank's international reserves, at around $15
billion, are available to intervene in the foreign exchange market if
necessary.



But he also suggested that he wasn't overly concerned with the current
exchange rate, and that intervention would require more than the peso
weakening only against the greenback, given the country's diversified
export markets.



"For intervention to be justified, we have to consider that the
situation is extraordinary, that is, that the peso is not moving with
the rest of the currencies, but that it has taken a loss by itself,"
said Massad, adding that this hasn't been the case until now.



He also noted that a weaker peso helps the export sector, which, along
with construction, is the main driver of the Chilean economy.



And unlike Argentina and Brazil, which are saddled with heavy
dollar-linked debt obligations, a weakening local currency actually
eases fiscal pressures in Chile, given that the government only has $7
billion in foreign debt, Massad added.


Chile last intervened in the foreign exchange market last year, in the
wake of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks on the U.S. that sent financial
markets reeling.



Massad said he felt comfortable that Chile will be able to meet its 3%
inflation target this year. He pointed out that yields on domestic debt
indicate that the market also believes annual inflation will be around
3%, not just this year, but over the next five years.

mike.esterl@dowjones.com

title: Chile  peso firms, cenbank says no  intervention  yet.
text:

The currency has lost 38 percent of its value since the beginning of the year, mainly on investor jitters that leftist presidential candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva could win on the Oct. 6 election but be incapable of managing the country's economy and $260 billion public debt.

title: Big peso drop may spur  Chile  CenBank  intervention .
text:
NEW YORK, Oct 1 (Reuters) - Chile is well positioned to withstand the current global economic turbulence but its central bank may intervene if the peso weakens more dramatically than the swooning currencies of other Latin American nations, the bank's governor said on Tuesday. 

 The peso hit historic lows on Monday amid fears that neighboring Brazil may be about to elect a president who will frighten investors away from the region. If the peso starts to fall independently of the regional weakness, which has hit not only Brazil but Mexico, Carlos Massad told a group of Wall Street analysts that the Chilean Central Bank may step in to buy the country's currency. 

 "For intervention to be justified, we have to consider the situation to be extraordinary, that the peso is not moving with the rest of the currencies, but that it is taking a loss by itself," Massad told a meeting hosted by the Americas Society. 

 "In that case, we would feel justified to intervene." 

 The Chilean peso strengthened slightly on Tuesday, following an uptick in Brazil's currency, the real . The peso gained 0.17 percent at midday to 747.50/747.80 pesos to the dollar. 

 Should intervention be necessary, Massad said the operation would be announced publicly. The Central Bank intervened several times in the currency market in the second half of 2001 to prop up a peso hit by fallout from Argentina's deep financial crisis. 

 Chilean interest rates are at historic lows as the country tries to continue growing in the face of a listless global economy that has depressed the price of the nation's main export, copper. 

 Analysts wonder if the Central Bank can continue lowering rates, given the peso's weakness. 

 "We do not discard the possibility of future action on interest rates either way, downward or upward, depending on the general conditions," Massad said. 

 Massad said he expects the country's inflation rate to be around 3 percent by the end of the year "unless oil prices shoot up substantially as a result of a war in the Middle East." 

 The threat of a U.S. attack on Iraq has jacked up oil prices, which places a burden on energy importers, such as Chile, while weighing on global equity markets. This atmosphere of fear has prompted a flight from risky emerging market assets and toward safe-haven U.S. Treasury bonds. 

 But Massad, citing Chile's strong export sector, urged his audience to discriminate among Latin American countries, saying that the economic problems of some should not be seen contaminating the whole region. 

 "We are in a position to continue growing despite the difficulties around us," said Massad, who predicted Chile's gross domestic product will expand by 2 percent to 2.5 percent this year.

title: Chile's Peso Calms As Fresh Reasons For Fall Fade
text:
By Stephan Kueffner 

 SANTIAGO -(Dow Jones)- After several plunges in a row, the Chilean peso on Tuesday found some solid footing. 

 The currency strengthened to CLP739.40 to the dollar from CLP748.90 Monday as the market began to fear central bank intervention. 

 While Chile's currency set record low after record low in the past two weeks, traders now expect it to trade in a CLP720-750 range unless major external pressures such as actual hostilities between the U.S. and Iraq or a further meltdown in the Brazilian real overwhelm domestic fundamentals. 

 "The dollar could rise a little more but these levels aren't sustainable for a long time because the market knows the authorities could intervene at any time," said Francisco Montaner, director of online brokerage Lemon Financial. 

 Others also think the big sell-off is over for the time being. 

 "While the uncertainty that has been pressuring the peso remains in place - a possible Iraqi war and elections in Brazil - there has been no concrete event that justifies a greater rise to the dollar," said Cristian Gardeweg, economist at Santander Investment. 

 So far, Chile's government has been more vocal than the Central Bank in supporting the peso. President Ricardo Lagos recently criticized peso speculators and Finance Minister Nicolas Eyzaguirre said Monday there were no economic reasons that justified current dollar levels. 

 When the peso was flirting with its previous historic low of CLP718.70, set last October, Central Bank President Carlos Massad had said the fall was justifiable considering low prices for copper, Chile's main export commodity, and the surge in crude oil prices. 

 While ruling out direct intervention at the time, he also said the bank might step in at any time to combat speculation, a stance he reiterated Monday, adding that the bank could move if inflation threatened to rise above an annual 3% due to the peso's devaluation. 

 The statements by Eyzaguirre and Massad helped calm the market since "even if Massad said nothing new and only said that it hasn't given up on its option to intervene, it's good to sometimes remind the market of these things," said Santander's Gardeweg. 

 While the Central Bank could feasibly buy pesos directly, a more likely course of action would be the issuance of dollar-denominated bonds, as it has done in the past, he added. 

 Indirect intervention could also stem from major state-owned companies, above all copper giant Codelco and energy company Enap, Lemon's Montaner said. 


Bank Could Have Taken Strong Stance Earlier, Some Say



Some economists criticize Massad's position as being too lax.



"Chile's foreign exchange market is far from being a deep market, so
it needs signals from the authorities to manage uncertainty," said
economist Patricio Arrau at think tank Gemines.



When the peso set its previous record low due to the Argentine crisis
and the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks on the U.S., "a signal that the
Central Bank had $2 billion to auction new dollar bonds and to intervene
directly was enough for the market to start correcting itself," he
added.



Monday, the Central Bank reported that as of Sept. 13 foreign reserves
had risen to $15.12 billion, up 1.2% from $14.94 billion on Aug. 31.



The high level of reserves and low external debt rates would enable
the bank to easily set aside $2 billion to $3 billion to stabilize the
exchange market, Arrau said.



He added he considered exchange rates around CLP650 to the dollar,
last seen in June, as fair.

report)

title: Chile Finance Minister: Peso Fall To Lows `Exaggerated'
text:
SANTIAGO -(Dow Jones)- The Chilean peso's fall to new lows Monday was "exaggerated," Chilean Finance Minister Nicolas Eyzaguirre said Monday. 

 Hit by higher crude oil prices due to fears of a war between the U.S. and Iraq, as well as a fall in the Brazilian real due to the popularity of a leftist presidential candidate in pre-election polls, the peso hit an intraday low of CLP750.80 earlier in the day. 

 However, "the price of the dollar is currently exaggerated and doesn't have anything to do with the fundamentals of the Chilean economy," Eyzaguirre told reporters. 

 The fall won't have a lasting effect on the economy and significantly raise inflation, he added. 

 Mid-term interest rates haven't risen and Chile's country-risk indicators have declined, demonstrating that the economy isn't worried about inflation and that there are no risks to stability, he said. 

 "Interest rates continue absolutely unchanged, which is what's important from the point of view of reactivating the economy," he said, adding that he expects the peso to return to equilibrium levels. 

 Chile's central bank has linked the peso's recent plunge to declining prices in copper, Chile's main export, as well as oil prices and developments in the Brazilian currency. 

 It has also ruled out direct intervention as long as the peso's fall is driven by market fundamentals. 

 Eyzaguirre said a decision on intervention should be left to the central bank alone. 

 Regarding Chile's 2003 budget, Eyzaguirre said the deficit would likely be lower than the 1% of gross domestic product estimated for this year. 

 The government is due to introduce next year's budget package in congress before the end of the month.

title: Chile's Peso Ends Lower On Low Copper, High Oil Prices
text:

 However, the drop in the U.S. unemployment statistics published during the session helped reduce fears of a double-recession there, shoring up equity prices and other currencies, including the peso, they added. 

 Despite the peso's fall, Chile's Central Bank has ruled out direct intervention since it reflects current economic fundamentals, particularly in the oil and copper markets.

title: Chile  Ctrl Bk Pres: Peso's Low No Reason For  Intervention
text:
SANTIAGO -(Dow Jones)- Fluctuations in copper and oil prices are behind the current weakness of Chile's peso, and that will keep the central bank from intervening to prop it up, Chile's Central Bank President Carlos Massad said Monday. 

 "What has been happening is reply of the dollar price  to international conditions. The price of copper has been  very low and the price of oil rising. We sell copper and buy oil, so both prices play against us," Massad said. 

 However, "the rise of the dollar tends to somewhat compensate (for) these negative effects, because it keeps stimulating exports despite the negative international price conditions," he added. 

 Once market conditions change, the peso will reverse course, he added. 

 The peso last week fell near its historic low of CLP718.70 to the dollar, but strengthened somewhat after the central bank said it would issue dollar-denominated debt worth $220 million as part of an overall revamp of its debt-issuance practice. 

 The central bank didn't link the timing of the announcement to the peso's drop, but market participants have called the issuance of bonds in dollars one method the bank could use to quietly prop up the peso ahead of outright intervention. 

 The Chilean currency closed Friday at CLP710.00 to the  dollar. 

 As long as there is no "exceptional situation," there would be no intervention, Massad said. 

 However, "there are some who, taking advantage of the  country's situation, want to make an easy profit, but they've encountered surprises in the past, and I think they will again encounter surprises," he added.

title: Chilean peso tumbles, cenbank won't  intervene  now.
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, Aug 28 (Reuters) - Chile's peso tumbled almost 1 percent on Wednesday, creeping toward historic lows, but the central bank ruled out intervening for now to defend the flagging currency. 

 The currency closed at 716.00/716.50, a depreciation of 0.94 percent compared to 709.30/709.80 on Tuesday and at its lowest since October 2001 as region-wary foreign banks stocked up on safe-haven dollars, traders said. 

Central bank chief Carlos Massad said he would leave the market to correct itself but left the door open to future intervention if necessary. 

 "The peso is falling due to foreign factors, meaning we have to leave it to correct itself," Massad said in an interview with local radio Chile Solo Noticias. 

 "Naturally, if there are extraordinary circumstances, the central bank has always reserved the right to intervene like it did last year but so far those circumstances haven't arisen," he added. 

 Traders noted a strong demand for dollars over recent days from foreign banks operating in Chile which fear contagion of the Chilean economy from its financially troubled neighbors Argentina and Brazil. 

 Finance Minister Nicolas Eyzaguirre commented, "The fall in the peso is natural in a flexible market economy when there is currency weakness in other countries." 

 "It's the way an economy defends itself against eventual competitiveness from countries which may have a very weak exchange rate," Eyzaguirre said. 

 Chile's peso, which last year weakened about 14 percent due to the Argentine crisis, has been under pressure more recently from investor jitters over Brazil's October presidential elections.

title: Chile's Peso Ends Lower, Again Tracks Brazil's Weakness
text:
SANTIAGO -(Dow Jones)- Chile's peso retreated against the dollar Monday, falling for the second session in a row after the Brazilian real weakened intraday. 

 Chile's currency ended at CLP700.80 to the dollar, compared with CLP697.00 Friday. 

 The real weakened again despite central bank intervention as international credit for companies who need to settle foreign debts failed to materialize despite the record $30 billion the International Monetary Fund has promised Brazil. 

 Monday, companies had to buy dollars in the spot market, thus pressuring the peso. 

 However, the Brazilian Central Bank's intervention did manage to stabilize Chile's peso above technical support around CLP701.50, traders said. 

 But the real is having a more immediate impact than technical trading, they added. 

 Brazil had been seeking IMF help after the popularity of leftist candidates in the run-up to that country's October presidential elections caused investors to flee the region, dragging down other currencies, such as the Chilean peso, with it. 

 Strongly influenced by the wavering fortune of the real, the peso has fluctuated largely in a CLP690-700 range, though dropping as far as close to CLP710 to the dollar. 

 Even after the IMF promised Brazil additional help last week, traders doubted the peso would recover to a higher level than CLP685 in a short time.
