title: IMF Sees Chile's GDP Growth At 2.6% For 2002
text:
WASHINGTON -(Dow Jones)- Thanks to "sound and consistent" economic policies, the outlook for Chile remains bright despite the financial troubles of its neighbors, the International Monetary Fund said Wednesday. 

 While others in South America are facing recession this year, the IMF predicts Chile will post gross domestic  product growth of 2.6%, a forecast on the conservative side of market expectations. 

 "This performance, in the face of an adverse external environment, is also a reflection of Chile's political stability, good governance, and credible institutions, which serve to reinforce the economic agenda of the authorities," the IMF said in a press summary of the IMF's  annual "Article IV" review of Chile's economy. 

 Chile's inflation-targeting framework combined with its floating exchange rate regime continues to serve well,  the IMF said. Considering the output gap and subdued inflation, the Fund expressed approval for recent reductions in interest rates by the central bank. The Fund  also lauded Chile's policy of using foreign-exchange intervention to slow movements in currency markets, rather  than to prop up an exchange-rate target. 

 The IMF said the results of staff tests, and indicators like prudential and earnings ratios, point to a   sound banking system. Some IMF directors urged Chile to aim for increased bank competition to help lower interest rates, particularly for small business loans. 

 The Fund did caution that its favorable forecast for Chile assumes that domestic demand will strengthen fairly soon in response to the monetary-policy easing. The slowdown in GDP growth from rates above 9% in the late 1990s is probably mostly the result of temporary factors, the IMF said. Still, the government should continue to boost economic activity through its ongoing program of market-friendly reforms, including development of a venture capital market, and improving regulation and the legal framework. 

 The government must work harder to reduce Chile's stubbornly high rates of unemployment, estimated above 9% for 2001 and well above the 6% rate seen before the 1999 recession. 

 The IMF "suggested that greater attention be placed on  education and job training for low-skilled workers and on  other ways of enhancing labor market flexibility more generally."

title: Chile's Peso Close To Historic Lows, But No Worries
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SANTIAGO -(Dow Jones)- After breaching technical support Wednesday, Chile's peso is once again poised to test historic lows against the dollar, but not even Chile's Central Bank looks worried. 

 Hit primarily by the fallout from troubled Brazil, the peso needs to lose only another 2.5% versus the dollar to reach Oct. 2001's historic low of CLP718.70. But Chilean inflation is under control and a weak peso will bring smiles to exporters - and help Chile overcome low growth. 

 That will keep fear of imported inflation at bay "as long as the peso continues to weaken in tandem with other Latin American currencies," helping Chilean products stay competitive, said Clyde Wardle, currency analyst at HSBC in New York. 

 Trading at or below CLP702 a dollar early Wednesday, the peso fell through technical support traders had put at CLP701.50. 

 While it recovered in intraday trading, traders said it could fall to CLP710 easily and then move on towards the historic low. 

 "The price of the dollar isn't excessive considering the effect uncertainty in Brazil and the international bourses are having on capital flows" to Latin America, said analyst Cristian Gardewerg at Santander Investment. 

 The peso has been trading in a CLP690-700 range for a number of weeks. 

 It has been at that low level due to worries concerning its exposure to crisis-stricken neighbor Argentina and, above all, troubled Brazil, South America's biggest economy. Several major Chilean companies have invested heavily in those countries. 

 Apparently, the Central Bank isn't worried. July 11, it surprised markets with an unexpectedly large 75-basis-point rate cut to 3.25% from 4%. 

 However, a currency fall to near historic lows would certainly alert it, analysts said. Knowing that, traders will be cautious once it gets below CLP715, they added. 

 "The peso will remain volatile but it will reach a maximum low around CLP715 a dollar because the market knows that the Central Bank could react at any time then," said Erick Haindl, economist at Universidad Gabriela Mistral in Santiago. 


   Direct Central Bank Intervention Unlikely



The peso might even go to CLP720 if the international stock market
crisis continues, but even there "the Central Bank won't have to
intervene directly and sell its reserve dollars," said trader Cristian
Donoso Banco de Chile.



Before intervening outright, the Central Bank could still let off a
loud warning shot by offering dollar-denominated two-to-four year
securities - so-called PRDs - that buyers can use to hedge against
currency losses, while injecting dollar liquidity, analysts said. It
last announced devaluation-inspired PRDs last August.



The Bank itself believes the peso's weakness is a passing thing, it
said recently. September and December are the next months PRDs will be
on offer.



If and when calm returns to international markets - in Latin American
currencies as well as major stock markets - the peso could easily return
back to CLP650-670, economists said.



However, that's unlikely before October's Brazilian presidential
elections, where the popularity of left-of-center candidates has been
enough to spark fear - and major selling - in the markets, they added.



The weakening of Latin America's currencies reflects investment moving
to Asia and Eastern Europe, analysts said. For Chile, this will be of
little concern as the country is still able to reliably pull in outside
capital, HSBC's Wardle said.



-By Stephan Kueffner, Dow Jones Newswires; 562-460-8546;
chiledowjones.com



(Patricia San Juan contributed to this report)

title: Chilean peso firms on Brazil  forex intervention .
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, July 3 (Reuters) - Chile's peso ended firmer on Wednesday, following gains in the Brazilian real after the Brazilian Central Bank announced it would intervene in the foreign exchange market to prop up the weakened currency, traders said. 

 At closing, the Chilean currency traded at 694.50/695.00 pesos per U.S. dollar, up 0.71 percent from Tuesday's close of 699.50/699.80 but still down about 5 percent since the start of the year. 

 Traders said the peso would remain volatile until turbulence in Brazilian markets subsided, probably after that country's presidential election in October. 

 "Even though the Central Bank injects liquidity to defend the real, there is still a lot of pressure in the market and that is affecting the peso," said Gabriela Clivio, analyst with Santiago brokerage. 

 Brazil's battered real currency rebounded on Wednesday after the Brazilian Central Bank announced it would inject $1.5 billion into the market in July to prop up the currency. The real firmed to 2.845 per dollar from Tuesday's close of 2.895. 

 Traders in Chile's peso, battered last year by the Argentine financial crisis, have now turned to Brazil's financial markets as a barometer of investor confidence in the region. 

 Chilean traders said they expected the real to continue losing ground despite the Central Bank move. 

 Brazil's financial markets have been whipped in recent weeks by fears economic problems could hinder its debt payments and by the lead in polls of a leftist presidential candidate.

title: UPDATE 2-IMF warns against big Argentine  forex interventions .
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, Jan 18 (Reuters) - A senior International Monetary Fund official on Friday warned against large central bank interventions in the Argentine foreign exchange market, which she said would be "questionable." 

 The IMF's Anne Krueger, who has been critical of Argentina's new dual exchange rate, said recent dollar sales by the country's central bank to prop up the newly-floated peso were small scale. 

 "They are small interventions that basically smooth out fluctuations and are in small amounts. I think one might make a case for it. I think large scale interventions would be probably very questionable," Krueger, the lending body's first deputy managing director, told a news conference in Chile. 

 The Argentine Central Bank stepped into the foreign exchange market for the fourth straight day Friday in an attempt to stop a devaluation of the peso from spinning out of control and adding to the bankrupt country's economic crisis. 

 Latin America's third-largest economy this month abandoned a decade-old currency peg to the U.S. dollar and introduced a dual exchange system, with one official fixed rate of 1.40 pesos a dollar and a floating peso for cash deals. 

 In the first week of trade, the floating currency has fallen sharply, forcing the central bank to intervene. 

 The bank sold an unspecified amount of dollars Friday at 1.85 pesos, although the currency later withered to 1.95/2.00 per dollar by midday as nervous buyers sought refuge in dollars on fears the country would sink even further into chaos. 

 The IMF has not looked kindly on the dual exchange rate, but was encouraged by Argentina's statement this week it hoped to float the currency completely within five months. 

 "A unified exchange rate system is the only system that is workable in the long term," Krueger said Friday. 

 LOAN ACCORD 

 Krueger also said she doubted Argentina would get a loan accord with the IMF within a month, a time frame Argentina said was feasible. 

 "I think it would be very difficult to have anything within a month," she said. 

 Argentina has said it could request up to $20 billion in fresh aid to see it through what promises to be a turbulent 2002. 

 Krueger said the new Argentine government had not yet formally asked for support and that, even if it did so now, the process of IMF approval would not be that fast. 

 The lender last month froze a $1.3 billion payment on its overall $22 billion package to Argentina because the government failed to curb spending as promised. 

 Krueger reiterated the IMF position that it will help Argentina, which has defaulted on part of its $141 billion public debt, once the country comes up with a sustainable economic plan. 

 In addition to scrapping the twin currency system, the lender wants to see Argentina craft a new monetary policy, restore the banking system, complete its budget and agree on mechanisms for renegotiating debt with creditors, she said. 

 "Those are the broad outlines of what would be required to get fund support, but how the authorities choose to do that is their choice," she said. 

 A technical mission is currently in Argentina, working with Argentine officials monetary and banking problems. A second mission to look at debt and fiscal issues will land in Buenos Aires early next week, Krueger said.

title: Chile 's Peso Ends Weaker As Ctrl Bank Ends  Interventions
text:
SANTIAGO -(Dow Jones)- Chile's peso softened to close at CLP660.50 to the dollar Friday, after the Central Bank announced it was wrapping up an intervention policy in effect since August. 

 The peso gained on the dollar early, but turned on its heels and began to weaken when Central Bank President Carlos Massad said the monetary authority won't pump any more dollars into the local market after Dec. 31. 

 The intervention policy, which fed $800 million in central bank reserves into the market over the past five months, was scheduled to end with the close of the year. 

 Before Friday, the peso had firmed for three straight sessions and closed Thursday at CLP655.20 per dollar. Local currency traders don't expect the peso to continue to depreciate significantly next week. 

 Market participants have a long weekend ahead to digest Friday's news. Banks in Chile will remain closed both Monday and Tuesday next week to celebrate the New Year's holiday.

title: Chile  Ctrl Bank Ends  Forex Intervention  Policy Jan 1
text:
SANTIAGO -(Dow Jones)- Chile's central bank president, Carlos Massad, said Friday the bank won't directly intervene in the foreign exchange market after Dec. 31, ending a policy in effect since August. 

 On Aug. 16, the bank said it was prepared to pump up to $2 billion in reserves into the market by the end of the year. In the weeks leading up to the announcement, the local currency shed whole percentage points in single trading sessions, largely due to pressures linked to Argentina's economic crisis. 

 Massad said Friday that the bank sold about 40% of the total $2 billion since the policy was launched. 

 Chile's peso, which was trading firmer early Friday, changed direction and is slipping weaker on the news. 

 Chile's peso finished weaker Friday, at CLP660.50 to the dollar, reversing significant gains made early in the session. 

Currency traders said the peso slipped primarily on news that the bank won't inject any more dollars into the market, but also on a bit of rate cut speculation sparked by some of Massad's comments. 

 When asked about local interest rates Friday, Massad suggested the bank might consider lowering its benchmark monetary policy rate, currently set at a nominal 6.50%. 

 "If inflation remains stable and external risks continue to be absorbed, we think that could open up possibilities for additional steps in the area of monetary policy," the central bank president said. 

 Tomas Flores, an economist with Chile's Liberty and Development think tank, sees Friday's rate cut speculation as overblown. 

 Flores expects the bank to wait and see if local and international growth continues to decline before deciding whether the economy needs more stimulus. Even so, controlled inflation does give the bank room to trim should they choose to go that route, he says. 

 A few months ago, rising international oil prices and a falling local currency were threatening to stir up inflation in Chile. But since early October, those pressures have begun to ease. 

 Weak domestic demand has also helped keep consumer prices in check. Economists see zero inflation for December, which would be a repeat of November's performance. 

 The underlying pressure on Chile's peso has also dissipated, at least temporarily. 

 The peso, which depreciated as much as 20% against the dollar this year, began to rebound in October as prices for copper, Chile's No. 1 export product, staged a meek recovery. A round of production cuts, while not convincing enough to override weak demand for the metal, at least fanned hopes that prices will respond quickly when demand does pick up. 

 Chile's currency also began to cut loose in October from the turmoil in neighboring Argentina. By last week, the peso had firmed to levels not seen since July. 

 But while pressures are continuing to ease, the central bank reserves the right to step into the foreign exchange market again should circumstances spin out of control, Massad said Friday. 

Chile's Central Bank swore off market interventions and floated the peso two years ago, finally putting in place an inflation targeting monetary policy system that was years in the making.

title: Chilean peso firms on  central bank intervention .
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, Oct 10 (Reuters) - Chile's peso posted a notable recovery on Wednesday following decisive intervention from the central bank, which sold $122 million in the market, traders said. 

 The currency climbed 1.28 percent to 710.10/710.40 from a historic low of 719.30/719.60 on Tuesday. 

 Traders said the bank stepped in twice just minutes before close with two auctions for $50 million each as well as selling dollars directly to banks. 

 "The central bank auctioned twice and this had an immediate effect as banks with surplus began to sell dollars immediately, allowing a rapid recovery of the peso. 

 A Reuters survey of market players found that, in addition to the $100 million auctioned, the central bank sold $22 million directly to banks. 

 "The peso was under too much pressure and there was a need for a more aggressive attitude by the central bank to avoid it weakening further...It did so today (Wednesday) and the effect was immediate," said Pedro Verdugo, exchange rate manager with travel agency Viajes Mercury. 

 "Now we have to see how long this lasts, because as the international scene continues to be unstable the central bank has a tough fight ahead to keep the peso from slipping," he added. 

 The central bank injected $285.5 million directly in the market in September and has sold an estimated $260 million so far this month.

title: Chile Cenbank cuts 2002 growth estimate to 3-4 pct.
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, Oct 9 (Reuters) - The Chilean Central Bank on Tuesday cut its 2002 economic growth forecast to between 3 percent and 4 percent from a previous forecast of 5 percent due to the worsening global economic outlook after the Sept. 11 attacks in the United States. 

 "Consensus estimates point to a downward revision of about one percentage point in the growth of Chile's trade partners toward the end of 2002," the Central Bank said in a statement following its monthly monetary policy meeting. 

 The institution opted to keep interest rates unchanged at 6.5 percent because of inflationary pressures caused in part by a sharp depreciation of the peso. 

 The central bank maintained its inflationary target of between 2 percent and 4 percent and said it will continue to intervene in the foreign exchange market to bolster the peso. 

Chile's export-driven economy grew 3.4 percent in the January to July period after posting 5.4 percent growth in all of 2000.

title: Chile's Peso Ends Stronger With Help From  Central Bank
text:
SANTIAGO -(Dow Jones)- Chile's peso ended at CLP693.00 against the dollar Friday, fighting its way back from Thursday's CLP696.20 record low close with some help from the central bank, local traders said. 

 The central bank began selling small quantities of dollars on the market around midsession, and that helped put the brakes on the Chilean peso's decline, traders said. 

 The peso slipped to an intraday low of CLP696.20 around the time the bank began selling dollars, but then changed directions as more U.S. currency flowed in, traders said. One trader estimated that the bank sold a total of only about $30 million over the course of the session. 

Chile's Central Bank has directly intervened in the foreign exchange market seven times in recent weeks, always selling U.S. currency reserves in small quantities. 

 The bank's policy is to confirm any interventions after the forex market closes.

title: Chilean peso firms on  central bank intervention .
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, Sept 28 (Reuters) - Chile's peso firmed on Friday following a decisive intervention by the central bank to break an initial slide in the currency, traders said. 

 The peso gained 0.46 percent to finish at 693.00/693.30 compared to record lows of 696.20/696.50 on Thursday. 

 The peso came under heavy pressure from a high demand for dollars early in the session, forcing the central bank to intervene three times. The final and most effective injection of dollars came moments before close. 

 "Early injection of dollars from the bank was too small, meaning the market absorbed them immediately and the peso continued to fall," one trader said. 

 According to an informal Reuters survey after the market closed, the central bank sold about $38 million. 

 Traders said a slowing world economy following the recent attacks on the United States, a lack of liquidity in the market and the constant prospect of central bank intervention would keep the exchange rate highly volatile. 

 "It's difficult to make predictions for the short term, its not even easy to predict trends on a day-to-day basis as there are so many factors that come into play," said Pedro Verdugo, foreign exchange manager at Mercury Travel in Santiago. 

 The central bank has now sold an estimated $302 million from its reserves in the money market since mid-August, when it broke with a two-year hands-off policy.

title: Chile central bank intervenes  again to back peso.
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, Sept 17 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank carried out another small intervention in the money market again on Monday, selling dollars to prop up the ailing peso , traders said. 

 It was the fourth such intervention in just two weeks. 

 The peso initially rose around 1.5 percent and ended trading at 690.00/690.50 from Friday's close of 690.30/690.80. 

 Traders said the central bank sold around $60 million. The Chilean central bank does not disclose the size of its interventions. 

 Before Monday, the central bank had sold an estimated total of $191.5 million in a series of interventions starting in mid-August, when it broke with a two-year policy of keeping out of the foreign exchange market. 

 The peso has lost some 16 percent of its value against the dollar since the start of the year, partly due to the economic crisis in neighboring Argentina. 

 But the currency has been shaky again in recent days since the attacks in the United States. 

 Chile's markets will be closed on Tuesday and Wednesday to mark the country's independence day celebrations.

title: Chile  Peso Firming, Traders Cite Ctrl Bank  Intervention
text:
SANTIAGO -(Dow Jones)- Chile's peso was firming against the dollar midsession Monday, after falling nearly to the 700-level early in the session. 

 Local traders attributed the rebound to the stronger than expected performance of U.S. and regional equities markets bolstered by a surprise central bank intervention. 

 At 1530 GMT, traders quoted the peso at CLP688.50 against the dollar, compared to Friday's CLP690.30 close. The currency had already rallied to CLP694.50 before the central bank stepped in. 

 Local traders said the peso plunged at the open on fears that U.S. equities might tank when markets reopened Monday after last week's closure. The peso quickly began to firm, they said, when the Dow Jones Industrial Average appeared to stabilize. At 1540 GMT, the DJIA was down 4.9%, fighting its way back from a more than 6% decline. 

 Rising regional markets were also supporting the peso, said a trader for Chile's Banco de Estado. At 1540, Brazil's Bovespa Index was up 4.3%, while Argentina's Merval was ahead 2.6%. 

 A surprise 50 basis point rate cut handed down by the Federal Reserve should lend support to the peso as the market begins to calm, said Roberto Guzman of the Covarrubias Y Cia brokerage.

title: Chile  peso falters despite Cenbank  intervening .
text:

 The peso closed at 680.50/681.00 to the U.S. dollar, losing 0.2 percent from Wednesday's close of 678.50/679.00 pesos.

title: Chile  Ctrl Bk Pres: Forex  Mkt  Intervention  Not To Fix Peso
text:
SANTIAGO -(Dow Jones)- Chile's central bank president Carlos Massad said Friday that the monetary authority's recent dollar sales on the foreign-exchange market aim to maintain liquidity, not set a fixed limit on the Chilean peso. 

 "The interventions are not seeking a determined price for the dollar, but maintaining a degree of liquidity and order on the foreign-exchange market," Massad said, speaking to reporters on the sidelines of a government seminar with local businessmen. 

 The bank announced in mid-August that it was willing to use up to $2 billion in international reserves to sell dollars directly on the forex market in an effort to halt the Chilean peso's free-fall in previous months. 

 The bank then made good on its warning on Aug. 28, surprising markets with its first direct intervention since abandoning its currency band two years ago. 

 The monetary authority has sold dollars on the market twice since then, the most recent time on Thursday. 

 At 1615 GMT Friday, the Chilean peso was trading at CLP666.50 to the dollar, weaker than Thursday's close of CLP664.30. 

 The currency, which had lost as much as 17% of its value this year, has strengthened 3.8% since the bank's mid-August announcement. 

 Market players, however, have been teasing the currency weaker since Aug. 28 to test at what levels the bank will intervene, traders have said. 

 In the meantime, total daily volumes on the spot market have sunk to between $200 million and $300 million, compared with the previously seen daily average volumes of about $500 million. 

 Massad said Friday that the bank will continue to intervene in the market "regularly but not mechanically" through the end of the year. 

 In the meantime, he said the weaker Chilean peso is helping the country's exports without risking the bank's 2% to 4% target range for its inflation outlook in the medium term. 

 The central bank's monetary policy-making board on Thursday opted to maintain its benchmark target lending rate at a nominal 6.50%, saying that inflation was still within its target range. 

 That's despite signs in the government's most recent inflation report that the weaker currency is passing through to prices. Inflation in August came in at a higher-than-expected 0.8%. 

 Massad on Thursday reiterated the bank's pledge to closely watch the effect of the weaker currency on inflation and act when necessary. 

 The central bank reported earlier Friday that in spite of selling $36.5 million on the forex market in August, its foreign reserves grew or 1.4% to $14.68 billion during the month, compared with July. 

 -By Christen A. Jamar, Dow Jones Newswires; 562-460-8546; chile@dowjones.com

title: Chile 's Ctrl Bank  Intervenes  In  Forex  Market - Traders
text:
SANTIAGO -(Dow Jones)- Chile's central bank sold dollars directly on the foreign-exchange market shortly before the close of Thursday's session, traders said, leading peso to end 0.5% stronger at CLP664.30 to the dollar. 

 The currency closed Wednesday at CLP667.50 a dollar. 

 The peso was trading at CLP667.30 at 1630 GMT, right before the monetary authority intervened. By 1645 GMT, the peso had jumped to CLP664.50 to the dollar. 

 The total amount of dollars that the Central Bank sold on the market was not known, though one local trader at an international bank estimated that it was about $30 million. 

 Thursday's intervention marks the third time in two weeks that the monetary authority has entered into the forex market after announcing its willingness to tap foreign reserves to shore up the peso in mid-August. 

 The bank first intervened on Aug. 28 when the peso hit CLP666.00, and then again on Aug. 31 when the currency had weakened to CLP663.00. 

 On both occasions, traders said that the amount that the bank sold on the market didn't surpass $50 million. The monetary authority, in turn, has only directed markets to its biweekly foreign reserves report, due out Friday. 

 The peso on Thursday opened official trading at CLP668.00, but then strengthened slightly to trade between CLP666.00-CLP667.00 on corporate sector dollar sales, traders said. 

 The currency's hit its intraday strong point of CLP666.00 at 1445 GMT. 

 Traders said the bank's monetary policy board meeting, later Thursday, was having no effect on the currency because markets expect local interest rates to remain at their current nominal 6.50%. Nor do traders expect the publication of the next schedule of dollar-denominated bond auctions, due out Friday, to have much of an impact. 

 Besides intervening directly in the market, the bank is also selling dollar-denominated notes, or PRDs, to provide the currency with additional cushion. As of Thursday's auction, the monetary authority will have sold about $1.4 billion in the notes in two months. 

 -By Christen A. Jamar, Dow Jones Newswires; 562-460-8546; chile@dowjones.com

title: SURVEY: Chile Aug CPI Seen +0.4%;  Forex  Effect Weighed
text:
Consumer Price Index:
           Aug     July   June    Aug/00    12-Mo/00
Forecast  +0.4%   +0.0%   +0.1%   +0.3%       ---
Actual     ---    -0.2%   +0.1%   +0.3%      +4.5%



By Christen A. Jamar


 SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--Chile's consumer price index likely climbed in August, driven principally by steady increases in fuel prices during the month. 

 While the fuel price effect has become a familiar story, markets will be closely watching the government's report - due out Wednesday at 1430 GMT - to see if the country's sharply weaker currency has finally started to trickle into consumer prices. 

 A Dow Jones Newswires survey of seven economists yielded a forecast of 0.4% inflation for August, after 0.2% deflation in July. 

 State-owned petroleum refiner ENAP implemented a series of hikes during August, translating into higher transportation costs and, to a lesser degree, housing costs. ENAP, which imports or produces about 90% of the fuel used in Chile, sets fuel prices to distributors on a weekly basis. 

 For much of the past year, the CPI has fluctuated in line with fuel prices and their subsequent affect on transportation costs. 

 Inflation in most other sectors, meanwhile, has stayed stable as Chile's depressed consumer spending environment prevented businesses from hiking prices. 

 That has held true even as the peso lost as much of 17% of its value against the dollar this year on concerns about Argentina and weak copper prices. 

 But economists say the softer currency might have led to "marginal" price increases in some areas of the economy during August. 

 Specifically, prices for some food products and housing appliances might have seen small incremental hikes. There's also a possibility that the weaker peso has led clothing prices higher, although that's seen offset by end-of-season sales. 

 If August's inflation comes in higher than expected, the focus is going to quickly shift to the Central Bank's monetary policy board monthly meeting, set for Thursday, as some economists banter around the idea of an interest rate hike. 

 The Central Bank's year-end target range for inflation is between 2% and 4%. Consumer prices were up 1.3% over the first seven months of the year. At its last meeting, in early August, the monetary authority left rates unchanged at a nominal 6.50%. 

 Chile's Central Bank announced in mid-August a two-tier attack on the falling peso, signaling to markets its concern about the currency's effect on inflation. 

 It said it would sell up to $2 billion more in dollar-denominated bonds, or PRDs, starting next week and through the end of the year, possibly bringing the total amount of the notes in circulation to about $4.5 billion. 

 But far more symbolic, economists say, is the bank's announcement that it would intervene directly on the market. 

 Last Tuesday, the monetary authority sold dollars on the foreign exchange market for the first time since it floated the currency two years ago. It intervened a second time on Friday. 

 "The only interpretation that can be made is that the Central Bank is worried about the effect of the (weaker peso) on inflation," say Universidad Gabriela Mistral economist Erick Haindl. 

 Still, many economists say a rate hike is still remote. 

 "The Central Bank can't give a negative signal," says Haindl, adding that the bank is likely to stick with intervention rather than risk Chile's nascent recovery in demand. 

Currency traders also said Tuesday that the market is expecting the bank to maintain rates on Thursday. 

 The peso closed Tuesday's session at 664.70 to the dollar, 3.7% stronger than when the Bank announced its willingness to intervene directly in the market. 

 -Christen A. Jamar, Dow Jones Newswires; 562-460-8547; chile@dowjones.com

title: Chile  peso dips in CenBank  intervention  aftermath.
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, Aug 29 (Reuters) - The Chilean peso fell slightly on Wednesday as hopes for a second Central Bank intervention in two days to prop up the currency were never realized, traders said. 

 The peso ended trading down 0.30 percent at 660.00/660.50 to the U.S. dollar. 

 The Central Bank on Tuesday intervened directly in the currency market - selling dollars for the first time since 1999 - to prop up the peso, which has sunk to record lows recently amid Argentina's ongoing financial woes. 

 Traders said the peso drooped towards the end of trading on Wednesday partly because the market had been primed for further similar dollar sales by the Central Bank which did not come. 

 On Tuesday, the peso had buckled in early trading under heavy dollar demand by banks, hitting a low of 666.70 pesos to the U.S. dollar. 

 Bankers surveyed by Reuters said the Central Bank, which never reveals the size of its interventions, had injected around $14 million to the market on Tuesday.

title: UPDATE 3-Chile  Central Bank  sells dollars to bolster peso.
text:
(Adds central bank statement and estimated amount of intervention) 

 SANTIAGO, Chile, Aug 28 (Reuters) - The Chilean Central Bank on Tuesday intervened directly in the currency market, selling dollars for the first time since 1999 to prop up the peso , which has sunk to record lows amid Argentina's financial woes, traders said. 

 The peso had buckled early in Tuesday's session under heavy demand for dollars by banks, hitting a low of 666.70 pesos to the U.S. dollar. It was the lowest rate of the session, but the peso has recovered somewhat from its record low close at 691.70 registered on Aug. 14. 

 The currency strengthened immediately as a result of the Central Bankoperation and closed at 658.00/658.50, up 0.92 percent from Monday's close of 664.10/664.40. 

 After markets closed, the central bank confirmed that it pumped money into the market but did not disclose the amount. 

 "Today, on August 28, the central bank carried out currency sale operations in the interbank market," it said in a brief statement, adding that it would report changes in its foreign reserves in a routine September 7 report. 

 Chile's foreign reserves stood at $14.473 billion at the end of July. 

 Traders in 20 banks surveyed by Reuters estimated that the institution sold about $14 million overall, saying they considered it a small-scale intervention but with a strong impact. 

 The Chilean Central Bank does not disclose details of its market transactions, but earlier this month it said it would inject up to $2 billion into the foreign exchange market during the remainder of this year, drawing from reserves. 

 It also had announced previously it would increase the amount of debt it issues in the form of dollar-denominated promissory notes by up to $2 billion, putting a ceiling of $4.5 billion on the issue of these notes by the end of 2001. 

 The institution had refrained from direct intervention in the currency market since 1999, when it abandoned an exchange-rate band regime and floated the peso. 

 The Chilean currency has depreciated about 15 percent since the start of the year amid widespread fears of a debt default or devaluation in neighboring Argentina, Latin America's third-largest economy. 

 The peso had a three-day rally last week - gaining 2.6 percent - after Argentina struck a deal for an $8 billion loan from the IMF, but began to lose ground on Monday.

title: Chile 's Peso Ends Firmer, 658.00/Dlr; Ctrl Bk  Intervenes
text:
SANTIAGO -(Dow Jones)- Chile's peso ended stronger at CLP658.00 to the dollar Tuesday, as the central bank directly intervened in the foreign exchange market for the first time since floating the local currency two years ago. 

 The monetary authority warned two weeks ago that it was prepared to spend up to $2 billion in reserves to defend the peso. Local traders weren't able to say immediately how many dollars the bank pumped into the market Tuesday. 

 The bank began selling dollars around midsession, traders reported, after corporate demand and rising speculation pressured the peso to a weak point of CLP666.60 against the dollar. The currency had closed Monday at CLP664.00. 

 Before this week, Chile's peso had gained 4.4% over seven sessions, an impressive rally after fears of an Argentine debt default pushed the currency to a record low of CLP691.70 per dollar on Aug. 14. 

 Traders and currency analysts attributed the rebound to the central bank's intervention warning, together with news that the International Monetary Fund will tack another $8 billion onto an emergency credit line for Argentina. 

 Chile's peso gained steadily on Argentina's good news last week, despite rising doubts about whether the IMF aid will be enough to help Argentina avoid default. 

 Two hours after official trading in Chile's peso closed Tuesday, foreign exchange traders were still unclear about the extent of the central bank intervention. 

 Several traders said spot market volumes were above average during the session, totaling about $700 million to $800 million. Given that daily volumes have typically averaged nearer the $500-million mark in recent months, traders deduced that the Central Bank sold a limited amount of dollars on the spot market. 

 One trader reported talk that the monetary authority sold as little as $30 million. The sale triggered a swift reaction from market players, he said, adding that foreign banks were active during the session.

title: Chile's Peso Ends 0.6% Stronger At CLP676.00/Dlr
text:
SANTIAGO -(Dow Jones)- Chile's peso firmed 0.6% against the U.S. currency Monday, ending the session at CLP676.00 per dollar compared with Friday's CLP680.00 close. 

 The peso opened moderately stronger at CLP678.30, but then leaped nearly 0.8% in the last hour of trading, climbing from just above the 678-level to CLP673.00 per dollar. 

 Local traders said the Central Bank put in a request to price dollars, immediately sparking rumors that the monetary authority might step in to sell some of its U.S. currency reserves into the market. 

 The Bank announced late last week that it had set aside $2 billion in reserves for possible interventions between now and the end of the year. 

 The peso then softened in the last few minutes of the session, easing back to CLP676.00 per dollar. 

 At the end of Monday's session, traders said the monetary authority hadn't intervened in the forex market. 

 "Most likely, they did it just to startle (market participants)," one trader commented. 

Chile's Central Bank hasn't directly intervened in the forex market since adopting a floating currency policy two years ago. The bank did, however, launch a program to sell dollar-indexed bonds into the market after the peso began to drop sharply in early July. 

 The bank announced last week that it was prepared to intervene directly, after watching the peso sink to a record low of CLP691.70 against the dollar. 

 Falling prices for Chilean commodity exports together with fears that Argentina's economic troubles will spark a regional financial crisis have pressured the peso to depreciate up to 17% against the dollar this year. 

 At Monday's close, the peso was off 15% against the dollar from Jan. 1.

title: Chile  cenbank  intervenes  to boost peso.
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, Aug 16 (Reuters) - The Chilean central bank on Thursday announced it would intervene in the currency market to prop up the beleaguered peso, which has fallen to record lows recently mainly because of financial woes in Argentina. 

 In a statement released after markets closed, the institution said it would withdraw up to $2 billion from its foreign reserves to sell dollars directly in the market over the remainder of this year. 

 This marks the central bank's first direct intervention in the exchange rate since it floated the currency in 1999. 

 It also announced it would increase its placement of dollar-denominated promissory notes by up to $2 billion above previously announced amounts, putting a ceiling of $4.5 billion on the issue of these notes by the end of this year. 

 "The objective (of the measures) is to give greater stability to financial markets in the country in a scenario in which negative external conditions persist," the central bank said, referring to Argentina. 

 The Chilean peso firmed slightly on Thursday to close at 689.20/689.50 pesos to the U.S. dollar on market speculation of a central bank intervention. 

 The central bank, which is autonomous but works closely with the finance ministry, first stepped in to break the peso's fall in early July, announcing an extra $1 billion in dollar-denominated promissory notes over the next six months to help banks hedge against the declining currency. 

 The move temporarily bolstered the peso, which was quickly swept down again by chronic fears of a debt default in Argentina, Latin America's third-largest economy. 

 The latest central bank move comes amid intense market speculation that Argentina may be on the verge of securing up to $9 billion in fresh loans from the International Monetary Fund, supplementing a $40 billion multi-lender rescue package already approved. 

 After seven days of loan negotiations in Washington, Argentine government officials and the IMF have given no hints about the possible outcome of the talks.

title: Chile's Peso Ends At 664.00/Dlr, Bounces Back From 669.50
text:
SANTIAGO -(Dow Jones)- Chile's peso ended at a record weak point of CLP664.00 against the dollar Wednesday, after fighting its way back from an historic intraday low of CLP669.50 to the dollar. 

 The peso plunged early, in line with other emerging-market currencies, as market players sought out dollars to hedge against a burgeoning crisis set off in part by economic troubles in Argentina, one of Chile's closest neighbors. 

 Traders reported that the heavy covering activity in Chile kicked off early Wednesday on Tuesday's report that Argentina had auctioned Treasury bills at a 14.01% annual rate. 

 The higher than expected rate reignited fears that Chile's neighbor will be forced to devaluate its own dollar-pegged currency or default on public debt, exacerbating regional dollar outflows. 

 "Corporate (players) and financial holdings can cover easily here given the lower financing costs in Chile," said Francisco Sanchez, a local trader with Hellernet Sud. 

 However, the peso bounced back after approaching the 670-mark as lack of direction ahead of the coming session led to some moderate profit-taking. 

 "The market's confused because it doesn't depend only on us," said BanEdwards trader Cristian Donoso, citing broad uncertainty about how emerging markets, particularly Argentina, might open up Thursday. 

 Many market players also suspect Chile's Central Bank might directly intervene in the foreign exchange market going forward, Donoso said. 

 The monetary authority announced last week that it will sell $1 billion in dollar-denominated bonds, or PRDs, into local financial markets by the end of the year. The Bank auctioned the first $100 million tranche Tuesday, and is set to sell another $100 million Thursday. 

 Talk is beginning to spread that the Bank might dip into its reserves to pump dollars directly into the spot market to prop up the peso, as the planned PRD auctions appear to have failed to fully offset external pressures on the currency. 

 "(The Central Bank governors) made a pretty overt statement...and now they've lost credibility," said FleetBoston currency analyst Greg Anderson. "It hurts to potentially lose reserves, but on the other hand the dollar-indexed debt didn't work."

title: ANALYSIS-Chile cenbank move boosts peso - for now.
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, July 6 (Reuters) - A Chilean central bank decision to intervene in the currency market to break the peso's fall will reap short-term success but the determining factor for the peso is the regional economic outlook, analysts said on Friday. 

 As the local currency hit record lows on Thursday, the central bank said it would inject $1 billion into the financial market by issuing dollar-denominated promissory notes over the next six months. The notes act as insurance for banks against financial losses caused by exposure to dollar positions. 

 "This announcement took the market by surprise, which makes me think that it will at least bring to an end the sharp decline," said Alejandro Fernandez, analyst with Gemines consultancy in Santiago. 

 "What is not clear is whether or not the amount announced by the central bank is sufficient to break that tendency," he added. 

 It was the first time the institution stepped in to influence the exchange rate since it floated the peso in 1999. 

 The move aims to soften the impact on the peso of neighbor Argentina's chronic political and economic troubles, which have helped drag the Chilean currency 11 percent lower so far this year. 

 Following the central bank announcement, the peso firmed almost 1 percent to close on Friday at 642.20/642.50 pesos to the dollar. 

 The currency had plunged to a record low of 649 pesos earlier on Thursday amid rumors that Argentine president Fernando de la Rua was about to resign. 

 DOLLAR FEVER 

 Ongoing fears that Argentina will abandon its dollar-pegged currency system or default on its debt have led to a feverish race among Chilean players to acquire dollars. 

 However, economists say the Chilean market is overreacting. 

 "My opinion is that Argentina is not going to default nor will it have a major crisis. Everything will be done to ensure that doesn't happen. The authorities would have to be totally inept to let things get to that point," said Guillermo Patillo, economist at the University of Santiago. 

 Argentina, Latin America's No. 3 economy, will continue to be key influence on regional markets through to year-end, analyst said. But they say there is no reason why the Chilean peso should tumble dramatically as a result. 

 "We are optimistic about Argentina. I think it is very unlikely for there to be a default or for the (currency) convertibility system to be dropped in the short term," said Sergio Quintana, economist with Forecast consultants. 

 The peso has fallen on more than just regional turmoil. The currency also teetered from a series of domestic interest rate cuts earlier this year to rekindle spending amid a broader economic slowdown. 

 The central bank's benchmark lending rate now stands at 3.5 percent. 

 "The anticipation of lower economic activity and therefore of another cut in rates, are factors that have affected the exchange rate," Fernandez said. 

 Some traders interpreted the central bank's indirect intervention as a sign that it set the 650 pesos-mark as the ceiling for the exchange rate and would actively defend that level. 

 But in theory, there is no limit. Some analysts see the peso hitting 700 pesos to the dollar if speculation is not restrained. 

 "It is impossible to say how high the dollar will go in Chile. It could reach the sky," Quintana quipped. 

 $1 = 642.5 Chilean pesos.

title: UPDATE 2- Chile  cenbank in $1 bln  currency intervention .
text:
SANTIAGO, Chile, July 5 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank said on Thursday it would inject $1 billion into the currency market to prop up the battered peso , its first such intervention since 1999. 

 The move came as several regional currencies buckled under pressure from the Argentine economic crisis. Brazil's Central Bank on Thursday pledged $6 billion to defend the real. 

 Chilean Central Bank Governor Carlos Massad told Reuters his institution will issue dollar-denominated promissory notes over the next six months as a hedging mechanism, effectively backing up commercial banks' dollar positions. 

 "Given the turbulence in the currency markets, there is strong demand for this type of coverage instrument," Massad said in an interview. 

 News of the intervention hit after markets had closed but caused Chile's currency to perk up immediately, gaining eight pesos or 1.2 percent in after-hours trading, traders said. 

 Details of the transaction will be made public on Friday. 

 The Chilean peso has hit historical lows in recent sessions in reaction to political and economic tension in neighboring Argentina, Latin America's third-largest economy. 

 After faltering from a series of domestic interest rate cuts earlier in the year, the local currency sank to fresh lows this week on rumors, later denied, that Argentine President Fernando de la Rua was about to resign. 

 The peso closed on Thursday at 648.50/648.80 pesos to the dollar, down 0.96 percent from Wednesday's close and down over 11 percent since the start of the year. 

 Massad said the $1 billion worth of the central bank notes, known locally as PRDs, would be injected into the market over and above the $1.5 billion already circulating in the market. 

 The institution will therefore have issued a total of $2.5 billion in PRD by year end. 

 The first $500 million will be placed as of July 9, he said. 

 NO MORE HANDS-OFF 

 Since 1999, when Chile adopted a free-floating currency system, the central bank has not intervened in the foreign exchange market. Before 1999, it frequently stepped in to buy and sell currency in order to keep the exchange rate within a target range. 

 Last month, however, Massad told markets the central bank still has the power to step in to support the currency. 

 The PRD is one of the instruments the central bank has at its disposal to influence the exchange rate without directly withdrawing from its reserves. 

 Massad said he did not expect the announced intervention to have a direct effect on the exchange rate but said it would provide some relief from pressure caused by regional instability. 

 "The situation in Brazil demonstrates how the turbulence is not internal but is affecting several markets and diverse currencies," he said. 

 Brazil's central bank said on Thursday it would spend $6 billion by the end of the year to shore up the beleaguered real currency. 

 The strong dollar in Chile has spawned fears of high inflation, which the central bank has pegged at 3.4 percent for 2001. But Massad ruled out inflationary pressure. 

 "So far, we have not seen any effect on inflation," he said. 

 Inflation in June was 0.1 percent, down from 0.4 percent in May due to falling oil prices. January-June inflation was 1.5 percent, according to the state statistics office. 

 Massad said Chilean authorities were closely monitoring Argentina, whose economy has been stalled for three years, prompting investors to doubt its ability to pay back its massive debt. 

 "What we want is for Argentina to recover and grow again. That would be the best thing that could happen to strengthen growth in Chile too," he said. 

 Chile recovered last year from an 11-month recession to post 5.4 percent economic growth. But low prices for copper, the country's top export, and a global slowdown have led to a slowdown this year. 

 First-quarter growth was 3.3 percent. In May, the central bank lowered its 2001 growth forecast to 4.3 percent from 5.6 percent.

title: UPDATE 1-Argentine stocks end at lows unseen since early 1999.
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, July 4 (Reuters) - Argentine shares edged down on Wednesday, sinking to their lowest levels since Brazil devalued its currency in 1999, in the wake of presidential resignation rumors on Tuesday, traders said. 

 In an interview with La Nacion newspaper, President Fernando de la Rua dismissed as "nonsense" talk that he was "overwhelmed" and about to quit as president of Argentina. 

 The center-left coalition leader said the rumors were spread by people "speculating against the country." 

 The benchmark MerVal dropped 0.80 percent to close at 385.96 points, near its lowest point since Brazil's steep devaluation in mid-January 1999. 

 The MerVal touched a low of 384.98 earlier in the session which was marked by anemic volume of $6.4 million. Decliners tripled advancers 18 to six while six issues were unchanged. 

 Frustration with the torpor that has afflicted Latin America's third-largest economy for the last three years is reaching new heights. 

 A member of De la Rua's own party, Chaco provincial Gov. Angel Rozas on Tuesday said the president was "overwhelmed" by the ongoing crisis, which fueled talk the 63-year-old leader, treated last month for arteriosclerosis, might step down. 

 "No one would seriously pull out of an investment based on rumors. I think yesterday's rumors were an expression of desire by investors for what they'd like to see done," said Leopoldo Olivario of Bacque brokerage. 

 The currencies of Brazil and Chile tumbled on Argentine woes and Uruguay's central bank intervened for the fourth consecutive business day to defend its battered money. 

 The currency of Argentina's top trade partner, Brazil's real , closed seven cents lower at 2.42 reais per U.S. dollar, a 2.85 percent depreciation from Tuesday's close and a level not seen since Brazil's central bank announced aggressive plans to prop up that money on June 21. 

 Argentina's country risk rating - the spread between Argentine bonds and safe-haven U.S. Treasuries - was up 17 basis points at 1,094 basis points. 

 "The market will continue to trend down as long as we have political noise which will lead to expectations the government will have to pay high interest rates at the next Letes (Treasury bill) auction," said Luis Corsiglia of Corsiglia y Cia. brokerage. 

 The next Letes T-bill auction is scheduled for July 10 when $500 million in 364-day T-bills and $350 million in 182-day T-bills will be sold. 

 Another factor that has unnerved foreign investors is an ongoing spat between opposition Peronist Party provincial governors who complain the central government owes them about $225 million in transfer funds for social and other programs. 

 De la Rua's government negotiated the deal last November in exchange for a commitment by the provinces to freeze their primary public spending at 2000 levels for five years. 

 The government Tuesday night failed to reach an accord with opposition Peronist Party provincial governors, who control most of Argentina's 23 provinces, on the disbursement of social program and other funds. 

 Argentine stocks and bonds have suffered most of the year amid concern over Argentina's ability to pay its $128 billion debt during an economic slump verging on three years. 

 Investors want to see positive numbers in economic indicators such as tax collection that show that pro-competition, pro-growth measures announced by Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo over the last three months are actually working to pull the Argentine economy out of its lull. 

 Investors have said that only with sustained growth will Argentina be able to meet its debt obligations. U.S. markets, meanwhile, were closed for the U.S. Independence Day holiday.

title: Chilean peso ends weaker, stocks flat at midday.

title: Chile 's cenbank says may  intervene  in  currency  market.
text:
SANTIAGO, June 20 (Reuters) - Chile's central bank on Wednesday said it has the power to intervene in the foreign exchange market to prevent the local peso, driven to historic lows on fears of instability in Argentina and Brazil, from depreciating further. 

 The peso sank to record lows this week after Argentina announced it would exclude exports from its currency's peg to the dollar, seen by the Chilean market as a "hidden devaluation." 

 A surprise cut in interest rates last week and a recent decline in Brazil's real also helped drive the peso lower. 

 "The market will have to decide where to set the price of the dollar, but I have always said that in exceptional circumstances the central bank reserves the right to intervene," Central Bank Governor Carlos Massad told reporters. 

 The peso closed on Wednesday at 624.00/624.30 pesos to the dollar, making for a depreciation of 2.6 percent in a little over a week and 8.2 percent so far this year. The local currency depreciated 7.7 percent in all of 2000. 

 Until 1999, when Chile adopted a free-floating peso, the central bank frequently stepped in to buy and sell currency in order to keep the exchange rate within a target range. 

 Massad said it would warn markets ahead of time if it decides to return to that kind of intervention. 

 The Argentine government on Friday announced changes to its currency system, varying the peso's exchange rate for importers and exporters in a bid to cheapen exports and pull the economy out of a three-year stagnation. 

 Massad dismissed fears that the measures would hurt the Chilean economy but said the country could be dragged down along with other emerging markets if Argentina eventually defaults on its debt. 

 "Even though now we are seen as distinct (from the rest of the region), my fear is that we won't be distinct enough," he said. 

 Massad said the Chilean economy, which last year recovered from an 11-month recession to post 5.4 percent growth, may grow less than 4.3 percent this year. Last month, the central bank slashed its 2001 growth forecast to 4.3 percent from 5.6 percent.

title: Chile may raise rates to curb inflation - economist.
text:
SANTIAGO, Nov 4 (Reuters) - One of Chile's top economists, Vittorio Corbo, on Thursday said he doubted the central bank would intervene in the foreign exchange market to shore up the softening peso, though that it could raise interest rates to keep a lid on inflation. 

 The peso, which has weakened nearly 15 percent this year, closed at 549.40/549.70 per dollar on Thursday compared with the previous session's 548.10/548.40. 

 "I believe that if we wake up tomorrow and see the exchange rate at 600 pesos, that will accelerate inflation very quickly," Corbo, an adviser to Banco Santander in Chile, told reporters. "That is when the central bank will intervene, but not by selling dollars but most likely by raising interest rates." 

Central Bank Governor Carlos Massad on Thursday said his institution is not thinking about intervening in the currency market. 

 "Right now, we are not worried about that," Massad said. "Naturally, we must continue observing the situation, but the exchange rate is not a worrisome element." 

 As a financial crisis took root in Asia, the peso began a sharp slide in October 1997, when it was trading around 412 per dollar. 

 In September 1999, the central bank abandoned its system for controlling the exchange rate.

title: Chile  Ctrl Bk/GDP -3: No  Forex Intervention  In 6 Months
text:
In a chart accompanying the release of Massad's speech, the Central Bank said it expects consumer prices to rise by 3.0% during the current year. In the period January through August, the consumer price index rose by 1.3%. 

 Chile's economy contracted by 2.9% in the first half of the year, compared to the same period a year earlier. The Central Bank said it expects the country's GDP to grow by between 2.5% and 3.5% during the second half of the year. 

 Massad laid a large part of the blame for the economic downturn on the financial crisis in Asia, which has been a key market for Chilean exports in recent years. A prolonged drought, macroeconomic problems in Brazil and a sharp increase in crude oil prices all added to the country's difficulties, Massad said. 

 The Central Bank president said the projected economic rebound will be driven by an increase in domestic demand. Net external demand could increase moderately next year due to a projected 16% increase in imports, offset somewhat by a reduction in the rate of growth of copper exports. 

 The Central Bank president said the higher import levels will come as a result of companies rebuilding diminished inventory levels and responding to stronger domestic demand. 

 Exports of goods are projected to grow by 9.0% this year, followed by a 5.0% increase during 2000. Copper exports are seen growing by 13% during 1999 and by 2.0% during the following year. Non-copper exports are projected to increase by 6.5% in both 1999 and 2000. 

 No estimates for exports of services were provided. 

 The Central Bank also said that it expects gross capital formation to equal 27.5% of GDP this year, growing to 28.5% during the year 2000. 

 In his speech, Massad referred to the Central Bank's decision last week to suspend its formal policy of intervening in foreign exchange markets when the price of the dollar exceeds the limits of the monetary authority's band. 

 Massad said that the Central Bank had not intervened in currency markets during the last six months.

text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean Central Bank said Thursday that it was suspending its "formal commitment" to intervene in the foreign exchange market to keep the peso within the country's currency band. 

 In a press statement, the monetary authority also said that it had set an inflation target of loosely 3.5% for next year, and an annual CPI target range of between 2% and 4% beginning in 2001. 

 The Bank said the exchange rate policy move is a step toward "incorporating growing exchange-rate flexibility."

 The exchange-rate measures will allow for a "freer float of the exchange rate", the Bank explained. 

 On the other hand, the monetary authority reaffirmed the current system for calculating the dolar acuerdo, a dollar-reference price that serves as the midpoint for the currency band. The dolar acuerdo is based on a trade-weighted currency basket.

title: D&P rates Chile $270 mln dlr-tied PRD notes A-plus.
text:
SANTIAGO, July 16 (Reuters) - Duff and Phelps Credit Rating Co. on Thursday said it assigned an A-plus rating to the Chilean Central Bank's programme to issue $270 million in three-year, dollar-linked readjustable promissory notes (PRDs). 

 The Central Bank placed $30 million of the notes on July 9 at 6.51 percent at an initial spread of 111 basis points over three-year U.S. Treasury rates, Duff said in a statement. 

 The ratings outlook is stable, it said. 

 Because the PRDs are payable in pesos, their credit profile is similar to Chile's local currency, long-term debt rating of AA-minus, Duff said. 

 However, the rating is limited because interest and principal payments are linked to the exchange rate between the dollar and peso, it said. 

 The rating also reflects the PRDs' relatively small amounts and long maturities, which limit potential pressure arising in the foreign exchange market upon their redemption, it said. 

 The Central Bank announced June 25 that it would offer money market instruments linked to the dollar to give players the option of buying paper with a built-in hedge against the forex volatility. 

 The aim is to steady the skittish foreign exchange market, which has been seriously shaken up by the Asian financial crisis. 

 The institution plans to auction $30 million in PRDs every Tuesday and Thursday from July 9 to August 8 for a total of $270 million. 

 The notes are specifically designed to reduce banks' and dollar-indebted companies' demand in the spot market for the Central Bank's dollars, Duff said. 

 Its reserves dropped in June by $1.32 billion to end the first half of the year at $15.55 billion. Traders attributed the fall to the Central Bank's intervention to prop up the peso. 

Chile's currency has weakened sharply since November on expectations that the crisis will reduce revenues from exports. The peso traded today at 461.50/461.80 to the dollar, down sharply from around 415 last fall.

title: Chile stocks swing lower in kneejerk sell-off.
text:
SANTIAGO, June 10 (Reuters) - Chile's key stock index swung lower early Wednesday in what traders said was a knee-jerk sell-off after Tuesday's sharp gains. 

 The benchmark index slumped 1.47 percent to 90.53 points, almost wiping out all the previous session gains when the blue-chip index jumped 2.03 percent. 

 Tuesday's sharp leap came after the Chilean government announced plans to introduce three reforms to rejuvenate stock market trading. 

 "The euphoria of yesterday has fizzled out," one trader said. "The general feeling is that the reforms are not profound enough to bring about a real change in attitude about the (equity) market." 

 The government stimulus package includes two proposals to tweak capital gains tax rules on equities trading to favour more volume and a third plan to broaden the sphere of tax deductions on equity investments. 

 Other traders said the fall on Wall Street and the general downturn in Asian markets also hurt stock prices in Chile. 

 Chile's peso saw opening pressure, which brought Central Bank dealers into the market selling an unspecified, "but not heavy" amount of dollars, one dealer said. 

 Other dealers said the Central Bank intervened when the peso weakened to 455.80/456.10 per dollar. The local currency edged back to 455.70/456.00. 

Chile's Central Bank has intervened in the money market for the past two months, holding the peso under a ceiling of 456.00 per dollar in an open stance to stabilise the local currency on the grounds that letting it weaken could bring inflationary pressures.

title: Chile econ minister comfortable with peso fall.
text:
SANTIAGO, Jan 13 (Reuters) - Chile's government is comfortable with the recent weakening of the peso against the dollar, seeing it as a readjustment of the peso's 1997 rise, Economy Minister Alvaro Garcia said on Tuesday. 

 "I am happy with the current price of the dollar despite its price of 438 pesos at the end of 1997 as it is only a rebalance of the rise of the peso (during that year)," Garcia told reporters. 

 The peso currently stands at 466.95 to the dollar. 

 Garcia said that the peso had gained an average eight percent in 1997, adding that its current price is similar to its price at the beginning of last year. 

 The peso's fall has been put down to the on-going Asian crisis and its impact on Chile's economy. The Central Bank has intervened in the forex market five times in the last 10 days in an attempt to smooth the fall. 

 Garcia said that the rate of the dollar against the peso was in line with the government's export policies and that the Central Bank's forex policies were sufficient to avoid speculative attacks against the peso. The bank raised rates last week. 

 "We mustn't forget that we have improved our foreign exchange position in relation to Europe and I would hope that when the traders finish changing their portfolios versus the dollar, the currency will stabilize," he said. 

 Garcia said there was no point in changing the country's restrictions on foreign capital inflows. 

 "In the middle of this turbulence we are not at the best time to consider changes in this sort of measure," he said. 

 Garcia said the depreciation of the peso in the last few weeks would strengthen Chile's export sector and would improve its competitive edge in the aftermath of the Asian crisis. ((Gabriela Donoso, Santiago Newsroom, 562 699-5595 x228))s

title: FOCUS - Chile raises rates after peso reels.
text:
SANTIAGO, Jan 8 (Reuters) - Chile's Central Bank raised rates Thursday after financial markets reeled on mounting concerns Latin America's star economy could be in for a rough ride in 1998 on contagion from Asia's financial crisis. 

 "This decision was taken due the potential impact of the new international situation," the Central Bank said in a statement referring to the Asian financial crisis. 

 "This new situation has made it necessary to moderate the evolution of aggregate demand to lower its affect on the current account and inflation." 

 The Central Bank announced late Thursday a rise in its interbank lending rate target to 7.0 percent from 6.5 percent. 

 The move followed an acceleration of the week's trend  Thursday in the pesos' losses against the dollar. Investors are worried about the growing likelihood that the country's exports to Asia will be hit hard as a result of the financial crisis, causing an economic slow-down in Chile. 

 The peso closed at 463.50 per dollar, way below Wednesday's close of 450. At the end of last week the currency stood at 440. 

 There have also been concerns that the Central Bank would be unable to meet this year's inflation target of 4.5 percent on the back of imported inflation from the weaker peso. Last year's inflation came in at 6.0 percent, overshooting the Central Bank's 5.5 percent target. 

 The Central Bank said together with the finance minister that it will continue to monitor the development of the economy at home and in international markets in order to, "adopt the necessary measures of sustaining the macroeconomic targets." 

 Analysts' responses were mixed. 

 "I see it as taking an aspirin...it does not contribute to resolving the root of the problem," said Henry Rudnick, manager of the CB Capitales consultancy. 

 "The measure also implies a recognition that country risk has increased on the external situation." 

 Tomas Flores, an economist at the Liberty and Development Institute said that, with the rate increase, the Central Bank will meet its inflation target. 

 The market slide this week has uncovered concerns about Chile's economy. As one of Latin America's biggest traders and with its similarities to Asia's little tigers, its high savings rates, aggressive exports and sustained growth over more than a decade, Chile could now be directly hit from the Asian fall-out. 

 About $5.3 billion of its total $17 billion in exports is expected, in 1997, to go to Asia. And the price of copper, the country's main export, has ratcheted lower amid the commodities slump induced by Asia's crisis. 

 Finance Minister Eduardo Aninat on Wednesday urged moderation in economic policy, but said, "Chile can resist this crisis perfectly well." 

 The Central Bank intervened in the foreign exchange market on Wednesday and Monday to smooth the pesos' fall, but did not intervene on Thursday, traders said. 

 "The foreign exchange market continues to show strong demand for dollars, which has not been halted by the Central Bank interventions," said one trader. 

 "In reality, the Central Bank has shown it does not have sufficient force to prevent the rise of the dollar." 

 The Central Bank has about $17 billion in foreign reserves. 

 Analysts said the continued performance of the peso will depend on how markets approve of the rate increase, but also on whether or not additional measures need to be taken. 

 One way to curb the pesos' drop would be to lower restrictions on the amount of foreign capital that can be taken into the country. Those restrictions, which aim to curb speculation, require foreigners to deposit 30 percent of their capital with the central bank for a year in a non-interest earning account. An easing of those restrictions would allow more dollars to flow into the economy, boosting demand for the peso. 

 As the Central Bank said, the current situation is compounded by the current account deficit, which is seen rising this year on lower raw materials exports. The government has raised its estimate for the 1998 current account deficit to 5.0 percent of gross domestic product from 4.5 percent. ((Santiago Newsroom, 562 699-5595))

title: Chile  Central Bank  says prepared to sell dollars.
text:
SANTIAGO, Dec 3 (Reuters) - Chile's Central Bank is prepared to intervene in the local foreign exchange market and sell dollars to counterbalance any exaggerated drop in the Chilean peso, Central Bank president Carlos Massad said on Wednesday. 

 The Central Bank stepped into the market on Thursday, Friday, Tuesday and again on Wednesday to sell dollars as the peso slid near or beyond 440 to a dollar, its lowest level in four years. 

 Massad, who has attributed the peso's sudden slide to shockwaves from the Asian financial crisis and a scarcity of dollars in the local market, declined to estimate how long he expects that lack of liquidity to last. 

 "We don't have a forecast, but we are prepared to face a scarcity (of dollars)," Massad told reporters. "We are more prepared for a scarcity of dollars than an abundance." 

 At around midday Wednesday, the Central Bank sold dollars with the peso trading at around 438.50, causing it to rise to 436.50, traders said. The dollar had closed at 437.00 pesos on Tuesday. 

 Massad refused to say how many dollars the Central Bank sold in previous sessions. According to foreign exchange traders quoted in the Chilean press, the Central Bank has sold about $200 million of its reserves since Thursday. 

 Chilean economic officials said this month that the Central Bank's reserves total about $19 billion and are large enough to fend off any attacks on the peso. 

 Massad also would not say what level the dollar must reach in order to merit the Central Bank's intervention, but traders have speculated the ceiling is 440 pesos. 

 "We prefer that the market form its own opinion about this rather than have the Central Bank give its opinion," he said. 

 Before the Asian crisis started softening the peso in September, the Chilean currency had appreciated about eight percent against the dollar this year, worrying local exporters.

title: PRESS DIGEST - Chile - December 3.

SANTIAGO, Dec 3 (Reuters) - The following are some of the stories on the Chilean front pages this morning. Reuters has not necessarily verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy. 

 EL MERCURIO

Inflation so far this year reaches 5.9 percent, making it impossible to reach the 5.5 target set for 1997.

 - Government concerned by delays in agreement over Campo de Hielo border with Argentina as any negotiations already completed may become null and void after Chile's December 11 elections.

 ESTRATEGIA

 - 0.1 percent rise in November's CPI brings inflation for 12- months to end November to 6.3 percent. 

 - U.S. dollar was the best investment in Chile in November as stock market crashes made currency buying more attractive. 

 - Price of copper could fall as low as $0.70 per pound in the next few months.

 EL DIARIO

title: Chile Peso Edges Dn Slightly On Dlr; Bond Yields Down
text:
SANTIAGO (Dow Jones)--The Chilean peso fell slightly Monday but closed above its session lows on a late round of dollar selling. Bond yields edged down. 

 In foreign exchange trading, the formal dollar used in trading operations closed at 407.50 pesos, up 0.20 pesos from Friday's close of 407.30, but down from its session highs of 408.40 pesos earlier in the session. 

 Dealers Monday said rumors had largely disappeared of imminent Central Bank action to widen or even eliminate the trading band in which the dollar trades against the peso. 

 Under the current scheme, the Central Bank must intervene to buy dollars when the greenback falls below the band's floor, which on Monday stood at 401.98 pesos. 

 Widening the band would ease the pressure for such intervention, which is costly in Chile's current high interest rate environment. 

 At the same time, widening the band would allow the dollar to weaken further, pushing up the peso. That would help offset the effects of a recent gas-price hike, by lowering the costs of importing fuel, whose price is denominated in dollars. 

 The gas hike has caused concerns about higher-than-projected monthly inflation in April. 

 But on Monday, the dollar's recent strength internationally helped put slightly more space between the dollar and the floor of its band, though a late round of dollar selling pushed the peso up from its session lows. 

 Among those reportedly selling dollars Monday was state-held Banco del Estado, which dealers on Friday had speculated was purchasing dollars on behalf of the Central Bank.

title: (WSJ): Chile Counts Mixed Blessings As Peso Rises Versus Dlr
text:
SANTIAGO (AP-DJ)--Buoyed by the country's strong export performance and a surge in foreign direct investment, the Chilean peso rose 11.5% against the dollar in May alone, the Wall Street Journal reports Tuesday. 

 But despite calls for relief by exporters and makers of manufactured goods for the domestic market, Chile's central bank isn't inclined to brake the peso's rapid rise. 

 Bank officials say that as long as the peso stays within a band calculated against a basket of currencies of Chile's trading partners and designed to keep the country's current-account deficit in check, there's no need to intervene aggressively. 

 They note that most of Chile's major exports, including copper, wood products and even wine, are surging despite the peso's appreciation. Nonetheless, the central bank and the government of President Eduardo Frei have begun tinkering with exchange-rate policy in recognition of the growing complaints. 

 In the past week, they have modified some of the capital and interest-rate controls credited with shielding Chile from the worst of the Latin American volatility stemming from Mexico's financial crisis, which began in December. 

 In one measure, the central bank stopped setting interest rates on 90-day government debt and instead began fixing overnight rates. In response, 90-day rates fell to 5.8% from 6.1% in real terms, making the peso less attractive as an investment. 

 The government also allowed private pension funds to invest abroad a bigger percentage of their $2.3 billion in holdings.
